A focused sub-agent working on one function should not automatically gain access to every unrelated document and session. A research branch that only needs read access should not automatically receive mutation capability.

Raw text and rendered projections remain available when exact presentation matters, but they are explicit capabilities rather than the universal access primitive.

docs.title: 12. Tool Invocations and Results Are First-Class Knowledge
docs.text:
A tool invocation should not exist only as prose in a transcript. The session should be able to preserve relationships such as:

ToolInvocation I
    operation -> inspect
    target -> Function F
    pinned_revision -> FR12
    initiated_by -> Branch B3

A tool result may reference structured or reusable derived knowledge:

ToolInvocation I1
    inspect -> Function F @ FR12

ToolResult R1
    produced -> FunctionSummary S9

The session records that R1 was observed in this branch, while FunctionSummary S9 may be reusable wherever the same immutable function revision and summary profile are requested.

This allows questions such as:

  • which branch inspected this entity;
  • which tool result supported this decision;
  • which migration caused a validation run;
  • whether an observation came from current or historical state.

It also connects session architecture directly to the broader derived-knowledge and caching model.

docs.title: 13. Agent Edits Produce Semantic Migrations
docs.text:
An agent is not a special mutation path. It should not write directly into canonical state merely because it has generated a plausible change.

The figure below separates speculative work from accepted state. The important boundary is validation and promotion: rejected work loops back into the branch, while accepted work becomes a normal semantic migration and new snapshot.

Figure 5. Agent edits follow the same migration and validation path as other clients; speculative work does not silently mutate canonical state.

A session branch and a project workspace are related but distinct. The branch represents conversational and semantic work; a workspace represents speculative project state derived from a base. One branch may compare several candidate workspaces before selecting a result.

Validation may include domain-appropriate checks such as schema validation, parsing, type checking, linting, tests, projection round trips, invariants, or human approval. Validation results are themselves structured objects linked to the branch, migration, and resulting state.

This change model is shared with human UI operations, CLI commands, API clients, and externally edited projections. Provenance differs; canonical transition semantics do not.

docs.title: 14. Decisions and Durable Project Knowledge
docs.text:
Sessions often produce information that remains useful after the conversation ends:

  • accepted architectural decisions;
  • facts discovered from project artifacts;
  • constraints;
  • open questions;
  • rejected alternatives;
  • tasks;
  • validated hypotheses.

These may be promoted to durable project knowledge while retaining provenance back to the branch and evidence that produced them.

For example:

Decision D19
    text -> "Canonical source nodes preserve chosen syntax"
    status -> accepted
    derived_from -> Branch B81
    concerns -> SourceModel

Promotion must be explicit or governed by clear policy. A conversational statement is not automatically authoritative knowledge merely because an agent generated it.

Useful states may include concepts such as proposed, accepted, rejected, superseded, or obsolete. Later agents should normally retrieve current accepted knowledge first while still being able to follow provenance into historical branches.

Summaries and model-generated interpretations are normally derived knowledge. They should preserve their source objects, source revisions, profile or policy, and provenance so that generated interpretation remains distinguishable from canonical facts.

docs.title: 15. Multi-Agent Work Uses the Same Branch Model
docs.text:
Multiple agents do not require a separate collaboration architecture. They operate on branches or workspaces derived from known bases, then use the same semantic merge model as other concurrent work. The reader should notice that the parent can consume compact branch results while merge operates on project state, not on combined conversation transcripts.

Figure 6. Multi-agent collaboration is expressed through ordinary branches, results, common ancestors, semantic merge, and explicit conflict resolution.

A parent agent may delegate to specialized child agents by giving each child:

  • a purpose;
  • a base state;
  • selected knowledge handles;
  • a capability scope;
  • an expected result shape.

The parent receives a BranchResult rather than an uncontrolled stream of the child's complete history. Full child branches remain inspectable for provenance and debugging.

Agent configuration is execution metadata, not session identity. A persistent session may involve different models, providers, tools, context policies, or specialized agent profiles over time.

docs.title: 16. Human, Agent, Audit, and Database Views Share One Session
docs.text:
A human-facing application may render the session as familiar conversation. An agent-facing context renderer may show goals, branch summaries, decisions, and relevant project handles. An audit view may show every tool invocation, exact revision, validation result, and migration. A raw database browser may expose the underlying entity and relation graph.

These are projections over the same session knowledge.

The same semantic handle should also cross interface boundaries. If a user selects a function in the integrated editor and asks an agent to work on it, the scope should conceptually be:

Function F at Snapshot S

rather than an informal conversion such as:

"look at lines 120-180 of src/foo.rs"

The same handle can be used by the object inspector, history view, semantic diff, agent branch, validation system, CLI, API, TUI, and third-party clients.

docs.title: 17. Search and Attention Metadata
docs.text:
Session search should be semantic rather than limited to text matching over transcripts.

Useful queries include:

find branches touching Function F
find decisions about snapshot identity
find migrations produced by Agent A
find failed validations for Module M
find observations derived from ToolResult R
find branches that superseded Decision D

Text search remains useful, but it should return semantic handles such as branches, decisions, tool results, and messages rather than only offsets.

Short descriptions are especially important for agents because they help decide what to inspect next without consuming the full object. Examples include:

Function F
"Reconciles an externally edited Markdown projection."

Branch B
"Investigates whether entity identity should change on edits."

Migration M
"Adds session branches and branch-result promotion."

Descriptions should include provenance when generated rather than authored. They are navigation metadata over canonical knowledge, not replacements for it.

Implementations may also expose approximate information cost—small descriptor, medium summary, large full history—so an agent can choose detail before paying the context cost.

docs.title: 18. Context Change Does Not Invalidate Unrelated Understanding
docs.text:
A session's global snapshot may change frequently as new turns, branches, and results are added. That should not force every cached description, summary, or analysis to be recomputed.

Derived knowledge should depend on the exact immutable objects it actually used.

For example:

FunctionSummary FS
    depends_on -> Function F @ FR12

A new session message does not invalidate FS. A different unrelated function changing does not invalidate FS. Only a relevant dependency change requires recomputation.

This is the same local-versus-global identity rule used throughout Scriberig: global snapshot identity gives certainty that something changed somewhere, while local immutable dependencies provide precise cache invalidation.

docs.title: 19. Security, Retention, and Auditability
docs.text:
Using one universal knowledge substrate does not imply that every object is visible to every agent.

Sessions may reference private repositories, external services, sensitive documents, local resources, or credentials-adjacent configuration. Authorization, provenance, retention, and capability scopes continue to apply when following session relations.

The session model should preserve enough structured provenance to reconstruct which knowledge and operations participated in important work. This does not imply deterministic replay of model behavior; models and external services may be nondeterministic or unavailable later.

The stronger guarantee is that historical inputs, exact referenced revisions, tool invocations, tool results, migrations, validations, and accepted outcomes remain inspectable.

Session data follows the same retention and reachability model as other immutable knowledge. Active sessions, pinned branches, accepted decisions, retained migrations, audit records, and referenced branch results may act as roots. Unreferenced transient work may become collectable when policy permits.

docs.title: 20. Relationship to Other Level 1 Designs
docs.text:
This document depends on and complements the other architectural documents rather than redefining their concepts.

  • Universal knowledge model: defines the substrate that sessions specialize.
  • Identity, revisions, and snapshots: defines exact historical references and evolving session state.
  • Changes, migrations, branches, and merge: defines the state-transition model used by agent workspaces and multi-agent collaboration.
  • Projections and bidirectional editing: defines the general projection model that also applies to transcripts and agent context.
  • Domain modeling and adapters: defines how the session domain coexists with code, Markdown, PDFs, and other domains.
  • Derived knowledge, caching, and incrementality: defines summaries, descriptions, reusable tool views, and precise invalidation.
  • Universal query and operation model: defines the detailed shared vocabulary agents use for navigation and action.
  • Trust, validation, capabilities, and provenance: defines authorization and promotion policies layered over the relationships described here.

The session layer coordinates and records work. It should not duplicate domain logic such as Rust parsing, PDF extraction, Markdown reconciliation, or source rendering.

docs.title: 21. Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
Implementations of agent interaction and sessions must preserve the following invariants.

  1. Sessions use the universal knowledge store. They are not a separate transcript database.
  2. A transcript is a projection. Chronological chat is one representation of richer session structure.
  3. Branches are first-class knowledge objects. They can be described, queried, nested, summarized, retained, or collected.
  4. Completed branches may collapse in context without disappearing from storage. A descriptor and result can stand in for full history until deeper inspection is needed.
  5. Session history does not require private reasoning traces. Durable semantics are built from observable actions, outputs, decisions, tool interactions, and explicit knowledge.
  6. Agent context is derived from the session; it is not the session itself. Different context policies may render the same session differently.
  7. Historical observations remain pinned to what was actually observed. Later revisions do not rewrite old tool results or decisions.
  8. Agents use semantic handles where available. Filenames, line numbers, and byte offsets are projection details.
  9. Agents do not require unrestricted file or database access. Capabilities can be scoped to objects, relations, domains, and operations.
  10. Agent edits use the universal change model. They produce semantic proposals and migrations rather than a separate mutation path.
  11. Speculative work is isolated. Failed or exploratory branches do not silently become canonical state.
  12. Validation evidence is first-class. Promotion can reference structured validation results.
  13. Session-derived knowledge has provenance. Decisions and summaries retain links to branches and evidence.
  14. Generated summaries are not automatically canonical truth. Derived interpretation remains distinguishable from accepted knowledge.
  15. Tool results may be persistent without being permanent context. Large outputs can be summarized and reopened on demand.
  16. One interaction grammar spans domains. Sessions, code, PDFs, documents, and future domains share universal navigation concepts.
  17. The agent runtime is a consumer, not a dependency of the knowledge system. Session and project data remain useful through ordinary libraries and applications.
  18. Multi-agent work uses the same branch, snapshot, migration, and merge concepts as other concurrent work.
  19. Project knowledge can outlive the session that produced it. Durable facts, decisions, and tasks are promoted explicitly with provenance.
  20. All projections remain subordinate to canonical structured knowledge. Human chat, agent context, audit views, and branch trees do not become independent sources of truth.

docs.title: 22. Non-Goals
docs.text:
This Level 1 design does not require:

  • storing every model token;
  • storing hidden chain-of-thought reasoning;
  • deterministic replay of nondeterministic models;
  • one fixed prompt format;
  • one model provider;
  • one fixed branch-depth limit;
  • one universal summary algorithm;
  • injecting every stored tool result into context;
  • replacing domain-specific semantic tools with only generic graph traversal;
  • giving agents unrestricted database or filesystem access;
  • making every conversational statement project truth;
  • keeping every abandoned branch forever;
  • defining concrete Rust crate boundaries, protocol messages, or API endpoints.

Those choices belong in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 23. Definition of a Session
docs.text:
A Scriberig session is a structured, versioned knowledge graph describing an interaction process around goals, observations, decisions, actions, branches, and results.

It is stored in the same universal knowledge system as the artifacts the agent works on.

A session can be rendered as a human transcript, an agent context, an audit history, a branch tree, or a decision view without changing its canonical meaning.

Branches allow focused and nested work to proceed without permanently expanding parent context. Short descriptions and branch results make completed work cheap to navigate while retaining exact provenance.

Agents interact with project and session knowledge through stable semantic handles, progressive disclosure, shared query operations, and capability-scoped actions. Their edits become semantic migrations subject to the same branching, validation, history, and merge rules as changes produced by humans and other clients.

The result is a session model in which conversation is not an append-only wall of text. It is a navigable part of the project's knowledge graph, capable of scaling with long-running work while preserving history, exact references, and durable outcomes.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig uses one universal typed knowledge model across source code, Markdown, PDFs, sessions, branches, decisions, migrations, styles, derived analysis, and future domains.

Consumers must therefore not need a separate interaction model for each domain.

A human interface, agent, CLI command, API client, TUI, web editor, or third-party application should be able to navigate and act on the same knowledge through one common grammar.

The central principle is:

The interaction model is universal; domains specialize meaning through types, relations, views, and higher-level operations rather than replacing the core grammar.

This document defines that common grammar.

It covers:

  • stable handles;
  • snapshot-bound reads;
  • inspection;
  • relation and collection traversal;
  • discovery and querying;
  • comparison and history;
  • rendering;
  • branching;
  • applying changes;
  • committing new state;
  • progressive disclosure;
  • result discoverability;
  • domain extensions;
  • operation lifecycle;
  • the relationship between low-level and high-level actions.

Concrete Rust traits, query AST types, HTTP endpoints, CLI syntax, TypeScript APIs, database indexes, pagination encodings, and UI components belong in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 2. Design Goals
docs.text: The universal interaction model must satisfy the following goals.

docs.title: 2.1 One grammar across domains
docs.text:
The same basic operations should work whether the target is:

  • a project;
  • a Rust module;
  • a function;
  • an AST expression;
  • a Markdown section;
  • a paragraph;
  • a table row;
  • a PDF page;
  • a session;
  • an agent branch;
  • a project decision;
  • a migration;
  • a style;
  • a derived result.

The details differ by type, but the user or agent should not need to learn a completely different navigation protocol for each one.

docs.title: 2.2 Semantic access before raw representation
docs.text:
Consumers should operate on semantic entities and relations when those exist.

A function should be addressed as a function, not primarily as a filename plus line range.

A paragraph should be addressed as a paragraph, not primarily as a byte span.

A session branch should be addressed as a branch, not primarily as a slice of transcript text.

Raw representations remain available through projections when necessary.

docs.title: 2.3 Progressive disclosure
docs.text:
A consumer should be able to discover structure before loading content.

For example, inspecting a function may reveal:

Function process_payment
  code groups: 7
  parameters: 2
  outgoing calls: 4

The consumer can then decide which relation or child collection to inspect.

The model should make the inexpensive representation useful enough to guide the next operation.

docs.title: 2.4 Stable references
docs.text:
Results must expose stable semantic handles that can be passed directly into later operations.

Consumers should not need to reconstruct a target from display text.

docs.title: 2.5 Exact read semantics
docs.text:
A read must be interpretable relative to an exact snapshot or exact immutable revision.

A consumer should always be able to answer:

Which state did this result describe?

docs.title: 2.6 Explicit change semantics
docs.text:
Write operations must not mutate canonical state invisibly.

They should operate through branches, workspaces, migration proposals, and commits so that:

  • the base state is known;
  • validation can run before promotion;
  • concurrent edits remain explicit;
  • failures do not corrupt the current root;
  • history remains inspectable.

docs.title: 2.7 Useful without agents
docs.text:
The universal query and operation model is application infrastructure, not an agent-only API.

A database browser, compiler integration, IDE, CLI, web application, or custom service should use the same model.

docs.title: 2.8 Discoverability
docs.text:
A consumer should be able to inspect an object and discover:

  • what it is;
  • what relations it exposes;
  • what collections it owns;
  • which views are available;
  • which operations apply;
  • what deeper information can be requested.

This reduces dependence on hard-coded domain knowledge in clients.

docs.title: 3. The Universal Interaction Grammar
docs.text:
The core interaction grammar is intentionally small.

At Level 1 the important operations are:

inspect
list
follow
find
query
diff
history
render
branch
apply
commit

These operations fall into four broad groups.

docs.title: 3.1 Observe
docs.text:
inspect
list
follow

These reveal known structure.

docs.title: 3.2 Discover and compare
docs.text:
find
query
diff
history

These locate, select, compare, and trace knowledge.

docs.title: 3.3 Project
docs.text:
render

This produces a representation for a human, model, external tool, or file.

docs.title: 3.4 Change
docs.text:
branch
apply
commit

These create isolated candidate state and explicitly promote accepted changes.

Domain-specific capabilities may add richer operations such as:

rename_symbol
extract_function
insert_table_row
resume_session_branch
accept_decision

Such operations extend the universal model.

They must not create a separate persistence or history path.

Conceptually, high-level domain operations eventually become changes expressed through the same branch, migration, validation, and commit machinery.

Figure 1 is the main mental model for the document: all four operation groups act on the same semantic knowledge substrate. Domains may add vocabulary, but they do not create parallel navigation, rendering, or mutation architectures.

Figure 1 — The universal interaction grammar groups all operations around one semantic knowledge substrate.

docs.title: 4. Universal Handles
docs.text:
The interaction model relies on references that preserve semantic identity.

The important handle classes are conceptually:

EntityRef
RevisionRef
SnapshotRef
RelationRef
ProjectionRef
OperationRef

The exact wire representation belongs in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 5. Entity References
docs.text:
An EntityRef identifies a conceptual entity across time.

Examples:

function F
paragraph P
session branch B
PDF page G

An entity reference alone does not necessarily identify exact content.

It must be resolved in a snapshot when exact state matters.

Conceptually:

resolve(Snapshot S, Entity F)
    -> Revision R

This is useful when a consumer wants:

the current state of this conceptual thing within this exact world state.

docs.title: 6. Revision References
docs.text:
A RevisionRef identifies one exact immutable state.

For example:

Function F @ Revision FR12

A revision reference remains meaningful even after the entity advances to a newer revision.

Historical observations, derived knowledge, diffs, validation results, and reproducible queries should prefer exact revision references when appropriate.

docs.title: 7. Snapshot References
docs.text:
A SnapshotRef identifies the exact canonical knowledge universe used for an operation.

A query against a snapshot must not silently drift to a newer state while being evaluated.

A consumer may begin with:

Snapshot S17

and receive results containing entities resolved within S17.

If the current project later advances to S18, the original result still describes S17.

This is essential for:

  • reproducibility;
  • agent reasoning;
  • concurrent edits;
  • semantic diff;
  • three-way merge;
  • debugging;
  • validation;
  • history inspection.

docs.title: 8. Selections and Anchors
docs.text:
User interfaces often need to identify not only an entity but a meaningful location within a representation.

For example:

  • a paragraph shown in rendered Markdown;
  • a function shown in source code;
  • a table cell shown in a PDF view;
  • a branch shown in a session tree.

A selection should resolve back to semantic handles.

Conceptually:

Selection
  snapshot: S
  entity: E
  revision: optional exact revision
  relation path: optional structural context
  projection anchor: optional rendered location

Projection anchors are not canonical identity.

They are bridges between rendered representations and semantic objects.

A line number, byte range, DOM node, page rectangle, or editor selection may be useful as an anchor, but the system should prefer semantic identity once correspondence is known.

Figure 2 separates the three kinds of identity that must not be conflated: the conceptual entity, the exact snapshot in which it is resolved, and the immutable revision that contains exact content. A UI selection can additionally carry structural or rendered context without making that context part of identity.

Figure 2 — Entity identity, snapshot context, exact revision identity, and projection anchors play distinct roles.

docs.title: 9. Read Operations Are Snapshot-Bound
docs.text:
Every canonical read should be evaluated against an explicit or resolved snapshot.

Clients may omit the snapshot for convenience only if the system resolves a concrete snapshot before executing the operation and reports that snapshot in the result.

This avoids ambiguous behavior such as:

inspect F

beginning under one project state and completing under another.

The architectural rule is:

Convenience may select a snapshot implicitly; execution and results must be tied to an exact snapshot explicitly.

For immutable RevisionRef inputs, the revision itself already provides exact state for that object, though surrounding graph traversal may still require a snapshot.

docs.title: 10. inspect
docs.text:
inspect answers:

What is this object, and what are the useful ways to continue exploring it?

It should usually be the first operation on an unfamiliar handle.

An inspection result may contain:

identity
type
short description
provenance
current revision
container counts
important properties
available relations
available collections
available views
available operations
information-size hints

For example:

Function F
name: process_payment
purpose: Validate an order and charge the payment provider.

parameters: 2
code groups: 7
outgoing calls: 4

relations:
  parameters
  body
  calls
  references
  comments

views:
  summary
  groups
  semantic body
  source projection

For a PDF page:

PDF Page P17

paragraphs: 12
tables: 2
figures: 1

relations:
  document
  paragraphs
  tables
  figures

For a session:

Session S

active branches: 1
completed branches: 14
open tasks: 3
current decisions: 8

relations:
  branches
  decisions
  tasks
  recent turns

inspect should emphasize orientation, not dump the entire object.

docs.title: 11. list
docs.text:
list enumerates an ordered or unordered collection associated with an object.

Examples:

list(Document, sections)
list(Section, paragraphs)
list(Function, code_groups)
list(Session, branches)
list(PDFPage, tables)

A listing should return compact entries suitable for navigation.

For example:

cg:1  validate request       4 statements
cg:2  load account           5 statements
cg:3  apply changes          8 statements
cg:4  persist account        3 statements

The list operation should support bounded results and continuation.

Consumers should not be forced to materialize a collection containing thousands of members merely to inspect the first few.

The exact pagination mechanism belongs in lower-level design.

docs.title: 12. follow
docs.text:
follow traverses a typed relation from one object to related objects.

Examples:

follow(Function F, calls)
follow(Symbol S, references)
follow(Decision D, supersedes)
follow(Migration M, produced_by)
follow(Paragraph P, derived_from)

The operation should preserve relation meaning rather than reduce every relationship to generic graph edges.

A domain schema may declare:

  • relation cardinality;
  • direction;
  • ordering;
  • expected target types;
  • whether reverse traversal is indexed;
  • whether the relation is canonical or derived.

Consumers should not need to know how relations are physically stored.

docs.title: 13. find
docs.text:
find is a discovery operation.

It answers questions such as:

Where does this text or concept occur in this scope?

Unlike raw text search, results should resolve to semantic objects whenever possible.

Example:

find(Project, "hash based caching")

may return:

Paragraph P81
section: Rendering
preview: "..."

A code result might be:

Function F91
name: render_cached

A session result might be:

Branch B42
"Investigate render caching"

A table result might be:

TableRow R19
within: supported styles

The key rule is:

Search discovers semantic handles, not merely offsets in opaque text.

Text offsets may be included as projection anchors when useful.

find may support different strategies, including:

  • exact text;
  • token search;
  • indexed terms;
  • structured names;
  • semantic similarity;
  • domain-specific matching.

If ranking depends on derived indexes or model-generated embeddings, the result should preserve provenance and derivation information where relevant.

docs.title: 14. query
docs.text:
query performs structured selection over the knowledge graph.

It is more precise than find.

Examples include:

functions that call service X

decisions that concern object identity

branches that touched migration M

paragraphs contained in section S

entities changed between snapshots A and B

The query model should be declarative and serializable.

It should express concepts such as:

scope
type constraints
property predicates
relation traversal
collection membership
revision constraints
snapshot constraints
ordering
limits

The universal query model must not expose the physical database as its public abstraction.

For example, clients should not need to know SQL table names or storage-specific join structure.

This preserves freedom to change persistence while keeping the semantic API stable.

Domain adapters may contribute optimized predicates or query expansions without changing the universal query semantics.

docs.title: 15. find and query Serve Different Purposes
docs.text:
The distinction should remain clear.

find is primarily for discovery.

It may be ranked, approximate, text-oriented, or semantic.

query is primarily for structural selection.

It should be as deterministic as its declared inputs and derivations allow.

For example:

find(Project, "payment retry")

may help locate relevant objects.

Then:

query(
  functions that call PaymentProvider.retry
)

produces an exact structural result.

Agents should often use find to orient themselves and query to establish facts.

Figure 3 shows the intended progression: find reduces uncertainty and returns semantic handles; those handles can then anchor a structured query that establishes a precise graph fact. The two operations are complementary rather than competing search syntaxes.

Figure 3 — find is for discovery; query is for precise structural selection using semantic handles.

docs.title: 16. diff
docs.text:
diff compares two exact states.

Inputs may include:

  • two revisions of one entity;
  • two snapshots;
  • two branches;
  • two projection results;
  • two related semantic objects when a domain defines comparison semantics.

The preferred result is semantic.

For example:

FunctionDiff

signature:
  unchanged

code group 2:
  condition changed
  error branch added

code groups 1 and 3:
  unchanged

A Markdown diff might say:

Section Storage
  paragraph changed

Section Sessions
  inserted

Section Rendering
  unchanged

A raw textual diff may be available as an additional rendering.

It should not be the only comparison representation when richer semantic structure exists.

docs.title: 17. history
docs.text:
history answers:

How did this entity, root, or branch evolve?

History is based on explicit migrations, revisions, snapshots, and lineage.

Useful views may include:

predecessor revisions
successor revisions
migrations touching this entity
branch ancestry
merge ancestry
who or what produced a change
validation associated with a change

For example:

Function F

R12 --Migration M8--> R18
R18 --Migration M11--> R21

or:

Project Snapshot P1
        /      \
      P2        P3
        \      /
          P4

History must preserve exact handles so a consumer can reopen the state that existed at any retained point.

docs.title: 18. render
docs.text:
render converts semantic state into a projection.

Conceptually:

render(subject, projection, style)
    -> representation

Examples:

Rust module + Rust style
  -> source file

Markdown document + Markdown style
  -> .md text

Session + human-chat style
  -> chronological transcript

Session + agent-context style
  -> model context

Migration + review style
  -> semantic change view

render does not change canonical semantic state.

A style change does not imply a semantic migration.

The result should retain correspondence back to semantic entities where possible so that user selections in rendered output can resolve to semantic handles.

docs.title: 19. branch
docs.text:
branch creates an isolated change context from an exact base state.

Conceptually:

branch(base = Snapshot S17)
    -> Branch B

The branch records the state from which work began.

A branch may be used by:

  • an agent;
  • a human editor;
  • a refactoring operation;
  • an import process;
  • a merge resolver;
  • a testing experiment;
  • a third-party application.

Branching is not agent-specific.

It is the general mechanism for safely constructing candidate state.

docs.title: 20. apply
docs.text:
apply adds a proposed change to a branch or workspace.

The input may be low-level or high-level.

Low-level examples:

replace entity revision
insert collection member
remove relation
move collection member

Higher-level examples:

rename symbol
replace paragraph
insert table row
extract function
resolve merge conflict

The architectural requirement is that high-level operations eventually produce explicit semantic changes against a known branch base.

They must not bypass history.

An apply operation may produce:

new candidate root
migration proposal
diagnostics
validation requirements
conflicts

The canonical project root does not advance merely because a change was applied to a branch.

docs.title: 21. commit
docs.text:
commit promotes a validated candidate state into a retained root or advances a named current root according to policy.

Conceptually:

Branch B
  base: S17
  candidate: S18

commit(B)
  -> accepted migration
  -> retained Snapshot S18

A commit should preserve:

  • the base state;
  • the resulting state;
  • the migration;
  • provenance;
  • validation results required by policy;
  • parent or merge ancestry.

The exact authorization and validation policy belongs partly to the trust and validation design.

The universal operation model only requires that canonical promotion be explicit.

docs.title: 22. Read and Write Paths Must Remain Distinct
docs.text:
Read operations:

inspect
list
follow
find
query
diff
history
render

must not silently mutate canonical knowledge merely to answer a question.

Derived indexes and caches may be populated as implementation details without advancing the canonical snapshot.

Write operations:

branch
apply
commit

must make state transitions explicit.

This distinction lets applications reason clearly about safety and reproducibility.

Figure 4 makes the write boundary explicit. branch isolates work from the current snapshot, apply constructs candidate state and a migration proposal, and validation either returns structured failure or allows commit to promote the candidate. A failed attempt never silently advances canonical state.

Figure 4 — Candidate state is isolated until validation succeeds and an explicit commit promotes it.

docs.title: 23. Results Must Be Referential
docs.text:
Every result should contain handles that can be used directly for the next operation.

Bad:

The payment code is in process_payment.

Better:

Function F82  process_payment
CodeGroup G4  charge provider
CodeGroup G5  persist transaction

The consumer should not need to search again merely to turn a display label into an actionable reference.

This rule applies equally to:

  • agents;
  • CLI users;
  • browser applications;
  • TUI applications;
  • API clients.

docs.title: 24. Results Should Advertise Useful Next Operations
docs.text:
A result should help the consumer understand what can be done next.

An inspection response for a function may advertise:

available relations:
  parameters
  groups
  calls
  references

available views:
  summary
  semantic body
  source

available operations:
  diff
  history
  render
  branch
  rename_symbol

A PDF page may advertise:

available relations:
  paragraphs
  tables
  figures

available views:
  extracted text
  page image
  semantic structure

A session branch may advertise:

available relations:
  turns
  decisions
  tool results
  result

available operations:
  inspect
  diff
  history
  resume
  summarize

This makes domain capabilities discoverable without requiring every client to encode all domain rules in advance.

docs.title: 25. Progressive Disclosure Is Part of the Protocol
docs.text:
Progressive disclosure should not exist only in user-interface code.

It should be visible in the interaction model itself.

A consumer should be able to request levels such as:

identity only
compact description
structure
selected children
full semantic representation
rendered representation

The exact profiles may vary by domain.

The invariant is that a consumer can begin cheaply and intentionally request more.

For example:

Project
  -> subsystem
     -> module
        -> function
           -> code group
              -> statement
                 -> expression

or:

Session
  -> branch
     -> episode
        -> turn
           -> tool result

The consumer should not need to read the deepest representation in order to discover that the deeper representation exists.

Figure 5 illustrates that progressive disclosure is a domain-independent navigation pattern. Code, documents, and sessions use different semantic types, but each lets the consumer start with a coarse object and request finer detail only when needed, keeping information cost proportional to the task.

Figure 5 — Progressive disclosure uses the same coarse-to-fine navigation pattern across domains.

docs.title: 26. Information Cost May Be Exposed
docs.text:
Where practical, the system may expose approximate information cost for deeper views.

For example:

Function F82

summary:            ~120 tokens
group overview:     ~300 tokens
semantic body:      ~1800 tokens
source projection:  ~2500 tokens

The estimates need not be exact.

Their purpose is to help clients and agents choose an appropriate level of detail.

This is particularly useful for model context, network transport, large documents, and remote clients.

docs.title: 27. Domain Extensions
docs.text: A domain may extend the universal model in three main ways.

docs.title: 27.1 Typed relations
docs.text:
Code may define:

calls
references
implements
parameters
body

Documents may define:

sections
paragraphs
rows
cells

Sessions may define:

branches
decisions
tasks
turns

docs.title: 27.2 Specialized views
docs.text:
Code may provide:

function summary
code groups
control-flow view
source projection

PDFs may provide:

page structure
extracted text
layout view
page image

docs.title: 27.3 High-level operations
docs.text:
Code may provide:

rename_symbol
extract_function

Documents may provide:

split_paragraph
move_section

Sessions may provide:

resume_branch
accept_decision

These domain capabilities should reuse universal identity, snapshot, branch, migration, provenance, validation, and commit semantics.

docs.title: 28. Domain Extensions Must Not Fragment the Tool Model
docs.text:
The system should avoid a tool explosion such as:

read_markdown_section
read_rust_function
read_pdf_page
read_session_branch

when the underlying action is conceptually the same.

Prefer:

inspect(handle)
list(handle, relation)
render(handle, view)

with type-aware results.

Specialized tools are justified when they represent genuinely specialized semantics rather than a different spelling of universal navigation.

For example:

rename_symbol

has language semantics that a generic apply operation may not know how to validate by itself.

But rename_symbol should still operate inside the same branch and migration system.

docs.title: 29. Universal Tools and High-Level Tools Should Coexist
docs.text:
Low-level universal operations are important because they make the system inspectable and composable.

High-level domain operations are important because they reduce error and express intent.

For example, an advanced user may inspect raw relations and manually construct a migration.

An agent may instead call:

rename_symbol(Foo, Bar)

Both should converge on the same semantic history.

The system should not force all clients to work at the lowest possible level.

Nor should it hide the lower-level structure so completely that advanced inspection and debugging become impossible.

docs.title: 30. Low-Level and High-Level Views Must Share Selection
docs.text:
A full editor may show the same entity simultaneously as:

  • a raw database object;
  • a semantic function or paragraph;
  • a rendered source or document projection;
  • an item in history;
  • an agent scope.

All of these views should resolve to compatible semantic handles.

For example, selecting a Rust function in rendered source should allow the application to:

inspect its raw revision
show its relations
show its history
show migrations touching it
ask an agent about it
render it under another style

without rediscovering the object through text search.

This universal selection model is one of the main benefits of the shared knowledge substrate.

Figure 6 shows why semantic selection is a first-class cross-view concept rather than UI-local state. Once a selection resolves to an entity in an exact snapshot, the raw database browser, semantic editor, rendered projection, history view, and agent scope can all act on the same object without searching for it again.

Figure 6 — One semantic selection can coordinate raw, semantic, rendered, historical, and agent views.

docs.title: 31. Query Results and Derived Knowledge
docs.text:
Some operations depend only on canonical structure.

Others may rely on derived information.

For example:

follow(Function F, parameters)

may be canonical.

But:

follow(Function F, inferred_callers)

may depend on compiler analysis.

Similarly:

find(Project, semantic similarity query)

may depend on embeddings.

Results should preserve enough provenance to distinguish:

canonical fact
derived fact
model interpretation
external observation

The interaction grammar remains the same, but authority is not flattened.

docs.title: 32. Query Evaluation Must Respect Exact Dependencies
docs.text:
A query result may be cached when its dependencies are exact and known.

For example:

query Q
against Snapshot S17
using QueryDefinition V3

may produce reusable derived result R.

If a newer snapshot appears, the old result still remains valid for S17.

Whether it can also be reused for S18 depends on its dependency model.

The query system should prefer exact dependency reasoning over global invalidation when possible.

This follows the broader incremental architecture of Scriberig.

docs.title: 33. Conflicts Are Structured Results
docs.text:
Operations should not reduce important conflicts to unstructured error strings.

For example, applying a migration to a branch may discover:

Conflict
subject: Paragraph P
base revision: R7
expected revision: R7
current branch revision: R9

A semantic merge conflict may expose:

both branches changed Function F
left changed signature
right changed body

Structured conflicts can be:

  • rendered for humans;
  • inspected by agents;
  • resolved by domain-specific tooling;
  • logged and audited;
  • transported consistently over API boundaries.

docs.title: 34. Errors Must Preserve Context
docs.text:
An operation failure should preserve enough information to understand:

  • which operation failed;
  • which snapshot or branch it used;
  • which entity or revision was involved;
  • whether the failure was validation, authorization, absence, ambiguity, or conflict;
  • which corrective actions may be available.

For example:

AmbiguousMatch
scope: Section S
candidates:
  Paragraph P7
  Paragraph P9

is more useful than:

Could not apply edit.

The exact error taxonomy belongs in lower-level protocol design.

The architectural requirement is structured, referential failure.

docs.title: 35. Long-Running Work Uses Operation Handles
docs.text:
Some operations may take significant time:

  • compilation;
  • test execution;
  • large imports;
  • semantic indexing;
  • agent runs;
  • reconciliation;
  • rendering large projections;
  • PDF extraction.

The interaction model should allow such work to be represented by an OperationRef.

Conceptually:

Operation O
state:
  queued
  running
  completed
  failed
  cancelled

Operation events may expose:

progress
structured output
diagnostics
produced objects
result handles

The CLI, API server, TUI, web application, and agent runtime should observe the same operation semantics.

Whether the operation is executed synchronously or asynchronously is a runtime concern.

Figure 7 captures the lifecycle that every surface should observe. The important point is not whether work is implemented with threads, tasks, jobs, or remote workers; it is that one OperationRef provides stable identity while progress, outputs, diagnostics, completion, failure, or cancellation are reported consistently.

Figure 7 — Long-running work uses one operation identity and one observable lifecycle across interfaces.

docs.title: 36. The Interaction Model Is Transport-Independent
docs.text:
The following should be different surfaces over the same application semantics:

Rust library call
CLI command
HTTP request
WebSocket/event stream
TUI action
React hook
agent tool call

For example, these may all ultimately perform the same semantic operation:

inspect(Entity F at Snapshot S)

The CLI may print text.

The API may return structured data.

The web UI may render an inspector.

The agent tool may return a compact semantic map.

The underlying operation must remain consistent.

docs.title: 37. User Interfaces Should Not Bypass the Universal Operations
docs.text:
The reference web application and TUI should be built on the same public application operations available to third parties.

A web editor should not have a private mutation path such as:

update database row directly

while an agent uses migrations.

Instead:

filesystem edit
web edit
CLI edit
agent edit
API edit

should converge toward:

branch
  -> apply semantic change
  -> validate
  -> commit

This keeps history, validation, conflict handling, and provenance coherent across surfaces.

docs.title: 38. Agents Use the Same Model as Ordinary Clients
docs.text:
Agents are not privileged database users.

They consume the same semantic interfaces as applications.

The main difference is presentation policy.

An agent-facing inspect result may emphasize:

  • short descriptions;
  • counts;
  • semantic handles;
  • next useful relations;
  • context cost;
  • provenance.

A human-facing inspector may display more metadata and interactive controls.

Both refer to the same underlying objects and operations.

This prevents the system from developing a hidden agent-only architecture that diverges from the public platform.

docs.title: 39. Raw Database Browsing Remains Possible
docs.text:
Universal abstractions should not make the underlying graph inaccessible.

Advanced users and debugging tools should be able to inspect:

entity
revision
properties
relations
collections
snapshot membership
lineage
derived objects

This raw view is still expressed through the same interaction grammar.

For example:

inspect(Revision R)
list(Entity E, relations)
history(Entity E)
diff(Revision A, Revision B)

The difference is level of abstraction, not a separate database access path.

docs.title: 40. Query Scope Must Be Explicit
docs.text:
Discovery and query operations should have a meaningful scope.

Examples:

entire snapshot
project
module
document
section
session
branch
subtree
explicit entity set

This improves:

  • performance;
  • relevance;
  • security;
  • agent context discipline;
  • reproducibility.

An agent working inside one branch or module should not need to search the entire knowledge universe by default.

Capability and trust policy may further restrict available scopes.

docs.title: 41. Operations Should Be Composable
docs.text:
A consumer should be able to chain handles from one result into the next operation.

Example:

inspect(Project P)
  -> relation modules

list(P, modules)
  -> Module M

inspect(M)
  -> relation functions

list(M, functions)
  -> Function F

follow(F, calls)
  -> Function G

diff(G@R3, G@R7)

The output vocabulary of one operation should naturally feed the input vocabulary of another.

This is especially important for simple agents.

They should not need custom glue logic between every pair of tools.

docs.title: 42. Generic Operations Should Prefer Semantic Defaults
docs.text:
When multiple representations exist, defaults should favor the most useful semantic level.

For example, inspecting a Rust file projection should normally orient the consumer toward:

module
functions
types
imports

rather than exposing the file first as an undifferentiated byte sequence.

Inspecting a PDF should normally expose:

pages
sections
paragraphs
tables
figures

when extraction exists.

Inspecting a session should normally expose:

goal
branches
decisions
tasks
recent activity

Raw content remains available when requested.

docs.title: 43. Absence of a Domain Adapter Must Be Representable
docs.text:
Not every resource will have a rich semantic adapter.

The universal system must still represent unsupported or partially supported objects.

For example:

Blob B
media type: application/octet-stream
size: ...
capabilities:
  inspect metadata
  render/download raw representation

A consumer should be able to discover that richer operations are unavailable rather than receive misleading semantic structure.

As adapters evolve, additional views and relations can become available without changing the universal grammar.

docs.title: 44. Domain-Specific Convenience APIs Are Allowed
docs.text:
Libraries may expose convenience methods such as:

code.find_callers(F)
session.list_branches(S)
document.list_sections(D)

These can improve ergonomics and type safety.

They should be understood as typed wrappers around shared application semantics, not independent systems.

This rule lets Scriberig provide pleasant APIs while preserving conceptual unity.

docs.title: 45. Cross-Surface Capability Parity
docs.text:
A user-level capability should not exist only in one interface unless there is a strong reason.

For example, when semantic diff becomes a supported capability, the architecture should allow it to become available through:

Rust application API
CLI
server protocol
TypeScript client
web UI
TUI
agent tool surface

The exact user experience may differ.

The semantic capability should remain shared.

This encourages vertical development rather than building a powerful backend with permanently lagging public surfaces.

Figure 8 shows the dependency direction that makes this possible. Client surfaces differ in presentation and transport, but they all call the same application operations, which delegate to query, history/diff, projection, and change subsystems over one knowledge graph. A UI or agent that bypasses this boundary would break capability parity and semantic consistency.

Figure 8 — CLI, server, web, TUI, agents, and embedded callers are peer surfaces over shared application semantics.

docs.title: 46. Example: Navigating a Markdown Document
docs.text:
A consumer starts with a document handle.

inspect(Document D)

returns:

title: Architecture
sections: 8
tables: 3
code blocks: 6

relations:
  sections
  references

Then:

list(D, sections)

returns compact handles:

Section S1  Storage
Section S2  Sessions
Section S3  Rendering

Then:

inspect(S2)

returns:

subsections: 2
paragraphs: 5

Then:

list(S2, paragraphs)

returns paragraph handles and descriptions.

The document never had to be read as one large text blob.

docs.title: 47. Example: Navigating Source Code
docs.text:
A consumer starts with a module.

inspect(Module M)

returns:

functions: 22
types: 8
imports: 14

Then:

list(M, functions)

returns compact function entries.

After selecting Function F:

inspect(F)

may expose:

code groups: 6
calls: 4
parameters: 3

Then:

list(F, code_groups)

allows the consumer to choose one group without reading the whole function.

The same function can later be rendered as source:

render(F, source, Style S)

or compared semantically:

diff(F@R12, F@R18)

docs.title: 48. Example: Navigating a Session
docs.text:
A consumer starts with:

Session S

Inspection may return:

goal:
  design universal query model

active branches: 1
completed branches: 12
current decisions: 6
open tasks: 2

Then:

list(S, branches)

may return:

Branch B17  Immutable identity model
Branch B18  Projection reconciliation
Branch B19  Render caching

The consumer can inspect one branch summary without loading its transcript.

Only if necessary does it continue into turns or tool results.

This uses the same navigation model as code and documents.

docs.title: 49. Example: Changing an Object
docs.text:
Suppose a user or agent wants to change a paragraph.

The operation flow is:

base = Snapshot S17

branch(S17)
  -> Branch B

apply(
  B,
  replace Paragraph P with candidate revision P2
)
  -> candidate Snapshot S18

validate(B)
  -> acceptable

commit(B)
  -> Migration M
  -> Snapshot S18 retained/promoted

A web editor, API client, CLI command, or agent may initiate this flow differently.

The semantic history is the same.

docs.title: 50. Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
The following rules must remain true across implementations.

  1. The same universal interaction grammar applies across domains.

  2. Domain adapters add types, relations, views, and high-level operations rather than replacing the core model.

  3. Canonical reads are tied to exact snapshots or immutable revisions.

  4. Results return semantic handles suitable for follow-up operations.

  5. Inspection favors orientation and progressive disclosure over complete dumps.

  6. Collection traversal is bounded and pageable.

  7. Search returns semantic objects whenever a semantic mapping exists.

  8. Structured queries do not expose physical storage schemas as their public abstraction.

  9. Semantic diff is preferred over raw text diff when semantic structure exists.

  10. Rendering is a projection and does not itself mutate canonical state.

  11. Writes occur through explicit branch/apply/commit semantics rather than hidden in-place mutation.

  12. High-level domain edits still produce ordinary migrations and history.

  13. Conflicts and failures are structured and referential.

  14. Long-running work can be represented by operation handles.

  15. The interaction model is transport-independent.

  16. The reference UI and agent runtime use the same public application semantics available to ordinary clients.

  17. Raw graph inspection remains possible for advanced tools and debugging.

  18. Capability discovery is part of inspection.

  19. Different views of the same object share semantic selection handles.

  20. Agent use is a specialization of the general application model, not a privileged storage path.

docs.title: 51. Non-Goals
docs.text:
This document does not define:

  • a concrete Rust query API;
  • SQL tables or indexes;
  • GraphQL, REST, or RPC endpoints;
  • a concrete query language syntax;
  • pagination tokens;
  • authorization policy;
  • capability token encoding;
  • CLI command names;
  • React hooks;
  • TUI key bindings;
  • concrete agent tool schemas;
  • compiler-specific operations;
  • transport event formats;
  • database transaction implementation.

Those belong in Level 2 and Level 3 designs.

docs.title: 52. Decision Summary
docs.text:
Scriberig will expose one universal semantic interaction model over the knowledge store.

The core operations are:

inspect
list
follow
find
query
diff
history
render
branch
apply
commit

The model is built around stable entity, revision, and snapshot references.

Reads are snapshot-bound.

Results contain handles and advertise useful next relations, views, and operations.

Navigation follows progressive disclosure so consumers can move from project-level summaries to individual statements, paragraphs, cells, tool results, or other fine-grained objects only when necessary.

Domains extend the model with typed relations, specialized views, and high-level semantic operations.

They do not create separate persistence or history semantics.

All mutation paths converge on explicit branch, migration, validation, and commit behavior.

The same semantic operations are intended to power Rust libraries, the CLI, API server, TUI, web libraries, the integrated editor, agents, and third-party applications.

This makes the knowledge store not only universal in representation, but universal in how it is explored and changed.

docs.title: Runtime Libraries, Protocol, and Product Surfaces
1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig is not one application with several wrappers around it.

It is a reusable knowledge platform with multiple consumers.

The same underlying capabilities must be usable by:

  • Rust applications embedding the libraries directly;
  • the command-line interface;
  • the TUI;
  • the HTTP/API server;
  • browser and desktop applications;
  • third-party clients;
  • the agent runtime;
  • the full Scriberig editor.

These consumers should not each develop their own version of project inspection, semantic editing, querying, migration handling, validation, or session control.

The central architectural rule is:

Product surfaces consume shared application operations. Lower-level storage and domain libraries never depend on product surfaces or on the agent runtime.

This document defines the separation between reusable runtime libraries, application operations, protocol types, transport adapters, command-line and interactive products, and the agent runtime.

It also defines how capabilities must evolve across those surfaces so that Scriberig does not become a powerful backend with incomplete or incompatible frontends.

Concrete crate names, Cargo features, endpoint paths, serialization formats, framework choices, process topology, command names, and UI component APIs belong in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 2. One System, Multiple Consumers
docs.text:
Scriberig has one semantic system and many ways to use it.

A small utility may link directly to the storage and graph libraries. The CLI may invoke application operations in-process. A browser may use the same operations through the server protocol. An external IDE may use a generated client library. An agent may use a constrained tool adapter over the same operation model.

Figure 1 shows the architectural center of gravity: reusable knowledge and domain libraries feed shared application operations, and every product surface is a consumer above that boundary. Embedded applications may call operations directly; remote applications cross a protocol boundary; agents receive an adapted tool surface but still rely on the same operations.

Figure 1 — Scriberig has one reusable semantic platform and several peer product surfaces.

The capability should remain conceptually the same in every case. For example, "inspect this entity" should not mean one thing to the CLI, another thing to the server, and a third thing to an agent.

docs.title: 3. The Lower Layers Must Be Useful Without Agents
docs.text:
The storage and semantic platform must not depend on the existence of an agent runtime.

A user may want Scriberig only as:

  • a versioned semantic database;
  • an immutable object and snapshot store;
  • a structured knowledge graph;
  • a query library;
  • a Markdown or code model;
  • a semantic diff engine;
  • a projection and reconciliation engine;
  • an API server for another application.

All of those must remain valid uses.

The storage layer must not import agent concepts. A Rust AST adapter must not know how prompts work. A Markdown reconciler must not know that a chat UI exists. The agent runtime is a consumer of the platform, not the platform's owner.

docs.title: 4. Logical Runtime Layers and Dependency Direction
docs.text:
The architecture is divided into logical layers. The exact number of crates may change, but the responsibilities and dependency direction must remain separated.

Figure 2 is the dependency rule in visual form. The key observation is that dependency arrows point toward more foundational layers, while each useful lower layer can stand on its own. Storage can be embedded without any agent or UI, and domain support can be used without running a server.

Figure 2 — Dependency direction preserves independent use of the lower libraries and prevents product concerns from leaking downward.

docs.title: 4.1 Core identity and value model
docs.text:
The bottom layer defines universal values and identities used throughout Scriberig, including concepts equivalent to entity identity, revision identity, snapshot identity, relation and collection identity, migration identity, operation identity, style identity, and type or schema identity.

This layer should have very few dependencies and should not know about SQLite, HTTP, Markdown, Rust source code, sessions, agents, React, or command-line parsing.

docs.title: 4.2 Persistence implementations
docs.text:
The persistence layer implements storage contracts such as immutable revision storage, snapshot storage, entity-to-revision mappings, transactions, deduplication, retained roots, storage-level indexes, and garbage-collection primitives.

The logical persistence API must not require consumers to know the backend representation. A first implementation may use SQLite, but SQLite must not become the public semantic API.

docs.title: 4.3 Universal graph and schema model
docs.text: This layer exposes domain-independent semantic operations over entities, revisions, properties, typed relations, collections, provenance, descriptions, and schemas. It turns raw immutable storage into a knowledge system.

docs.title: 4.4 Query and change infrastructure
docs.text:
Shared query and change mechanisms belong above the universal graph. They include traversal, filtering, search, semantic diff, migration construction and application, history inspection, common-ancestor lookup, and merge support.

They remain domain-independent where possible.

docs.title: 4.5 Domain adapters
docs.text:
Domain libraries specialize the knowledge store for Markdown and structured documents, programming-language-independent code concepts, Rust, PDFs, sessions, and future languages or formats.

A domain adapter defines its own schemas, parsers, renderers, validators, relations, derived analyses, and specialized operations. It does not replace the shared persistence, query, history, or operation models.

docs.title: 4.6 Projection infrastructure
docs.text:
Projection infrastructure owns common concerns around projection identity, rendering lifecycle, style selection, external modification detection, reconciliation lifecycle, projection state, dirty-state tracking, and synchronization events.

Domain adapters provide domain-specific parse, render, and reconciliation behavior.

docs.title: 4.7 Application operations
docs.text:
Above the reusable libraries sits the application-operation layer.

This layer expresses user-visible capabilities rather than low-level storage calls. Examples include:

inspect an entity
list semantic children
follow a relation
run a query
show history
compare two revisions
create a branch
apply a migration
render a projection
reconcile an edited projection
validate a candidate change
open a session
submit an agent command

The CLI, server, TUI, web application, and agent adapters should reuse these operations. This layer is the principal boundary between reusable semantic libraries and product surfaces.

docs.title: 5. Application Operations Are the Shared Product Core
docs.text:
The application layer must prevent product-specific business logic from spreading into each frontend.

A bad architecture would allow the CLI to implement one semantic diff, the server to implement another, the web app to own reconciliation, and the agent runtime to mutate database tables directly.

Scriberig instead requires one semantic operation to be presented in several ways.

The same principle applies to mutations. A web edit, agent edit, CLI edit, external-file edit, or third-party API edit should not have unrelated write paths.

Figure 3 shows the required convergence. The source of a change may differ, and that source should be recorded as provenance, but every canonical write becomes a migration proposal, passes the same validation and conflict rules, and advances canonical state through an explicit snapshot transition.

Figure 3 — All user-visible mutation paths converge on the same migration, validation, conflict, and snapshot machinery.

This shared path is important for correctness, auditability, permissions, testing, history, merge behavior, and alternative clients.

docs.title: 6. The Protocol Is a First-Class Architectural Boundary
docs.text:
The server protocol must not be treated as an accidental serialization of internal Rust structures.

It is a public architectural contract.

The protocol should represent stable semantic concepts such as:

  • entity, revision, and snapshot references;
  • typed object summaries;
  • relation and collection summaries;
  • descriptions;
  • query expressions;
  • semantic diffs;
  • migrations;
  • validation results;
  • sessions and branches;
  • operations and events;
  • projection state;
  • machine-readable errors;
  • compatibility metadata.

Clients should receive semantic references such as EntityReference, RevisionReference, or ObjectSummary, not SQLite row IDs, page numbers inside a database file, or internal table names.

This allows the persistence implementation to evolve without redesigning every client.

docs.title: 7. One Wire Model
docs.text:
Protocol types must have one authoritative definition or one authoritative generation path. Rust server types and TypeScript client types must not evolve independently by hand.

Figure 4 shows the intended relationship. The canonical contract defines semantic payloads and compatibility rules; Rust, TypeScript, and future clients either derive from that contract or are mechanically checked against it. The server is an adapter from application operations to this contract, not the owner of a separate semantic model.

Figure 4 — Scriberig has one wire contract even when many languages and clients represent it differently.

The exact generation mechanism belongs in lower-level design. The invariant is that a protocol concept has one canonical contract.

This applies especially to IDs and references, operation states, errors, event forms, query forms, migration forms, and compatibility metadata.

docs.title: 8. Embedded Use and Server Use Must Share Semantics
docs.text:
Scriberig should support both embedded and service-oriented use.

An embedded Rust application may call application operations directly:

application.inspect(...)
application.query(...)
application.apply(...)

A remote client may perform conceptually the same actions through a transport:

client.inspect(...)
client.query(...)
client.apply(...)

The transport may add authentication, authorization, serialization, request IDs, retries, streaming, deadlines, subscriptions, and remote cancellation. It must not redefine the meaning of the operation.

This lets product behavior be tested once at the application layer and each transport be tested for faithful exposure.

docs.title: 9. Product Surfaces
docs.text: Scriberig has several product surfaces. They serve different users but should expose the same conceptual platform.

docs.title: 9.1 CLI
docs.text:
The CLI is both a product and a diagnostic surface.

It should support low-level operations such as inspecting entities, revisions, snapshots, relations, queries, and migrations, as well as high-level operations such as rendering a project, reconciling projections, validating a branch, starting a session, issuing an agent command, running a one-shot task, starting the server, or starting the TUI.

The CLI should contain minimal business logic. Its purpose is to bind command-line input and output to shared application operations.

docs.title: 9.2 API server
docs.text:
The server exposes the application layer to remote clients.

Its responsibilities include transport, authentication and authorization where configured, request lifecycle, protocol compatibility, event delivery, long-running operation management, remote cancellation, and connection or subscription handling.

The server must not become a second implementation of the domain model.

docs.title: 9.3 TUI
docs.text:
The TUI is an interactive client of the same operations. It may combine graph navigation, session navigation, agent interaction, migration review, validation output, and projection inspection.

It should not receive privileged semantic access unavailable to other clients unless a capability explicitly requires local process access.

docs.title: 9.4 Web and desktop applications
docs.text:
Browser and desktop applications should use public protocol and client libraries. They may provide richer interaction and visualization but must not depend on private server internals.

The full reusable web/editor architecture is defined separately.

docs.title: 9.5 Agent runtime
docs.text:
The agent runtime consumes the same platform through a deliberately constrained tool layer. It may combine several application operations into agent-oriented tools, but it must not bypass the public semantic model.

An inspect tool should ultimately use the same semantic inspection facilities available to ordinary clients. An editing tool should produce the same migration forms used by non-agent clients.

docs.title: 10. The Agent Runtime Is an Adapter, Not a Privileged Backend
docs.text:
The agent runtime has special requirements: progressive disclosure, context budgeting, session state, tool schemas, branch management, model interaction, summarization, and capability restriction.

Those requirements justify an agent-specific layer. They do not justify direct access to private storage details.

The correct relationship is:

agent request
  -> agent tool adapter
  -> application operation
  -> knowledge platform

The incorrect relationship is an agent reaching directly into backend tables or bypassing validation and migration semantics.

This boundary matters for safety, testing, compatibility, third-party agent implementations, alternative storage backends, and non-agent use of the same platform.

Agent tools may be coarser than application operations. A simple inspect(object, detail_level) tool may compose several application operations, and a high-level edit_function(...) tool may construct and validate several semantic changes before yielding one migration.

The agent adapter composes platform capabilities; it does not invent a second persistence model.

docs.title: 11. Universal Operation Identity and Events
docs.text:
Long-running and externally visible work should have stable operation identity.

Examples include an agent command, validation run, large query, import, projection reconciliation, render, compiler analysis, migration application, or test run.

An operation conceptually includes:

id
kind
requested_by
input_snapshot
status
progress
result
diagnostics

Lifecycle states may include queued, running, completed, failed, and cancelled.

Figure 5 highlights the separation between operation identity, streaming delivery, and final state. A running operation can emit progress, partial output, or diagnostics to any observer, while its final result remains independently addressable. Events tell a client that something happened; they do not become an alternative database representation.

Figure 5 — Stable operation identity unifies CLI, TUI, web, API, and agent observation without making streaming a separate semantic API.

Useful event categories include snapshot changes, entity changes, projection changes, branch changes, migration creation, operation lifecycle changes, validation completion, and agent output.

A client receiving an EntityChanged(E) event should resolve the new state through the normal application or protocol model.

docs.title: 12. Queries and Commands Must Be Distinguishable
docs.text:
The runtime should distinguish operations that inspect state from operations that may create new canonical state.

Queries include concepts such as:

inspect
list
follow
find
diff
history

Commands include concepts such as:

branch
apply migration
reconcile
commit
merge
update projection configuration

Some expensive queries may populate derived caches, but they must not advance canonical snapshots merely because they ran.

This distinction supports clear permissions, retries, idempotency, audit history, agent capabilities, and UI behavior.

docs.title: 13. Product Surfaces Must Not Own Canonical State
docs.text:
A UI, CLI process, agent runtime, or server connection may maintain local view state such as current selection, expanded nodes, scroll position, command history, temporary form state, unsent text, and cached responses.

Those are product concerns.

Canonical project and session knowledge remains in the shared semantic system. A frontend must not silently become authoritative for data the rest of the system cannot see.

When product state becomes durable project knowledge, it must be committed through the normal semantic change model.

A product may intentionally persist durable workspace layouts, named views, bookmarks, saved queries, or similar state inside Scriberig, but those should become explicit domain entities rather than hidden implementation tables masquerading as project knowledge.

docs.title: 14. One Capability, Multiple Presentations
docs.text:
The same capability may look different in different surfaces.

Inspecting an entity may appear as:

CLI        scriberig inspect <id>
TUI        selected object panel
Web        object inspector
Agent      inspect tool result
API client inspect(entity)

Semantic diff may appear as machine-readable protocol data, a colored terminal diff, a structured web visualization, or a compact agent summary.

Presentation may differ greatly. The underlying semantic result must remain consistent.

docs.title: 15. Vertical Capability Development
docs.text:
Scriberig must avoid developing one subsystem far ahead of all product surfaces.

A common failure mode is a mature backend with many capabilities, a partially complete CLI, a smaller server API, and a web or agent layer that exposes only a small subset. That produces several incompatible products sharing only a repository.

Instead, meaningful user-facing features should normally be developed vertically.

Figure 6 uses semantic diff as an example. The capability begins in shared knowledge and application semantics, then gains a protocol representation, server and client exposure, relevant presentations, agent exposure where useful, and conformance tests. The capability matrix beside it makes omissions explicit instead of allowing a feature to exist accidentally in only one surface.

Figure 6 — User-level capabilities should be cross-surface slices, with explicit capability status and semantic conformance tests.

A capability is not considered broadly available until the relevant surfaces expose it. Not every internal primitive needs a button in every UI, but meaningful user-facing gaps must be visible and intentional.

A project-level capability matrix should therefore record whether a capability exists in the reusable library, application layer, protocol, CLI, server, web, TUI, and agent surfaces. Status should reflect evidence rather than aspiration.

docs.title: 16. Third-Party Applications Are First-Class Consumers
docs.text:
The protocol and reusable libraries must be designed for consumers other than the reference Scriberig applications.

A third party may want to build a custom IDE, CAD or GIS application using the knowledge store, documentation editor, code-analysis service, CI integration, alternate agent runtime, specialized browser, or proprietary application embedding only the storage layer.

This implies:

  • stable public boundaries;
  • transport-independent semantic models;
  • documented compatibility expectations;
  • client libraries that do not require the full editor;
  • no dependency from foundational crates to agent-specific code;
  • no requirement to adopt the reference UI style.

The reference products should prove these public boundaries rather than bypass them.

docs.title: 17. Client Libraries
docs.text:
Remote use should be supported through reusable clients rather than requiring every application to manually construct transport requests.

A client library should expose semantic operations in the host language, conceptually including:

client.inspect(entity)
client.query(query)
client.diff(a, b)
client.apply(migration)
client.subscribe(...)

The client may provide request construction, protocol version negotiation, typed decoding, operation tracking, event subscriptions, retry helpers where safe, cancellation, and common error handling.

It must not implement a separate semantic model. The server remains one transport realization of application operations.

docs.title: 18. The Reference Products Must Use Public Boundaries
docs.text:
The full Scriberig products should behave like demanding external consumers.

The reference web editor should use public client and UI libraries. The CLI should use the shared application layer rather than private shortcuts. The TUI should use the same semantic operations. The agent runtime should use the same public platform interfaces expected of alternate agents.

This gives a strong architectural test:

If the reference product needs a private path to implement an important capability, the reusable boundary is probably incomplete.

Carefully justified local-only capabilities may exist, but they must be explicit exceptions.

docs.title: 19. Deployment Shapes
docs.text:
Scriberig should support several deployment shapes without changing its semantic architecture.

Figure 7 compares three common forms. In-process use links an application directly to operations and a local store. A desktop environment may run a local server used by CLI, TUI, or browser clients. A shared environment may use a remote service and managed store. The process boundary changes, but inspect, query, apply, snapshot, and error semantics should remain recognizably equivalent.

Figure 7 — Scriberig supports embedded, local-server, and remote-service deployments without changing the semantic model.

A convenient distribution may expose several modes from one executable, such as server mode, TUI mode, one-shot commands, agent commands, and maintenance operations. That is a packaging choice, not an architectural requirement.

The important property is that these modes remain thin hosts over reusable libraries so they can later be split into separate processes without redesigning the knowledge model.

docs.title: 20. Shared Error and Snapshot Semantics
docs.text:
Errors are part of the protocol contract.

The system should distinguish machine-readable categories such as entity not found, revision not found, snapshot not found, schema violation, stale base snapshot, semantic conflict, validation failure, permission denied, unsupported domain operation, projection out of sync, operation cancelled, and transport failure.
