  8. Query traversal and derived views respect effective access scope.
  9. Secrets are not ordinary semantic objects by default.
  10. Changes are proposed against exact revisions or snapshots.
  11. Candidate work normally occurs outside the canonical root.
  12. Validation results are bound to exact inputs and configurations.
  13. Validators produce evidence; promotion policy decides acceptance.
  14. Ambiguous reconciliation does not silently become canonical history.
  15. External imports retain provenance to captured evidence where practical.
  16. Sessions do not automatically become canonical project knowledge.
  17. Tool results remain attributable to their invocation and input state.
  18. External side effects require explicit authority distinct from local semantic edits.
  19. Official product surfaces enforce the same application-level trust rules.
  20. Low-level reusable storage APIs may intentionally exist below those application policies.
  21. Failed validations and conflicts are representable without becoming canonical project state.
  22. Capability delegation does not implicitly increase authority.
  23. Derived caches cannot be used to bypass access restrictions.
  24. Promotion records enough evidence to explain why a candidate became canonical.
  25. Trust, freshness, confidence, authority, validation, and integrity remain distinct concepts.

docs.title: 22. Failure Modes the Architecture Must Prevent
Model output becomes authoritative merely because it was generated
docs.text: Prevented by provenance and explicit promotion.

docs.title: A web page or imported document instructs an agent to perform a privileged action
docs.text: Prevented by separating data from runtime capabilities.

docs.title: An agent validates snapshot A and promotes different snapshot B
docs.text: Prevented by binding validation to exact candidate state.

docs.title: An external file edit silently overwrites concurrent canonical work
docs.text: Prevented by snapshot-aware reconciliation and merge.

docs.title: A restricted object is exposed through search or a cached summary
docs.text: Prevented by capability-aware queries and derived-data access rules.

docs.title: A parser guesses an ambiguous correspondence and records false lineage
docs.text: Prevented by first-class ambiguity and conflict handling.

docs.title: A local write capability is used to mutate an unrelated external service
docs.text: Prevented by separate, destination-aware external-operation capabilities.

docs.title: A successful external action is retried because local persistence failed
docs.text: Mitigated by external receipts, idempotency where possible, and explicit reconciliation states.

docs.title: A historical validation result is presented as current after relevant inputs changed
docs.text: Prevented by immutable dependency tracking and freshness rules.

docs.title: Product surfaces implement inconsistent bypass paths
docs.text: Prevented by shared application operations and common promotion and validation semantics.

docs.title: 23. Relationship to Other Level 1 Designs
docs.text:
This trust model depends on the rest of the Level 1 architecture rather than replacing it.

  • The universal knowledge model defines the objects and relations that carry provenance.
  • Identity, revisions, and snapshots define the exact states against which evidence and capabilities operate.
  • Persistence provides immutable storage and retained roots.
  • Migrations and branches provide isolated candidate states and explain change lineage.
  • Projections define external edit boundaries and reconciliation.
  • Domain adapters define specialized validators and provenance vocabulary.
  • Derived knowledge and caching define how evidence can be reused safely from immutable dependencies.
  • Sessions define agent investigation history and promotion of durable decisions.
  • The universal operation model defines the common interaction grammar through which capabilities are enforced.
  • Runtime and product-surface design ensures the same trust path is used by CLI, server, web, TUI, third-party clients, and agent runtime.

Trust is therefore not a security subsystem attached at the end. It is a property of how these layers compose.

docs.title: 24. What Belongs in Level 2
docs.text:
Level 2 designs should make these principles concrete without changing them.

They may define:

  • actor and principal representation;
  • capability scope and delegation;
  • application authorization boundaries;
  • provenance schemas and relation vocabulary;
  • validation-result schemas;
  • validator orchestration;
  • project promotion policy;
  • secret-reference handling;
  • query authorization and redaction;
  • external connector receipts and idempotency;
  • projection-conflict persistence;
  • capability-aware cache behavior;
  • API and protocol representations for denial, validation, approval, and trust metadata;
  • web and CLI presentation of provenance and validation state.

Level 2 should preserve the distinction between reusable low-level libraries and application-level policy.

docs.title: 25. What Belongs in Level 3
docs.text:
Level 3 tasks should be small enough for a focused implementation agent.

Examples include:

implement one validation-result object type
add provenance links to one import path
reject promotion when candidate snapshot differs from validated snapshot
add one capability check to a query operation
render validation status in one API response
persist one projection conflict type
add tests proving generated summaries retain source provenance

A Level 3 task should not need to rediscover the trust model. It should point back to the relevant Level 1 and Level 2 rules and implement a narrow part of them.

docs.title: 26. Final Model
docs.text:
Scriberig is a universal knowledge system in which information can move through several states without those states being confused.

At every stage:

  • provenance explains where information came from;
  • capabilities determine what an actor may inspect or do;
  • validation provides evidence about exact immutable inputs;
  • policy determines what evidence is sufficient for promotion;
  • branches and candidate snapshots keep speculative work separate from accepted state;
  • conflicts and failures remain representable without becoming canonical;
  • external effects remain explicit and reconcilable;
  • all official product surfaces use the same trust-enforcing application semantics.

The same rules apply whether a change originates from a human, an agent, a file editor, a compiler, a web importer, an API client, or a third-party integration.

The result should be a system where powerful agents and rich integrations can operate deeply on project knowledge without forcing the storage layer to trust them, without treating generated content as authority, and without allowing ambiguous or insufficiently validated changes to become canonical silently.

docs.title: Vertical Product Completion and End-to-End Usability
1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig is built from reusable semantic libraries, application operations, protocol types, adapters, CLI/TUI/web surfaces, projections, and an agent runtime. Those layers are necessary, but the existence of those layers is not itself a useful product.

This document adds a durable architectural rule that applies to all future implementation work:

A user-facing capability is not complete because its storage model, library API, protocol endpoint, UI component, adapter, or isolated test exists. It is complete only when a real user workflow reaches a meaningful outcome through the intended product surface and that workflow is protected by end-to-end acceptance tests.

This rule extends the vertical capability requirements in 011. runtime libraries protocol and product surfaces.md and the integrated-editor requirements in 012. web platform and integrated editor.md.

It exists because horizontal subsystem completion can otherwise produce a repository with substantial infrastructure but no continuous workflow that a user can depend on.

docs.title: 2. Three Different Meanings of Completion
docs.text: Scriberig must distinguish three kinds of completion.

docs.title: 2.1 Subsystem implemented
docs.text:
A subsystem is implemented when its own public contract exists and its focused tests pass.

Examples include:

  • an immutable snapshot store exists;
  • a Rust parser emits semantic entities;
  • an HTTP endpoint exposes an application operation;
  • a reusable React component renders a semantic object;
  • a TUI reducer handles a command;
  • an agent provider adapter can execute a model request.

Subsystem implementation is valuable engineering progress, but it is not product completion.

docs.title: 2.2 Surface integrated
docs.text:
A capability is surface-integrated when a real product surface invokes the shared capability through its public boundary and presents the result correctly.

Examples include:

  • the web application can invoke project import;
  • the TUI can inspect a selected entity;
  • the CLI can request history;
  • the agent adapter can call semantic inspection.

Surface integration still does not prove that the result composes into a useful workflow.

docs.title: 2.3 Product verified
docs.text:
A capability or milestone is product-verified only when an end-to-end workflow starts from a realistic user entry point, traverses the real boundaries that matter, and reaches a useful observable outcome.

For interactive products, this normally means launching the actual executable or browser application against an actual local server/runtime and interacting through the same controls a user sees.

A mock-only component test cannot establish product verification.

A protocol-only test cannot establish product verification.

A test that asserts only HTTP status codes cannot establish product verification when the user outcome is navigation, editing, review, or filesystem change.

docs.title: 3. Product Verification Is a Release Gate
docs.text:
For milestones explicitly designated as product milestones, product verification is mandatory.

A milestone must not be described as complete, usable, finished, supported, or verified unless all required product-verification scenarios pass from a clean checkout.

Historical task checklists may continue to record that a subsystem was implemented. They do not override this rule.

In particular, a previously checked Level-3 task does not prove a current product workflow. If later integration shows that its output cannot be reached or composed through a product surface, the subsystem may remain implemented while the product capability remains unverified.

Documentation, capability matrices, release notes, and agent reports must use these distinctions truthfully.

docs.title: 4. The First Useful Software-Project Workflow
docs.text:
The first mandatory product milestone for Scriberig is a continuous workflow over a small real Git-backed source project.

A user must be able to perform the following sequence without leaving Scriberig or using an undocumented internal API:

open or import project
        |
        v
project becomes active workspace
        |
        v
browse recognizable semantic structure
        |
        v
select a named code object
        |
        v
view its real source projection
        |
        v
ask an agent about it and/or edit it
        |
        v
produce a candidate semantic migration
        |
        v
review semantic and source differences
        |
        v
validate candidate
        |
        v
accept/apply migration
        |
        v
write the resulting projection to the working tree
        |
        v
observe the successor snapshot/history and continue

This is called the first useful project workflow or golden path in lower-level designs.

The first implementation may intentionally limit the editable golden path to one well-supported source language, initially Rust. The architecture must remain domain-extensible.

docs.title: 5. Active Workspace Is Explicit Product State
docs.text:
Importing a project and working on a project are different operations.

After a project is imported, a product surface must be able to make that project's semantic root and current snapshot its active workspace.

The active workspace includes at least:

  • stable project identity;
  • canonical filesystem location when local filesystem access is relevant;
  • current project snapshot;
  • semantic root for that snapshot;
  • current selection/navigation state.

Active-workspace state is per client/session/product instance. It must not be implemented as one mutable global "current project" in a shared server or database.

Selecting a project in one browser or TUI must not silently change another client's active project.

docs.title: 6. Imported Knowledge Must Be Human-Navigable
docs.text:
A semantic store containing entities is not enough.

For supported domains, users must be able to recognize what they are browsing without decoding entity IDs, revision IDs, array positions, or labels such as path :: kind #N.

Supported domain adapters must expose stable display information and meaningful containment/navigation relationships.

For code, useful navigation includes recognizable concepts such as:

project
  source path / module
    type / trait / function
      method / nested semantic object

Exact hierarchy varies by language, but symbol names and semantic kinds must be available through public semantic data, not reconstructed privately in each frontend.

Raw IDs remain available for diagnostics. They are not the primary product label when a semantic name exists.

docs.title: 7. Projection Is the Human Representation, Not Another Inspector
docs.text:
A projection view must show the domain's human-oriented representation.

For source code this means source text associated with the selected semantic object or source artifact, together with mapping back to semantic identity.

For the editable golden path, the product must expose a real editable projection or a structured edit interaction that results in the same shared change machinery.

A generic property/object inspector does not satisfy the source-projection requirement.

A browser-local edited buffer is never canonical state by itself.

docs.title: 8. Every Mutation Uses the Shared Change Path
docs.text:
Human web edits, TUI edits, CLI changes, agent proposals, external-file reconciliation, and third-party client edits must converge on the shared migration/change model.

The required conceptual path is:

intent or edited projection
        -> candidate semantic change
        -> migration with exact base snapshot
        -> validation
        -> reviewable semantic/source diff
        -> compare-and-swap application
        -> successor canonical snapshot
        -> projection materialization / external effect

A product surface must not write canonical database rows directly.

An agent must not write the working tree directly as a privileged shortcut when the same change is expected to be reviewable through migration semantics.

A web editor must not invent a private mutation endpoint.

docs.title: 9. Filesystem Write-Back Is Part of the Software-Project Product
docs.text:
For a software project backed by ordinary source files, accepting a change is not useful if the resulting source never reaches the working tree.

The first useful project workflow therefore includes controlled projection materialization back to the project filesystem.

Write-back must:

  • remain inside the project's configured/canonical root;
  • use the projection ownership and atomic-I/O rules;
  • reject stale or conflicting external changes rather than silently overwrite them;
  • retain enough effect/recovery information to explain partial external-effect failures;
  • never escape through symlinks or path traversal;
  • update only files owned/targeted by the accepted projection operation.

The canonical semantic snapshot and filesystem projection may have different failure domains. Lower-level design must make recovery explicit rather than pretending both writes form one filesystem/database transaction.

docs.title: 10. Agent Use Must Be Semantically Scoped
docs.text:
The agent is a peer consumer of the same platform.

When a user asks an agent about a selected code object, the request must contain the semantic selection and exact/current snapshot context, not only a copied line range or an unstructured full repository dump.

When an agent proposes a code change for the golden path, that proposal must become the same reviewable migration that a human-generated edit would produce.

End-to-end tests for this behavior must not depend on an external commercial model service. A deterministic test provider may emulate the required provider/tool interaction while still exercising the real Scriberig agent/application/protocol/product boundaries.

docs.title: 11. Surface Parity for the Golden Path
docs.text:
The web application and native TUI are both first-class interactive products.

The first useful project milestone is not complete if one surface can perform useful work and the other remains only a database inspector, unless a Level-1 design explicitly marks a step not applicable to that surface.

Presentation may differ, but both interactive surfaces must support the core semantic sequence:

  • choose/open an imported project;
  • browse named semantic objects;
  • inspect source projection;
  • create or receive a candidate change;
  • review/validate/apply it;
  • observe the resulting current state.

The web surface is expected to support direct editable projection interaction in the first golden path.

The TUI may use a command/editor-buffer interaction appropriate to a terminal, but it must still use the same public operations and migration model.

CLI remains a diagnostic/automation peer and should expose the same underlying operations where command-line use is meaningful.

docs.title: 12. End-to-End Tests Must Observe User Outcomes
docs.text:
Product E2E tests must assert outcomes at the layer where the user experiences them.

Examples of valid assertions include:

  • after import and project activation, the explorer visibly contains the known fixture symbol Calculator;
  • selecting add shows the source containing left + right;
  • after editing, a migration review visibly contains the changed expression;
  • before acceptance, the fixture file on disk is unchanged;
  • after acceptance and write-back, the fixture file on disk contains the accepted expression;
  • the current snapshot ID changes;
  • history shows a successor state or migration entry;
  • reloading the web application or restarting the TUI still observes the accepted state;
  • an agent request receives the selected entity/snapshot and its candidate follows the same review/apply path.

Examples that are insufficient by themselves include:

  • endpoint returned HTTP 200;
  • a React component mounted;
  • a reducer action was dispatched;
  • a database row count increased;
  • an import operation ended with status=imported;
  • an object inspector displayed some entity ID.

Those may remain useful lower-level tests but cannot replace product E2E acceptance.

docs.title: 13. Deterministic Product Fixtures
docs.text:
Golden-path tests must use repository-controlled deterministic fixtures copied into a temporary working directory.

Fixtures must:

  • be small enough to understand completely;
  • contain no network dependencies;
  • be initialized or copied as a real Git project when Git behavior is under test;
  • contain stable symbol names used by assertions;
  • permit source mutation without modifying the Scriberig checkout itself;
  • support deterministic validation such as parsing and, where applicable, cargo check with no dependency downloads.

Tests must not edit this repository's own tracked source as their golden-path workspace.

docs.title: 14. No Placeholder Completion
docs.text:
The following do not satisfy a required workflow step:

  • a route that displays unsupported when that capability is required by the current milestone;
  • a button wired to a stub operation;
  • a projection panel that displays generic semantic metadata instead of source;
  • a fake symbol label generated only in the UI while public semantic data remains unnamed;
  • a migration preview that cannot be applied;
  • an apply operation that changes the semantic store but not the required filesystem projection;
  • an agent UI that can chat but cannot preserve semantic scope;
  • a test that mocks away the boundary whose integration is being claimed.

Unsupported states remain correct behavior for optional capabilities and older servers. They are not evidence that a milestone requiring that capability is complete.

docs.title: 15. Product-First Development Order
docs.text:
Until the first useful project workflow is product-verified, work should preferentially close gaps in that workflow rather than expand unrelated horizontal breadth.

New adapters, formats, storage features, generic UI components, or agent features are justified during this period when they:

  • directly unblock a golden-path step;
  • fix correctness/security required by that step; or
  • are necessary to keep shared abstractions honest across the required surfaces.

This is a prioritization rule, not a permanent ban on platform development.

Once the golden path is verified, additional capabilities should be developed as new vertical slices with their own user outcomes.

docs.title: 16. Capability Matrix Semantics
docs.text:
The capability matrix remains useful, but surface statuses must not be interpreted as product usability by themselves.

implemented means code for that capability exists on the surface.

verified means the capability's surface semantics have dedicated verification.

Product milestones must additionally identify their required workflow-level E2E scenarios.

A future matrix extension may add workflow/milestone references, but no status vocabulary change is required to adopt this design.

docs.title: 17. Definition of Done for the First Useful Project Milestone
docs.text:
The milestone is complete only when all of the following are true:

  1. a clean build can launch the real local server/runtime, web app, and native TUI;
  2. a deterministic Git/Rust fixture can be copied to a temporary directory and onboarded;
  3. both web and TUI can make that project their active workspace without changing global server state;
  4. both surfaces expose recognizable semantic names including a known type and method/function from the fixture;
  5. source projection for the known selected symbol displays exact fixture source;
  6. the web surface can create a candidate source edit through the shared change path;
  7. the candidate has an exact base snapshot, semantic/source diff, and validation result;
  8. accepting the candidate creates a successor snapshot and writes the accepted source to the fixture working tree through controlled projection materialization;
  9. the refreshed product state and history show the successor state;
  10. a deterministic agent-provider scenario receives the same semantic selection and can produce a candidate that enters the same review path;
  11. stale/conflicting filesystem content is not silently overwritten;
  12. browser E2E, native TUI E2E, cross-surface conformance, and repository quality gates pass from a clean checkout.

No individual subsystem checklist can waive these requirements.

docs.title: 18. Relationship to Earlier Designs
docs.text:
This document does not invalidate the architecture in Levels 1-3.

It changes how completion is judged.

Earlier documents that mark project onboarding, the integrated editor, TUI views, projections, or agent surfaces as implemented remain useful records of subsystem work. Their checked boxes must not be read as proof that the first useful project workflow is product-verified.

Lower-level designs created under this Level-1 rule must specify the exact active-workspace contract, golden fixture, product interactions, mutation/write-back sequence, and E2E tests required to close the workflow.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig must be able to use its own project knowledge, agent runtime, change model, validation system, and product surfaces to evolve Scriberig itself.

Self-hosting is not a special privileged mode. It is the composition of ordinary Scriberig capabilities into a complete loop:

trusted local runtime context
    -> project scan
    -> reviewed persisted manifest
    -> semantic import
    -> active project P@S0
    -> semantic discovery
    -> agent candidate C
    -> isolated validation
    -> explicit acceptance
    -> safe materialization
    -> active project P@S1

The reference proof begins in the native TUI with an empty database, asks an agent to onboard the current Scriberig checkout, then asks the agent to add support for ingesting PHP source files.

This document defines the durable invariants behind that proof. Concrete operation shapes belong in Level 2, and focused implementation work belongs in Level 3.

docs.title: 2. Bootstrap Context Is Not Project Knowledge
docs.text:
An agent may start when there is no active project and no project snapshot in the database.

The local product composition may provide bounded trusted environmental context such as:

  • current working directory;
  • database/runtime identity;
  • authenticated principal;
  • provider configuration;
  • capabilities authorized for the local process.

That context is enough to bootstrap project onboarding, but it is not itself a semantic project.

A filesystem path must not be treated as an EntityId, project root, or current semantic snapshot merely because the TUI was launched from that directory.

The transition from external environment to semantic project state is explicit:

filesystem path
    -> project.scan
    -> persisted manifest
    -> project.import
    -> ProjectId + SnapshotId + semantic root

docs.title: 3. Onboarding Is an Agent-Usable Application Capability
docs.text:
Project onboarding must be available to an authorized agent through the same application boundary used by other clients.

The agent does not implement onboarding by:

  • recursively reading one file at a time through model-visible filesystem calls;
  • opening SQLite;
  • writing project catalog tables;
  • inventing source ownership records;
  • constructing project snapshots directly.

The project subsystem owns deterministic scan, manifest persistence, adapter classification, import, ownership reconciliation, and atomic project promotion.

The agent's responsibility is orchestration: discover the capability, select the intended project context, review bounded results, invoke import for the exact reviewed manifest, and verify that the resulting semantic workspace is useful.

docs.title: 4. Progressive Semantic Transition
docs.text:
Before onboarding, filesystem/environment references are unavoidable bootstrap evidence.

After onboarding, project work should preferentially use stable semantic scope:

ProjectId
SnapshotId
root EntityId
selected EntityId when applicable
projection identity when applicable

The agent should not continue to treat arbitrary paths and raw grep output as its primary project model once equivalent semantic objects are available.

Filesystem/source paths remain important provenance and projection metadata. They do not replace semantic identity.

This transition is central to Scriberig's purpose: the tool should become more useful to an agent after it has ingested a project than before.

docs.title: 5. Capability Discovery Remains Progressive
docs.text:
Self-hosting does not justify giving every tool to every model turn.

The bootstrap catalog should contain only the capabilities needed to orient and make progress, with additional capabilities disclosed from trusted registries as scope becomes more specific.

For the reference flow, the agent can progress conceptually from:

capabilities
project.scan
project.import
project.workspace

to project-scoped semantic reads such as:

inspect
list
follow
find
query
render
history

and only then, for authorized change work, to:

branch.start
change.propose
change.inspect
validate

change.apply remains governed by the product's acceptance policy and must not be implicitly granted merely because the change was produced by an agent.

docs.title: 6. Nested Branches Are Context Boundaries
docs.text:
Substantial self-hosting work should be decomposable into nested agent branches.

A child branch receives an explicit subset of parent context, including as appropriate:

  • purpose;
  • exact project and snapshot;
  • semantic selection;
  • authorized capabilities;
  • expected result shape.

A child must not inherit ambient mutable state accidentally.

When a child completes, its durable BranchResult is the normal input returned to the parent. The entire child transcript is not automatically injected into the parent's active model context.

The detailed child conversation remains inspectable through session/history tools when needed.

This property makes branches a real context-scaling mechanism rather than only a visual grouping feature.

docs.title: 7. Agents Use the Same Change Model as Humans
docs.text:
An agent has no privileged canonical mutation path.

A source change produced by an agent must become the same normal candidate/migration consumed by review, diff, validation, apply, history, and materialization operations for human-produced changes.

The canonical provenance may distinguish:

initiator = agent
session
branch
operation

but provenance must not select a weaker mutation path.

In particular, the agent must not:

  • write live project files as the canonical edit mechanism;
  • create an agent-only patch type that bypasses migration semantics;
  • advance a project root directly;
  • write semantic records directly to storage;
  • silently auto-apply its own candidate unless an explicit future policy authorizes that behavior.

docs.title: 8. Project-Wide Changes Are Coherent Candidates
docs.text:
Self-hosting commonly requires more than changing one existing source range.

A normal candidate must therefore be able to represent a coherent project-wide source change containing, as needed:

  • creation of new source files;
  • updates to existing source files;
  • deletion of owned source files;
  • package/workspace metadata changes;
  • lockfile changes;
  • tests and fixtures;
  • documentation or registry changes.

All file effects belong to one exact-base candidate when they jointly implement one semantic capability.

The candidate must remain inspectable and renderable without making it current project state.

The live project snapshot and live working tree remain at the base until normal acceptance.

docs.title: 9. Validation Binds to Exact Candidate State
docs.text:
Validation evidence is meaningful only when bound to the exact candidate content it validated.

Self-hosting validation may include:

  • semantic/reconciliation checks;
  • focused crate/unit tests;
  • workspace compile/lint/test profiles;
  • end-to-end project ingestion tests;
  • product tests in real processes.

Validation that needs filesystem/process execution uses isolated candidate materialization or an equivalent safe workspace. It must not validate by overwriting the user's live project before acceptance.

External dependency acquisition, if required, is an explicit bounded capability. It is not implicit unrestricted network access for the agent.

docs.title: 10. Acceptance Separates Proposal From Authority
docs.text:
A validated agent candidate is still a proposal.

Before normal acceptance:

project current snapshot == candidate base snapshot
live project files == expected base projections
candidate is durable and inspectable
validation evidence is durable and inspectable

Acceptance uses exact-base compare-and-swap semantics and the shared external-effect/materialization design.

The database and filesystem are not falsely described as one atomic transaction. Effect status and recovery remain explicit.

After successful apply/materialization, clients refresh the authoritative project workspace instead of locally inventing the successor snapshot.

docs.title: 11. Extending Domains Must Extend the Shared Model
docs.text:
A self-hosted request such as "add support for ingesting PHP source files" must extend Scriberig's existing domain architecture, not create a private format-specific storage system.

A new source-code adapter is expected to:

  • preserve exact source evidence;
  • use versioned adapter/schema metadata;
  • normalize parser output into the universal/code domain model;
  • preserve deterministic syntax/source mappings appropriate to the language;
  • expose named declarations through common semantic discovery when available;
  • produce structured adapter diagnostics;
  • participate in normal project ownership and re-import reconciliation;
  • remain inert with respect to executing imported user code.

Language-specific richness is encouraged. Language-specific isolation from universal operations is not.

docs.title: 12. Self-Hosting Must Be Proven From a Baseline That Lacks the New Capability
docs.text:
A golden self-extension test is invalid if the requested feature already exists in the starting product and the agent merely reports success.

For the PHP reference scenario, the starting Scriberig checkout used by the product gate must not already have first-class PHP semantic ingestion registered.

The agent-produced candidate must be what introduces the PHP domain adapter and its integration into the tested checkout.

Test-only fixtures may describe the required PHP extension and deterministic provider behavior, but they must not make PHP a production adapter before the scenario begins.

This invariant preserves the meaning of self-hosting.

docs.title: 13. Durable Session and Provenance Requirements
docs.text:
The complete loop must remain inspectable after model streaming ends and after the product restarts.

Durable state must be sufficient to answer questions such as:

  • Which user request started the work?
  • Which session and branch performed architecture discovery?
  • Which exact project snapshot did the implementation branch use?
  • Which tool operations were executed?
  • Which candidate did the agent produce?
  • Which validations evaluated it?
  • Who accepted it?
  • Which successor snapshot became current?
  • Which external file effects succeeded or require recovery?

The original provider stream is not the canonical historical record.

docs.title: 14. Cross-Surface Invariant
docs.text:
The reference scenario is intentionally TUI-first, but none of its semantic state is TUI-owned.

Stable project, snapshot, entity, session, branch, operation, candidate, validation, history, and effect references must remain meaningful through the shared embedded application and supported protocol/client surfaces.

The TUI is a client of application semantics, not an alternate implementation of them.

docs.title: 15. Non-Goals
docs.text:
This principle does not require:

  • autonomous unreviewed repository rewrites;
  • unrestricted shell or network access for models;
  • a full IDE implementation for every source language;
  • compiler/type analysis for every newly ingested language;
  • replaying full historical transcripts into every continuation;
  • making every imported language bidirectionally editable;
  • treating every self-hosted task as a special product mode.

The objective is stronger shared semantics and safe composition, not maximal agent privilege.

docs.title: 16. Completion Standard
docs.text: Scriberig satisfies this principle when a real product test can begin with an empty project database, use the TUI agent to onboard the current Scriberig checkout, continue from the resulting exact semantic workspace, produce a validated multi-file candidate that adds a previously absent source format, review and accept that candidate through the normal change path, observe the authoritative successor snapshot and safe filesystem effects, restart, and recover the resulting project/session/history state without relying on hidden test mutation paths.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig is both a product and a reusable platform.

The universal knowledge store, query model, projection system, domain adapters, client libraries, and web libraries should be useful independently of the integrated Scriberig application and independently of the agent runtime.

The project should make it straightforward for third parties to:

  • define new schemas and semantic domains;
  • add parsers, renderers, validators, and reconciliation logic;
  • provide alternative storage backends;
  • add derived indexes and analysis;
  • build clients in different languages;
  • create custom user interfaces;
  • build domain-specific editors;
  • integrate Scriberig into existing applications;
  • build alternative agent runtimes or omit agents entirely.

At the same time, the integrated Scriberig server, agent runtime, and editor should remain an open shared product rather than becoming a proprietary hosted fork whose improvements are never returned to users.

This document defines the architectural extension boundaries, ecosystem expectations, compatibility principles, and licensing split that support both goals.

The central rule is:

Reusable infrastructure should be easy to adopt. The integrated Scriberig product should remain open when modified and offered as a service.

docs.title: 2. Platform and Product Are Different Layers
docs.text:
Scriberig should not be designed as one indivisible application.

The architecture has two broad layers.

docs.title: 2.1 Reusable platform
docs.text:
The reusable platform includes capabilities such as:

  • immutable storage;
  • snapshots and revisions;
  • the universal semantic graph;
  • schemas;
  • queries;
  • migrations;
  • projections;
  • domain adapters;
  • protocol definitions;
  • client libraries;
  • reusable web models and UI primitives;
  • reusable agent-facing abstractions that do not require the integrated runtime.

These parts should be useful to applications that are not Scriberig.

A CAD application, documentation system, code-analysis service, research tool, IDE, knowledge browser, or proprietary internal system should be able to reuse the platform without adopting the full Scriberig product.

docs.title: 2.2 Integrated product
docs.text:
The integrated product combines the reusable platform into an opinionated end-user system.

It includes capabilities such as:

  • the reference server;
  • the complete Scriberig web editor;
  • the integrated agent runtime and orchestration;
  • opinionated workflows that coordinate sessions, tools, migrations, validation, and UI;
  • product-specific operational behavior.

The integrated product should itself be built on the public platform interfaces.

It must not rely on private shortcuts that are unavailable to third-party applications.

This distinction is architectural before it is legal.

The licensing boundary follows the same separation.

Figure 1 shows the intended dependency and licensing direction. The reusable Apache-2.0 platform sits below the integrated AGPL-3.0 product, and third-party applications may stop at the platform layer. The important point is that the legal boundary follows an architectural boundary that already exists for reuse, dependency direction, and product composition.

Figure 1 — The licensing split follows the platform/product architecture: reusable building blocks stay permissive while the integrated product remains AGPL-covered.

docs.title: 3. Extensibility Is a Core Requirement
docs.text:
Extensibility is not a later plugin feature.

The universal knowledge model exists specifically so new domains can be added without replacing the storage and interaction architecture.

A new extension should specialize the shared system rather than fork it.

For example, adding a new programming language should not require a new persistence model.

Adding a new document format should not require a separate query engine.

Adding a new browser view should not require a separate server API.

Adding a new agent should not require unrestricted database access.

The project should preserve stable extension seams from the beginning even when the first implementation supports only a small number of domains.

docs.title: 4. Public Extension Categories
docs.text: Scriberig should support several independent classes of extension.

docs.title: 4.1 Schemas
docs.text:
A schema defines domain meaning over the universal knowledge substrate.

Schemas may define:

  • entity types;
  • properties;
  • relation types;
  • collection semantics;
  • constraints;
  • validation rules;
  • canonical versus derived fields;
  • supported operations;
  • supported projections;
  • description strategies.

A third party should be able to define a domain without changing the universal store.

docs.title: 4.2 Domain adapters
docs.text:
A domain adapter connects an external representation or domain system to semantic knowledge.

An adapter may provide:

  • parsing;
  • canonicalization;
  • import;
  • rendering;
  • reconciliation;
  • validation;
  • semantic operations;
  • derived analysis;
  • domain-specific queries;
  • domain-specific UI metadata.

Examples include Markdown, Rust, PDF, TypeScript, notebooks, CAD data, or a proprietary business format.

Adapters should depend on public graph, schema, migration, query, and projection abstractions rather than internal storage details.

docs.title: 4.3 Storage backends
docs.text:
The logical storage model must not be permanently coupled to one physical backend.

The initial implementation may use one preferred backend, but the architecture should permit alternatives for:

  • embedded use;
  • testing;
  • server deployments;
  • distributed storage;
  • specialized indexing;
  • constrained environments.

A storage implementation must preserve the logical guarantees of revisions, snapshots, consistency, and identity.

Consumers above the storage boundary should not need to know which backend is used.

docs.title: 4.4 Queries and derived analysis
docs.text:
Extensions may add derived knowledge and specialized query capabilities.

Examples include:

  • compiler analysis;
  • reference indexes;
  • call graphs;
  • embeddings;
  • PDF layout analysis;
  • search indexes;
  • domain-specific validation;
  • summaries and descriptions.

Derived extensions must declare their provenance and dependencies so their results can be reused or invalidated correctly.

docs.title: 4.5 Projections
docs.text:
Extensions may define new external representations of knowledge.

A projection may be:

  • a text file;
  • a source file;
  • HTML;
  • a transcript;
  • a model context;
  • a UI representation;
  • an interchange format;
  • a generated report.

Editable projections may additionally provide parsing and reconciliation so external changes can become semantic migrations.

docs.title: 4.6 Clients and protocols
docs.text:
Third parties should be able to use Scriberig remotely without depending on internal Rust libraries.

The public protocol must therefore be treated as an extension surface.

Client libraries may exist for Rust, TypeScript, and other languages.

The protocol should expose semantic concepts rather than backend-specific details.

docs.title: 4.7 User-interface libraries
docs.text:
The web interface must be layered so third parties can choose how much opinion they adopt.

Reusable layers may include:

  • protocol types;
  • transport clients;
  • client-side semantic models;
  • framework bindings;
  • headless editor and navigation controllers;
  • neutral components;
  • opinionated component libraries such as MUI-based components.

A third party should be able to use the behavior without using Scriberig's visual style.

docs.title: 4.8 Agent integrations
docs.text:
The integrated Scriberig agent runtime is one consumer of the platform.

Other agents should be able to consume the same semantic APIs.

Reusable agent abstractions may define:

  • semantic tool descriptions;
  • context providers;
  • capability descriptions;
  • operation events;
  • workspace abstractions.

They should not require the integrated Scriberig orchestration runtime.

Figure 2 summarizes the extension model as a composition problem rather than a plugin ownership hierarchy. Schemas, adapters, storage backends, derived analysis, projections, protocol clients, UI libraries, and agent integrations all meet at the same public semantic boundary. A new extension enriches or implements one capability without becoming the exclusive owner of the entities it touches.

Figure 2 — Independent extension categories compose around the universal semantic platform instead of forking the architecture.

docs.title: 5. Extensions Must Use Public Semantic Boundaries
docs.text:
Extensions should not depend directly on database tables, private serialization details, undocumented internal identifiers, or application-specific state.

The preferred dependency direction is:

extension
    -> public semantic API
        -> application/domain layer
            -> graph and storage abstractions

Not:

extension
    -> SQLite tables

or:

extension
    -> private server implementation

This rule allows the persistence implementation, cache layout, server framework, and internal indexing strategy to evolve independently.

The public semantic model is the compatibility boundary.

docs.title: 6. Extension Capabilities Should Be Discoverable
docs.text:
A consumer should be able to discover what an entity, domain, or server supports.

For example, inspecting an entity may reveal:

entity type: Function

relations:
  body
  parameters
  calls
  references

operations:
  inspect
  diff
  rename
  validate
  render

A different domain may expose:

entity type: PDFPage

relations:
  paragraphs
  tables
  figures

operations:
  inspect
  render
  find

This allows clients and agents to adapt to installed capabilities rather than requiring every possible domain to be hard-coded into the universal interface.

Capability discovery also allows simpler clients to ignore functionality they do not understand.

docs.title: 7. Extensions Should Compose
docs.text:
The extension model should favor composition over exclusive ownership.

A domain entity may participate in several independent extension systems at the same time.

For example, a function may have:

  • a Rust syntax adapter;
  • compiler-derived type information;
  • a call-graph index;
  • model-generated descriptions;
  • a source projection;
  • a custom UI inspector;
  • organization-specific annotations.

These extensions should attach knowledge through typed relations, derived objects, projections, and public operations instead of forcing all behavior into one monolithic adapter.

This is important for the universal knowledge premise.

The same entity may be interpreted and enriched by several independent producers.

docs.title: 8. Canonical and Derived Extensions Must Stay Distinct
docs.text:
An extension may contribute canonical knowledge, derived knowledge, or both.

The distinction must remain explicit.

A parser importing an editable source file may contribute canonical syntax.

A compiler may contribute derived type information.

A model may contribute a generated description.

A user may contribute an authoritative annotation.

These must not become indistinguishable merely because they are stored in the same database.

Every extension that produces derived knowledge should identify:

  • its producer;
  • its profile or version;
  • its exact dependencies;
  • its provenance;
  • whether its output is authoritative, imported, validated, inferred, or generated.

The extension mechanism must preserve the trust model of the knowledge store.

docs.title: 9. Compatibility Is Defined at Several Layers
docs.text:
Scriberig should not use one global version number as the only compatibility mechanism.

Different contracts evolve at different rates.

Important compatibility layers include:

  • object and canonical encoding versions;
  • schema versions;
  • domain adapter versions;
  • protocol versions;
  • projection formats;
  • style/profile versions;
  • query language versions;
  • derived-analysis profile versions;
  • client-library APIs.

Compatibility should be explicit at the boundary where it matters.

For example, changing an internal SQLite index should not require a protocol version change.

Changing canonical encoding rules may require migration support but should not automatically require a new UI API.

Changing a model-generated summary profile should not redefine the canonical entity schema.

docs.title: 10. Evolution Must Prefer Additive Change
docs.text:
Public extension contracts should prefer additive evolution.

Where practical:

  • add new fields rather than reinterpret old fields;
  • add new relation types rather than silently changing existing semantics;
  • add new operations rather than changing unrelated operation behavior;
  • preserve unknown fields or capabilities when forwarding data where the protocol permits it;
  • allow clients to ignore unsupported optional capabilities;
  • version incompatible canonical formats explicitly.

This is especially important because the ecosystem may contain clients and extensions that do not upgrade at the same time as the reference product.

The integrated editor must not assume that every server or adapter was compiled from the same commit.

Figure 3 makes the compatibility rule concrete. Canonical encoding, schemas, adapters, query profiles, protocol, projection formats, and client APIs are separate contracts that can evolve at different rates. An internal storage-index change should therefore leave all of those public versions untouched unless their actual contract changes.

Figure 3 — Version the compatibility boundary that changed; do not use one global version number as a proxy for unrelated contracts.

docs.title: 11. Extensions Must Not Circumvent Migrations
docs.text:
A public extension that changes canonical knowledge must use the normal change model.

It must not update storage behind the graph, migration, validation, or snapshot systems.

All canonical write paths should converge conceptually on:

proposed semantic change
    -> migration
    -> validation
    -> new snapshot

This rule applies equally to:

  • built-in adapters;
  • third-party adapters;
  • web editors;
  • CLI extensions;
  • agents;
  • external API clients;
  • importers.

An extension may provide specialized semantic operations, but those operations must ultimately produce ordinary semantic changes visible to the same history and validation system.

docs.title: 12. Extensions Must Respect Capabilities and Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
Being installed does not imply unrestricted authority.

Extensions should operate under explicit capabilities where practical.

Capabilities may constrain:

  • which entities can be read;
  • which relations can be followed;
  • which domains can be modified;
  • which external resources can be accessed;
  • whether canonical migrations may be proposed;
  • whether migrations may be promoted;
  • which validations may be invoked;
  • which tools may be exposed to agents.

A third-party parser, renderer, UI component, or agent integration should not receive broad database or filesystem access merely because it participates in the system.

The extensibility model must remain compatible with the trust and validation model defined elsewhere.

docs.title: 13. The Reference Product Is a Conformance Consumer
docs.text:
The full Scriberig application should be built from the same public abstractions available to other applications.

This includes the web editor.

The reference editor should consume public protocol, client, model, navigation, and component libraries rather than use hidden server endpoints or direct database access.

The same principle applies to CLI and agent surfaces where appropriate.

This gives the reference product a second role:

It is a conformance test for the public platform.

If the integrated product requires a private capability that third parties cannot access, the preferred response is to improve the public platform boundary rather than keep the shortcut private.

Figure 4 shows why this is a strong architectural test. Third-party consumers and Scriberig's own CLI, server, editor, and agent runtime enter through the same public semantic surface. Neither side should jump directly to database details; if the reference product needs such a shortcut, the public abstraction is incomplete.

Figure 4 — The reference product validates the public platform by consuming the same semantic APIs that third parties receive.

docs.title: 14. Third-Party User Interfaces Are Expected
docs.text:
Scriberig should explicitly support applications that do not look like the reference editor.

A third party may want:

  • a minimal code-review interface;
  • a document editor;
  • a project-specific dashboard;
  • a CAD-oriented semantic browser;
  • a read-only knowledge explorer;
  • a mobile application;
  • an IDE integration;
  • a custom design system.

Reusable web behavior should therefore be separated from visual opinion.

Headless navigation, selection, commands, history, diff, and editing behavior should be usable without MUI.

Opinionated component libraries may be provided on top.

The reference MUI implementation is a convenience and product choice, not the required rendering architecture.

docs.title: 15. Third-Party Domains Are Expected
docs.text:
The project should assume that important future domains will be implemented outside the main repository.

The core must therefore avoid assumptions such as:

  • every entity belongs to a built-in type;
  • every projection is textual;
  • every validator is known at compile time;
  • every relation is understood by the reference UI;
  • every query result can be rendered by a built-in component;
  • every domain has source files;
  • every extension uses an agent.

Unknown domain objects must remain inspectable at the universal graph level even when no specialized UI is installed.

The raw graph browser in the reference editor is therefore not only a debugging tool. It is also a compatibility fallback for unknown extensions.

docs.title: 16. The Ecosystem Should Have a Small Stable Core
docs.text:
The most durable extension contracts should be the smallest ones.

The universal concepts should change more slowly than domain adapters and product UI.

A healthy dependency direction is conceptually:

identity and storage
    -> graph and schemas
        -> queries and migrations
            -> domains and projections
                -> application operations
                    -> server, CLI, UI, agents

Higher layers may evolve quickly.

Lower layers should remain intentionally conservative.

This makes it possible for experimental domains and products to evolve without destabilizing storage or semantic identity.

docs.title: 17. Licensing Goals
docs.text: The licensing model should support four goals simultaneously.

docs.title: 17.1 Encourage adoption of the reusable platform
docs.text: Organizations should be able to embed the storage, graph, query, protocol, client, projection, domain, and UI libraries in commercial or proprietary software without being required to open the rest of their application.

docs.title: 17.2 Encourage an ecosystem around shared primitives
docs.text: Third parties should be able to build alternative editors, domain systems, services, and integrations on top of Scriberig without requesting a special license.

docs.title: 17.3 Keep the integrated Scriberig product open
docs.text: A company should not be able to take the complete Scriberig server or editor, make substantial private modifications, offer the modified product as a network service, and avoid making those covered modifications available under the same open-source terms.

docs.title: 17.4 Keep the boundary understandable
docs.text:
The repository may contain more than one license, but a developer should be able to determine the license of a component from its architectural role and package metadata.

The licensing split should follow package boundaries rather than individual implementation details whenever practical.

docs.title: 18. Reusable Infrastructure Uses Apache-2.0
docs.text:
Reusable platform libraries should use the Apache License 2.0.

This includes, by default, libraries whose primary purpose is reusable infrastructure rather than the integrated Scriberig product.

Examples include:

  • identity and core types;
  • immutable storage abstractions and implementations;
  • the universal graph;
  • schemas;
  • query libraries;
  • migration libraries;
  • projection libraries;
  • domain adapters;
  • protocol definitions;
  • Rust and TypeScript clients;
  • client-side semantic models;
  • framework bindings;
  • headless editor libraries;
  • reusable neutral UI components;
  • opinionated reusable UI libraries such as MUI-based components;
  • reusable agent-facing interfaces that do not implement the integrated runtime.

Apache-2.0 is intentionally permissive.

Consumers may combine these components with closed-source applications.

This supports the goal that the universal knowledge platform become useful infrastructure beyond Scriberig itself.

Apache-2.0 is preferred over a minimal permissive license because it also provides explicit patent terms for contributors and users.

docs.title: 19. The Integrated Product Uses AGPL-3.0
docs.text:
The integrated Scriberig product should use the GNU Affero General Public License version 3.

This includes, by default, components whose primary purpose is operating the complete Scriberig product rather than serving as a reusable primitive.

Examples include:

  • the reference Scriberig server application;
  • the integrated agent runtime and orchestration layer;
  • the complete Scriberig editor application;
  • product-specific workflows that combine platform capabilities into the hosted or locally operated Scriberig product.

The AGPL boundary is intended to preserve openness for modified network-accessible versions of the integrated product.

A user or company remains free to build a different proprietary application from the Apache-licensed platform libraries.

The distinction is intentional:

Apache-2.0
    reusable platform and building blocks

AGPL-3.0
    integrated Scriberig product and runtime

The project should avoid moving generally reusable functionality into AGPL components merely to make the licensing boundary more restrictive.

If a capability is broadly useful as infrastructure, it belongs in the reusable Apache-licensed layer.

docs.title: 20. Agent Functionality May Be Split Across the Boundary
docs.text:
Agent functionality is not automatically part of the AGPL layer.

Reusable agent abstractions may remain Apache-2.0 when they define general concepts such as:

  • tool interfaces;
  • semantic context providers;
  • operation event types;
  • capability descriptions;
  • workspace interfaces;
  • model-independent agent protocol structures.

The integrated agent execution and orchestration system may be AGPL-3.0.

This follows the same platform/product distinction used elsewhere.

The knowledge store must remain fully usable without any AGPL agent runtime.

docs.title: 21. CLI and Client Tools Should Remain Reusable Where Practical
docs.text:
A command-line client that primarily exposes public platform or server capabilities should normally remain Apache-2.0.

Likewise, client SDKs and protocol tools should remain Apache-2.0.

Product-specific executables that embed substantial integrated AGPL runtime behavior may themselves belong on the AGPL side.

The decision should follow architectural responsibility rather than executable format.

A binary is not automatically part of the product layer merely because it is a binary.

docs.title: 22. Package Boundaries Must Make Licensing Clear
docs.text:
Mixed licensing is acceptable only if the boundaries are easy to understand.

Each distributable package or crate should declare its own license.

Repository-level documentation should explain the split.

Where appropriate, source files may use SPDX identifiers.

The repository should retain complete license texts for the licenses it uses.

A package should not silently contain code under incompatible expectations from another architectural layer.

Dependencies from AGPL product components to Apache platform components are expected.

The reverse dependency should generally not exist for architectural reasons independent of licensing.

docs.title: 23. Third-Party Dependencies Keep Their Own Licenses
docs.text:
Scriberig's license does not replace the licenses of its dependencies.

The project must preserve notices and attribution required by third-party libraries, assets, generated code, fonts, parsers, UI frameworks, and other dependencies.

An Apache-licensed Scriberig package may depend on permissively licensed third-party software under its own terms.

An AGPL Scriberig application may likewise include dependencies under compatible licenses.

Dependency license review should be part of adding a new externally distributed component.

docs.title: 24. Extensions Do Not Become Scriberig Merely by Using the Platform
docs.text:
A third-party extension or application using Apache-licensed platform components is not required to adopt Scriberig's AGPL product license merely because it interoperates with Scriberig.

Examples include:

  • a proprietary application using the knowledge store;
  • a custom editor using the TypeScript client;
  • an internal service using a domain adapter;
  • a proprietary UI built from headless Scriberig editor primitives.

The AGPL applies to the covered AGPL components and modifications or combinations governed by that license, not to every application that uses the permissively licensed platform independently.

The architectural separation should make that distinction practical as well as legal.

Figure 5 captures the practical consequence of the split. An independent application can build on the Apache-2.0 platform under its own license, while the integrated Scriberig server, editor, and agent runtime remain AGPL-3.0. If that integrated product is modified and offered as a hosted service, the covered AGPL modifications remain subject to the obligations of that license; the platform itself does not become AGPL merely because the product depends on it.

Figure 5 — Apache-licensed building blocks can support independent products, while the integrated Scriberig product remains AGPL-covered.

docs.title: 25. Protocol Interoperability Must Not Require the Reference Product
docs.text:
The protocol should be usable by independent implementations.

A third party should be able to build:

  • another client;
  • another UI;
  • another server implementation;
  • a test harness;
  • an automation service;
  • an embedded integration.

without importing the reference product runtime.

Protocol specifications, schemas, and test fixtures should therefore live with the reusable platform rather than only inside AGPL application code.

This is important both for ecosystem health and for keeping the server from becoming the accidental architecture boundary.

docs.title: 26. Conformance Is More Important Than Central Registration
docs.text:
The ecosystem should not initially require every extension to be registered with a central Scriberig service.

An extension should be able to work locally if it satisfies the relevant public interfaces and compatibility contracts.

The project may later provide registries, package indexes, signatures, trust metadata, or curated catalogs, but these should be ecosystem conveniences rather than prerequisites for the extension architecture.

A local or private domain extension must remain possible.

docs.title: 27. Reference Implementations Should Not Become Mandatory Implementations
docs.text:
Scriberig may provide preferred implementations for:

  • storage;
  • Markdown;
  • Rust;
  • web components;
  • reconciliation;
  • rendering;
  • query execution;
  • agent orchestration.

These are reference or production implementations, not definitions of the architecture itself.

Where a public abstraction exists, another implementation should be possible without pretending to be the reference implementation internally.

This rule is particularly important for storage backends, parsers, renderers, clients, and UI systems.

docs.title: 28. Lower-Level Designs May Choose Concrete Packaging
docs.text:
This document defines architectural and licensing responsibilities, not final package names.

Lower-level designs may split or combine implementation packages as experience requires.

For example, a reusable agent layer may later be separated from an integrated runtime, or a domain adapter may be split into parser, renderer, and analysis packages.

Any such packaging should preserve the rules in this document:

  • reusable primitives remain independently usable;
  • lower layers do not depend on the integrated product;
  • extensions use public semantic boundaries;
  • the public protocol remains independent of one server implementation;
  • canonical writes use the shared migration model;
  • licensing follows the reusable-platform versus integrated-product boundary.

docs.title: 29. Contribution Policy Must Preserve the Licensing Model
docs.text:
Contributions should be accepted under terms compatible with the license of the component being modified.

Apache-licensed platform contributions should remain reusable under Apache-2.0.

AGPL product contributions should remain available under AGPL-3.0.

If the project later intends to offer a separate commercial license for AGPL-covered components, contributor terms must be designed deliberately before that becomes a requirement.

The project should not assume it can relicense third-party contributions later without having obtained the necessary rights.

Commercial dual licensing is therefore a possible future product decision, not an implicit property of the initial open-source model.

docs.title: 30. Ecosystem Health Principles
docs.text:
The following principles should guide future extension and packaging decisions.

  1. The universal store must be useful without agents.
  2. Domain adapters must be useful without the integrated product.
  3. The full product must use public platform interfaces.
  4. Extensions must not depend on private database representation.
  5. Canonical writes must use migrations and snapshots.
  6. Unknown domains must remain inspectable through universal graph tools.
  7. Reusable UI behavior must be separable from visual style.
  8. The protocol must support independent clients and implementations.
  9. Public contracts should evolve additively where possible.
  10. Derived extension data must preserve provenance and dependency information.
  11. Capabilities and permissions apply to extensions as well as agents.
  12. Reusable infrastructure should default to Apache-2.0.
  13. The integrated server, editor, and agent runtime should default to AGPL-3.0.
  14. Licensing boundaries should follow architectural package boundaries.
  15. A proprietary application may build on the Apache platform without becoming the Scriberig product.

docs.title: 31. Definition of Success
docs.text:
The extensibility model is successful when the following are simultaneously true.

A developer can use only the storage and graph libraries without installing an agent runtime.

Another developer can add a new semantic domain without changing the universal database architecture.

A third party can build a proprietary application using the reusable Apache-licensed libraries.

A UI developer can use Scriberig behavior with a custom design system instead of the reference MUI components.

An unknown extension can still be explored through generic graph browsing and query tools.

The full Scriberig editor can be built entirely from the same public APIs and libraries available to external developers.

A modified hosted version of the integrated AGPL Scriberig product remains subject to the open-source obligations of that license.

These outcomes are not separate goals.

Together they define the intended ecosystem:

A permissively reusable semantic knowledge platform underneath an integrated open product, with stable public extension points connecting the two.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
The Scriberig terminal user interface is a first-class product surface over the same semantic platform used by the CLI, API server, web editor, third-party clients, and agents.

It is not a second backend, a direct database browser that bypasses application rules, or a terminal-only implementation of semantic behavior.

This document specializes the product-surface principles from design/level-1/011. runtime libraries protocol and product surfaces.md for interactive terminal use. It defines durable interaction and architectural invariants. Concrete Rust modules, terminal libraries, key bindings, layout thresholds, command-line flags, and implementation tasks belong in Level 2 and Level 3.

The controlling rule is:

The TUI makes Scriberig's semantic operations visible, navigable, and composable in a keyboard-first environment without creating a parallel semantic system.

docs.title: 2. Role of the TUI
docs.text:
The TUI is the native interactive workbench for users who want more continuity than one-shot CLI commands but do not need or cannot use the browser editor.

It should support the same broad classes of work as other product surfaces:

  • inspect semantic entities and exact revisions;
  • navigate relations, collections, and snapshots;
  • search and query knowledge;
  • inspect history and semantic diffs;
  • inspect rendered projections and synchronization state;
  • review branches, migrations, conflicts, validation, and trust evidence;
  • navigate sessions and their nested branches;
  • issue agent commands and observe operation progress;
  • discover which operations are available for the current context.

The terminal presentation may be compact and keyboard-oriented, but the meaning of an operation must remain shared with the application layer.

docs.title: 3. TUI Invariants
docs.text: Every lower-level TUI design and implementation must preserve these invariants.

docs.title: 3.1 Shared semantic operations
docs.text: The TUI invokes application operations or a public client that exposes those operations. It must not implement storage queries, migration semantics, projection reconciliation, validation rules, session semantics, or agent mutation semantics itself.

docs.title: 3.2 Explicit semantic context
docs.text: The interface must make important context visible rather than hiding it in process-global state. At minimum, users must be able to determine the active project or database context, branch or snapshot context, current selection, trust or validation state when relevant, and whether an operation is pending.

docs.title: 3.3 Stable semantic handles
docs.text: Navigation is based on stable Scriberig handles and references, not terminal row numbers or backend record identifiers. A row may move after refresh without changing what it means.

docs.title: 3.4 Capability-driven actions
docs.text: The TUI must not advertise mutations or privileged operations merely because a widget knows their names. Available actions are derived from application capability discovery and the current semantic context. A denied or unavailable action must remain denied or unavailable in the TUI.

docs.title: 3.5 No alternate mutation path
docs.text: A TUI edit, branch action, migration application, projection reconciliation, session command, or agent action must pass through the same proposal, validation, conflict, trust, and snapshot-transition machinery used by other surfaces.

docs.title: 3.6 Presentation state is disposable
docs.text: Pane focus, scroll offsets, expanded rows, filters, open overlays, and cached view models are TUI state. Canonical knowledge is not. Losing the terminal process may lose presentation state, but must not silently lose or corrupt committed semantic state.

docs.title: 3.7 Rendering is observational
docs.text: Drawing the screen must not change canonical state, invoke hidden mutations, or perform semantic work whose result changes merely because a frame was rendered.

docs.title: 4. Semantic Navigation Before File Navigation
docs.text:
Scriberig is not fundamentally file-oriented, so the TUI must not reduce the product to a filesystem tree with an inspector attached.

A user should be able to move among semantic objects such as:

project -> collection -> entity -> revision
entity -> relation -> related entity
entity -> history -> earlier revision
snapshot -> diff -> changed entity
session -> branch -> turn -> tool result
projection -> source entity -> synchronization state
operation -> result -> affected semantic object

Filesystem paths remain useful projection metadata and may be exposed when a domain uses them. They are not the universal navigation model.

The primary selection is therefore a semantic reference plus enough snapshot or branch context to interpret it.

docs.title: 5. Progressive Disclosure
docs.text:
The TUI must support progressive disclosure rather than showing every property, relation, provenance record, operation, and diagnostic at once.

The default flow is:

summary -> inspect -> related knowledge -> history/diff -> provenance/trust -> operation

A compact summary should be cheap to render and should advertise useful next operations. Deeper inspection may request additional detail only when the user asks for it.

This principle is shared with agent interaction: both humans and agents should be able to begin with a small semantic handle and deliberately ask for more context.

docs.title: 6. One Selection, Several Views
docs.text:
The TUI may show the same selection through several views without inventing separate identities for each presentation.

For example, one selected entity may drive:

  • a semantic inspector;
  • relation and collection navigation;
  • history;
  • a diff against another revision;
  • a rendered Markdown or source-code projection;
  • provenance and trust evidence;
  • contextual commands.

Changing the active view changes presentation, not the identity of the selected knowledge.

When a view introduces a comparison target, base snapshot, branch, or projection, that extra context must be explicit and visible.

docs.title: 7. Keyboard First, Discoverable, and Composable
docs.text:
The terminal interface is keyboard-first. Every core workflow must be usable without a mouse.

Keyboard-first must not mean mnemonic-only or undiscoverable. The interface must provide:

  • contextual key hints for common actions;
  • a searchable command or action palette;
  • an always-available help surface;
  • visible focus;
  • clear indication when keys are captured by a text input or modal review.

Navigation commands and semantic operations should compose predictably. The same conceptual action should not use unrelated interaction patterns in different views without a strong reason.

Optional mouse support may improve convenience, but it must not be required to reach product functionality.

docs.title: 8. Review Before Canonical Change
docs.text:
Read operations may execute immediately. Canonical changes require explicit intent.

The TUI should make the transition from exploration to mutation visible. When an action can advance canonical state, the user should be able to inspect the proposed change, base context, conflicts, validation result, and important trust evidence before confirmation when those concepts apply.

Confirmation is not permission. Permission and capability checks belong to the application layer and remain authoritative even after a user confirms in the TUI.

A terminal prompt must never be used as a substitute for semantic validation or conflict detection.

docs.title: 9. Sessions and Agents Are Peers of Other Knowledge
docs.text:
Agent interaction is integrated into the TUI but does not own the TUI.

Sessions, branches, turns, tool invocations, results, summaries, and promoted knowledge are semantic objects that can be navigated like other Scriberig knowledge. An agent panel may provide a convenient conversational flow, but durable results still resolve to the same entities, revisions, snapshots, branches, migrations, and operations visible elsewhere.

Transient exploratory branches should remain visibly distinct from canonical project state until promoted through normal change machinery.

docs.title: 10. Live Work Without Hidden State Divergence
docs.text:
The TUI may observe long-running operations, application events, server events, filesystem reconciliation, or agent output.

Live updates are observations, not a second source of truth. When an event says that something changed, the interface resolves authoritative state through normal operations before treating the new state as canonical.

Cached summaries and rows may be invalidated or refreshed incrementally, but stale cache entries must not become silent substitutes for current semantic state.

The interface must distinguish at least:

loading
current
stale or refresh-needed
failed
cancelled

where those states are meaningful.

docs.title: 11. Local and Remote Use Share Interaction Semantics
docs.text:
A TUI may run embedded in the srig process against local application operations or may later use the public client/server boundary.

The interaction model must not depend on privileged local access. If an operation is available only in local mode, that fact must be represented as a capability or product limitation rather than as an invisible bypass.

Local and remote modes may differ in latency, authentication, event delivery, and cancellation mechanics, but an operation such as inspect, history, diff, or apply must preserve the same semantic meaning.

docs.title: 12. Terminal Robustness Is a Product Requirement
docs.text:
A terminal interface temporarily changes terminal state, so failure recovery is part of correctness.

The TUI must be designed so that normal exit, application errors, user cancellation, resize events, and unexpected panics do not intentionally leave the user's terminal in an unusable raw or alternate-screen state.

Rendering must tolerate terminals of different sizes and capabilities. A smaller terminal may collapse panes or reduce decoration, but it should preserve access to the same semantic workflows whenever practical.

Important state must not be communicated only through color. Focus, trust, validation, conflicts, errors, and operation status need textual or symbolic cues that remain understandable with limited color support.

Unicode may improve presentation, but the essential interface must not depend on a specific font or glyph repertoire.

docs.title: 13. Performance and Responsiveness
docs.text:
The terminal event loop must remain responsive while semantic work is in progress.

Potentially expensive queries, rendering, validation, agent work, and remote requests must not be performed inside frame rendering.
