Long-running work should expose progress or an operation identity where the application layer supports it, and users should be able to continue inspecting unrelated state when that is semantically safe.

Large collections should be navigable without materializing or drawing the entire universe at once. Pagination, bounded result sets, and incremental loading should reuse shared query semantics rather than inventing TUI-only truncation rules.

docs.title: 14. Non-Goals
docs.text:
The initial TUI is not required to be:

  • a full terminal IDE;
  • a replacement for the richer web editor;
  • a general-purpose text editor;
  • a direct SQL/database administration console;
  • a second implementation of Markdown, code, PDF, or session domain semantics;
  • a privileged shell around internal Rust objects;
  • dependent on an agent or model provider in order to browse ordinary knowledge.

A later terminal editor may support editing projections or structured semantic forms, but such editing must still produce normal Scriberig changes and preserve the invariants in this document.

docs.title: 15. Lower-Level Design Direction
docs.text:
Level 2 must define the concrete TUI package boundary, terminal runtime, state/effect loop, selection and navigation model, responsive shell, view contracts, command palette, application/client adapters, and conformance strategy.

Level 3 must break that design into implementation slices that can be completed and verified independently.

No Level 2 or Level 3 convenience may override the central rule: the TUI is an interactive semantic client of shared Scriberig capabilities.

docs.title: Model-Driven Agent Execution and Branch Isolation
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines how a model reached through an OpenAI-compatible API participates in Scriberig's agent architecture.

It refines, but does not replace, the principles in:

  1. 009. agent interaction and sessions.md;
  2. 010. universal query and operation model.md;
  3. 011. runtime libraries protocol and product surfaces.md;
  4. 013. trust validation capabilities and provenance.md.

The central rule is:

The model is a replaceable reasoning engine operating inside a Scriberig session branch. Scriberig owns context construction, tools, capabilities, branch topology, canonical state, provenance, validation, and promotion.

The model does not own the project database, session store, tool implementation, branch structure, or product UI. It receives a bounded projection of those things and returns model output or tool requests that Scriberig interprets through trusted runtime boundaries.

This document is intentionally architectural. Concrete Rust modules, request DTOs, HTTP paths, cache records, UI components, and command flags belong in Level 2 and Level 3.

docs.title: 2. Relationship to the Existing Session Model
docs.text:
009. agent interaction and sessions.md already establishes that:

  • sessions are structured knowledge graphs rather than transcript blobs;
  • branches are first-class focused work units;
  • branches may nest;
  • completed branches may collapse to descriptors and results in parent context while remaining fully stored;
  • agent context is a projection rather than canonical state;
  • tool calls and tool results are structured session knowledge;
  • speculative work does not become canonical project state without normal validation and promotion.

This document defines the missing execution rule that makes those ideas operational:

Every integrated model-driven agent execution occurs in an explicit session branch, and every model request is compiled from the exact state visible to that branch.

A model request is therefore not "the session." It is one derived execution input for one step of one branch.

docs.title: 3. Architectural Roles
docs.text: The architecture separates four roles that must not collapse into each other.

docs.title: 3.1 Scriberig knowledge and application layers
docs.text:
These own canonical and derived semantic state, snapshots, migrations, validation, capability checks, operations, and session-domain persistence.

They remain useful without a model provider.

docs.title: 3.2 Agent runtime
docs.text:
The agent runtime coordinates:

  • branch creation and completion;
  • context projection;
  • tool exposure;
  • model requests;
  • tool execution loops;
  • child-branch delegation;
  • model-result caching policy;
  • cancellation and operation lifecycle;
  • conversion of completed work into session objects and result handles.

The runtime is trusted orchestration code, but it still cannot bypass the shared application mutation model.

docs.title: 3.3 Model provider
docs.text:
The provider is an external or local service reached through an OpenAI-compatible model API or another future provider adapter.

The provider receives a serialized model request and may return:

  • assistant text;
  • structured output;
  • tool/function calls;
  • usage metadata;
  • stream fragments;
  • provider diagnostics.

The provider is not authoritative over project state.

docs.title: 3.4 Product surfaces
docs.text:
One-shot CLI, TUI, web application, API clients, and future surfaces start or observe the same agent operations.

They do not assemble provider requests independently and do not implement their own branch semantics.

docs.title: 4. The Model Is Replaceable
docs.text:
Scriberig must not make session identity or project semantics depend on one model vendor.

A configured model provider is execution metadata. Conceptually it includes:

provider profile
base endpoint
model identifier
compatibility capabilities
request options
credential reference

Credentials are runtime secrets and are never session knowledge.

The same session may use different model providers or model identifiers over time. Historical model invocations record sufficient non-secret provenance to identify what was requested and which provider profile/model handled it, but the session graph remains provider-neutral.

A branch result is meaningful because of its semantic outcome and provenance, not because it came from a particular vendor payload format.

docs.title: 5. One Model Step
docs.text:
A model step follows this logical flow:

Branch state
  + current goal/purpose
  + parent branch descriptors/results
  + selected semantic knowledge
  + recent branch activity
  + capability-filtered tool catalog
  + context policy
        |
        v
Compiled model context
        |
        v
Provider adapter
        |
        v
OpenAI-compatible model endpoint
        |
        v
Model output
  text / structured result / tool calls
        |
        v
Agent runtime interpretation

The compiled context must preserve stable handles and enough provenance to reopen omitted detail.

No provider response directly mutates canonical knowledge.

docs.title: 6. Branches Are Execution Isolation Boundaries
docs.text:
A session branch is the primary isolation boundary for agent work.

A branch has, conceptually:

identity
parent branch, if any
purpose
goal or requested task
base semantic scope
base snapshot/workspace when applicable
capability scope
context policy
status
child branches
observable execution events
result references
compact descriptor

The active branch owns the local sequence of model invocations, tool calls, observations, and outputs produced while completing its purpose.

A child branch inherits only explicitly selected context and capabilities from its parent. It does not automatically inherit the complete parent transcript.

A parent consumes a completed child primarily through BranchResult and the child's compact descriptor. Full child history remains available by reference.

docs.title: 7. Not Every Tool Call Requires a Child Branch
docs.text:
Branching is semantic isolation, not a requirement to create a node for every atomic read.

The runtime distinguishes two broad classes of tool execution.

docs.title: Atomic in-branch tool execution
docs.text:
A bounded operation that can be executed and returned without an independent reasoning loop may stay in the current branch. Examples include inspecting one entity, following one relation page, or reading operation status.

The invocation and result are still recorded as structured session objects.

docs.title: Child-branch execution
docs.text:
Work that can require its own model/tool back-and-forth, speculative mutations, retries, validation, conflict handling, or independent delegation should execute in a child branch.

Examples include:

  • editing a function;
  • reconciling a projection;
  • investigating a failing test;
  • comparing alternative implementations;
  • resolving a merge conflict;
  • performing a delegated research task.

The runtime or an explicit tool contract decides whether an operation is atomic or branch-producing.

This prevents branch explosion while preserving the context-isolation property that motivated the session tree.

docs.title: 8. Nested Branch Execution
docs.text:
Branches may recursively create child branches.

Conceptually:

Root branch: implement feature
|
+-- child: inspect architecture
|   +-- atomic semantic reads
|   +-- BranchResult: relevant constraints
|
+-- child: edit module A
|   +-- model/tool loop
|   +-- child: validate candidate
|   |   +-- compiler/tests
|   |   +-- BranchResult: validation evidence
|   +-- BranchResult: candidate migration
|
+-- root continues using compact child results

A branch-depth limit, step budget, wall-clock budget, token budget, or operation policy may bound execution. Such limits are runtime policy, not canonical session semantics.

Nested branches must remain inspectable even when their detailed histories are omitted from the active parent context.

docs.title: 9. Branch Completion and Collapse
docs.text:
A completed branch produces a durable BranchResult or an explicit no-result outcome.

A useful branch result contains, conceptually:

branch identity
status
short outcome summary
result kind
result handles
important touched entities
produced migration/workspace handles, if any
validation handles, if any
unresolved questions, if any

The parent context normally receives this compact result rather than every model/tool exchange from the child.

The parent may later reopen the child branch through a stable handle when the compact result is insufficient.

This is the principal mechanism by which long-running sessions avoid permanent context growth.

docs.title: 10. Model Context Is a Deterministic Projection Input
docs.text:
The context compiler constructs a provider-neutral context plan from exact branch and project state.

Its inputs include, when applicable:

  • agent/profile instructions;
  • current branch purpose and goal;
  • current user instruction;
  • exact parent branch descriptors/results selected for inheritance;
  • recent activity in the current branch;
  • accepted decisions and open tasks relevant to the branch;
  • explicitly selected semantic objects and exact revisions;
  • derived descriptions or summaries with provenance;
  • capability-filtered tool definitions;
  • context budget and policy revision.

The context plan records the exact semantic dependencies used to construct it.

The provider adapter then serializes that plan into the provider's request format.

This separation lets Scriberig change providers without changing the session model and lets context compilation be tested without a network.

docs.title: 11. Progressive Tool Disclosure
docs.text:
A model should not receive every operation in the system by default.

The runtime exposes a compact initial tool set suitable for orientation and capability discovery. Additional operations become available from semantic context, domain capabilities, stable result handles, or explicit branch policy.

Tool definitions therefore form part of model context and must participate in request identity.

A tool result should advertise useful next semantic handles and operations rather than forcing the model to infer hidden endpoint names or database structures.

Provider-native function/tool calling is a serialization mechanism for these trusted Scriberig tool contracts. It is not the source of tool semantics.

docs.title: 12. Tool Execution and Trust Boundary
docs.text:
A model-requested tool call is a proposal to invoke a named capability with structured arguments.

The runtime must:

  1. resolve the advertised tool definition;
  2. validate arguments against the trusted tool schema;
  3. apply the caller/branch capability scope;
  4. execute through application/session operations;
  5. record the invocation and result;
  6. return an appropriately bounded result projection to the model.

The model cannot bypass authorization by inventing a tool name or supplying arbitrary raw transport data.

Canonical mutations follow the same migration, validation, review, conflict, and promotion rules as human-initiated mutations.

docs.title: 13. Observable Reasoning, Not Hidden Chain of Thought
docs.text:
Scriberig does not require hidden model chain-of-thought for correctness, provenance, replay, or audit.

Durable execution records consist of externally meaningful artifacts such as:

  • model invocation metadata;
  • compiled context identity and dependency manifest;
  • assistant output intended for use by the runtime/user;
  • structured tool calls;
  • tool results;
  • branch creation and completion;
  • decisions and observations;
  • migrations and validation evidence;
  • final branch results.

If a provider exposes opaque reasoning tokens or internal traces, they are not required canonical session content.

The system should prefer explicit concise observations or summaries that can be attributed and inspected.

docs.title: 14. Model Invocation Identity and Cacheability
docs.text:
Model invocations are derived computations and should support hash-based identity.

A request fingerprint is derived from all output-relevant, non-secret inputs, including conceptually:

fingerprint schema version
provider compatibility profile
provider/model identifier
output-affecting model parameters
agent/profile revision
context-policy revision
canonical compiled context
exact semantic dependency identities/revisions
tool definition schema hashes
requested structured-output schema, if any

Credentials and secret header values are excluded.

The fingerprint identifies the request Scriberig intended to make, not necessarily the provider's hidden model binary.

Cache policy is explicit. Supported policies may include:

record only
reuse exact successful result
disable cache

A reused model result keeps provenance to the original invocation and records that the new execution reused it.

Providers may be nondeterministic or silently update a model behind the same identifier. Cache metadata must therefore preserve provider/model identity and any provider fingerprint/version information that is available, and reuse must remain policy-controlled rather than pretending the provider is mathematically deterministic.

docs.title: 15. Streaming Is Observation, Not Canonical State
docs.text:
Provider streaming may expose partial text, tool-call fragments, usage updates, or progress.

Streams are useful for TUI, web, logs, and cancellation responsiveness, but partial fragments are not canonical project knowledge.

The runtime may emit transient operation events while assembling a complete model output. Durable session objects are committed at semantic boundaries such as:

  • accepted assistant message/output;
  • complete tool call;
  • complete tool result;
  • branch state transition;
  • branch result;
  • final agent output.

A client that disconnects and reconnects must be able to recover durable state by querying the session/operation rather than depending on replay of every stream fragment.

docs.title: 16. Cancellation and Failure
docs.text:
Agent execution is a long-running application operation.

Cancellation may be requested at any time through the shared operation boundary.

The runtime should propagate cancellation to:

  • an in-flight provider request where transport support permits;
  • pending child branches;
  • cancellable application operations initiated by the branch.

Cancellation does not erase already durable session history.

Failure is also structured. A branch may fail because of:

  • provider transport failure;
  • provider protocol incompatibility;
  • context compilation failure;
  • tool validation failure;
  • permission denial;
  • semantic application failure;
  • validation failure;
  • budget/limit exhaustion;
  • explicit cancellation.

The parent receives a compact failure result and may decide whether to retry, delegate differently, or stop.

docs.title: 17. One Shared Agent Operation across Product Surfaces
docs.text:
TUI, web, one-shot CLI, remote clients, and future product surfaces must use the same semantic agent operation.

Conceptually a start request identifies:

prompt/instruction
session selector or create-new intent
parent branch or create-root intent
semantic selection/scope
agent profile
context policy
authorized capabilities
runtime limits/retention policy

Starting work returns immediately with stable handles such as:

OperationId
SessionRef
RootBranchRef

The operation can then be observed through status/events and the session graph.

A product surface may choose to wait synchronously for the final result, but this is presentation behavior over the same long-running operation.

docs.title: 18. One-Shot CLI Semantics
docs.text:
The native one-shot surface is a non-interactive presentation of the same branch-aware runtime.

A one-shot invocation:

  1. composes the local application and configured model provider;
  2. creates or selects a session;
  3. creates a root execution branch;
  4. starts the shared agent operation;
  5. waits for terminal completion while optionally rendering bounded progress;
  6. prints the final agent output or structured failure;
  7. leaves the session/branch/result inspectable according to retention policy.

One-shot mode does not implement a simplified direct-to-provider shortcut for normal agent work.

If a provider-diagnostic command exists, it is a separate diagnostic concern and must not be confused with the integrated one-shot agent semantics.

The existing srig run <PROMPT> command is the intended one-shot product surface. If srig agent <PROMPT> remains for compatibility or advanced profile selection, both commands must converge on the same integrated runtime rather than maintain two independent agent loops.

docs.title: 19. TUI Semantics
docs.text:
The TUI is an interactive observer/controller of shared agent operations.

It must be able to:

  • start agent work against the current semantic selection/session/branch;
  • show root and nested branch topology;
  • show compact branch descriptors and results;
  • expand a branch to inspect turns, tool calls, results, and provenance;
  • display streaming/progress as transient operation state;
  • navigate away while execution continues;
  • cancel when authorized;
  • activate result handles through normal semantic navigation;
  • review/promote candidate changes through shared mutation workflows.

The TUI never stores provider credentials, builds provider requests, or owns branch completion logic.

docs.title: 20. Web Application Semantics
docs.text:
The browser application uses the public Scriberig protocol/client/model packages and does not contact the model provider directly.

The integrated web agent experience must be able to:

  • start or continue agent work;
  • bind work to the universal semantic selection;
  • observe operation progress;
  • render the session/branch tree;
  • collapse completed child branches to compact result cards;
  • expand any retained branch on demand;
  • navigate result handles into raw/semantic/projection/history views;
  • show candidate changes and validation through existing review surfaces;
  • reconnect and rehydrate durable session state after stream interruption.

Reusable branch/session interaction belongs in public web packages, not only in the reference application.

docs.title: 21. Remote and Embedded Execution
docs.text: The same agent semantics support both local and server-hosted composition.

docs.title: Embedded/local
docs.text: A native one-shot command or local TUI may invoke the application/agent runtime in-process.

docs.title: Remote/server
docs.text:
The web application, remote TUI, or third-party client invokes the public Scriberig server protocol. The server hosts or delegates to the agent runtime and model provider.

The remote client must not need provider credentials or provider-specific request logic.

Embedded and remote results should be semantically equivalent for the same configured runtime and base state, subject to ordinary model nondeterminism/cache policy.

docs.title: 22. Retention and Reachability
docs.text:
Agent execution can generate large amounts of transient session knowledge.

Retention policy may distinguish:

  • active root sessions;
  • completed root branches;
  • child branches referenced by retained BranchResult objects;
  • audit-required model/tool records;
  • abandoned/retry branches;
  • raw provider payload artifacts;
  • stream fragments.

A compact parent result may keep a child branch reachable even when the parent does not include its full contents in context.

Raw provider payload retention should be optional and sanitized because such payloads can contain duplicated context or external data. Canonical session semantics must never require raw provider JSON to remain forever.

docs.title: 23. Cross-Surface Invariants
docs.text:
The following must hold for one-shot, TUI, web, embedded use, and remote use.

  1. The same semantic request starts agent work.
  2. The same branch/session objects represent execution.
  3. The same capability checks gate tools.
  4. The same operation lifecycle represents progress and cancellation.
  5. The same branch results are queryable after completion.
  6. The same canonical mutation path handles proposed changes.
  7. Provider details stay below the agent-runtime boundary.
  8. Product surfaces may differ in presentation, waiting behavior, and navigation, not semantic ownership.

docs.title: 24. Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
Implementations must preserve these invariants.

  1. Every integrated model-driven execution belongs to an explicit session branch.
  2. The model is replaceable execution infrastructure, not canonical authority.
  3. The session schema remains provider-neutral.
  4. Model context is a derived projection with exact semantic dependencies.
  5. Child branches inherit selected context, not an implicit complete parent transcript.
  6. Completed child branches may collapse to descriptors/results in parent context without losing stored history.
  7. Nested branches are allowed and use the same model recursively.
  8. Atomic tools may stay in-branch; complex/delegated work may create child branches.
  9. Tool requests are validated and capability-checked by trusted runtime code.
  10. The model cannot directly mutate canonical state.
  11. Model invocations support hash-based request identity over non-secret output-relevant inputs.
  12. Cache reuse is explicit and provenance-preserving.
  13. Streaming fragments are observations, not canonical project mutations.
  14. Cancellation and failure preserve already durable provenance.
  15. One-shot, TUI, web, and remote clients converge on the same agent operation and session model.
  16. The browser and TUI never require direct model-provider credentials.
  17. No correctness property depends on storing hidden chain-of-thought.
  18. Durable branch results remain reopenable through stable handles.

docs.title: 25. Non-Goals
docs.text:
This design does not require:

  • one permanent model vendor;
  • OpenAI-specific session schemas;
  • exposing all tools in every request;
  • creating a child branch for every atomic tool call;
  • storing hidden reasoning traces;
  • deterministic provider behavior;
  • storing every stream fragment forever;
  • direct provider access from browser or TUI code;
  • bypassing normal migration/review because the model requested a mutation;
  • flattening nested branches into the parent transcript;
  • making one-shot mode a separate semantic agent implementation.

docs.title: 26. Definition of Model-Driven Agent Execution
docs.text:
A Scriberig model-driven agent execution is a long-running, branch-scoped application operation that compiles a bounded semantic context, invokes a replaceable model provider, validates and executes model-requested tools through trusted capabilities, recursively delegates complex work into child branches when useful, and returns compact branch results while retaining full provenance by reference.

The same execution model powers interactive and non-interactive product surfaces. The TUI and web app expose the tree; one-shot mode waits for the root branch to finish. In all cases, Scriberig—not the model—owns the branch graph, tools, canonical state, validation, and durable meaning of the result.

docs.title: Recursive Agent Decomposition and Context Isolation
1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig sessions are trees because agent work is recursively decomposed into focused units whose internal reasoning/tool activity should not automatically pollute the context of parents, siblings, later workers, or the long-running coordinator.

This document makes that principle explicit and easy to reference. It refines, but does not replace:

  1. 009. agent interaction and sessions.md;
  2. 014. agent native semantic self hosting.md;
  3. 015. terminal user interface principles.md;
  4. 016. model driven agent execution and branch isolation.md;
  5. 018. durable plans dependency scheduling and multi-model execution.md;
  6. 019. semantic agent operations and projection-first editing.md;
  7. design/level-2/023. agent runtime model provider and branch orchestration.md.

The controlling rule is:

A branch is a context-isolation boundary for one focused goal. It may perform arbitrary model/semantic-operation/tool back-and-forth and may recursively create children. Its parent normally receives only a compact result, exact semantic handles, validation/candidate references, and the small amount of information needed to continue.

A branch is not primarily a visual indentation feature and it is not primarily a user-created chat fork. User continuations, agent delegation, planned work, retries, focused semantic edits, research, validation, conflict resolution, and alternative attempts all use the same branch model.

docs.title: 2. Why the Session Is a Tree
docs.text:
A linear transcript forces every later model step to inherit noise from all earlier work. That is acceptable for short chats but scales poorly for implementation work.

Consider a root goal:

Implement feature X

A semantic agent may decompose it into work such as:

Root: Implement feature X
|
+-- Understand architecture
|
+-- Implement parser capability
|   |
|   +-- Decide semantic structure
|   +-- Create/update module/function entities
|   +-- Repair semantic/API incompatibilities
|   +-- Validate candidate projection
|
+-- Add tests against the completed semantic result
|
+-- Integrate sibling candidates
|
+-- Validate feature

The parser branch may require many model invocations, semantic reads, semantic edits, child branches, compiler diagnostics, corrections, and local validation. The later test-writing task does not need that conversational history. It needs the completed semantic result, exact handles/revisions, candidate/workspace state, public behavior, relevant decisions, and validation evidence.

The root also does not need the full implementation dialogue. It needs a compact result equivalent to:

Parser capability implemented.
Touched semantic entities: Module M, Function F1, Function F2.
Candidate: C18.
Validation: passed.
Relevant source projection: src/php/parser.rs.

The tree exists so detailed work can remain durable and inspectable without becoming permanent context for unrelated later work.

docs.title: 3. Branches May Be Created by Humans, Agents, Plans, or Runtime Policy
docs.text:
Do not treat human-created forks as a special branch architecture.

A branch may begin because:

  • the user chooses to continue from an earlier replyable session location;
  • the current agent delegates a focused subtask;
  • /plan materializes or starts a planned node;
  • a branch-producing semantic tool contract starts isolated work;
  • the runtime isolates a speculative mutation or retry;
  • validation failure triggers a repair branch;
  • the agent compares alternatives in sibling branches;
  • two different model profiles are asked to attempt the same goal independently;
  • conflict resolution requires focused work;
  • a child agent recursively decomposes its own task.

The same canonical branch semantics apply in every case.

Origin, assignment, model/provider, plan membership, and coordinator/worker role are useful provenance. They must not create incompatible kinds of session trees.

docs.title: 4. Recursive Decomposition Is Expected Behavior
docs.text:
A model-driven agent is expected to decompose work when doing so improves context quality, isolation, validation, recoverability, scheduling, parallelism, or semantic scope.

A child branch may create another child branch using the same rules. There is no architectural distinction between the first delegation level and deeper delegation levels.

Conceptually:

Root task
|
+-- Child A
|   |
|   +-- Grandchild A1
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Great-grandchild A1a
|   |
|   +-- Grandchild A2
|
+-- Child B

Runtime budgets may limit depth, child count, token use, cost, operation count, or elapsed time. Those limits are execution policy. They do not change the semantic fact that branches may nest recursively.

docs.title: 5. Atomic Operations and Branch-Producing Work Are Different
docs.text:
Do not create a branch for every small operation.

An atomic operation can remain inside the current branch when it does not need an independent reasoning loop. Examples include:

inspect one semantic entity
list one bounded child collection
follow one relation page
query one bounded semantic fact
render one selected source/document fragment
read one operation status
apply one small capability-scoped semantic operation whose result is immediately known

Create or delegate to a child branch when the work can require its own model/operation loop, speculative state, retries, validation, reconciliation, merge, or further decomposition. Examples include:

implement one semantic module/capability
edit one complex function
investigate a failing validation
reconcile an ambiguous projection
research one architectural question
compare alternative implementations
resolve a semantic merge conflict
validate and repair a candidate

This distinction prevents branch explosion while preserving context isolation where it matters.

docs.title: 6. Semantic Operations Are the Normal Work Primitive
docs.text:
For understood domains, branch activity should primarily use semantic knowledge and domain operations rather than generic raw file manipulation.

A branch working on source code may operate on:

Module
Type
Function
Parameter
CodeGroup
Statement
Expression
Comment

A branch working on Markdown may operate on:

Document
Section
Paragraph
List
Table
TableRow
TableCell

Typical operations are semantic/capability driven:

inspect
list
follow
find
query
render
code.add_function
code.insert_statement
code.replace_expression
document.insert_paragraph
validate

Source files and documents are projections of canonical semantic state. Raw write and shell capabilities remain fallback/bootstrap/interoperability/validation mechanisms as defined by 019. semantic agent operations and projection-first editing.md.

Do not describe branch isolation as though its ordinary purpose were to hide a sequence of write_file and bash calls. Its ordinary purpose is to hide local semantic implementation detail while returning exact semantic results.

docs.title: 7. Child Context Is Selected, Not Copied
docs.text:
Creating a child branch does not copy the complete parent transcript.

The child receives an explicit inheritance plan containing only the information required for its goal. Depending on the task, that may include:

child purpose and expected result
parent branch descriptor
selected parent result handles
fulfilled plan dependency results
accepted decisions or constraints
semantic selection and exact snapshot/workspace
specific entity/revision handles
candidate/workspace handles
capability subset
agent/model profile and branch policy
explicit delegation instruction
small bounded parent excerpt when policy deliberately allows it

Unrelated parent activity is omitted.

This is important in both directions:

  • the child does not automatically inherit all parent history;
  • the parent does not automatically inherit all child history.

Context construction is a projection over session knowledge, plan/dependency results, and project semantic knowledge—not transcript concatenation.

docs.title: 8. Branch Completion Produces a Compact Contract
docs.text:
A completed branch produces a durable BranchResult or an explicit no-result/failure outcome.

A useful result contains concepts equivalent to:

branch identity
status
short outcome summary
result kind
important semantic handles and exact revisions
produced candidate/migration/workspace handles
important touched entities
projection/materialization references when relevant
validation handles
unresolved questions
failure summary when unsuccessful

The result is the normal information boundary between parent and child and the normal fulfillment artifact for plan dependencies.

The full child history remains stored and inspectable by stable reference. It can be reopened if the result is insufficient, but it is not implicitly inserted into the parent's next model request.

docs.title: 9. Parent Context Uses Results, Not Child Transcripts
docs.text:
After a child finishes, the parent normally continues with context equivalent to:

current parent goal
recent parent-local activity
child descriptor
child BranchResult
relevant semantic project/candidate state
selected completed child/dependency results

It does not normally receive:

every child model response
every child tool/semantic-operation invocation
every failed semantic edit attempt
every compiler diagnostic already resolved
every correction step
every grandchild transcript
raw provider streams

The omitted history remains available for audit and inspection.

This is the principal mechanism that prevents a long implementation session from degrading into an ever-growing prompt.

docs.title: 10. Sibling Branches Communicate through Results and Semantic State
docs.text:
Sibling tasks should not depend on one another's internal conversational history.

For example:

Root: implement feature
|
+-- Child A: implement parser capability
|     -> BranchResult: semantic handles + candidate + validation
|
+-- Child B: write parser tests

Child B may receive the result of Child A, exact created/updated semantic state, relevant dependency handles, and design constraints. It does not need the back-and-forth that Child A used to arrive there.

If Child B discovers a defect, it may create/request another focused repair branch. That repair branch returns a new result rather than causing all previous implementation history to be copied into Child B's permanent context.

docs.title: 11. User Continuations Use the Same Tree
docs.text:
A user may navigate to a historical replyable node and continue from that semantic location.

That continuation is another branch operation over the same session graph. It is not a separate chat-fork mechanism.

The context compiler resolves the exact continuation location and constructs context from the branch path, semantic state, decisions, and results relevant to that point. Later sibling work is not silently injected merely because it occurred later in wall-clock time.

The default user behavior may continue from the current root/coordinator position so ordinary use feels fluid, but the canonical session remains tree-shaped.

docs.title: 12. Plans Reuse the Branch Tree but Add Dependency Edges
docs.text:
/plan creates durable planned work that is shown in the same tree used by executed branches.

Structural parent/child relations still mean context ownership and decomposition.

Plan dependencies are separate edges that mean execution ordering/readiness.

Conceptually:

Root
  Parser
  Importer
  Integration

Dependencies:
  Integration depends_on Parser
  Integration depends_on Importer

Do not fake dependencies by nesting siblings under one another.

A planned node can be visible before its branch executes. When execution begins, it becomes or binds to the branch that owns the work.

The complete scheduling model is defined by 018. durable plans dependency scheduling and multi-model execution.md.

docs.title: 13. Multiple Models Share the Same Tree
docs.text:
Different branches may be assigned to different model/provider profiles.

For example:

Discover architecture   -> local model
Implement parser        -> OpenAI/Codex profile
Research edge cases     -> OpenRouter profile
Documentation           -> local inexpensive profile

This does not create separate sessions.

One plan has at most one auto-advancing coordinator, but many workers may execute ready branches concurrently.

One branch normally has one active executing owner. If two models should independently attempt the same goal, create sibling attempt branches and compare their results explicitly.

docs.title: 14. Plan Dependencies Carry Compact Results, Not Transcripts
docs.text:
A dependent node should become ready because required result contracts were fulfilled, not because predecessor output happened earlier in a transcript.

For example:

ParserImplementationResult
  Function parse_type @ R22
  Function parse_union_type @ R1
  Candidate C18
  Validation V7

may satisfy the dependency of a test branch.

That test branch does not inherit the parser worker's model/tool history.

This makes dependency edges useful context declarations as well as scheduling constraints.

docs.title: 15. Branch Tree, Plan Dependency Graph, Knowledge Graph, and Activity Causality Are Distinct
docs.text: Four different structures coexist:

docs.title: Session branch tree
docs.text:
root task
  child task
    grandchild task

docs.title: Plan dependency graph
docs.text:
A ----\
       -> C
B ----/

docs.title: Semantic knowledge graph
docs.text: Project -> Module -> Function -> Statement -> Expression

docs.title: Local execution/activity causality
docs.text:
model invocation
  semantic operation/tool invocation
    operation/tool result
  model invocation
  branch result

Do not collapse these into one canonical relation.

A UI may combine them into one visual tree, but it must preserve the underlying meanings.

docs.title: 16. The Default TUI Is a Tree-Aware Conversation Projection
docs.text:
The default TUI should feel like a conventional coding-agent conversation while faithfully representing recursive agent decomposition, planned work, dependencies, assignments, and user continuations.

Normal root interaction may look nearly linear when no branching is visible.

When the agent or plan creates focused children, the TUI inserts them structurally at the location where they belong rather than appending them only by timestamp.

A compact completed child may render like:

▏ Implement parser capability
▏ ✓ parser entities created and validated

An active/expanded child may reveal its internal activity:

▏ Implement parser capability
▏
▏ ▏ inspect Function parse_type
▏ ▏ ✓ 4 code groups
▏
▏ ▏ replace expression in nullable-suffix group
▏ ▏ ✓ Expression E17 -> Revision R9
▏
▏ ▏ Validate parser candidate
▏ ▏ ▏ cargo test -p scriberig-domain-php ...
▏ ▏ ▏ ✓ 12 tests passed
▏
▏ ✓ parser capability implemented

The external cargo test is displayed as a shell-like process because it actually is one. Semantic edits are displayed as semantic operations.

The fact that the UI can expand the child does not mean the parent model received the expanded history.

docs.title: 17. Depth Rails Encode Structural Nesting
docs.text:
Terminal presentation should encode branch/activity nesting with visible vertical rails.

Conceptually:

▏ depth 1
▏ ▏ depth 2
▏ ▏ ▏ depth 3

Each depth uses a stable theme color from a finite palette. The palette may cycle at deep levels.

Color is supplemental. Nesting must remain understandable through rail count/position when color is unavailable.

For narrow terminals, older ancestor rails may be compacted with an explicit marker such as:

… ▏ ▏ deeply nested activity

Do not persist depth color or indentation as semantic state. Derive them from branch/activity ancestry.

docs.title: 18. Completed Children Are Compact by Default, Expandable on Demand
docs.text:
The ordinary conversation projection should prefer attention-efficient presentation.

Recommended behavior:

  • planned node: compact state/assignment/dependency indicator;
  • active branch: show enough live activity to understand progress;
  • completed child branch: collapse to descriptor + result by default;
  • failed child branch: show compact failure result and status;
  • selected/expanded child: render retained detail on demand;
  • parent branch: continue after the compact child result without reproducing child history.

Expansion is presentation state only.

Collapsing or expanding a branch must not change model context, branch semantics, durable plan state, or result dependencies.

docs.title: 19. Per-Activity Presentation Is Independent from Context
docs.text:
Each visible activity/message kind may have its own client presentation policy.

Examples include:

semantic/tool invocation:
  hidden
  compact/truncated
  full one-line/wrapped
  structured parameters one per line

tool/operation result:
  hidden
  summary
  preview
  full bounded detail

reasoning summary:
  hidden
  shown

model request/prompt:
  hidden
  summary
  structured full

branch:
  compact result
  expanded activity

plan node:
  compact
  dependencies/assignment detail

A compact semantic invocation may look like:

▏ add function parse_union_type to php::parser

A structured version may look like:

▏ code.add_function
▏   module: php::parser
▏   after: parse_named_type
▏   name: parse_union_type

An actual process invocation may use shell-command formatting.

These settings affect rendering only. They must not change captured activity, ancestry, continuation identity, context compilation, tool execution, provider execution, or scheduling.

docs.title: 20. Navigation Cursor, Reply Anchor, and Coordinator Cursor Are Distinct
docs.text:
A user-facing row number, terminal cursor position, scroll offset, indentation level, or current rendering mode is never a continuation identity.

The TUI needs three distinct concepts:

navigation cursor
  where the user is browsing

reply anchor
  where the next human message will attach

coordinator cursor
  where the single auto-advancing plan coordinator is currently operating/evaluating

Normally the reply anchor may auto-follow the coordinator cursor while the user is idle.

When the user deliberately selects a historical/sibling node or starts typing against it, the reply anchor becomes pinned. Coordinator progress must not move it underneath an in-progress draft.

All anchors resolve to stable session/plan identities, never terminal row numbers.

docs.title: 21. The Reply Anchor Is Visually Distinct
docs.text:
The current reply anchor should use a background highlight or equivalent strong focus treatment.

Depth rail color must not double as reply-anchor state.

The background answers:

Where will my next message attach?

The rails answer:

What structural ancestry does this content have?

The composer may show a compact Replying to ... label when the anchor is not the ordinary current/coordinator head.

Important state must not depend on color alone.

docs.title: 22. New Activity Is Placed Structurally, Not Appended by Time
docs.text:
The UI must not treat the conversation as an append-only list.

When a planned branch, autonomous child, historical user continuation, worker result, or nested repair branch produces new activity, the view recomputes a deterministic tree projection and places that activity beneath its semantic parent.

Creation time and event sequence remain useful for ordering siblings/activity where the session model defines them, but wall-clock append position is not the canonical layout rule.

This applies equally to:

  • user-created continuations;
  • agent-created children;
  • planned nodes and their later execution;
  • recursively delegated grandchildren;
  • repair branches;
  • validation branches;
  • alternative model attempts;
  • concurrent worker results.

docs.title: 23. Auto-Follow Is Presentation State
docs.text:
When a long-running plan is active, the TUI may automatically keep the viewport near the coordinator cursor.

Recommended behavior:

user idle -> follow coordinator
user scrolls/selects -> pause follow
user explicitly resumes follow -> follow coordinator again

This is presentation state only. It has no effect on scheduling or context.

docs.title: 24. Guiding Example
docs.text:
A synchronized mental model is:

Root: Add PHP ingestion
|
+-- Discover architecture                     [local-fast]
|   +-- inspect code-domain conventions
|   +-- inspect project import registry
|   `-- Result: required semantic extension points
|
+-- Implement PHP adapter                     [OpenAI profile]
|   |
|   +-- Add PHP syntax/domain entities
|   |   +-- create/update semantic schema nodes
|   |   +-- create parser functions/code groups
|   |   `-- Result: parser semantic candidate
|   |
|   +-- Register adapter
|   |   `-- Result: source-domain registry candidate
|   |
|   +-- Validate parser
|   |   +-- materialize candidate projection
|   |   +-- external compiler/test validation
|   |   `-- Result: validation evidence
|   |
|   `-- Result: validated adapter candidate
|
+-- Research PHP edge cases                   [OpenRouter profile]
|   `-- Result: accepted edge-case constraints
|
+-- Add tests                                 [local/other profile]
|   depends_on: adapter result, research result
|   `-- Result: semantic test entities + validation
|
+-- Integration
|   depends_on: adapter, tests
|   `-- Result: merged candidate
|
`-- Root result: PHP ingestion candidate ready for review

The root model does not need every operation under every descendant.

The test branch receives exact adapter/research results, not their transcripts.

The complete histories remain durable and inspectable for provenance, debugging, audit, and later reopening.

docs.title: 25. Product-Surface Invariant
docs.text:
CLI, TUI, web, server clients, and future agents must agree on the same branch topology, plan-node identities, dependency results, semantic handles, compact-result semantics, and execution assignments.

The TUI may offer the richest immediate visualization, but it does not own recursive decomposition, plan scheduling, semantic editing, or model assignment.

The session domain stores the tree; the plan subsystem records intended work/dependencies; the runtime orchestrates branch execution; the semantic application/domain layers own reads and mutations; the context compiler selects what each branch sees; product surfaces render and navigate the resulting shared semantics.

docs.title: 26. Non-Negotiable Summary
docs.text:
Future design and implementation work must preserve these rules:

  1. A session is a graph/tree, not a transcript log.
  2. Branches are context-isolation boundaries for focused work.
  3. Agents are expected to create branches recursively when useful.
  4. Users, plans, agents, and runtime policy use the same branch model.
  5. Atomic semantic operations may remain inside a branch; independent reasoning loops belong in child branches.
  6. Known source/document work is semantic-first; raw file/shell primitives are fallback/runtime mechanisms.
  7. A child receives selected parent/dependency context, not the complete parent transcript.
  8. A parent normally receives BranchResult, not the complete child transcript.
  9. Siblings communicate through semantic state/results, not inherited conversational noise.
  10. Plan dependencies are separate from branch parentage and are satisfied by durable results.
  11. Many model profiles may execute different branches; one plan has one auto-advancing coordinator.
  12. Full child history remains durable and inspectable by reference.
  13. Context compilation is independent from UI expansion and verbosity.
  14. The default TUI renders the same recursive/planned tree, with completed children compact by default and expandable on demand.
  15. New activity is inserted at its structural location, not blindly appended by wall-clock time.
  16. Vertical depth rails are derived presentation of ancestry, not canonical data.
  17. Navigation cursor, reply anchor, and coordinator cursor are distinct stable concepts.
  18. The current reply anchor uses a strong visual highlight separate from rail colors.
  19. Per-activity detail modes are presentation only and include semantic-operation-specific forms.
  20. No product surface may rebuild these semantics independently.

docs.title: Durable Plans, Dependency Scheduling, and Multi-Model Execution
1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig must support long-running agent work that is planned, inspectable, interruptible, revisable, and executable by more than one model without collapsing into one ever-growing transcript.

This document refines the session and agent architecture defined by:

  1. 009. agent interaction and sessions.md;
  2. 016. model driven agent execution and branch isolation.md;
  3. 017. recursive agent decomposition and context isolation.md;
  4. design/level-2/023. agent runtime model provider and branch orchestration.md.

The controlling rule is:

A plan is durable semantic knowledge that describes intended branch work and explicit dependencies. The plan is rendered through the same session tree as executed work, while scheduling remains a separate graph over that tree.

The session branch tree remains the canonical structure for context ownership and recursive decomposition. A plan does not replace it with a generic DAG. Instead, plan nodes bind intended work to branch identities or future branch identities, and explicit dependency edges determine when those nodes are eligible to run.

docs.title: 2. Why Plans Are First-Class
docs.text:
A prose checklist in one model response is insufficient for long-running work because it has no durable identity, cannot be safely revised, cannot be assigned to another executor, cannot express scheduling dependencies precisely, and cannot survive product restart without reparsing text.

Scriberig therefore treats a plan as structured session knowledge.

A plan must be able to answer:

  • what is the overall goal;
  • which focused tasks exist;
  • how those tasks are nested;
  • which tasks are blocked by which other tasks;
  • which tasks are ready, running, completed, failed, skipped, or cancelled;
  • which model/profile/provider is assigned to a task;
  • which branch and semantic scope execute a task;
  • which result fulfills a dependency;
  • which revision of the plan is current;
  • who or what changed the plan;
  • which single coordinator is allowed to auto-advance the plan.

The full plan remains inspectable after execution completes.

docs.title: 3. /plan Creates Structured Planned Work
docs.text:
The TUI command:

/plan <goal>

is a local product command that starts or requests plan construction through shared application semantics. It is not sent to the model as ordinary conversation text.

A generated plan is represented conceptually as:

Plan
  identity
  session
  anchor
  goal
  revision
  status
  coordinator assignment
  root plan nodes

and:

PlanNode
  identity
  plan
  parent plan node, if any
  branch or future branch identity
  purpose
  expected result shape
  semantic scope
  dependencies
  assignment
  scheduling state
  branch policy
  capability scope

Exact storage types belong in lower-level design. The architectural requirement is stable identity and structured relations rather than text parsing.

docs.title: 4. The Plan Reuses the Session Tree
docs.text:
Planned work should be visible in the same tree that later contains execution.

A node may begin as:

○ Implement PHP parser

then become:

◉ Implement PHP parser

and finally:

✓ Implement PHP parser
  PHP parser domain entities created and validated

The logical node should retain stable identity through these states.

The execution branch associated with the plan node is the context-isolation boundary. Planning metadata does not replace branch semantics.

A plan may reserve future branch identities before execution begins, or bind a plan node to a branch when the node is claimed. The lower-level design may choose either strategy as long as stable plan-node identity is preserved and product surfaces can correlate planning with execution.

docs.title: 5. Tree Structure and Dependency Structure Are Different
docs.text: Two different relations coexist.

docs.title: 5.1 Structural parent/child relation
docs.text:
This means:

  • context ownership;
  • decomposition;
  • result collapse;
  • provenance;
  • visible nesting.

Example:

Implement feature
  Implement parser
    Validate parser

docs.title: 5.2 Dependency relation
docs.text:
This means:

this node is not eligible to execute until another node has produced the required terminal result.

Example:

Parser --------\
                -> Integration
Importer ------/

Parser and Importer may both be structural children of the same parent while Integration depends on both.

Do not encode dependency by inventing fake parentage. Do not infer dependency only from display order.

The structural branch relation is tree-like. Dependency edges form an acyclic graph over plan nodes.

docs.title: 6. Dependency Satisfaction Is Result-Based
docs.text:
A dependency is not fulfilled merely because another process stopped running.

The prerequisite node must reach a dependency-satisfying terminal state and publish the result required by its contract.

Normally this is a durable BranchResult or another explicit result handle.

Conceptually:

PlanNode parser
  expected result:
    ParserImplementationResult

BranchResult BR42
  fulfills: ParserImplementationResult
  status: completed
  semantic handles: ...
  candidate/workspace: ...
  validation evidence: ...

A dependent node receives the compact result and selected semantic state, not the prerequisite branch transcript.

A failed, cancelled, or budget-exhausted prerequisite does not satisfy a success dependency unless the dependency explicitly accepts that result class.

Initial implementation should support strict successful dependencies before introducing optional or soft dependencies.

docs.title: 7. Dependency Graph Rules
docs.text:
The plan subsystem must enforce at least these invariants:

  1. dependency edges refer to stable plan-node identities;
  2. dependency cycles are rejected;
  3. a node cannot become Ready while a required dependency is incomplete;
  4. a node cannot be claimed by two executors simultaneously;
  5. completion is recorded before dependents become ready;
  6. dependency-result handles are exact and revision/snapshot aware;
  7. removing or replacing a dependency creates a new plan revision rather than rewriting historical meaning;
  8. dependency order is not inferred from wall-clock creation order;
  9. sibling nodes may run concurrently when their dependencies and workspaces permit it.

A simple readiness rule is:

Ready(node) =
  node is planned
  AND every required dependency has an accepted terminal result
  AND node is not claimed or terminal
  AND branch/capability/runtime policy permits execution

docs.title: 8. One Auto-Advancing Coordinator
docs.text:
A plan has at most one auto-advancing coordinator at a time.

The coordinator is responsible for plan-level orchestration such as:

  • inspecting plan state;
  • selecting ready unassigned work;
  • dispatching work according to policy;
  • consuming compact child results;
  • reacting to failures;
  • adding further decomposition when necessary;
  • updating dependencies;
  • revising the plan;
  • deciding when the plan is complete.

The coordinator is not the only model allowed to execute work. It is the single owner of automatic plan advancement.

This prevents several concurrent models from racing to reorganize the same global plan.

Coordinator ownership must be represented as a claim/lease or equivalent application-level concurrency contract rather than process-local UI state.

docs.title: 9. Workers Execute Focused Branches
docs.text:
A worker is assigned one branch or one ready plan node at a time.

A worker receives a bounded execution contract equivalent to:

plan node identity
branch identity
purpose
expected result
selected dependency results
selected ancestor results
semantic scope
exact base snapshot/workspace
capability subset
agent/model profile
thinking level
context policy
branch policy
runtime budgets

A worker does not automatically gain authority over unrelated siblings or the whole plan.

A worker may recursively decompose its own branch when branch policy allows it. Such descendants remain under the worker's branch and return compact results according to ordinary branch-isolation rules.

docs.title: 10. Multiple Models May Work on One Plan Concurrently
docs.text:
Scriberig intentionally supports different executors on different branches of the same session tree.

For example:

Discover architecture
  model/profile: local-fast

Implement parser
  model/profile: openai-codex-high

Research language edge cases
  model/profile: openrouter-research

Documentation cleanup
  model/profile: local-cheap

These assignments are ordinary execution metadata and provenance, not different session architectures.

Each branch resolves and snapshots its effective execution configuration when execution begins.

Changing the assignment of a node that has not started affects that future execution. Changing defaults does not mutate an already-running model invocation.

docs.title: 11. Per-Branch Execution Configuration
docs.text:
Model selection must remain hierarchical and explicit.

Resolution should follow an order equivalent to:

explicit invocation override
  > plan-node assignment
  > branch override
  > session selection
  > project/user default
  > runtime fallback

A plan-node or branch assignment may select a reusable profile containing concepts such as:

provider profile
model profile
credential reference
thinking level
context policy
branching policy
capability scope
runtime budgets
default generation parameters

Secrets remain opaque credential references. They are never stored in session history, plan records, prompts, or protocol traces.

The existing model-library and thinking-level architecture remains the source of model capability truth. Do not create a second planner-only model registry.

docs.title: 12. One Executing Owner per Branch
docs.text:
Multiple models may execute different branches concurrently, but one branch should normally have at most one active executing owner.

Use an application/runtime claim equivalent to:

BranchExecutionLease
  branch
  executor identity
  operation
  observed revision
  lease/heartbeat metadata when remote execution requires it

If two models should independently attempt the same goal, create sibling attempt branches:

Implement parser
  Attempt A — model X
  Attempt B — model Y
  Compare/select — depends on A and B

Do not allow two providers to race mutations inside one branch merely because parallel execution is available.

docs.title: 13. Concurrent Project Work Remains Isolated
docs.text:
Two completed worker branches may produce two independent candidate workspaces derived from the same base snapshot.

Dependency completion makes both results available. It does not silently merge them.

A later integration node must explicitly combine them using the normal semantic merge/change machinery.

For example:

Parser branch -> Candidate PA
Importer branch -> Candidate PB

Integration branch
  depends on Parser, Importer
  merges PA + PB against common base
  resolves semantic conflicts if any
  produces Candidate PC

This preserves exact history and prevents dependency scheduling from becoming a hidden canonical mutation path.

docs.title: 14. Plan Revisions Are Durable
docs.text:
Long-running plans evolve.

A failure may reveal missing work. A user may reorder priorities. New semantic facts may require additional branches. A dependency may become unnecessary.

Changes to plan structure create a new durable plan revision or equivalent immutable historical state.

For example:

Plan revision 1
  Parser -> Tests

Parser discovers unsupported type representation

Plan revision 2
  Investigate representation
    -> Extend type model
    -> Parser
    -> Tests

The normal UI shows the current plan. History/debug views can inspect earlier revisions and provenance.

Do not overwrite a completed historical plan shape as though it never existed.

docs.title: 15. Replanning Is an Explicit Coordinator Operation
docs.text:
Replanning may be triggered by:

  • user request;
  • failed branch result;
  • blocked dependency;
  • conflict;
  • budget exhaustion;
  • newly discovered semantic requirement;
  • coordinator policy.

The coordinator may propose a revised plan through shared application semantics.

Plan revision must validate:

  • parent/child structure;
  • dependency acyclicity;
  • references to existing completed work;
  • assignments and capability compatibility;
  • preservation of terminal historical nodes;
  • consistency of any migrated or superseded node relationships.

Replanning is not hidden chain-of-thought. The durable plan is the externally meaningful planning artifact.

docs.title: 16. /plan Lifecycle
docs.text:
Product surfaces should expose semantics equivalent to:

/plan <goal>      create/propose a structured plan at the current anchor
/plan start       begin coordinator auto-advancement
/plan pause       stop new automatic dispatch while preserving running work policy
/plan resume      resume automatic dispatch
/plan replan      request a revised plan from current state
/plan stop        request cancellation/terminal stop according to policy
/plan show        return to/focus the plan tree

Exact command spelling is a product-surface detail, but the underlying operations must be shared.

Recommended initial behavior is that /plan <goal> creates a reviewable plan before execution. A separate explicit start action begins long-running autonomous work.

An optional later shortcut such as /plan --run <goal> may combine those actions when policy permits it.

docs.title: 17. Coordinator Cursor and User Reply Anchor Are Distinct
docs.text:
A running plan has a coordinator position indicating the node the auto-advancing coordinator is currently working from or evaluating.

The user interface also has a reply anchor indicating where the next human message will attach.

These concepts normally coincide while the user is simply watching, but they must not be the same state.

Rules:

  1. while the user is idle and following the plan, the reply anchor may auto-follow the coordinator cursor;
  2. if the user deliberately selects a historical or sibling node, the reply anchor becomes pinned there;
  3. coordinator progress must not move the user's anchor out from under a partially written message;
  4. the user can explicitly resume following the coordinator;
  5. both positions resolve to stable session/plan identities, never terminal row numbers.

This distinction becomes necessary as soon as more than one worker can run concurrently.

docs.title: 18. TUI Rendering
docs.text:
The default TUI conversation/tree projection should render planned and executed work together.

A compact example:

You
Implement PHP ingestion.

/ Plan: PHP ingestion
▏ ✓ Discover architecture                      local-fast
▏ ◉ Implement parser                           openai-codex
▏ ○ Implement importer                         openrouter-claude
▏   waits: parser
▏ ◉ Research PHP edge cases                    local-research
▏ ○ Integration                                openai-codex
    waits: parser, importer, research

Expanded execution may show nested semantic operations and child branches beneath a running node.

Planned/blocked/running/completed state must have textual or symbolic cues in addition to color.

Dependency information should be compact by default and inspectable in more detail on demand.

docs.title: 19. Auto-Follow Is Presentation State
docs.text:
While a plan runs, the TUI may follow coordinator progress automatically.

Recommended behavior:

user idle -> viewport follows coordinator
user scrolls/selects -> follow pauses
explicit follow action -> resume coordinator follow

Viewport following is disposable presentation state. It does not affect scheduling, branch context, or plan state.

docs.title: 20. Human Intervention Uses the Same Tree
docs.text:
The user may:

  • select a planned node and change its assignment before it runs;
  • add a message at a historical or current branch anchor;
  • request replanning;
  • pause automatic dispatch;
  • cancel a branch when authorized;
  • create an explicit alternative branch;
  • inspect or expand any retained child branch;
  • assign a specific model/profile to a ready node;
  • leave some nodes unassigned for coordinator policy to select.

Human intervention does not require a parallel session model.

docs.title: 21. Context Compilation for Planned Work
docs.text:
A worker context is compiled from exact semantic dependencies, not from everything visible in the TUI.

Conceptually:

Worker context =
    branch purpose and expected result
  + selected ancestor descriptors/results
  + fulfilled dependency results
  + exact semantic selection and project state
  + current branch local history
  + accepted decisions/open tasks selected by policy
  + capability-filtered tool catalog
  + model/profile instructions

It normally excludes:

sibling transcripts
resolved implementation chatter from dependencies
unrelated plan history
collapsed or expanded UI state
other models' raw provider streams

Dependency result handles therefore become first-class context inputs.

docs.title: 22. Streaming and Durable Scheduling State
docs.text:
Streaming model/tool activity is transient observation. Scheduling state changes are durable semantic/application state at meaningful boundaries.

Examples of durable events/records include:

plan created
plan revision accepted
node became ready
node claimed
branch execution started
branch result committed
node completed/failed/cancelled
coordinator changed
assignment changed

A reconnecting TUI or web client must be able to rebuild plan state from durable records plus current live events. It must not require replaying provider token streams.

docs.title: 23. Failure Behavior
docs.text:
A failed worker does not automatically destroy the whole plan.

The plan/coordinator policy decides whether to:

  • retry the same branch;
  • create a repair child;
  • create an alternative sibling attempt;
  • replan;
  • mark dependents blocked;
  • skip optional future work;
  • stop the plan.

Failure results remain compact durable BranchResult/node results with inspectable provenance.

The coordinator must not silently treat failure as successful dependency satisfaction.

docs.title: 24. Cancellation and Pause
docs.text:
Pause and cancellation are distinct.

pause means the coordinator stops dispatching new automatic work according to policy. Existing workers may continue or may be paused only if the runtime supports safe suspension.

cancel targets a specific operation/branch/plan and follows ordinary application cancellation semantics.

Stopping a plan does not erase completed branch history or accepted candidate state.

docs.title: 25. Cross-Surface Invariant
docs.text:
The durable plan, dependency edges, assignments, branch claims, results, and coordinator state are shared application semantics.

TUI, web, CLI, server, and third-party clients must observe the same plan topology and execution status.

The TUI may provide /plan and /assign shortcuts, but it must not become the owner of planning/scheduling state.

docs.title: 26. Non-Negotiable Summary
docs.text:
Future designs and implementations must preserve these rules:

  1. /plan produces structured durable planned work, not only prose.
  2. Planned work is visible in the same session tree as executed work.
  3. Branch parentage expresses context/decomposition; dependency edges express scheduling and form a DAG.
  4. Dependencies are satisfied by explicit durable results, normally BranchResult, not by transcript completion.
  5. One plan has at most one auto-advancing coordinator at a time.
  6. Many worker models may execute different branches concurrently.
  7. One branch normally has one active executing owner; parallel attempts use sibling branches.
  8. Each branch may have its own provider/model/profile/thinking/context/capability configuration.
  9. Secrets remain opaque credential references.
  10. Plan revisions are durable and historical; replanning does not rewrite the past.
  11. Concurrent candidate states are not silently merged merely because dependencies completed.
  12. Worker context contains selected dependency results and semantic state, not sibling transcripts.
  13. Coordinator cursor and user reply anchor are distinct even when they usually auto-follow together.
  14. Scheduling and auto-follow are shared/application and presentation concerns respectively; neither may redefine branch semantics.
  15. All product surfaces consume the same durable plan and execution model.

docs.title: Semantic Agent Operations and Projection-First Editing
1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig agents must operate primarily on structured semantic knowledge rather than treating the repository as a bag of opaque text files manipulated through generic shell and file-writing tools.

This document connects the universal knowledge model, domain adapters, migrations, projections, agent execution, and recursive branch architecture into one explicit rule for agent behavior.

It refines and ties together:

  1. 002. universal knowledge model.md;
  2. 005. changes migrations branches and merge.md;
  3. 006. projections and bidirectional editing.md;
  4. 007. domain modeling and adapters.md;
  5. 010. universal query and operation model.md;
  6. 014. agent native semantic self hosting.md;
  7. 016. model driven agent execution and branch isolation.md;
  8. 017. recursive agent decomposition and context isolation.md;
  9. 018. durable plans dependency scheduling and multi-model execution.md.

The controlling rule is:

Once Scriberig understands a domain, the agent edits semantic entities, relations, collections, and revisions through domain/application operations. Source files and documents are projections of that semantic state. Generic raw file and shell operations are fallback, bootstrap, interoperability, or validation mechanisms—not the ordinary canonical editing interface.

docs.title: 2. The Repository Is Not the Canonical Model
docs.text:
A source path remains useful projection metadata and external interoperability state, but it is not the primary identity of known source knowledge.

For understood source code, Scriberig should be able to represent structure such as:

Project
  Module
    Type
    Function
      Parameter
      CodeGroup
        Statement
          Expression
    Comment

For Markdown:

MarkdownDocument
  Section
    Heading
    Paragraph
    List
      ListItem
    Table
      TableRow
        TableCell

The exact domain schemas vary, but the agent should operate on stable semantic handles whenever those handles exist.

A path, line number, byte span, rendered source fragment, or terminal row is an anchor into a projection. It is not a substitute for semantic identity.

docs.title: 3. Source Files Are Projections
docs.text:
For understood source domains, the conceptual flow is:

canonical semantic state
        |
        v
source projection adapter
        |
        v
.rs / .ts / .php / .md / other file

A canonical agent edit goes in the opposite conceptual direction only through the semantic change model:

semantic operation
    -> candidate semantic state
    -> migration/change proposal
    -> validation
    -> accepted snapshot/workspace
    -> deterministic projection/materialization

A model should not normally construct the entire final file text and call a generic write_file tool when a structure-preserving domain operation exists.

docs.title: 4. Semantic Reads Come Before Raw Reads
docs.text:
For known knowledge, agents should orient themselves using universal semantic operations such as:

inspect
list
follow
find
query
history
diff
render

Examples:

inspect(Function parse_type)
list(Function parse_type, code_groups)
follow(Function parse_type, calls)
query(functions that implement DomainAdapter)
render(Function parse_type, source)

render is available when exact presentation/syntax is needed. It should not be the first and only way to understand the object.

Raw file reads may remain available for opaque or unsupported resources, bootstrap situations, external evidence, or exact projection inspection, but they are a lower-confidence/lower-semantics path.

docs.title: 5. Semantic Writes Are Domain Operations
docs.text:
The universal change model provides primitives equivalent to:

create entity
replace entity revision
add relation
remove relation
insert collection member
remove collection member
move collection member
replace collection structure

Domain adapters expose higher-level operations that preserve domain meaning.

Source-code examples may include:

code.add_function
code.remove_function
code.rename_symbol
code.add_parameter
code.remove_parameter
code.insert_statement
code.replace_statement
code.replace_expression
code.add_comment
code.extract_function
code.move_declaration

Markdown examples may include:

document.add_section
document.insert_paragraph
document.replace_paragraph
document.move_block
document.insert_table_row
document.update_table_cell

The exact capability catalog is domain-specific and discoverable. The architectural requirement is that rich semantic operations extend the universal change model rather than bypass it.

docs.title: 6. Tool Discovery Is Selection- and Capability-Driven
docs.text:
The model should not receive one giant static catalog of filesystem and shell commands.

The runtime builds a capability-filtered tool catalog from the current semantic scope.

For a selected function, a compact tool catalog may advertise:

inspect
list body/code_groups/parameters
follow calls/references
render source
code.insert_statement
code.replace_expression
code.add_comment
history
diff
validate

For a Markdown section, it may advertise:

inspect
list subsections/blocks
render markdown
document.insert_paragraph
document.add_subsection
document.move_block

For an opaque artifact, the catalog may degrade to projection/raw capabilities.

Capability discovery should make this degradation explicit instead of pretending every artifact has rich semantics.

docs.title: 7. Raw File Operations Are a Fallback, Not the Default
docs.text:
Generic file operations remain useful when:

  • the project has not yet been onboarded;
  • a file type has no semantic adapter;
  • exact external bytes are evidence that must be preserved;
  • an interoperability flow explicitly edits a projection;
  • a generated/opaque artifact must be handled as opaque data;
  • a domain adapter is being bootstrapped for a previously unsupported format;
  • recovery or diagnostics require direct projection inspection.

When semantic capabilities exist, the runtime should prefer them and may avoid advertising unrestricted raw write operations to the model entirely.

If a raw projection edit is permitted, it must reconcile back through the projection adapter and normal semantic migration path before becoming canonical.

docs.title: 8. Shell Execution Is Also a Narrow Capability
docs.text:
Scriberig does not need to ban process execution, but it should not make unrestricted shell access the normal model-facing editing mechanism.

A model should prefer application capabilities such as:

validate(candidate, profile)
dependency.add(...)
project.scan(...)
project.import(...)
projection.render(...)

The implementation behind those capabilities may run external processes such as compilers, linters, test runners, formatters, or package managers in controlled workspaces.

For example:

validate(candidate C, rust-focused)

may internally:

materialize candidate projection
run cargo check
run focused tests
collect diagnostics
map diagnostics back to semantic handles

The model receives a structured ValidationResult, not merely a terminal transcript.

Direct shell execution, when exposed, should be capability-scoped, auditable, bounded, and treated as external-effect/runtime functionality.

docs.title: 9. Diagnostics Should Resolve Back to Semantic Knowledge
docs.text:
Compiler, parser, linter, test, or external-tool diagnostics may initially arrive in projection coordinates such as path/line/column.

Adapters should resolve those coordinates back to semantic entities where possible.

A useful diagnostic result is conceptually:

ValidationDiagnostic D42
  projection: src/php/parser.rs
  anchor: line/column range
  semantic target: Function parse_type / Expression E17
  severity: error
  message: ...
  producer: rustc / parser / test runner / ...

The agent can then inspect or edit the semantic target instead of repeatedly manipulating raw source ranges.

docs.title: 10. “Create a File” Means Create Semantic Knowledge Plus a Projection
docs.text:
When a task conceptually creates a new source file, the semantic interpretation should be something like:

create Module M
insert Module M into project/module structure
create Function F1
create Function F2
create Type T1
insert declarations into Module M
associate/update source projection specification
render/materialize projection at path P

The path remains important for source layout and interoperability, but the knowledge being authored is the module and its contents.

For Markdown:

create MarkdownDocument D
create Section S
create Paragraph P1/P2
attach semantic projection location docs/foo.md

This rule prevents file paths from becoming accidental canonical identities.

docs.title: 11. Semantic Identity Makes Planning More Stable
docs.text:
Plan nodes should prefer semantic goals and scopes over textual file-edit instructions.

Prefer:

Extend PHP union-type parsing
  scope: Function parse_type

rather than:

Edit src/php/parser.rs

Prefer:

Register PHP source adapter
  scope: SourceDomainRegistry

rather than:

Modify registry.rs

Projection paths may be shown as helpful metadata, but plan identity should survive moves, rerendering, style changes, or source-layout refactors when the semantic object remains the same.

docs.title: 12. Semantic Results Improve Branch Isolation
docs.text:
