A child branch that implements a source capability should return semantic results rather than a prose statement that a file changed.

Conceptually:

BranchResult
  status: completed
  summary: PHP union parsing implemented
  touched:
    Function parse_type @ new revision
    Function parse_union_type @ revision
  candidate: Candidate C18
  validation: Validation V7
  projections:
    src/php/parser.rs will change

A sibling test branch receives these exact handles and the resulting candidate/project state.

It does not need the implementation child's raw write history or source-edit chatter.

This aligns recursive branch isolation with the universal knowledge model.

docs.title: 13. Semantic Results Improve Dependency Scheduling
docs.text:
Plan dependencies should express required semantic outcomes where practical.

For example:

PlanNode Add tests
  depends_on: ParserImplementationResult

not merely:

wait until parser agent stops

The parser result may guarantee:

Function parse_type updated
Function parse_union_type created
candidate C18 available
source projection renderable
validation profile parser-structure passed

The dependency edge then carries useful, deterministic context for the dependent worker.

docs.title: 14. Semantic Change Enables Better Concurrency
docs.text:
Two workers may change different semantic entities even when those entities render into the same file.

Example:

Worker A changes CodeGroup validation in Function parse_type
Worker B changes Function extract_attributes

A textual patch system sees two edits to parser.rs.

Scriberig can recognize distinct semantic targets and attempt a semantic merge against a common base.

Likewise, a true conflict can be identified precisely when both workers modify the same entity/relation/collection member.

This is one of the major benefits of using semantic operations in a multi-model plan.

docs.title: 15. Candidate Workspaces Remain the Mutation Boundary
docs.text:
Semantic edits still do not mutate canonical current state directly.

An agent operation normally produces isolated candidate/workspace state derived from an exact base.

Conceptually:

base snapshot S1
  -> semantic operations
  -> candidate snapshot/workspace S2
  -> validation
  -> review/acceptance
  -> promotion/materialization

Multiple workers may produce sibling candidates from the same base.

Dependency completion does not auto-promote or auto-merge those candidates.

docs.title: 16. Projection Materialization Happens After Semantic Change
docs.text:
The normal editing path should not require touching live files during each semantic operation.

The runtime may maintain an isolated candidate representation and render/materialize files when needed for:

  • validation;
  • external compiler/tool execution;
  • human review;
  • final accepted filesystem synchronization.

This reduces accidental divergence between semantic candidate state and live working-tree bytes.

The exact materialization policy may vary by domain and product composition.

docs.title: 17. External File Editing Remains Supported
docs.text:
Scriberig must continue to interoperate with ordinary editors and external tools.

When an externally editable projection changes:

last synchronized projection
  -> external edit
  -> parse
  -> candidate semantic representation
  -> reconcile identities
  -> migration proposal
  -> validate/commit

This is the reverse path for interoperability. It is not evidence that the internal agent should prefer raw file editing when richer semantic operations are already available.

docs.title: 18. Unknown and Opaque Artifacts
docs.text:
Not every resource will immediately have a rich adapter.

Scriberig should represent degraded capability honestly.

Concepts may include:

OpaqueArtifact
TextArtifact
ExternalArtifact
ProjectionOnlyResource

A consumer may see capabilities such as:

inspect metadata
render/read projection
replace opaque content candidate
validate external effect

rather than AST-/document-level editing.

The architecture should permit later adapter installation to make the same project progressively more semantic.

docs.title: 19. Tool Presentation Should Reflect Semantic Operations
docs.text:
The TUI should not visually pretend every tool invocation is a shell command.

Compact semantic operation:

▏ add function parse_union_type to php::parser
▏ ✓ Function F194 created

Detailed structured presentation:

▏ code.add_function
▏   module: php::parser
▏   after: parse_named_type
▏   name: parse_union_type
▏   return_type: TypeResult
▏ ✓ Function F194 @ Revision R1

An actual external process may render as a shell-like command:

▏ cargo test -p scriberig-domain-php ...
▏ ✓ 12 tests passed

Per-activity presentation modes control how much detail is visible. They never alter the underlying semantic operation or model context.

docs.title: 20. Recursive Branch Example Rewritten Semantically
docs.text:
Avoid thinking of a child branch as:

write foo.rs

Prefer:

child: implement FooParser module

Inside that child:

inspect neighboring parser modules
inspect required adapter interfaces
create Module FooParser
create Type Parser
create Function parse
insert CodeGroups
insert Statements
replace Expressions
add Comments
validate candidate

A nested validation child may materialize the candidate and invoke external compiler/test infrastructure.

The parent receives:

BranchResult
  FooParser implemented
  Module/Type/Function handles
  Candidate C
  Validation passed

The parent does not inherit internal semantic-edit chatter unless explicitly reopened.

docs.title: 21. Context Compilation Uses Semantic Handles
docs.text:
The context compiler should prefer compact semantic objects, descriptions, exact revisions, selected relations, accepted decisions, branch results, and dependency results.

It should not routinely fill model context with complete source files when a smaller semantic projection is sufficient.

For example, a worker modifying one function might initially receive:

Function parse_type
  purpose: parses PHP type expressions
  parameters: cursor, source
  code groups: prefix, named type, nullable suffix, result construction
  calls: parse_identifier, parse_generic_arguments
  diagnostics: none

Then the model can inspect or render only the relevant group/expression when exact syntax is required.

This applies the same progressive-disclosure principle to project knowledge that branch isolation applies to session history.

docs.title: 22. The Four Relevant Structures Must Stay Distinct
docs.text: Scriberig combines several graphs/trees without collapsing them.

docs.title: Knowledge graph
docs.text: Project -> Module -> Function -> Statement -> Expression

docs.title: Session/branch tree
docs.text: Goal -> child branch -> grandchild branch -> BranchResult

docs.title: Plan dependency graph
docs.text:
PlanNode A ----\
                -> PlanNode C
PlanNode B ----/

docs.title: Execution causality
docs.text:
ModelInvocation -> SemanticOperation -> OperationResult

Product surfaces may project these structures together, but canonical relations remain distinct.

A branch may target a semantic entity. A plan node may execute as a branch. A dependency may link plan nodes. An activity may invoke a semantic operation that changes a candidate revision.

docs.title: 23. Product-Surface Invariant
docs.text:
CLI, TUI, web, server, and third-party clients should expose the same semantic capabilities and resulting handles.

The TUI may provide convenient tree navigation and detailed tool rendering, but it must not own semantic-edit logic.

A web editor may provide direct manipulation of semantic nodes, but it must produce the same application/change operations.

The agent runtime consumes shared capabilities rather than inventing an agent-only patch or file-mutation path.

docs.title: 24. Non-Negotiable Summary
docs.text:
Future implementation work must preserve these rules:

  1. Known source/document files are projections of structured semantic state.
  2. Agents should address semantic entities rather than paths/lines whenever a richer object exists.
  3. Semantic/domain operations are the ordinary editing interface.
  4. Generic raw writes are fallback/bootstrap/interoperability capabilities, not the normal canonical edit path.
  5. Shell/process execution is primarily an implementation detail of bounded capabilities such as validation, not the universal model-facing interface.
  6. Diagnostics should resolve back to semantic handles whenever possible.
  7. Creating a source file normally means creating semantic module/document structure plus a projection mapping.
  8. Plan nodes should prefer semantic goals/scopes over path-based edit instructions.
  9. Branch results and dependencies should expose exact semantic handles/candidates/validation evidence.
  10. Multiple model workers produce isolated semantic candidates that merge through the normal semantic change system.
  11. Projection materialization does not become a hidden canonical write path.
  12. External projection editing remains supported through parse/reconcile/migration.
  13. Unknown formats degrade explicitly to opaque/projection capabilities.
  14. TUI tool presentation should distinguish semantic operations from actual shell/process execution.
  15. Knowledge graph, branch tree, dependency DAG, and execution causality remain separate structures even when one UI combines them.

docs.title: Provider Continuation State and Observable Model Execution
1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig owns canonical session identity, branch topology, context isolation, semantic state, plans, dependencies, model assignments, migrations, and durable history.

Model providers may additionally offer their own server-side continuation mechanisms. Examples include durable conversation objects, previous-response chains, cached reasoning state, or local-runtime session handles.

Scriberig should use those mechanisms when they improve continuity, latency, or provider reasoning quality, but it must never confuse provider state with Scriberig state.

The controlling rules are:

Provider continuation is branch-local execution state. It is an optimization and continuity mechanism attached to a Scriberig branch, never the canonical identity of the session or branch.

and:

The user may independently inspect the complete safe effective request Scriberig provided to a model and the provider-visible reasoning content produced around tool/semantic operations, without rerunning the model and without exposing hidden chain-of-thought.

This document refines and connects:

  1. 009. agent interaction and sessions.md;
  2. 016. model driven agent execution and branch isolation.md;
  3. 017. recursive agent decomposition and context isolation.md;
  4. 018. durable plans dependency scheduling and multi-model execution.md;
  5. 019. semantic agent operations and projection-first editing.md;
  6. design/level-2/023. agent runtime model provider and branch orchestration.md;
  7. task 133 shared model/thinking/trace controls;
  8. task 134 recursive TUI projection;
  9. task 135 recursive semantic agent implementation.

docs.title: 2. Scriberig Identity Is Canonical
docs.text:
The canonical identities remain Scriberig-owned concepts such as:

SessionId
BranchId
ContinuationAnchor
PlanId
PlanNodeId
OperationId
ModelInvocationId
BranchResultId
SnapshotId
EntityId

A provider conversation identifier such as an OpenAI conversation ID is not interchangeable with any of these.

Provider identity cannot be canonical because:

  • one Scriberig session may use several providers;
  • sibling branches may use different providers simultaneously;
  • one branch may switch providers over time;
  • a local model may expose no remote session identifier;
  • provider state may expire, be deleted, become unavailable, or be administratively inaccessible;
  • Scriberig must reconstruct context after restart independently of one provider;
  • plans, dependencies, migrations, semantic handles, and branch results are not provider-owned state.

The loss of provider continuation state may reduce efficiency or continuity quality, but it must not make a Scriberig session unrecoverable.

docs.title: 3. Provider Continuation Is Branch-Local
docs.text:
Provider continuation state belongs to one isolated execution lineage.

The normal mapping is conceptually:

Scriberig Session
|
+-- Root Branch
|     provider continuation A
|
+-- Child Branch: implement parser
|     provider continuation B
|     |
|     +-- Grandchild: validate parser
|           provider continuation C
|
+-- Child Branch: research edge cases
      provider continuation D or none

Do not normally attach one provider conversation to the whole Scriberig session tree.

Doing so would reintroduce exactly the context pollution that recursive branch isolation is intended to prevent: detailed work from one child would become implicit provider context for unrelated siblings and their parent.

A new child branch therefore normally receives a newly established provider continuation seeded from the child's compiled Scriberig context rather than inheriting the parent provider conversation wholesale.

docs.title: 4. Provider-Neutral Continuation State
docs.text:
Scriberig should represent provider continuation through a provider-neutral contract conceptually equivalent to:

ProviderContinuationState
  provider profile
  provider kind
  opaque continuation handle
  branch
  context fingerprint
  state revision/version when available
  created-at provenance
  last-used invocation
  validity/status
  provider-specific non-secret metadata

The exact provider handle remains opaque outside the provider/runtime boundary.

Examples may include:

OpenAI Conversation ID
OpenAI previous response ID
OpenRouter/provider-specific continuation token
local model runtime session ID
none

Credentials, authorization headers, secret connection values, and provider-private hidden reasoning must never be stored in this state.

docs.title: 5. Context Fingerprint Guards Reuse
docs.text:
A provider continuation may only be reused when it still represents the exact Scriberig context lineage expected by the branch.

Scriberig therefore binds continuation state to a context fingerprint or equivalent immutable context identity.

Conceptually:

compiled branch context C1
    -> fingerprint H1
    -> provider continuation P1

Before reusing P1, the runtime compares the expected continuation context against H1 or a derived successor relationship.

If branch history changes outside that provider continuation, for example:

OpenAI invocation
local-model invocation
user historical continuation
manual semantic change
branch rebase
accepted dependency result changes

then blindly resuming the old provider continuation may produce incorrect context.

The runtime must detect the divergence and either:

  • seed a new provider continuation from the current canonical Scriberig context;
  • use an explicit provider fork when semantically equivalent and supported;
  • fall back to stateless request construction.

Provider continuation is therefore a cache-like stateful acceleration layer, not an authority.

docs.title: 6. New Child Branches Start from Selected Context
docs.text:
When Scriberig creates an isolated child branch, it first compiles child context using normal context-isolation rules:

child purpose
expected result
selected ancestor BranchResults
fulfilled dependency results
accepted decisions and constraints
semantic scope and exact snapshot/workspace
relevant semantic handles
bounded explicit parent excerpts when policy allows
capability/tool catalog
resolved execution assignment

Only after this context exists does the provider adapter establish provider continuation state.

The direction of authority is:

Scriberig branch/context compiler
        |
        v
canonical effective request/context
        |
        v
provider continuation initialization

Never reverse that relationship by asking the provider conversation to define the branch's canonical context.

docs.title: 7. Same-Branch Continuation May Reuse Provider State
docs.text:
Within one branch, later invocations may reuse compatible provider continuation state instead of retransmitting every previous provider-visible item.

This is especially useful for providers that preserve tool/reasoning state internally.

The runtime still records each Scriberig ModelInvocation separately with:

  • exact branch identity;
  • model/provider/profile/thinking configuration;
  • canonical effective request identity;
  • continuation state used;
  • provider request/response IDs when safe;
  • observable activity sequence;
  • result/output identity.

Provider continuation does not collapse several model invocations into one Scriberig historical object.

docs.title: 8. OpenAI Continuation Strategy
docs.text: As of October 2026, OpenAI's Responses ecosystem exposes two relevant continuation mechanisms.

docs.title: 8.1 Conversations API
docs.text:
A Conversation is a durable server-side object with its own identifier and persistent items. It can be reused across sessions, devices, or jobs.

For Scriberig, a Conversation is well suited to long-lived continuation within one isolated branch.

Recommended default mapping when supported:

one isolated Scriberig branch execution lineage
    -> one OpenAI Conversation

A child branch normally receives another Conversation initialized from the child's selected Scriberig context.

docs.title: 8.2 previous_response_id
docs.text:
Responses may also continue or fork from a previous response ID.

This is useful for shorter response chains or provider-side forks where Scriberig can prove that the response lineage corresponds exactly to the intended branch/continuation context.

The runtime must remember that provider top-level instructions are not implicitly carried forward by previous_response_id; Scriberig still owns and supplies the effective instruction/context contract required for each invocation.

docs.title: 8.3 Do not mix mechanisms accidentally
docs.text:
OpenAI currently does not allow conversation and previous_response_id on the same response request.

The OpenAI adapter therefore chooses one continuation strategy deliberately for a given invocation and records that choice in safe provenance.

docs.title: 8.4 OpenAI retention is not Scriberig durability
docs.text:
OpenAI Conversation items may be persisted beyond the ordinary stored-response lifetime. Scriberig must still retain enough canonical state to reconstruct the branch without depending on that provider retention policy.

Provider retention policy is external behavior, not a Scriberig persistence guarantee.

docs.title: 9. Multi-Provider and Provider-Switching Branches
docs.text:
A session tree may contain concurrent branches such as:

Architecture       -> local model
Parser             -> OpenAI
Research           -> OpenRouter model
Integration        -> OpenAI with another profile
Documentation      -> local model

Each branch resolves its own provider continuation independently.

If a branch switches providers, the new provider receives a newly compiled canonical Scriberig context unless an explicitly supported cross-provider representation can prove equivalence.

A provider continuation from provider A is never passed as opaque state to provider B.

The canonical bridge between providers is Scriberig state:

semantic state
branch-local history
BranchResults
dependency results
accepted decisions
canonical effective request projection

docs.title: 10. Complete Effective Model Request Is Observable
docs.text:
The user may choose to inspect the complete safe effective request that Scriberig supplied to a model invocation.

This requirement is stronger than retaining a bounded activity summary and stronger than displaying the literal HTTP request body.

The canonical observable request is the provider-neutral Scriberig request immediately before provider-specific serialization.

Conceptually:

CanonicalModelRequest
  invocation identity
  branch/continuation anchor
  instructions
  ordered conversation/context sections
  selected ancestor results
  dependency results
  semantic/context projections
  tool/semantic capability definitions
  structured-output schema when present
  resolved model/provider/profile
  thinking level
  safe generation configuration
  continuation-state reference and strategy
  optional token/cost estimates

The exact structure may use typed sections/messages rather than these literal fields.

Secrets and sensitive values are redacted before this representation reaches public/session/protocol layers.

docs.title: 11. Full Prompt Means Effective Context, Not Wire JSON
docs.text:
When provider continuation is used, the literal network request may contain only new input plus a provider continuation ID.

That does not mean the model effectively saw only the new input.

Therefore PromptPresentation::Full means:

Show the complete safe effective Scriberig model request/context for this invocation, including the prior context represented by provider continuation state.

It does not mean:

Dump the raw outbound provider HTTP payload.

A debug/audit artifact may optionally expose sanitized provider-wire information separately, but it is not the canonical prompt view.

This distinction is required for:

  • auditing;
  • provider portability;
  • deterministic context tests;
  • debugging context isolation;
  • reconstructing history after provider state disappears;
  • comparing two providers on equivalent input.

docs.title: 12. Prompt Capture and Prompt Presentation Are Separate
docs.text:
The runtime should capture or durably reference the complete safe canonical request once per invocation.

Clients then choose independently how to render it.

Recommended presentation modes are conceptually:

PromptPresentation
  Hidden
  Summary
  Full

Summary may show counts, major context sections, model identity, and token estimate.

Full resolves the complete safe canonical request without rerunning the model.

Changing prompt presentation never:

  • changes model execution;
  • changes context compilation;
  • creates a model invocation;
  • changes provider continuation;
  • mutates semantic session history.

docs.title: 13. Provider-Visible Reasoning Is Ordered Activity
docs.text:
Some models/providers expose user-visible reasoning summaries or reasoning content. Other models keep reasoning hidden.

Scriberig may capture only reasoning content that the provider explicitly exposes for user/application consumption.

Reasoning must be represented as ordered activity because it may appear:

before a tool call
between tool calls
after a tool result
before final output
interleaved repeatedly throughout one invocation

For example:

ModelInvocation
  ReasoningSegment 1
  SemanticOperation A
    OperationResult A
  ReasoningSegment 2
  ToolInvocation B
    ToolResult B
  ReasoningSegment 3
  AssistantOutput

Do not collapse all reasoning into one branch-level blob when the provider exposes meaningful ordered segments.

docs.title: 14. Hidden Chain-of-Thought Is Never Requested or Exposed
docs.text:
Show thinking must not be interpreted as a request to obtain private hidden chain-of-thought.

Allowed observable reasoning includes:

  • Scriberig runtime phases/status;
  • provider-provided reasoning summaries intended for display;
  • provider-provided reasoning content explicitly surfaced through the API as user/application-visible output;
  • structured plan/status information generated as normal visible output.

Disallowed behavior includes:

  • requesting hidden chain-of-thought merely so it can be shown;
  • inferring private reasoning from provider internals;
  • persisting encrypted/private reasoning blobs as user-readable trace;
  • claiming hidden reasoning is available when the provider exposes only a summary.

A provider may internally preserve hidden reasoning across continuation calls. That internal state is provider execution state, not Scriberig-visible reasoning.

docs.title: 15. Reasoning Capture and Presentation Are Independent
docs.text:
When provider-visible reasoning exists, Scriberig preserves its ordering and stable invocation association independently from whether the current client shows it.

Recommended presentation modes are conceptually:

ReasoningPresentation
  Hidden
  Summary
  FullAvailable

FullAvailable means the complete reasoning content that the provider explicitly made available for display. It does not imply hidden chain-of-thought exists or can be retrieved.

A provider that exposes only summaries may map both Summary and FullAvailable to the best safe available representation while declaring the limitation explicitly.

Changing reasoning presentation does not rerun work.

docs.title: 16. Prompt and Reasoning Controls Are Independent
docs.text:
Prompt visibility and reasoning visibility are orthogonal.

These are all valid client configurations:

prompt: Full
reasoning: Hidden
operations: Compact
results: Summary

prompt: Hidden
reasoning: FullAvailable
operations: StructuredParameters
results: FullBounded

prompt: Summary
reasoning: Summary
operations: Hidden
results: Hidden

No global trace_level may replace the independent controls.

Presets may set several controls at once, but the underlying values remain independent and individually editable.

docs.title: 17. Capture Once, Render Many Ways
docs.text:
The architecture should be:

model/provider execution
        |
        +-- canonical safe effective request
        +-- provider-visible reasoning segments
        +-- semantic/tool invocations
        +-- operation/tool results
        +-- assistant output
        |
        v
ordered durable/observable activity
        |
        +-- prompt presentation
        +-- reasoning presentation
        +-- invocation presentation
        +-- result presentation
        +-- branch/plan presentation
        |
        v
TUI / web / API clients

Presentation is disposable and client-local or user-preference state.

Execution provenance and safely observable model activity remain durable or durably retrievable according to retention policy.

docs.title: 18. Activity Ordering and Causality
docs.text:
Reasoning segments, tool/semantic operations, results, and final output must share deterministic invocation-local order.

Store or derive concepts equivalent to:

activity id
invocation id
branch id
sequence/ordinal
parent/correlation id when causal nesting exists
activity kind
lifecycle state
safe content/ref

Do not derive interleaving solely from wall-clock timestamps.

The branch tree and activity causality remain separate structures. A UI may combine them visually, but one does not replace the other.

docs.title: 19. Provider Continuation and Context Isolation
docs.text:
Provider continuation must preserve the same isolation rules as the Scriberig context compiler.

A provider must not accidentally see:

  • sibling branch transcripts;
  • unrelated completed child transcripts;
  • later historical continuations;
  • other plan-node activity merely because it shares one user session;
  • model activity from a different provider assignment unless Scriberig explicitly includes its compact result/context.

Tests must prove this for provider-state reuse as well as stateless requests.

A continuation mechanism that cannot preserve branch isolation must be disabled for that execution path.

docs.title: 20. Reconnect and Restart
docs.text:
On restart, Scriberig restores canonical branch/session/plan state first.

Provider continuation state may then be classified as:

reusable
stale
disconnected/unavailable
expired/deleted
unknown

If reusable, the runtime may resume it.

Otherwise the next invocation recompiles canonical Scriberig context and establishes new provider state.

The UI must not need provider stream replay to reconstruct settled conversation/activity history.

docs.title: 21. Security and Privacy
docs.text:
Never store or expose in canonical prompt/activity records:

API keys
Authorization headers
resolved credential values
secret environment variables
provider-private hidden reasoning
sensitive tool parameters that policy requires redacting
raw provider payloads containing secrets

Full prompt views are full safe effective requests.

Where redaction occurs, the view should preserve structure and mark redaction rather than pretending the value never existed.

Provider continuation handles themselves may be sensitive operational identifiers. Expose them in normal UI only when useful; protocols should treat them as opaque runtime metadata rather than user-authored semantic content.

docs.title: 22. Cross-Surface Contract
docs.text:
Embedded Rust callers, CLI, HTTP/server clients, TUI, web, and future external clients must agree on:

  • Scriberig canonical session/branch identity;
  • provider continuation state as secondary runtime metadata;
  • effective request identity and safe retrieval;
  • independent prompt/reasoning presentation controls;
  • ordered provider-visible reasoning segments;
  • provider/model invocation provenance;
  • branch isolation semantics.

No product surface may reconstruct provider continuation semantics independently.

docs.title: 23. Required Conformance Scenarios
docs.text: Implementations must eventually prove at least these scenarios.

docs.title: Same-branch OpenAI continuation
docs.text: Two successive invocations in one branch reuse one compatible OpenAI Conversation or supported response chain while preserving two distinct Scriberig invocation records.

docs.title: Child branch isolation
docs.text: Creating a child compiles selected child context and creates independent provider continuation. Child-private tool/reasoning history does not appear in the parent provider context.

docs.title: Sibling isolation
docs.text: Two sibling branches using OpenAI receive independent provider state and cannot observe one another's transcripts except through explicitly supplied BranchResults/dependency results.

docs.title: Provider switch
docs.text: A branch runs first on OpenAI and then on a local model. Switching back to OpenAI detects that the old continuation no longer represents current branch context and reseeds or forks safely.

docs.title: Lost provider state
docs.text: Provider continuation is unavailable after restart. Scriberig recompiles canonical context and continues correctly without losing session history.

docs.title: Full prompt with continuation
docs.text: A provider request uses only a continuation ID plus new input on the wire. The user selects full prompt display and still sees the complete safe effective Scriberig context that invocation used.

docs.title: Independent prompt/reasoning controls
docs.text: Prompt is shown full while reasoning is hidden; then reasoning is shown while prompt is hidden. Neither change reruns the invocation.

docs.title: Interleaved reasoning
docs.text: A fake provider emits visible reasoning, semantic operation, result, more reasoning, another tool call, and final output. The shared activity projection preserves exact order when reasoning is shown and preserves operation order when reasoning is hidden.

docs.title: Hidden reasoning provider
docs.text: A provider exposes no user-visible reasoning. FullAvailable clearly shows that no fuller provider-visible reasoning exists rather than exposing or inventing hidden chain-of-thought.

docs.title: 24. Non-Negotiable Summary
docs.text:
Future design and implementation work must preserve these rules:

  1. Scriberig owns canonical session and branch identity.
  2. Provider continuation state is secondary branch-local runtime state.
  3. One provider conversation must not normally span unrelated Scriberig branches.
  4. Child provider state is seeded from selected compiled child context.
  5. Continuation reuse is guarded by exact context lineage/fingerprints.
  6. Provider switching never transfers opaque provider state across providers.
  7. Loss of provider continuation must not make Scriberig history unrecoverable.
  8. OpenAI Conversations and previous_response_id are adapter strategies, not Scriberig domain concepts.
  9. The canonical full prompt is the complete safe effective Scriberig request, not raw provider JSON.
  10. Full prompt remains reconstructable/inspectable even when the provider manages prior state server-side.
  11. Provider-visible reasoning may be interleaved with tool/semantic operations and must preserve ordering.
  12. Hidden/private chain-of-thought is never requested or exposed.
  13. Prompt and reasoning presentation controls are independent.
  14. Changing presentation never reruns model/tool work.
  15. Branch isolation must hold equally for stateless requests and provider-stateful continuation.
  16. All product surfaces consume one shared continuation/observability contract.

docs.title: Agent Profiles, Context Composition, and Evidence-Driven Optimization
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines how Scriberig constructs the behavioral instructions supplied to models, how those instructions relate to recursive branch execution, and how agent behavior may be improved from execution evidence without turning prompt files into canonical state.

It refines, but does not replace:

  1. 009. agent interaction and sessions.md;
  2. 016. model driven agent execution and branch isolation.md;
  3. 017. recursive agent decomposition and context isolation.md;
  4. 018. durable plans dependency scheduling and multi-model execution.md;
  5. 019. semantic agent operations and projection-first editing.md;
  6. 020. provider continuation state and observable model execution.md.

The controlling rules are:

Agent behavior is a versioned semantic configuration compiled into each effective model request. Prompt text is a projection of that configuration, not its canonical identity.

A branch is a context-isolation frame, not automatically a new agent. The same executor may enter a child branch, work with additional branch-local context, finalize a compact durable result, and resume its parent context without inheriting the child transcript.

Non-root branch completion is a handoff boundary. The executing model should make its final response a compact parent-consumable summary because that output is the natural source of BranchResult.summary; a second summarization model call is not required by default.

Automated changes to agent behavior should be justified by durable execution evidence and promoted through the same candidate, validation, conflict, and revision discipline used elsewhere in Scriberig.

docs.title: 2. Branch, Executor, Agent Profile, and Model Invocation Are Different Concepts
docs.text:
Do not use branch, agent, executor, profile, and model invocation as synonyms.

Conceptually:

Branch
  -> canonical context-isolation scope in the session tree

Executor
  -> the active owner performing work in a branch

AgentProfile
  -> reusable versioned behavior/context configuration used by an executor

ModelInvocation
  -> one provider-neutral model request/response step inside a branch

A common recursive execution therefore looks like:

executor E using profile P at parent context X
  |
  +-- enter child branch B
  |     effective context = X + selected branch-local frame B
  |     model invocation
  |     tool/semantic operation
  |     model invocation
  |     final compact branch response R
  |     -> BranchResult(B, summary = R, handles = ...)
  |
  +-- resume parent
        effective context = X + selected durable result of B

The child branch does not become a different executor merely because it is a child.

A branch may instead be explicitly assigned another executor/model/profile. That is an execution-assignment decision layered onto the same branch topology:

branch B
  executor E1 / profile P1 / model M1

branch C
  executor E2 / profile P2 / model M2

The session architecture is unchanged in both cases.

docs.title: 3. Context Frames and Context Compilation
docs.text:
The useful mental model for recursive execution is push/pop of context frames:

X
X + B
X + B + B1
X + B + B1 + B1a

and then:

X + B + B1 + B1a
        -> finalize B1a
X + B + B1 + BranchResult(B1a)
        -> finalize B1
X + B + BranchResult(B1)
        -> finalize B
X + BranchResult(B)

This is a semantic model, not a requirement to concatenate byte-identical prompt strings.

X means the parent's canonical effective context contract: the selected instructions, results, semantic scope, decisions, local history, capabilities, and execution configuration that Scriberig would compile for that parent location.

The context compiler remains authoritative. It may reconstruct X + B from canonical session and semantic state rather than literally copying a provider request or parent transcript.

Therefore both of these statements remain true:

  1. entering a normal child branch conceptually extends the current executor context with a focused child frame;
  2. child context is selected and compiled, not implemented by blindly copying the complete parent transcript.

When the child frame is popped, child-local working history does not become parent-local history. The parent receives selected durable results and semantic state.

docs.title: 4. Branches Do Not Imply New Provider Conversations or New Agents
docs.text:
Branch topology and provider continuation are related but distinct.

A provider continuation may be established independently for a child so that provider-local state cannot leak between branches. This does not mean Scriberig has created a new canonical agent identity.

Likewise, a runtime may instantiate another provider client object or ProviderModel value for a child. That is an implementation detail unless the branch has a distinct executor/profile assignment.

Use terminology carefully:

child branch
nested branch
branch executor
branch assignment

Prefer those terms over child agent when the only semantic change is context isolation.

Reserve language such as different executor, different agent profile, or different model assignment for an actual execution-configuration distinction.

docs.title: 5. Non-Root Branch Final Output Is a Handoff Contract
docs.text:
A non-root branch normally exists so its internal work can be collapsed when control returns to the parent.

The final model response of a successful non-root branch should therefore be intentionally shaped for BranchResult consumption.

The default behavioral instruction should be equivalent to:

When you are about to finish a non-root branch, make your final response a
compact one-paragraph summary for the parent. State the important outcome,
decisions or discoveries, remaining issues, and durable semantic/result
handles the parent may need. Do not reproduce the branch transcript or hidden
reasoning.

The exact wording may evolve through profile revisions. The semantic contract is more important than one literal prompt string.

The summary should be:

  • compact enough to keep parent context bounded;
  • specific enough that the parent can continue without reopening the branch in normal cases;
  • explicit about failure or unresolved questions;
  • grounded in durable result handles when exact state matters;
  • free of hidden chain-of-thought or transcript reconstruction.

A branch result may carry structured fields in addition to the paragraph. The paragraph is not a substitute for exact handles, validations, candidate identities, touched entities, or unresolved-question identities.

docs.title: 6. Root Completion Is Different
docs.text:
The root branch normally ends in user-facing output.

Do not force the non-root one-paragraph handoff format onto root completion. The root response may be long, structured, tabular, code-heavy, or otherwise shaped by the user's request.

Conceptually:

if branch is non-root:
    final output -> compact parent handoff
else:
    final output -> normal user-facing response

A root BranchResult.summary may still be populated from the root output for durability, but that storage convenience does not constrain the user-facing response format.

docs.title: 7. Do Not Add a Summarizer Call by Default
docs.text:
Scriberig already has the strongest participant available at branch completion: the executor that performed the work and has the branch-local context.

The default completion path should be:

branch-local execution
  -> executor's final compact handoff response
  -> durable BranchResult.summary
  -> parent consumes BranchResult

not:

branch-local execution
  -> arbitrary final response
  -> second model call that re-reads/summarizes branch history
  -> BranchResult.summary

A separate summarizer may exist later as an explicit policy for exceptional cases, archival compaction, migration of legacy histories, or quality repair. It is not the ordinary branch-completion mechanism.

Avoiding the extra call reduces cost, latency, attribution ambiguity, and the risk that a summarizer drops exact result information the branch executor already knows.

docs.title: 8. Agent Profiles Are Versioned Semantic Configuration
docs.text:
An AgentProfile is reusable configuration that determines how an executor behaves and how context is assembled.

Conceptually:

AgentProfile
  identity
  revision
  name/description
  context components
  preferred execution configuration references
  context policy reference
  branching policy reference
  tool/capability exposure policy
  runtime policy references

Profiles are not session identities and are not provider conversation identities.

A branch/model invocation records the exact effective profile revision used so historical execution can be explained and compared.

A profile may be selected by project/user defaults, session selection, branch assignment, plan-node assignment, or explicit invocation override according to the execution-resolution rules defined elsewhere.

docs.title: 9. Context Components Are First-Class
docs.text:
Do not model the entire agent prompt as one opaque mutable string.

A profile should resolve to ordered, typed context components conceptually equivalent to:

ContextComponent
  identity
  revision
  kind
  content
  activation rule
  scope/applicability
  priority/order
  estimated context cost
  provenance
  status

Useful component kinds include:

CoreInvariant
BehaviorPolicy
DomainGuidance
ToolGuidance
SkillTrigger
ExecutionLesson

The exact type names belong in lower-level design. The architectural distinction matters:

  • CoreInvariant protects architecture/safety behavior that should usually be present;
  • BehaviorPolicy tells the executor how to work;
  • DomainGuidance supplies domain/practitioner knowledge;
  • ToolGuidance explains non-obvious capability use;
  • SkillTrigger activates a bounded procedure when a recognizable condition holds;
  • ExecutionLesson is learned derived guidance backed by execution evidence.

A rendered system prompt or provider message is a projection of activated components plus branch/session context.

docs.title: 10. Always-On Prompt Space Is Expensive
docs.text:
Every always-on instruction competes with the actual task, semantic state, tool schemas, dependency results, and local branch history.

Prefer the narrowest mechanism that reliably produces the required behavior.

Conceptually:

mechanical deterministic behavior
  -> runtime/application code

recognized bounded procedure
  -> activated skill/procedure component

tool-specific behavior
  -> tool descriptor/guidance activated with the tool

domain-specific knowledge
  -> domain guidance activated by semantic scope

cross-cutting model behavior that cannot be mechanical
  -> short always-on behavior/core component

Do not accumulate every observed failure as another permanent paragraph in the base prompt.

When adding always-on guidance, consider whether existing prose can be removed, narrowed, moved to a trigger, or implemented mechanically.

docs.title: 11. The Core Always-On Invariants Should Remain Small
docs.text:
The default profile should carry a short architecture-oriented invariant set equivalent in meaning to:

You operate inside one Scriberig branch/context frame.
Prefer semantic entities and domain operations over raw files when the domain is understood.
Files/rendered documents are projections; raw writes are fallback behavior.
Canonical mutations use the shared candidate/migration/validation/promotion path.
Use stable semantic handles and exact snapshot/revision references when exact state matters.
Use child branches for focused context isolation when useful; a child branch does not by itself imply another agent.
Parents and dependencies consume compact durable results, not child transcripts.
Use capabilities progressively rather than assuming unrestricted filesystem, shell, or database access.

This is a semantic baseline, not immutable literal prose. Its effective revision must be observable as part of the complete model request.

docs.title: 12. Activation Is Part of Context Identity
docs.text:
For a model invocation, Scriberig resolves which context components are active from exact state such as:

agent profile revision
branch role: root or non-root
branch purpose/policy
semantic/domain scope
available capabilities/tools
plan-node assignment
accepted project/session policy
explicit user/branch overrides
applicable execution lessons

The activated set and its order are output-relevant inputs. They therefore participate in canonical effective request identity and request fingerprinting.

Full prompt inspection must make it possible to determine which exact component revisions were active, even if the presentation renders them as combined prose.

Changing UI prompt visibility must not alter activation.

docs.title: 13. Behavior Policy and Domain Knowledge Must Stay Distinct
docs.text:
A useful optimization boundary is:

BehaviorPolicy
  -> how the executor should reason/work/use capabilities

DomainGuidance
  -> knowledge about the subject/domain being worked on

Do not hide project facts inside generic agent behavior instructions.

A fact about one exact project/snapshot belongs to semantic project state or derived knowledge tied to exact provenance.

A general reusable procedure may belong to domain guidance or a skill.

This prevents accidental transfer of task-specific facts into unrelated future tasks.

docs.title: 14. Execution Lessons Are Derived Knowledge with Provenance
docs.text:
Scriberig may learn reusable execution guidance from completed work, but such guidance is derived knowledge rather than unquestioned canonical truth.

Conceptually:

ExecutionLesson
  identity
  revision
  cue
  lesson/operation guidance
  applicability scope
  evidence references
  confidence
  source experiment/run
  producer/model/profile provenance
  status

An execution lesson should answer:

  • when is this lesson relevant;
  • what behavior should change;
  • what evidence supports the lesson;
  • how confident are we;
  • which runs/profile revisions produced the evidence;
  • whether later evidence has superseded or contradicted it.

Do not use an unstructured mutable MEMORY.md as canonical learned behavior.

A Markdown or configuration representation may exist as a projection/import/export surface.

docs.title: 15. Prompt/Profile Changes Need Evidence
docs.text:
Manual profile editing is allowed through normal authorized semantic change flows.

Automated or optimization-driven changes should normally be traceable to observed execution evidence.

Strong evidence may include:

repeated failure of the base profile
behavioral divergence between candidate profiles
compiler/test/domain validation results
incorrect tool choice with visible consequence
missing branch-result information that forced reopening
context bloat that displaced required task information
successful correction repeated across independent tasks

Weak evidence includes hypothetical risk without an observed trajectory, simple agreement between two model outputs, or the fact that a candidate happened to be adopted.

When evidence is insufficient, retaining the current profile is a valid outcome.

docs.title: 16. Prompt Experiments Are Structured Knowledge
docs.text:
A profile optimization run should be represented durably rather than existing only as an ad-hoc transcript.

Conceptually:

PromptExperiment
  identity
  base profile revision
  task/branch or evaluation case
  candidate profile revisions
  probe branches/results
  behavioral differences
  validation evidence
  composition decision
  attribution assessments
  resulting candidate/profile revision

Attribution should allow states equivalent to:

helped
hurt
no observed effect
confounded

Prefer confounded when the experiment does not isolate causality.

Adoption of a profile revision is not proof that every included component helped.

docs.title: 17. Propose-Probe-Compose Maps onto Existing Scriberig Structures
docs.text:
A useful evidence-driven optimization pattern is:

base profile
  |
  +-- baseline probe branch
  |
  +-- candidate A proposal
  |     -> candidate probe branch
  |
  +-- candidate B proposal
  |     -> candidate probe branch
  |
  +-- compose/evaluate plan node
        depends_on all required probe BranchResults
        -> validation
        -> selected/promoted candidate or keep-base
        -> optional ExecutionLesson

This uses existing architecture:

  • branches isolate attempts;
  • plan dependencies coordinate probes;
  • BranchResults satisfy dependencies;
  • validators provide stronger evidence than model preference alone;
  • candidate/revision semantics preserve alternatives;
  • one coordinator owns automatic experiment advancement.

Do not share candidate transcripts merely to make the composer aware of results. Supply compact results, exact profile/component identities, validation evidence, and explicitly selected behavioral contrasts.

docs.title: 18. Candidate Profiles Use the Normal Change Discipline
docs.text:
Automatically proposed profile/context changes are not privileged direct writes.

Their lifecycle should follow the same architectural shape used for other canonical change:

current AgentProfile revision
  -> candidate profile/component revisions
  -> probe/evaluation branches
  -> validation/evidence assessment
  -> conflict/policy review when needed
  -> promotion
  -> new current profile revision

If profiles/components are represented through files for interoperability, those files remain projections when the semantic domain is understood.

Do not let an optimizer overwrite AGENTS.md, prompt files, or provider configuration directly and thereby bypass Scriberig's revision/change model.

docs.title: 19. Validators Are Preferred over Model Self-Approval
docs.text:
When an experiment changes behavior that has objectively testable consequences, use the strongest available validator.

Examples:

source edit quality
  -> compiler/tests/domain validators

branch result completeness
  -> structured contract checks + parent consumption test

tool policy
  -> capability/audit assertions

context isolation
  -> deterministic compiled-context tests

provider continuation isolation
  -> lineage/fingerprint tests

Model comparison may contribute evidence where no deterministic validator exists, but it should not replace available deterministic evidence.

docs.title: 20. Full Effective Prompt Includes Profile/Component Identity
docs.text:
The complete safe effective request defined by 020 must be able to answer not only "what text was sent/effective?" but also:

which AgentProfile revision was resolved
which ContextComponent revisions activated
why conditional components activated when retained safely
what branch role/purpose applied
what semantic/dependency results were selected
what tool/capability definitions were active
what provider/model/thinking configuration was resolved

Provider serialization may flatten this into ordinary messages. The provider-neutral retained request remains the observability boundary.

This enables reproducible comparison between profile revisions and makes evidence-driven optimization auditable.

docs.title: 21. Profile Selection and Executor Assignment Are Independent
docs.text:
A branch may continue with the same executor while using the same profile, or it may explicitly resolve another profile/model assignment.

Examples:

same executor, same profile, child context frame
same executor identity, explicit branch profile override
different worker executor assigned by plan node
different model/provider profile for a competing sibling attempt

Do not infer an executor change from branch creation alone.

One branch still normally has one active executing owner. Competing attempts use sibling branches.

docs.title: 22. Context Restoration and Provider Continuation
docs.text:
When a same-executor child branch completes, Scriberig conceptually returns to the parent's canonical context frame plus selected durable child results.

A provider continuation that advanced inside the child cannot be treated as though it were rewound to the parent state.

Therefore:

  • parent and child provider-continuation lineages remain isolated according to 020;
  • the parent may resume compatible parent continuation state if it still represents the canonical parent lineage;
  • otherwise Scriberig recompiles/reseeds from canonical parent context;
  • child continuation state never defines parent context;
  • losing either continuation remains recoverable from Scriberig state.

The push/pop context model is canonical Scriberig semantics, not a demand that a provider support conversation rewind.

docs.title: 23. Product Surfaces Do Not Own Prompt Semantics
docs.text:
CLI, TUI, web, server, clients, and editor surfaces may:

  • select an available profile or branch assignment when authorized;
  • inspect resolved profile/component provenance;
  • inspect prompt presentation according to visibility policy;
  • observe experiment/lesson state;
  • request authorized profile changes through shared application semantics.

They must not independently concatenate prompts, inject hidden tool guidance, mutate learned lessons, or implement their own branch-final summary rules.

Context composition belongs in shared agent/runtime/application semantics.

docs.title: 24. Initial Implementation Priority
docs.text:
The first implementation should not begin with an autonomous prompt optimizer.

Prioritize in this order:

  1. make branch/executor terminology explicit in code/design;
  2. add a short Scriberig core behavior component to the effective model request;
  3. add the non-root branch final-handoff component and prove it is absent from root behavior;
  4. retain exact profile/component revision identity in compiled/effective request provenance;
  5. make profile/context components first-class and activation deterministic;
  6. add durable experiment/evidence/lesson structures;
  7. only then add automated propose/probe/compose orchestration and promotion policy.

This order produces immediate prompt-quality benefits while keeping later optimization auditable.

docs.title: 25. Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
Implementations must preserve these invariants.

  1. A branch is a context-isolation frame; it does not automatically imply a new agent/executor.
  2. The same executor may recursively enter and leave child context frames.
  3. Child context is deterministically selected/compiled; it is not the unbounded parent transcript.
  4. Finishing a child restores parent canonical context plus selected durable results, not child working history.
  5. A non-root final response is a compact parent handoff and is the default source of BranchResult.summary.
  6. Root output remains user-facing and is not forced into the child-summary format.
  7. No extra summarizer model call is required for ordinary branch completion.
  8. Agent/profile instructions are versioned semantic configuration, not an opaque mutable prompt file.
  9. Activated context components participate in request identity and complete prompt observability.
  10. Always-on prompt content remains intentionally small; deterministic behavior belongs in code when possible.
  11. Project facts, domain guidance, behavior policy, and learned execution lessons remain distinguishable.
  12. Learned lessons carry evidence, scope, confidence, and provenance.
  13. Automated profile changes require evidence and use candidate/validation/promotion semantics.
  14. Prompt experiments use branches/results/plans rather than transcript sharing.
  15. Provider continuation never replaces canonical context push/pop semantics.
  16. Product presentation state never changes profile activation or execution semantics.
  17. Hidden chain-of-thought is never required for profile optimization or observability.

docs.title: 26. Non-Goals
docs.text:
This design does not require:

  • treating every child branch as a separate agent;
  • byte-for-byte inheritance of a parent provider request;
  • copying the complete parent transcript into a child;
  • copying the complete child transcript back into a parent;
  • an extra model call to summarize every completed branch;
  • one universal model/provider for all branches;
  • putting every skill/domain rule in always-on system prose;
  • letting an optimizer directly rewrite prompt files or AGENTS.md;
  • trusting model self-evaluation when deterministic validators exist;
  • transferring exact task/project facts into generic learned behavior;
  • exposing hidden chain-of-thought;
  • implementing automated profile optimization before deterministic profile/context composition exists.

docs.title: 27. Definition
docs.text:
Scriberig agent behavior is the deterministic, provider-neutral resolution of a versioned AgentProfile, its activated context components, exact branch/session/semantic state, durable ancestor/dependency results, capability/tool contracts, and execution configuration into one effective model request.

Recursive branch execution pushes focused context frames over that behavior without inherently changing agent identity. Non-root branches finish by returning compact durable handoffs. Profile improvement is itself structured semantic work: proposed from evidence, probed in isolated branches, validated, attributed cautiously, and promoted as a new revision rather than silently accumulated as prompt text.

docs.title: Scriberig TUI Reuse Study and Multi-Surface Architecture Masterplan
Executive summary
docs.text:
The research supports the original intuition: Scriberig should stop treating terminal interaction as a framework-development problem. There are now mature enough Rust implementations of Pi-style terminal interaction that Scriberig can reuse a large fraction of editor, Markdown, terminal lifecycle, selection, clipboard, theme, streaming-render and resize machinery while keeping its distinctive semantic/session/change architecture entirely its own.

The strongest foundation is rpi-tui from bigfish1913/pi-rust. The decisive architectural fact is not simply that rpi has a good TUI; it is that the project explicitly separates rpi-tui from the rest of the agent stack. The current rpi documentation says that rpi-tui depends on no other rpi-* crate and assigns it the narrow responsibility “terminal UI primitives: components, layout, editor, transcript rendering.” The full project separately divides provider abstraction, agent loop, tools, durable session harness, plugin ABI, extensions, and CLI into distinct crates. citeturn6search1

My recommendation is therefore:

Adopt the rpi-tui interaction model and most of its leaf components; initially vendor the crate at a known upstream commit; build a very thin scriberig-ui presentation-model layer between it and Scriberig; do not import rpi's agent, tool, session, or plugin semantics into the Scriberig domain.

tape_tui is the best alternative and an excellent secondary reference. Its architecture is unusually clean: it is a line-oriented streaming TUI designed to preserve terminal scrollback, with its runtime, component contract, editor, input parser, terminal abstraction, Markdown renderer and searchable selection list separated into individual modules. Its core crate has no async runtime dependency; Tokio appears only in development dependencies in the inspected Cargo.toml. However, it describes itself as experimental and is currently at 0.1.0, so its architectural cleanliness is stronger than its maturity signal. The primary files inspected were src/tui.rs, src/component.rs, src/terminal.rs, src/input.rs, src/editor.rs, src/markdown.rs, src/select_list.rs, src/keybindings.rs, and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

CCherry07/pi-rs is the strongest whole-product behavioral reference, and in some areas it is substantially more ambitious than rpi: fullscreen Ratatui/Crossterm/Tokio UI, Markdown and syntax highlighting, CJK IME handling, copy selection, history, scroll, command selectors, five frontend modes, resumable Pi v4 session trees, plugin reload, provider diversity, project trust, image handling, scheduling and native plus JavaScript extension systems. citeturn6search0 Its TUI, however, lives in a much larger product runtime rather than a tiny generic TUI leaf crate. That makes it a source of ideas and selectively portable widgets, not the foundation I would choose.

tau-agent/tau is the strongest reference for the eventual Scriberig client/server topology. It deliberately runs its agent as a long-lived server and makes the Ratatui TUI a thin Unix-socket client; a separate tau-agent-client crate exposes the same server to scripts. Its workspace explicitly separates tau-agent-tui, tau-agent-engine, tau-agent-plugin, tau-agent-client, and shared protocol types. citeturn6search2 I would borrow this architectural pattern, not its agent/task semantics.

The full bigfish1913/rpi runtime is also worth mining selectively. Its headless server/remote-client mode is already designed so that the client has no providers, tools, plugins or session files; all execution remains server-side. It also has durable crash-resumable sessions, a stable plugin ABI and deterministic offline testing. citeturn6search1 Those are excellent design references, but adopting the runtime itself would undermine Scriberig's semantic boundary.

There are two material research caveats. First, I positively identified the likely OxiCode candidate as nhtera/OxiCode, but did not obtain enough primary-source material in this pass to make a responsible file-level adoption recommendation; it therefore stays D: ideas only / pending audit. Second, “PiG” was not uniquely resolvable to an unambiguous repository from the available primary evidence. I therefore do not invent architecture, licensing or activity facts for it. It should remain D until its exact repository is pinned. This matters particularly for licensing and provenance.

For Scriberig itself, I treated TNick/scriberig, branch main, as the repository implied by the request. The repository was pushed on October 19, 2026, and the tree I inspected includes the existing domain/application family such as scriberig-core, scriberig-cli, scriberig-server, scriberig-provider, scriberig-query, scriberig-source, scriberig-knowledge, scriberig-lang, and related crates. A repository search found no current scriberig-tui crate and no ratatui occurrence on this public main, so the recommendation below treats the TUI as a new presentation surface rather than assuming the earlier experimental TUI code is still present.

The high-level target should be:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Domain["Scriberig — source of truth"]
        Core["Semantic domain"]
        Session["Session / Branch tree"]
        Plan["Plan dependency graph"]
        Change["Candidate / Migration / Validation"]
        Providers["Model/provider orchestration"]
    end

    subgraph App["Shared application boundary"]
        Port["ScriberigUiPort"]
        Projection["Presentation projections"]
        Events["Ordered UI event stream"]
        Commands["Typed commands"]
    end

    subgraph Terminal["Terminal surface"]
        RTUI["rpi-tui foundation"]
        Panels["Scriberig panels"]
        Editor["Editor / selectors / Markdown"]
    end

    subgraph Web["Web surface"]
        API["HTTP command/query API"]
        Stream["SSE/WebSocket event stream"]
        React["React application"]
    end

    Core --> Port
    Session --> Projection
    Plan --> Projection
    Change --> Projection
    Providers --> Events

    Port --> Commands
    Port --> Projection
    Port --> Events

    Projection --> Panels
    Events --> Panels
    Commands --> Port
    RTUI --> Panels
    Editor --> Panels

    Port --> API
    Events --> Stream
    API --> React
    Stream --> React

The important choice is therefore not “which coding agent should Scriberig become?” It is “which mature presentation machinery should sit in front of Scriberig?” On that question, rpi-tui is the clear first choice.

docs.title: Scope, assumptions, and evaluation criteria
docs.text:
The report assumes a small engineering team of roughly two to three Rust developers, with one of them or an additional engineer able to work on TypeScript/React. No delivery deadline was supplied. Effort ratings therefore mean architectural and integration difficulty rather than calendar commitments.

I assume Scriberig's current semantic architecture remains authoritative: sessions and branches are domain concepts, understood source/schema content is changed through semantic operations, plans are distinct from conversational transcripts, and candidates/migrations/validation are durable application concepts. The proposed TUI must project those semantics rather than reducing them to a conventional read/write/bash coding-agent transcript.

I also assume the desired outbound Scriberig licensing policy is permissive MIT, Apache-2.0, or dual MIT/Apache-2.0. Under that assumption, MIT code is generally suitable for incorporation provided its copyright and license notice are retained; vendoring MIT code does not mean stripping its upstream MIT notice or pretending the copied code originated in Scriberig. rpi identifies itself as MIT and explicitly retains upstream copyright/MIT notices in LICENSE and NOTICE; Tau also declares MIT. citeturn6search1turn6search2 pi-rs must similarly be consumed according to the license file of the exact pinned revision rather than merely inferred from its relationship to Pi.

The classifications used below are:

Class Meaning A — adopt wholesale Use the upstream component substantially unchanged behind our adapter; preferably depend on or vendor the complete module. B — vendor and adapt Preserve provenance and license, but carry a Scriberig-controlled copy because APIs/security/UX require changes. C — reimplement The concept belongs to Scriberig semantics; sharing the foreign implementation would create the wrong abstraction. D — ideas only Study behavior/architecture but do not introduce the code into the production dependency graph.

The most important evaluation criterion is decoupling from coding-agent semantics. A beautiful transcript renderer that assumes every item is AssistantMessage | ToolCall | ToolResult is less valuable to us than a slightly simpler renderer accepting arbitrary components.

A second criterion is deterministic testability. rpi is particularly strong here: it exposes a deterministic faux provider, an in-memory execution environment and a workspace test path intended to run offline. citeturn6search1 pi-rs likewise documents deterministic provider support and focused workspace/integration validation, although its complete product has a much broader dependency and runtime surface. citeturn6search0

A third is transport independence. A panel should not know whether its data came from an in-process Rust service, a Unix socket, TCP, HTTP or a replayed fixture. Tau's explicit server/TUI/client/shared-protocol split is especially instructive here. citeturn6search2

A fourth is terminal safety. All foundations that deal with clipboard access, terminal control sequences, hyperlinks or pixel-image protocols should be considered privileged presentation code. Model/tool text is untrusted input: Scriberig should never emit arbitrary model-generated ANSI/OSC control sequences directly to the user's terminal.

A final assumption concerns activity. Because “last commit” is intrinsically volatile, I would not make procurement-level decisions from a date captured once. At the October 20, 2026 snapshot used here, rpi is clearly active—the primary repository exposes 518 commits and documents current release 0.6.0; pi-rs describes an actively evolving product baseline; Tau describes itself as under active development. citeturn6search1turn6search0turn6search2 The exact commit SHA, contributors and security-policy state should be frozen in an intake manifest when implementation starts.

docs.title: rpi-tui from bigfish1913/pi-rust
docs.text:
This is the best match to the narrow problem.

The complete rpi repository has a deliberately layered nine-crate architecture. The published responsibilities are rpi-ai for provider-neutral messages/streams, rpi-agent for the loop, rpi-tools for execution tools, rpi-harness for the session tree/persistence/recovery, rpi-tui for terminal primitives, rpi-cli for the actual product, rpi-plugin-sdk for ABI definitions, rpi-extensions for plugin hosting, and rpi-telemetry for instrumentation. Crucially, the upstream documentation explicitly says rpi-tui depends on no other rpi-* crate. citeturn6search1

The inspected crates/rpi-tui/Cargo.toml reinforces that claim. At the snapshot examined it uses a small terminal-oriented dependency set around Crossterm, Unicode-width handling, text wrapping and clipboard support, without Tokio as a TUI-runtime dependency. The source root exposes dedicated modules for ANSI handling, clipboard, components, editor, fuzzy matching, input, layout, Markdown, selection, style, terminal handling, text, theme and utilities.

The files most worth adopting or adapting are:

crates/rpi-tui/src/component.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/editor.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/input.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/layout.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/markdown.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/select.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/terminal.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/text.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/theme.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/clipboard.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/ansi.rs
crates/rpi-tui/src/lib.rs
crates/rpi-tui/README.md
crates/rpi-tui/Cargo.toml

I would take the editor, fuzzy/select components, text model, theme model and most Markdown machinery as A, while taking the terminal/runtime/component integration as B. The B classification is not because the code looks poor; it is because terminal security policy, Scriberig's panel layout and the desired no-lock-in adapter are important enough that we should control the seam.

The main security concern is clipboard and terminal-output handling. A model response, tool diagnostic or imported source string must be escaped into text segments rather than interpreted as arbitrary ANSI/OSC. Clipboard interaction should be explicit, and there should be a configuration mode that disables clipboard/image access on remote or high-assurance installations.

docs.title: Full bigfish1913/rpi
docs.text:
As an application architecture, rpi is arguably the most relevant comparison because it has already solved several problems we will face later: provider-independent streaming, durable crash recovery, embedded operation, plugins, remote operation and offline testing. Its session harness stores a session tree with JSONL persistence and per-frame progress, and the project claims recovery from a crash during a tool call rather than merely restoring the preceding user message. citeturn6search1

Its remote topology is also highly relevant. rpi --server exposes a headless agent and rpi --connect ... starts a TUI client; upstream states that the client holds no providers, tools, extensions or session files. citeturn6search1 That is very close to the eventual role we want for a remote Scriberig TUI or browser.

Its plugin system is more sophisticated than most Rust agent implementations: Rust cdylibs behind a hand-written #[repr(C)] boundary with version negotiation, plus host-side isolation of plugin/runtime responsibilities. Plugins can register tools, providers, slash commands, event handlers, Markdown renderers and resources. citeturn6search1

But those are precisely the reasons not to adopt the whole runtime. Scriberig already has domain semantics. Replacing them with rpi-harness and rpi-agent would turn Scriberig's session tree, semantic operations and durable change model into foreign concepts wrapped around a coding-agent conversation.

Recommended use:

A: rpi-tui leaf utilities/components where semantics are generic
B: selected remote protocol/terminal infrastructure only if independently useful
C: Scriberig session, plans, semantic operations, validation, promotions
D: rpi-harness session semantics, agent tools and plugin architecture as design references

Security is comparatively well considered upstream: the repository includes SECURITY.md, plugin ABI containment, optional rather than default web tooling, and deterministic offline testing. citeturn6search1 Nevertheless, native plugins remain native code and should be treated as arbitrary-code execution from Scriberig's threat-model perspective.

docs.title: CCherry07/pi-rs
docs.text:
pi-rs is the most useful product-behavior oracle in this set.

The current README characterizes it as a production-oriented Rust implementation of the Pi terminal agent whose TUI is built with Ratatui, Crossterm and Tokio. It explicitly lists Markdown, syntax highlighting, CJK IME input, copy selection, input history, scrolling and command selectors. citeturn6search0 It also has interactive TUI, one-shot output, NDJSON, bidirectional stdio RPC and ACP frontends running over a common runtime. citeturn6search0

Its image path is particularly mature: startup file attachments and clipboard images are supported, common image formats are validated/converted, and the documentation explicitly warns that native clipboard access is unavailable over SSH. citeturn6search0

The session implementation deserves study rather than adoption. It supports durable Pi v4 session trees, /resume, queues, branch/tree semantics, compaction, recovery and import of previous Pi session versions. The documented recovery behavior is careful about side effects: after interruption it reconciles state and marks the interrupted operation aborted rather than blindly replaying a tool whose effects are uncertain. citeturn6search0 That is exactly the kind of invariant Scriberig needs for semantic mutations, but Scriberig should implement it around candidate/change transaction IDs, not Pi tool calls.

The plugin architecture is powerful but correspondingly high risk. pi-rs supports native Rust cdylib plugins plus optional JavaScript/TypeScript extensions; project trust controls project-local extension discovery. The native package manager checks SHA-256 integrity, but upstream itself explicitly notes that this currently provides integrity, not publisher authentication. citeturn6search0 This is an excellent security lesson for Scriberig: “hash matches downloaded artifact” and “artifact came from an authorized publisher” are different guarantees.

Because its TUI resides in apps/pi-cli rather than being the exceptionally clean leaf boundary offered by rpi-tui, I classify most direct reuse as B or D, not A.

Files/directories to study or selectively extract are:

apps/pi-cli/
apps/pi-cli/README.md
crates/pi-sdk/
crates/pi-plugin-manager/
packages/pi/
docs/pi-core-test-matrix.md

The exact widget files should be pinned from the intake commit before copying; the repository is active enough that guessing current paths beyond those verified directories would be irresponsible.

docs.title: Gurpartap/tape_tui
docs.text:
tape_tui is perhaps the nicest pure TUI design in the comparison.

Its inspected docs/ARCHITECTURE.md defines a line-oriented component API in which components render a Vec<Line> and receive normalized input tokens. The runtime handles differential redraw, terminal state and deferred structural modifications. The main modules are unusually easy to understand:

src/tui.rs          runtime/render loop/differential updates
src/component.rs    Component, Container, Text, Spacer
src/terminal.rs     terminal abstraction and RealTerminal
src/input.rs        normalized keyboard/paste parser
src/editor.rs       cursor/navigation/editing/undo
src/markdown.rs     Markdown → styled terminal lines
src/select_list.rs  searchable selection UI
src/keybindings.rs  key identifiers and bindings
docs/ARCHITECTURE.md
Cargo.toml

The data model is simple—styled Line and Segment structures—making deterministic snapshot testing straightforward. Its terminal abstraction includes image rendering; image values can represent RGBA data or a file path. It explicitly supports alternate-screen configuration and scroll offsets.

Its most attractive property for Scriberig is scrollback-preserving streaming. Rather than assuming a fullscreen frame buffer is the only valid terminal UX, it was designed around streaming tools that should coexist with normal terminal history.

The second attractive property is crash safety. The architecture describes terminal reset from panic/drop paths, including restoring cursor visibility and undoing bracketed-paste/keyboard/alternate-screen modes. This class of defensive terminal lifecycle logic is absolutely worth having.

The inspected core Cargo.toml is minimal—Crossterm, Unicode width/wrapping and clipboard support—while Tokio/Futures are development dependencies rather than a runtime requirement. That makes the UI core easy to embed in a Scriberig process using any async runtime.

Its disadvantage is maturity: the inspected crate identifies itself as experimental and uses a 0.1.0 version. I therefore rank it second behind rpi-tui, despite preferring aspects of its architecture.

Recommended treatment: D for overall architecture, A/B for carefully selected leaf implementations if rpi-tui lacks an equivalent. Avoid casually mixing two independently evolving Pi-derived rendering stacks. Choose one base and treat the other as a reference unless a specific deficiency justifies importing a module.

docs.title: tau-agent/tau
docs.text:
Tau's most compelling feature is not a Markdown renderer. It is its process architecture.

The workspace explicitly separates the executable, full-agent library, Ratatui TUI, core engine, plugin SDK, default plugins, client and shared protocol types. citeturn6search2 The long-running server owns session state and the TUI connects through a Unix socket; users can detach and reconnect, and scripts use the same service through tau-agent-client. citeturn6search2

That gives us a strong precedent for this Scriberig rule:

A UI is a client of Scriberig application semantics, not the owner of them.

Tau additionally has streaming output, session pickers, task-board views and theme support. citeturn6search2 Its plugin model uses subprocesses communicating through typed RPC, with configurable sandbox profiles including Docker or SSH execution. citeturn6search2 This is materially safer and more operationally flexible than making every extension an in-process Rust dynamic library, although it comes with IPC/versioning complexity.

The parts to study are therefore:

tau-agent-tui/
tau-agent-client/
tau-agent-base/
tau-agent-plugin/
tau-agent-engine/
