The reuse classification is D for TUI widgets, because we already have a cleaner generic foundation; D/B for client protocol concepts; and D for plugin isolation, potentially becoming C if Scriberig later designs its own capability-oriented plugin protocol.

Do not import Tau's worktree/task/merge semantics. Its task model is designed for a coding agent editing Git repositories; Scriberig's plans, branches and semantic migrations have different invariants.

docs.title: OxiCode and PiG
docs.text:
The likely OxiCode repository is nhtera/OxiCode, described in GitHub search metadata as a high-performance Rust AI coding agent. I did not obtain enough primary-source file-level evidence during this research snapshot to certify its TUI decoupling, license, exact runtime surface, test quality, plugin model or session persistence. A deep-reuse recommendation without that evidence would be false precision.

It therefore remains:

OxiCode:
    D — ideas/reference only until a source/provenance audit is completed.

“PiG” is more problematic: the name did not resolve unambiguously enough to tie the request to one repository with confidence. Consequently, no claims about its language, license, architecture or maintenance are made here.

PiG:
    D — do not consume code until the exact OWNER/REPOSITORY and revision are pinned.

That is not merely a research nicety. An ambiguous project identity is a licensing/provenance blocker.

docs.title: Scriberig
docs.text:
For the repository treated as current Scriberig, the major strategic advantage is that the application is already decomposed into domain-oriented crates rather than being one terminal executable. The tree inspected contained, among others:

crates/scriberig-cli
crates/scriberig-core
crates/scriberig-enterprise
crates/scriberig-knowledge
crates/scriberig-provider
crates/scriberig-query
crates/scriberig-server
crates/scriberig-source
crates/scriberig-lang
...

The current public main did not yield a scriberig-tui or ratatui search hit. That actually makes the proposed boundary easier to establish cleanly.

I would add:

crates/
  scriberig-ui/          # transport-neutral presentation models + intents/events
  scriberig-tui/         # executable/application adapter
  scriberig-tui-kit/     # vendored/wrapped terminal foundation, if desired
  scriberig-protocol/    # network DTOs/event envelope/versioning

web/
  scriberig-web/         # React/TypeScript application

third_party/
  rpi-tui/               # optional pinned vendor location
  LICENSES/

The single most important architectural constraint is that scriberig-tui and scriberig-web may depend on scriberig-ui; scriberig-core must never depend back on either UI.

docs.title: Reuse decisions and comparison
docs.text:
The component-level decision is clearer than a project-level winner-takes-all decision.

Component Preferred source Decision Reason Terminal lifecycle rpi-tui B Mature and isolated, but terminal-safety policy warrants Scriberig-controlled adapter/vendor layer. Generic component primitives rpi-tui A/B Generic and agent-independent; wrap public interfaces so replacement remains possible. Editor rpi-tui A Solved commodity problem; no semantic value in rewriting it. Input/key handling rpi-tui A/B Reuse parser; retain Scriberig command/keymap layer. Markdown renderer rpi-tui A Commodity presentation; sanitize untrusted input. Search/select/fuzzy UI rpi-tui A Directly useful for command and semantic selectors. Theme primitives rpi-tui A Presentation-only; inexpensive to wrap. Scrollback model rpi-tui, informed by tape_tui B Preserve terminal-native history; copy behavior rather than mix runtimes unnecessarily. Image terminal support tape_tui/pi-rs reference B/D Useful but nonessential; protocol support and remote behavior complicate it. Generic textual diff widget upstream/reference B Rendering can be reused; semantic diff production stays Scriberig-owned. Semantic change diff Scriberig C Must understand entities/migrations/validation rather than raw files. Session tree Scriberig C Fundamental domain object. Resume/recovery Scriberig, informed by rpi/pi-rs C Side-effect semantics differ; foreign session format is inappropriate. Plans/dependency DAG Scriberig C Core product semantics, not a TUI concern. Model invocation projection Scriberig C Needs provider-neutral Scriberig telemetry/history. Client/server protocol Scriberig, informed by Tau/rpi C Protocol must expose Scriberig commands/events, not coding-agent calls. Remote reconnect semantics Tau/rpi ideas D → C Excellent precedent, but implement around our sequence IDs/snapshots. Native plugins rpi/pi-rs ideas D ABI is impressive but extension authority conflicts with semantic-operation controls. Out-of-process plugins Tau ideas D → C later Better security boundary if extensions become important. Command palette rpi-tui select/fuzzy + Scriberig registry A/C Widget A; command semantics C. Provider layer Existing Scriberig C No architectural reason to replace it with an agent project's provider abstraction.

The project-level conclusion is consequently:

Project Presentation Editor Renderer Session/resume Client/server Plugins Themes Overall rpi-tui B A A/B n/a n/a n/a A Foundation rpi D via rpi-tui D D D/B patterns D via rpi-tui Architectural reference pi-rs B/D B/D B/D D D D D Product/UX oracle tape_tui B/D A/B B n/a n/a n/a B/D Backup TUI foundation Tau D D D D D → C D → C D Distributed architecture reference OxiCode D D D D D D D Pending audit PiG D D D D D D D Exact repository required Scriberig C panels no semantic rendering C C C product config Source of truth

There is an important licensing implication to the A/B distinction. For vendored upstream source:

third_party/rpi-tui/
    UPSTREAM.md       # repository, exact SHA, intake date
    LICENSE           # exact upstream license
    PATCHES.md        # intentional local differences
    src/...

UPSTREAM.md should record the source revision and paths. An automated CI check should report divergence from the pinned upstream tree. Do not periodically “copy the newest files” by hand without preserving provenance.

For components classified A but used through a dependency, pin a semver range plus lockfile. For components B, pin a commit and carry explicit local patches.

rpi's current repository is especially attractive from a maintenance perspective because it has documentation per crate, offline workspace tests, architecture/user/security docs, and an explicitly library-first structure. citeturn6search1 pi-rs has similarly substantial validation, including workspace tests, Clippy, Node/NAPI checks and deterministic provider fixtures, but its broader product footprint creates more possible integration surface. citeturn6search0

Security should be enforced above all of these libraries:

Risk Scriberig policy Model-generated terminal escapes Render model/tool strings as escaped text segments; prohibit raw ANSI except trusted theme/render code. Clipboard leakage Clipboard disabled/configurable in secure mode; explicit user action only. Image escape/protocol vulnerabilities Off by default for first release; validate dimensions/size/format before enabling. Session persistence contains proprietary code/secrets Redaction hooks, configurable retention, file permission hardening, no credentials in session events. Native plugin compromise No native-plugin ABI in initial Scriberig TUI. Project-local plugin surprise Explicit project trust/capability grant if extensions are later introduced. Remote unauthenticated daemon Never bind remotely without authentication; loopback/Unix socket by default. Duplicate semantic operations after reconnect Commands carry idempotency IDs; application layer records accepted operations. UI optimistic state diverges from server Optimism only for ephemeral UI state; semantic mutation completes on authoritative event/ack. Markdown/XSS in browser Treat Markdown and model content as untrusted; no unsanitized HTML injection.

The pi-rs experience is useful here: its project-trust boundary governs project resources and plugins, and its documented interrupted-session recovery explicitly avoids blind re-execution of unknown-side-effect operations. citeturn6search0 Tau's out-of-process/sandboxable plugin model provides the other useful security precedent. citeturn6search2

docs.title: TUI architecture and custom panel design
docs.text:
The proposed implementation adds one presentation abstraction above Scriberig and below every UI.

Do not expose scriberig-core structures directly to a widget. Core structures inevitably evolve for persistence/domain reasons. Instead, create immutable presentation projections that are deliberately optimized for UI consumption.

// scriberig-ui/src/model.rs

use std::sync::Arc;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct SessionId(pub Arc<str>);

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct BranchId(pub Arc<str>);

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct UiSnapshot {
    pub revision: u64,
    pub session: SessionTreePm,
    pub branch_activity: BranchActivityPm,
    pub plan: PlanPm,
    pub invocation: Option<ModelInvocationPm>,
    pub semantic_selection: SemanticSelectionPm,
    pub change_review: ChangeReviewPm,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct SessionTreePm {
    pub root: BranchNodePm,
    pub selected: BranchId,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct BranchNodePm {
    pub id: BranchId,
    pub title: String,
    pub state: BranchStatePm,
    pub children: Vec<BranchNodePm>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct PlanPm {
    pub nodes: Vec<PlanNodePm>,
    pub selected: Option<Arc<str>>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct ChangeReviewPm {
    pub candidate_id: Option<Arc<str>>,
    pub operations: Vec<ChangeOperationPm>,
    pub diagnostics: Vec<DiagnosticPm>,
    pub can_promote: bool,
}

The application-facing port should distinguish queries, durable event subscription and commands:

// scriberig-ui/src/port.rs

use async_trait::async_trait;
use futures_core::Stream;
use std::{pin::Pin, sync::Arc};

pub type UiEventStream =
    Pin<Box<dyn Stream<Item = Result<UiEventEnvelope, UiError>> + Send>>;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct EventCursor(pub u64);

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct UiEventEnvelope {
    pub cursor: EventCursor,
    pub session_revision: u64,
    pub event: UiEvent,
}

#[async_trait]
pub trait ScriberigUiPort: Send + Sync {
    async fn snapshot(&self, session: &SessionId)
        -> Result<UiSnapshot, UiError>;

    async fn dispatch(
        &self,
        command: UiCommand,
    ) -> Result<CommandReceipt, UiError>;

    async fn subscribe(
        &self,
        session: &SessionId,
        after: Option<EventCursor>,
    ) -> Result<UiEventStream, UiError>;
}

The significant detail is that rpi-tui itself should not acquire Tokio as a requirement just because Scriberig is asynchronous. A shell task bridges async application events into a synchronous TUI inbox:

pub enum TuiMessage {
    Snapshot(UiSnapshot),
    Event(UiEventEnvelope),
    CommandAccepted(CommandReceipt),
    CommandFailed {
        command_id: String,
        message: String,
    },
    Disconnected,
}

pub enum TuiIntent {
    SelectBranch(BranchId),
    SubmitPrompt(String),
    CancelInvocation,
    SelectPlanNode(String),
    SelectSemanticItem(String),
    AcceptCandidate(String),
    RejectCandidate(String),
    RunCommand(CommandId),
}

sequenceDiagram
    participant Key as Terminal input
    participant Panel as Active panel
    participant Store as UiStore
    participant Bridge as Async bridge
    participant App as ScriberigUiPort
    participant Core as Scriberig domain

    Key->>Panel: normalized event
    Panel->>Store: local focus/scroll update
    Panel->>Bridge: TuiIntent
    Bridge->>App: dispatch(UiCommand)
    App->>Core: validated domain command
    Core-->>App: committed transition
    App-->>Bridge: CommandReceipt
    Core-->>App: durable UiEvent
    App-->>Bridge: event stream
    Bridge-->>Store: TuiMessage::Event
    Store-->>Panel: updated projection
    Panel-->>Key: next rendered frame

The panels should share a tiny interface. The exact adapter can conform to the selected rpi-tui::Component API; Scriberig's side should remain independent of upstream signatures:

pub trait ScriberigPanel {
    fn id(&self) -> PanelId;

    /// Presentation-state update only; never performs domain mutations.
    fn sync(&mut self, snapshot: &UiSnapshot);

    /// Returns a semantic intent. The shell owns dispatch.
    fn handle(&mut self, event: &UiInput) -> Option<TuiIntent>;

    /// Render into our small abstraction, later translated to rpi-tui lines.
    fn render(&self, width: usize, height: usize) -> Vec<UiLine>;
}

A simple PlanView might look like:

pub struct PlanView {
    model: PlanPm,
    selected: usize,
    scroll: usize,
}

impl ScriberigPanel for PlanView {
    fn id(&self) -> PanelId {
        PanelId::Plan
    }

    fn sync(&mut self, snapshot: &UiSnapshot) {
        self.model = snapshot.plan.clone();
        self.selected = self.selected.min(
            self.model.nodes.len().saturating_sub(1)
        );
    }

    fn handle(&mut self, event: &UiInput) -> Option<TuiIntent> {
        match event {
            UiInput::Down => {
                self.selected =
                    (self.selected + 1)
                        .min(self.model.nodes.len().saturating_sub(1));
                None
            }
            UiInput::Up => {
                self.selected = self.selected.saturating_sub(1);
                None
            }
            UiInput::Enter => self.model.nodes
                .get(self.selected)
                .map(|node| TuiIntent::SelectPlanNode(node.id.to_string())),
            _ => None,
        }
    }

    fn render(&self, width: usize, height: usize) -> Vec<UiLine> {
        self.model
            .nodes
            .iter()
            .skip(self.scroll)
            .take(height)
            .map(|node| {
                UiLine::from_segments([
                    UiSegment::muted(status_glyph(node.state)),
                    UiSegment::plain(" "),
                    UiSegment::plain(truncate(&node.title, width.saturating_sub(2))),
                ])
            })
            .collect()
    }
}

Then a small translation layer converts UiLine to rpi-tui's native text representation. This extra translation may seem redundant, but it buys us the ability to replace the entire terminal foundation without changing a single semantic panel.

The required panel responsibilities should be sharply separated:

Panel Projection owned Local UI state Emits SessionTreeView recursive session/branch structure, branch status/result summary expanded nodes, cursor, scroll select/focus/fork/navigate branch BranchActivityView ordered human/model/operation/result activity scroll, follow-tail, collapsed entries submit input, inspect event, cancel PlanView plan nodes, dependency/blocking state, results selection, filters select/run/cancel plan action ModelInvocationView provider/model, lifecycle, usage, tool/operation calls, continuation detail tabs, scroll cancel, inspect invocation SemanticSelectionView symbols/schema entities/context selection search/filter/check state add/remove semantic context ChangeReviewView candidate operations, semantic diff, diagnostics/validation selected operation, diff mode validate/promote/reject CommandPalette applicable commands generated from capabilities/context query, selected row typed UiCommand

The relationship should be:

classDiagram
    class ScriberigUiPort {
        +snapshot(session)
        +dispatch(command)
        +subscribe(session,cursor)
    }

    class UiStore {
        +UiSnapshot snapshot
        +EventCursor cursor
        +apply(event)
    }

    class PanelHost {
        +focus
        +layout
        +handle(input)
        +render()
    }

    class SessionTreeView
    class BranchActivityView
    class PlanView
    class ModelInvocationView
    class SemanticSelectionView
    class ChangeReviewView
    class CommandPalette
    class RpiTuiAdapter

    ScriberigUiPort --> UiStore
    UiStore --> PanelHost
    PanelHost *-- SessionTreeView
    PanelHost *-- BranchActivityView
    PanelHost *-- PlanView
    PanelHost *-- ModelInvocationView
    PanelHost *-- SemanticSelectionView
    PanelHost *-- ChangeReviewView
    PanelHost *-- CommandPalette
    PanelHost --> RpiTuiAdapter

The crucial distinction between domain state and interaction state should remain explicit:

Domain / durable                  UI-local / disposable
────────────────────────          ─────────────────────────
selected active branch            scroll offset
branch results                    focus
plan execution state              expanded/collapsed rows
candidate migration               palette query
validation result                 cursor position
model invocation history          selected tab
semantic selection                hover state
session revision                  visual animation state

Nothing in the right column should need to be persisted as part of Scriberig's semantic session except deliberately chosen user preferences.

For streaming output, do not append raw token strings directly to terminal state forever. Keep an in-progress projection keyed by invocation/message ID:

pub enum UiEvent {
    ModelStarted { invocation: InvocationPm },
    ModelDelta {
        invocation_id: String,
        sequence: u64,
        text: String,
    },
    ModelCompleted {
        invocation_id: String,
        final_message: MessagePm,
    },
    BranchChanged { branch: BranchPm },
    PlanChanged { plan: PlanPm },
    CandidateChanged { change: ChangeReviewPm },
}

The store folds deltas into the current projection. The TUI renderer receives a coherent state snapshot. The browser follows the same event semantics.

docs.title: TypeScript and React web application
docs.text:
The web application should not be a second Scriberig implementation. It should be a second adapter around the same application interface.

The clean structure is:

Rust
├── scriberig-core
├── scriberig-ui
├── scriberig-protocol
└── scriberig-server
        │
        ├── REST/HTTP commands + snapshots
        └── SSE event stream
              │
TypeScript    ▼
└── scriberig-web
    ├── src/api/
    ├── src/state/
    ├── src/panels/
    ├── src/components/
    └── src/routes/

I recommend HTTP for queries/commands plus SSE for the authoritative server→client event stream rather than starting with WebSockets.

Scriberig interaction is overwhelmingly asymmetric: the server streams model output, diagnostics and session state; the client occasionally sends a command. HTTP gives command requests clear authorization, idempotency and observability; SSE gives ordered reconnectable streaming with Last-Event-ID. WebSockets should be added only if later requirements genuinely require high-frequency bidirectional data.

The minimal API should resemble:

Method Endpoint concept Purpose GET /api/v1/sessions list resumable sessions POST /api/v1/sessions create session GET /api/v1/sessions/{id}/snapshot complete presentation snapshot GET /api/v1/sessions/{id}/events?after=… SSE ordered event feed POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/commands dispatch typed UI/domain command GET /api/v1/sessions/{id}/branches/{id} optional detailed branch projection GET /api/v1/capabilities feature/provider/server capabilities GET /api/v1/health liveness/readiness without sensitive session information

The command envelope should support retries safely:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
pub struct CommandEnvelope {
    pub command_id: uuid::Uuid,       // idempotency key
    pub expected_revision: Option<u64>,
    pub command: UiCommand,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
pub struct EventEnvelope<T> {
    pub sequence: u64,
    pub session_revision: u64,
    pub timestamp: time::OffsetDateTime,
    pub payload: T,
}

Client synchronization then becomes deterministic:

connect
  │
  ├─ GET snapshot
  │     revision = 418
  │     event_cursor = 9812
  │
  └─ subscribe events after 9812
          │
          ├─ 9813
          ├─ 9814
          └─ disconnect
                │
                └─ reconnect after 9814

If the cursor has fallen outside server retention, the server returns a “snapshot required” condition and the client atomically refreshes.

In React, the network layer can be small:

export interface UiSnapshot {
  revision: number;
  cursor: number;
  session: SessionTreePm;
  branchActivity: BranchActivityPm;
  plan: PlanPm;
  invocation: ModelInvocationPm | null;
  semanticSelection: SemanticSelectionPm;
  changeReview: ChangeReviewPm;
}

export interface EventEnvelope<T extends UiEvent = UiEvent> {
  sequence: number;
  sessionRevision: number;
  payload: T;
}

export interface ScriberigClient {
  snapshot(sessionId: string): Promise<UiSnapshot>;

  command(
    sessionId: string,
    command: UiCommand,
    expectedRevision?: number
  ): Promise<CommandReceipt>;

  subscribe(
    sessionId: string,
    after: number,
    onEvent: (event: EventEnvelope) => void,
    signal: AbortSignal
  ): Promise<void>;
}

The React store should use exactly the same reducer logic conceptually as the Rust UiStore:

export function applyUiEvent(
  state: UiSnapshot,
  envelope: EventEnvelope,
): UiSnapshot {
  if (envelope.sequence <= state.cursor) {
    return state; // duplicate after reconnect
  }

  const next = reducePayload(state, envelope.payload);

  return {
    ...next,
    cursor: envelope.sequence,
    revision: envelope.sessionRevision,
  };
}

A web PlanView consequently remains almost embarrassingly simple:

type Props = {
  plan: PlanPm;
  onSelect: (id: string) => void;
};

export function PlanView({ plan, onSelect }: Props) {
  return (
    <section aria-label="Plan">
      <header>
        <h2>Plan</h2>
      </header>

      <ol>
        {plan.nodes.map((node) => (
          <li key={node.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              onClick={() => onSelect(node.id)}
              aria-current={plan.selected === node.id}
            >
              <span aria-hidden="true">
                {statusGlyph(node.state)}
              </span>
              <span>{node.title}</span>
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ol>
    </section>
  );
}

The recommended frontend library set is deliberately conservative:

Need Recommendation Build/application shell React + TypeScript + Vite unless routing/SSR requirements justify a larger framework Server query cache TanStack Query Small ephemeral UI state Zustand or plain React context/reducer API type generation OpenAPI → openapi-typescript, or a Rust-side generator if Scriberig standardizes on one Runtime boundary validation Zod where generated/static typing cannot protect network input Markdown react-markdown, with raw HTML disabled; sanitize if HTML support is later enabled Syntax highlighting Shiki or another renderer that returns controlled markup Virtualized long activity/session lists TanStack Virtual Accessible primitives Radix UI where useful, but keep Scriberig styling independent Graph visualization lightweight custom SVG first; a React graph package only for genuinely interactive plan DAGs Tests Vitest + React Testing Library, plus Playwright for reconnect/auth/streaming scenarios

The server should produce an OpenAPI contract for request/response endpoints and a versioned schema for event payloads. Type generation should happen in CI so Rust and TypeScript cannot silently drift.

Authentication depends on deployment mode.

For local desktop/developer mode, default to a Unix-domain socket for TUI access where possible, or loopback-only HTTP with an ephemeral high-entropy token. Do not expose an unauthenticated service on 0.0.0.0.

For remote/team mode, use an external OIDC provider with Authorization Code + PKCE. A browser-facing deployment should prefer a secure, HttpOnly, SameSite session cookie rather than handing a durable bearer token to JavaScript. Mutating cookie-authenticated endpoints need CSRF protection. Authorization should be checked server-side against workspace/project/session capabilities, not merely hidden in the UI.

The security boundary is:

flowchart TB
    Browser["Browser — untrusted presentation client"]
    Auth["OIDC / authenticated session"]
    API["Scriberig Server"]
    ACL["Project/session authorization"]
    App["Application commands"]
    Semantic["Semantic operation layer"]
    Store["Sessions / candidates / revisions"]
    Provider["External model providers"]

    Browser --> Auth
    Auth --> API
    API --> ACL
    ACL --> App
    App --> Semantic
    Semantic --> Store
    App --> Provider

    Provider -. "untrusted model text" .-> API
    API -. "escaped structured events" .-> Browser

Most importantly, neither the browser nor the TUI receives authority to bypass semantic operations simply because it can formulate an arbitrary command. The command enum should represent allowed application actions. There should be no generic remote “execute Rust method,” “write arbitrary persistence record,” or hidden raw-shell escape masquerading as an API.

Tau and rpi validate the broader architectural direction: both demonstrate the value of separating the interactive terminal client from the long-lived execution/runtime owner. citeturn6search2turn6search1

docs.title: Masterplan, milestones, risks, and rollback strategy
docs.text:
The implementation should be incremental enough that Scriberig never enters a state where completing the TUI rewrite is necessary to keep the product usable.

Assuming roughly two to three engineers, a reasonable program is several engineering months rather than a multi-quarter terminal-framework project. The uncertainty lies mostly in Scriberig's semantic projections and remote protocol, not in rendering.

Phase Outcome Effort Principal risk Rollback Foundation intake Pin rpi-tui, license/provenance manifest, compile minimal shell Low upstream/API mismatch remove vendor/dependency; no domain code touched Interaction parity editor, Markdown, key handling, selection, resize, clipboard policy, streaming demo Medium terminal edge cases retain existing CLI output path Presentation model scriberig-ui, snapshots, events, typed intents High leaking domain internals into UI keep facade additive; core remains unchanged Semantic panels all seven required views High hierarchy/layout becomes too complex panels individually feature-gated Durable synchronization revisions, idempotency, reconnect, event cursor High duplicate semantic effects disable remote mode; in-process port remains Server protocol versioned HTTP/SSE surface Medium/High auth/protocol churn keep server API experimental/versioned React application browser feature parity for core workflows High two surfaces drift shared contract + generated types + conformance fixtures Hardening/release fuzz/snapshot/e2e/security/accessibility/docs Medium obscure terminal/network failures release TUI/web as opt-in preview first

A practical timeline is:

gantt
    title Scriberig presentation modernization — illustrative, assuming 2–3 engineers
    dateFormat  YYYY-MM-DD

    section Foundation
    Upstream intake and provenance       :a1, 2026-10-26, 1w
    rpi-tui integration spike            :a2, after a1, 2w
    Terminal parity harness              :a3, after a1, 2w

    section Shared UI model
    Presentation projections             :b1, after a2, 3w
    Event and command contracts           :b2, after a2, 3w

    section Terminal
    Session and activity panels           :c1, after b1, 3w
    Plan and model panels                 :c2, after b1, 3w
    Semantic and change panels            :c3, after c1, 3w
    Command palette and polish            :c4, after c2, 2w

    section Remote architecture
    Protocol and reconnect semantics      :d1, after b2, 3w
    Authentication and authorization      :d2, after d1, 2w

    section Web
    React shell and generated client      :e1, after d1, 2w
    Web semantic panels                   :e2, after e1, 4w
    Streaming and reconnect UX            :e3, after e1, 3w

    section Release
    Security and portability hardening    :f1, after c3, 3w
    Cross-surface conformance             :f2, after e2, 2w

These dates are illustrative, not a delivery commitment. Parallel work is intentional.

The foundation milestone should have a brutally simple success criterion: an executable that uses the selected upstream editor/Markdown/select/terminal machinery without importing rpi-agent, rpi-harness, or provider types. If that cannot be achieved cleanly, abort the choice and run the same adapter against tape_tui.

The presentation milestone is more important than feature polish. A fixture should be able to load a UiSnapshot from JSON and render every TUI panel without initializing a provider, database, parser or server. That is the point at which the architecture is genuinely decoupled.

The cross-surface conformance milestone should replay the same recorded sequence:

Snapshot R100
Event 501: branch started
Event 502: model started
Event 503: model delta
Event 504: semantic operation proposed
Event 505: candidate created
Event 506: validation completed
Event 507: model completed

against both the Rust UiStore and TypeScript reducer and assert equivalent final presentation state. This will be worth far more than large numbers of widget-specific mocks.

For rendering tests, use golden fixtures for tree rails, narrow widths, Unicode, RTL/CJK where supported, large Markdown, malformed Markdown, enormous unbroken tokens and resize sequences. rpi's deterministic/offline testing philosophy is a good precedent here. citeturn6search1 pi-rs is also useful as a behavioral corpus because its product explicitly exercises IME, scrolling, copy selection, resumable trees and multiple presentation modes. citeturn6search0

The principal architectural risks and mitigations are:

Upstream churn. rpi is active, which is both positive and a source of API risk. citeturn6search1 Pin a commit, put it behind scriberig-tui-kit, and upgrade intentionally rather than continuously.

Accidental agent-semantic contamination. The easiest path during implementation will sometimes be to copy ToolCallComponent or session structures wholesale. Resist it. Only terminal-generic types cross the vendor boundary.

Event-model overengineering. Do not turn every hover/focus change into a durable event. Durable events correspond to authoritative Scriberig state; UI state stays local.

Remote side-effect replay. This is the most dangerous correctness failure. Use command UUIDs, optimistic-concurrency revisions and durable command receipts. pi-rs's explicit refusal to blindly replay interrupted side-effecting operations is the right conceptual precedent. citeturn6search0

Plugin enthusiasm. Both rpi and pi-rs demonstrate sophisticated plugin capabilities, while Tau offers sandboxed subprocess plugins. citeturn6search1turn6search0turn6search2 Scriberig does not need to solve that problem in the TUI migration. Defer a public plugin ABI until the semantic capability model is stable.

Browser security. Provider/model output is attacker-controlled text from the perspective of a renderer. Never use React dangerouslySetInnerHTML for model Markdown. Sanitize links and any future HTML extension. Do not put provider credentials in the browser.

Supply-chain/provenance drift. Every copied upstream file must remain attributable to its precise source/revision. This is especially important if code is selectively taken from more than one Pi-derived implementation.

OxiCode/PiG uncertainty. These should not block the project because neither is needed for the preferred design. Before any code is copied from them, perform a fresh license, path and revision audit. For PiG in particular, first identify the repository unambiguously.

The master rollback architecture is deliberately simple:

                    ScriberigUiPort
                    /            \
                   /              \
         old CLI/text path      new presentation
                                  /       \
                            rpi-tui       web

As long as all new presentation work hangs below ScriberigUiPort, we can replace rpi-tui, disable remote mode, postpone the React application, or revert individual panels without changing Scriberig's semantic core.

The final recommendation is consequently more precise than “clone Pi in Rust”:

Do not clone Pi. Do not fork an entire coding agent. Pin and reuse rpi-tui as presentation infrastructure, with tape_tui as the fallback/reference; mine full rpi and pi-rs for recovery and UX patterns; mine Tau for transport and plugin-isolation architecture; keep Scriberig's session, plan, semantic-operation, candidate, validation and promotion machinery entirely Scriberig-owned.

That allocates engineering effort to the layer where Scriberig can actually differentiate, while reusing the terminal engineering that the Rust/Pi ecosystem has already paid for.

docs.title: Semantic Plan Entities, Evidence, Gates, and Recoverable Execution
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document refines 018. durable plans dependency scheduling and multi-model execution.md so durable planning follows the same universal semantic identity, revision, snapshot, relation, and derived-knowledge rules as the rest of Scriberig.

It does not replace the session tree, dependency DAG, coordinator model, branch isolation, or shared application-operation model from earlier designs.

The controlling rule is:

A Plan, PlanNode, gate, dependency, summary, and execution attempt are semantic knowledge with stable identities and exact revisions where their meaning requires independent history. A plan is not canonically stored as one opaque aggregate containing mutable vectors of all nodes and edges.

A second rule is:

Scriberig has one plan-node lifecycle vocabulary. Do not introduce a parallel PlanNodeWorkState or another user-visible state machine merely to represent rollups.

The lifecycle remains conceptually:

Planned
Ready
Running
Completed
Failed
Abandoned

Lower-level designs may refine exact Rust names, but they must preserve this single-state-model principle.

docs.title: 2. Relationship to Existing Plan Design
docs.text:
018 remains authoritative for:

  • the distinction between structural decomposition and dependency scheduling;
  • result-based dependency fulfillment;
  • one auto-advancing coordinator per plan;
  • many concurrent workers on independent branches;
  • per-node execution assignment;
  • branch isolation and compact BranchResult handoff;
  • explicit replanning and durable history;
  • cross-surface plan semantics.

This document is authoritative where it refines 018 on:

  • canonical persistence shape;
  • independent plan-node identity and revisioning;
  • plan summaries;
  • evidence;
  • gates;
  • derived parent/subtree status;
  • ignored/abandoned descendants;
  • recoverable failure;
  • execution-attempt history;
  • incremental status materialization.

If older implementation documents describe the complete plan as a serialized Plan { nodes: Vec<PlanNode>, dependencies: Vec<...> } persistence unit, that representation is transitional and not the target architecture.

docs.title: 3. Plans and Plan Nodes Are Ordinary Semantic Entities
docs.text:
A plan has stable semantic identity:

Plan P

Each node has its own independent stable semantic identity:

PlanNode N1
PlanNode N2
PlanNode N3

Each meaningful canonical mutation creates a new immutable revision of the affected entity while preserving stable identity.

For example:

N2@R1  status = Planned
N2@R2  status = Ready
N2@R3  status = Running
N2@R4  status = Failed
N2@R5  status = Ready
N2@R6  status = Running
N2@R7  status = Completed

The surrounding plan does not need a new semantic revision merely because a child node received a new content revision unless the plan's own canonical fields changed.

The current exact world remains fixed by a snapshot that resolves stable entity identities to revisions.

docs.title: 4. A Plan Is a Semantic Root, Not a Container Blob
docs.text:
The plan entity owns plan-level meaning such as:

identity
session / continuation anchor association
goal
plan lifecycle
coordinator policy/reference
coordinator cursor/reference when canonical
default policy or assignment references

The plan must not canonically embed the complete mutable graph as opaque fields equivalent to:

nodes: Vec<PlanNode>
dependencies: Vec<PlanDependency>
history: Vec<PlanRevision>

Instead, plan topology is represented by semantic entities, collections, and relations.

Conceptually:

Plan P
  --contains--> N1
  --contains--> N2
  --contains--> N3

N1 --decomposes_to--> N1a
N1 --decomposes_to--> N1b

N3 --depends_on--> N1
N3 --depends_on--> N2

Exact relation storage belongs to lower-level design.

docs.title: 5. Structural Decomposition and Dependency Scheduling Remain Distinct
docs.text:
The following structures must never be collapsed:

Session tree:
Goal -> Branch -> Child Branch -> BranchResult

Plan structural tree:
PlanNode -> child PlanNode

Plan dependency DAG:
PlanNode -> depends_on -> PlanNode

Structural child relations mean decomposition/context ownership/provenance.

Dependency relations mean scheduling constraints.

Adding a child must not silently invent a dependency edge between arbitrary siblings.

Likewise, adding a dependency must not silently reparent either node.

docs.title: 6. Plan Dependencies Need Independent History When They Carry State
docs.text:
A dependency may carry meaning beyond a bare graph edge, including:

prerequisite
dependent
required result contract
fulfilled_by exact result reference
optional/required policy when later supported
provenance

When that state needs independent revision/history/provenance, represent the dependency as a first-class revisioned relation or semantic entity rather than hiding it in one node's payload.

The target model is conceptually:

PlanDependency D7
  prerequisite -> N1
  dependent -> N3
  required_result -> Contract C
  fulfilled_by -> BranchResult BR42

A failed or abandoned prerequisite does not fulfill a successful dependency unless an explicit dependency/gate policy says otherwise.

docs.title: 7. Keep One PlanNodeStatus Vocabulary
docs.text:
Do not create a second lifecycle concept such as:

PlanNodeWorkState
Planned / Implementing / Stalled / Ignored

Use the existing plan-node lifecycle vocabulary for execution/scheduling semantics:

Planned
Ready
Running
Completed
Failed
Abandoned

Reasons and annotations refine a status without creating a second state machine.

For example:

Abandoned
  reason = Ignored

Abandoned
  reason = Superseded

Abandoned
  reason = Cancelled

Failed
  failure = exact attempt/result/evidence reference

The exact reason vocabulary may evolve independently.

docs.title: 8. Direct Status and Subtree Presentation Use the Same Status Vocabulary
docs.text:
A node's canonical revision records its own lifecycle state.

A product surface often needs the effective state of the complete structural subtree rooted at that node.

That subtree state is a derived projection, not a second lifecycle model. It uses PlanNodeStatus values and is rebuildable from exact node/relationship revisions.

Conceptually:

PlanNodeView
  node
  direct_status: PlanNodeStatus
  effective_status: PlanNodeStatus
  contains_ignored: bool
  contains_abandoned: bool
  child counts
  unsatisfied gate counts

effective_status and aggregate flags are derived/cache data. They must not participate in the canonical revision identity of the node merely because descendants changed.

A backend may materialize these values for efficient reads.

docs.title: 9. Effective Status Rollup
docs.text:
The derived rollup must be deterministic and backend-independent.

The default precedence is:

1. explicitly Abandoned node -> Abandoned
2. any required self/descendant Failed -> Failed
3. any self/descendant Running -> Running
4. any executable self/descendant Ready -> Ready
5. any unresolved self/descendant Planned -> Planned
6. completion policy and completion gates satisfied -> Completed

The precise treatment of optional descendants is controlled by their gate/dependency policy, not by presentation order.

A descendant abandoned because it was ignored does not automatically make the parent Abandoned.

Instead the parent exposes a derived flag:

contains_ignored = true

Likewise a generic:

contains_abandoned = true

may be exposed when useful.

The rollup rule may be extended later, but all backends and product surfaces must consume the same semantic definition.

docs.title: 10. Incremental Rollup Is Derived Knowledge
docs.text:
Reading the status of a top-level plan node must not require recursively walking every descendant every time.

Backends may maintain materialized child-status counts or equivalent derived indexes:

planned_children
ready_children
running_children
completed_children
failed_children
abandoned_children
ignored_descendants

When one descendant changes, the backend may update only the affected ancestor chain and stop when an ancestor aggregate no longer changes.

Typical update complexity should be proportional to tree depth rather than total subtree size.

Database triggers are an allowed backend implementation when the database has suitable normalized/indexed rows to react to.

However:

trigger behavior is an optimization of a backend-neutral semantic rule, not the semantic definition itself.

An in-memory backend, SQLite backend, server cache, or future database must produce equivalent effective status.

Derived rollups are rebuildable and excluded from canonical identity computation.

docs.title: 11. Summary Is First-Class Plan Knowledge
docs.text:
A plan node should support a concise current summary independent of its purpose and final result.

Keep these concepts distinct:

purpose
  what the node is intended to accomplish

summary
  compact current understanding/progress/state

result
  durable outcome produced by successful execution

The preferred target is a normal semantic Summary entity/relation rather than permanently embedding an unversioned string inside every plan node.

Conceptually:

PlanNode N
  --summarized_by--> Summary S

A generated summary should identify the exact node/child/result revisions it summarizes so staleness can be determined precisely.

Do not deterministically concatenate child summaries into a parent summary. Status rollup is deterministic; semantic summarization is interpretive derived knowledge.

docs.title: 12. Evidence Is Referential and Exact
docs.text:
Plan work may accumulate evidence before, during, and after execution.

Evidence should normally reference existing durable semantic objects rather than copy opaque blobs into the plan node.

Evidence sources may include:

BranchResult
ValidationResult
Decision
Candidate / Migration / Workspace
EntityRevision
Snapshot
Artifact
HumanApproval
ExternalObservation
structured failure result

Evidence associations may carry a small typed role such as:

Supports
Contradicts
Informational

Conceptually:

PlanNode N
  --supported_by--> ValidationResult V1
  --contradicted_by--> ValidationResult V2

If the association itself needs independent author/provenance/history/waiver semantics, represent that association as a first-class relation/entity.

Evidence must remain exact-revision/snapshot aware where the source is versioned.

docs.title: 13. Gates Are Independent Semantic Requirements
docs.text:
A gate expresses a condition that must be satisfied before a node may enter a phase or be considered complete.

A gate has independent identity because it may be inspected, revised, evidenced, failed, or waived.

Conceptually:

PlanGate G
  owner -> PlanNode N
  phase = Entry | Completion
  requirement = typed requirement
  waiver = optional explicit waiver

Initial typed requirements should remain simple and queryable, for example:

ValidationPassed(profile/reference)
EvidencePresent(kind)
DecisionResolved(decision)
HumanApproval(policy/role)
SemanticCondition(reference/predicate)
RequiredChildCompleted(child)

Do not begin with a general arbitrary Boolean-expression language.

Gate evaluation state is normally derived from canonical gate definition plus exact evidence:

Pending
Satisfied
Failed
Waived

A waiver is canonical knowledge and must retain who/what authorized it, why, and the relevant exact revision/provenance.

Do not make a gate disappear merely because it was waived.

docs.title: 14. Dependencies and Gates Serve Different Purposes
docs.text:
Dependencies express ordering/readiness relationships between independently schedulable plan nodes.

Gates express requirements on one node's entry or completion.

Do not duplicate every dependency as a gate.

The default readiness concept is:

Ready(node) =
  direct node state permits execution
  AND all required dependencies are fulfilled
  AND all entry gates are satisfied or explicitly waived
  AND no active claim owns the node
  AND execution policy permits dispatch

The default completion concept is:

Completed(node) =
  required result contract is satisfied
  AND all completion gates are satisfied or explicitly waived

A failed dependency remains a failed dependency; a gate must not silently reinterpret it as success.

docs.title: 15. Decomposition May Create Completion Obligations
docs.text:
Creating a structural child does not itself create a dependency edge.

However, decomposition often means the parent cannot truthfully complete until required child work is complete.

The semantic operation that decomposes a node should therefore distinguish required and optional child work.

For required decomposition, the operation should normally create or update a completion obligation equivalent to:

RequiredChildCompleted(child)

For optional/informational decomposition, no such completion obligation is required.

This keeps structural parentage distinct from dependency scheduling while preventing a parent from silently reaching Completed with known required child work unfinished.

docs.title: 16. Failed Is Recoverable
docs.text:
Failed records that the current execution path/attempt did not satisfy the node.

It is not semantic destruction of the intended work.

A failed node may later:

Failed -> Ready -> Running -> Completed

through an explicit retry/repair/resume operation.

Recovery must not erase the failed attempt or its evidence.

A failed node continues to block success dependencies until a later accepted successful result fulfills them or the plan is explicitly revised/waived according to policy.

The same principle applies at plan level:

Plan Failed

means automatic progress stopped and explicit recovery/replanning is required. It is recoverable.

Only plan states equivalent to completed success or explicit cancellation/abandonment should be treated as irreversible terminal outcomes by ordinary mutation guards.

docs.title: 17. Execution Attempts Preserve Failure and Retry Provenance
docs.text:
Once failure is recoverable, a durable plan node may have more than one execution attempt.

The node identity represents intended work.

Each attempt represents one concrete execution lineage.

Conceptually:

PlanNode N
  --attempted_by--> Attempt A1
  --attempted_by--> Attempt A2

Attempt A1
  branch -> B1
  claim/generation -> ...
  outcome = Failed
  failure/result evidence -> ...

Attempt A2
  branch -> B2 or resumed B1 according to policy
  outcome = Completed
  result -> BR2

The existing session branch and execution records may provide most attempt provenance. Lower-level design should avoid inventing redundant objects when a typed relation to existing branch/claim/result entities is sufficient.

The requirement is durable attempt history, not a specific extra Rust struct.

docs.title: 18. Normal Plan Evolution Is Not Replanning
docs.text:
A running plan is expected to grow as work reveals more work.

Ordinary plan evolution may include:

add next step
add structural child/decomposition
add dependency
add gate
attach evidence
update summary
change assignment before execution
retry failed node

These operations do not require the plan to enter a special failed/paused replan mode merely because new knowledge was discovered.

Replanning is reserved for structural replacement/invalidation such as:

supersede obsolete work
remove or replace dependencies after changed assumptions
replace failed strategy with a different strategy
perform broader restructuring

The current coordinator/mutation mechanism remains the owner of plan change authorization and concurrency.

docs.title: 19. Keep the Existing Plan Mutation/Coordinator Mechanism
docs.text:
Independent storage does not mean callers mutate plan objects directly in the database.

Shared semantic/application operations remain the mutation boundary.

Existing concepts equivalent to:

add_node
add_dependency
set_assignment
start/claim node
settle worker
retry failed node
complete node
replan

remain useful domain operations.

Their implementation changes from mutating one in-memory aggregate for persistence to producing one atomic semantic change set over the independently stored plan entities/relations.

One accepted mutation may update:

one Plan revision when plan-level state changed
one or more PlanNode revisions
relation/dependency/gate/evidence revisions
execution-attempt/result references
derived rollup/index state
current snapshot/root

The operation remains atomic at the application/storage transaction boundary.

docs.title: 20. Plan Mutation Revision Remains Useful
docs.text:
A plan may retain a monotonic mutation/coordinator revision used for:

compare-and-swap
coordinator concurrency
client stale-write detection
operation ordering
inspection/debugging

That revision is not the same thing as serializing a full copy of every node and dependency into the plan entity.

Historical exact state is obtained from semantic revisions, relation history, change provenance, and snapshots.

A lightweight plan mutation record may summarize why a plan changed without duplicating the whole graph.

docs.title: 21. Storage and Indexes Must Remain Backend-Neutral
docs.text:
Canonical plan knowledge belongs in the universal semantic revision/snapshot store.

Backend-specific tables/indexes may accelerate:

plan membership lookup
parent/child lookup
dependency traversal
ready-node lookup
active claim lookup
gate lookup/evaluation
rollup counts
contains_ignored / contains_abandoned

Those indexes are derived/rebuildable unless a lower-level design explicitly identifies canonical relation state.

Do not make SQLite table layout part of the public semantic API.

docs.title: 22. Product Views Consume Shared Plan Views
docs.text:
CLI, server, Rust client, web, integrated editor, TUI, and agents must consume the same plan semantics.

A shared plan-node view may expose concepts equivalent to:

node identity
exact revision
parent identity
direct status
effective subtree status
contains_ignored / contains_abandoned
summary reference/preview
assignment reference
branch/attempt references
dependency counts/blockers
gate counts/failing gates
evidence counts/result references

Product surfaces do not recompute semantic rollups from visual rows.

docs.title: 23. TUI Builds on the Upstream-First RPI Design
docs.text:
Any terminal implementation of these plan semantics must build on the design in:

  • design/level-2/032. upstream first agent runtime and terminal product ownership correction.md;
  • design/level-3/148. rebuild scriberig semantic session plan and review surfaces as upstream tui components.md.

The plan surface remains a Scriberig semantic component because upstream cannot know Scriberig plan meaning.

It must render through upstream rpi-tui component/layout/focus/overlay/scroll/theme contracts after task 148 establishes that product framework.

Do not introduce a parallel Ratatui shell, plan-only widget framework, terminal lifecycle, or plan-local event runtime.

Useful plan presentation includes:

direct/effective status
contains ignored/abandoned indicator
summary
blocked dependency reason
failing/pending gates
evidence/result counts
execution attempts and current branch
coordinator location

Detail inspection should use upstream component/overlay/navigation primitives around shared Scriberig views and operations.

docs.title: 24. Migration from Aggregate Session Plan Storage
docs.text:
The current implementation may temporarily store complete sessions/plans as serialized aggregates.

Migration to semantic entities must preserve existing stable plan/node identities and accepted results where possible.

During transition:

  1. choose one authoritative representation for each operation path;
  2. avoid uncontrolled dual-write semantics;
  3. provide deterministic import/upgrade of legacy plan aggregates;
  4. prove restart/reconnect preserves topology, statuses, results, and coordinator safety;
  5. remove aggregate plan persistence after semantic-store conformance is proven.

Compatibility serialization may remain at protocol boundaries as a projection. It must not remain canonical storage merely because older clients expect aggregate DTOs.

docs.title: 25. Non-Negotiable Summary
docs.text:
Future designs and implementations must preserve these rules:

  1. Plan and PlanNode have stable independent semantic identities.
  2. Meaningful node changes create immutable node revisions resolved by snapshots.
  3. The complete plan graph is not canonically one opaque serialized aggregate.
  4. Structural decomposition and dependency scheduling remain distinct relations.
  5. Dependency state with history/provenance is first-class relation/entity state.
  6. There is one PlanNodeStatus lifecycle vocabulary; no parallel work-state enum.
  7. Effective parent/subtree status uses the same status vocabulary and is derived/rebuildable.
  8. Derived rollups and ancestor counters do not contaminate canonical revision identity.
  9. Backends may use triggers/materialized indexes for incremental ancestor updates.
  10. Nodes support first-class summaries distinct from purpose and result.
  11. Evidence references exact durable semantic objects.
  12. Gates are typed independent requirements with explicit evidence and waivers.
  13. Dependencies and gates remain distinct concepts.
  14. Required decomposition normally creates an explicit completion obligation rather than an implicit dependency.
  15. Failed is recoverable; retries preserve prior failure provenance.
  16. Failed work never silently satisfies successful dependencies.
  17. Normal plan growth while running is ordinary evolution, not automatically a replan.
  18. Existing coordinator/application mutation semantics remain the only normal write path.
  19. Plan mutation revision may remain a CAS/coordinator mechanism without embedding the whole graph.
  20. All product surfaces consume shared semantic plan views/operations.
  21. TUI work extends the upstream-first rpi-tui design and task 148 rather than competing with it.

docs.title: Projection Styles, Personalized Representations, and Materialization Policy
1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig treats source files and other familiar representations as projections of canonical semantic knowledge. 006. projections and bidirectional editing.md already establishes that style is an explicit projection input and that the same semantic object may be rendered in several styles without becoming several semantic objects.

This document refines that principle for personalized source-code presentation, shared filesystem materialization, style discovery, comments and other selectively visible content, and editable projections whose chosen style intentionally omits canonical information.

The central rule is:

A user's preferred representation of canonical knowledge is not itself a mutation of that knowledge, and a user's private presentation preferences must not silently become the shared materialization policy of a project.

A second rule is:

Style is allowed to change representation, including intentional omission of safely omittable presentation content, but it must not silently perform semantic program transformations or erase canonical knowledge.

This document refines rather than replaces:

  • level-1/002. universal knowledge model.md;
  • level-1/003. identity revisions and snapshots.md;
  • level-1/005. changes migrations branches and merge.md;
  • level-1/006. projections and bidirectional editing.md;
  • level-1/007. domain modeling and adapters.md;
  • level-1/011. runtime libraries protocol and product surfaces.md;
  • level-1/019. semantic agent operations and projection-first editing.md.

For terminal-product integration this document is additionally constrained by the active RPI adoption work, especially level-2/032. upstream first agent runtime and terminal product ownership correction.md.

docs.title: 2. Canonical Knowledge and Representation Preferences Are Separate
docs.text:
Consider one exact semantic TypeScript module M in snapshot S.

Two users may legitimately prefer:

User A
  indentation: 2 spaces
  line width: 100
  ordinary comments: visible

User B
  indentation: 4 spaces
  line width: 120
  ordinary comments: hidden

Both users may view the same module at the same time:

M@S + Style A -> projection A
M@S + Style B -> projection B

The semantic identity and semantic revision of M do not change merely because the rendered bytes differ.

Style changes may invalidate derived projection caches. They do not, by themselves, create program migrations.

The architecture must therefore avoid any hidden equation of:

current user style == current project source state

or:

rendered bytes changed == semantic code changed

docs.title: 3. Style Is Exact Semantic Configuration
docs.text:
A style that affects deterministic output must resolve to an exact immutable input before rendering.

Conceptually:

StyleProfile
  stable conceptual identity
  immutable revisions
  domain/projection applicability
  domain-defined properties

Examples of code-style properties may include:

indentation kind
indentation width
maximum line width
quote preference
semicolon policy
trailing-comma policy
brace/layout policy
comment visibility/presentation policy

The universal projection layer must not define the meaning of these properties. A Rust adapter, ECMAScript adapter, Markdown adapter, or another domain owns the properties that are meaningful for that domain and projection kind.

Before rendering, the selected style must become an exact resolved value or immutable style revision so that rendering, caching, synchronization, and later reconciliation can identify precisely what produced the representation.

docs.title: 4. Generic Style Identity and Domain Style Semantics Are Different Responsibilities
docs.text:
Keep the following responsibilities separate.

The universal projection layer owns:

exact style identity/reference
exact resolved style input boundary
render/cache identity participation
style provenance sufficient for reproduction
projection synchronization association

A domain adapter owns:

style property schema
allowed values
default values
normalization
property merging where supported
rendering semantics
whether a property is safe for editable projections
whether a style is lossless or lossy for a projection kind

Application/product layers may own:

which profile is selected for a user/view/workspace
precedence between applicable style sources
persistence of user preferences
repository/workspace materialization policy
cross-surface commands and discovery

The TUI, web application, CLI, and server do not independently implement source-language formatting rules.

docs.title: 5. Style Schemas Must Be Discoverable
docs.text:
A client should not need hard-coded knowledge that TypeScript supports two-space indentation while another projection supports unrelated settings.

Projection/domain capabilities should make style options discoverable enough that shared application surfaces can answer questions equivalent to:

what style schema applies to this projection?
what properties are supported?
what are their allowed values/defaults?
which properties affect editability or fidelity?
what style is currently resolved?
where did each resolved choice come from?

The exact lower-level schema is defined by Level 2.

A client may present a specialized opinionated editor for a known schema, but generic clients must still be able to inspect and select style configuration without becoming the owner of domain semantics.

docs.title: 6. Style Resolution Has Purpose
docs.text:
A style is not selected in a vacuum. Resolution must know why a projection is being produced.

At minimum distinguish:

InteractiveView
SharedMaterialization
ExplicitExport

Additional purposes such as agent context or diagnostic rendering may be added when their semantics require them.

The distinction matters because a user's private display preference must not automatically affect shared external artifacts.

docs.title: 7. Interactive View Resolution
docs.text:
For an ordinary personal view, the preferred conceptual precedence is:

domain defaults
    < repository/project conventions
    < user preferences
    < explicit view override
    -> ResolvedViewStyle

A domain may reject or diagnose incompatible combinations instead of blindly merging arbitrary properties.

This ordering permits Alice and Bob to inspect the same exact semantic snapshot through different source representations without either user's preference mutating the project.

View-local changes such as choosing two spaces instead of four should normally be presentation state. They must not move a session reply anchor, change a branch, rerun a model invocation, alter a plan, or create a code migration.

docs.title: 8. Shared Filesystem Materialization Resolution
docs.text:
Shared checked-out files have a different purpose.

The preferred conceptual precedence is:

domain defaults
    < repository/project conventions
    < workspace/materialization policy
    -> ResolvedMaterializationStyle

Personal user view preferences are deliberately absent from the default path.

Therefore opening a project as User A must not rewrite shared .ts, .rs, or .md files into User A's preferred layout, followed by User B rewriting the same files into User B's layout.

A user may explicitly request an export using a personal style, but that is an explicit export/materialization action with an explicit target and policy. It is not an incidental consequence of looking at the project.

docs.title: 9. Repository Conventions Are Inputs, Not Accidental Canonical Truth
docs.text:
Existing ecosystems contain style/configuration sources such as:

.editorconfig
rustfmt.toml
Prettier configuration
Biome configuration
language/tool-specific formatter settings

Scriberig should be able to interpret applicable conventions through domain/configuration adapters.

When Scriberig understands such configuration, the architectural direction is:

external convention source
  -> parse/interpret
  -> domain style candidate or policy input
  -> resolve to exact Scriberig projection style

The raw external file does not automatically become a privileged global variable read by renderers.

All output-affecting settings must still become declared exact render inputs.

If a project intentionally treats an external configuration artifact as authoritative input, that relationship must be explicit and synchronized under the normal projection/import rules rather than hidden inside renderer process state.

docs.title: 10. Style and Semantic Transformation Must Remain Distinct
docs.text:
Ordinary representational differences include things such as:

2 versus 4 spaces
line wrapping
spacing
brace layout
quote spelling where the language semantics are unchanged
presentation of safely representable comments

Style must not silently choose a different semantic or author-significant program construct merely because two constructs currently behave similarly.

For example, a formatter/style must not silently turn one control-flow form into another semantic syntax choice when that choice belongs to canonical authoring structure.

If a transformation should change canonical semantic/syntactic structure, represent it as an explicit semantic operation and migration, not as a style side effect.

docs.title: 11. Comment Policy Is Typed, Not a Single Boolean
docs.text:
strip_comments: true is too coarse for a semantic projection system.

Comments and comment-like source elements may include materially different categories:

ordinary explanatory comments
documentation comments
license/header comments
lint directives
compiler/type-check directives
formatter directives
source-map/tooling directives
generated-code markers
other domain-specific directives

A domain adapter must classify the categories it understands and define which projection treatments are safe.

A style may request policies such as:

Show
HideInProjection
RenderAsLineComment
RenderAsBlockComment
PreserveRequiredForm

but the adapter may reject a requested treatment when it would change program/tool behavior, violate policy, or lose author-significant structure.

For example, a TypeScript suppression directive is not equivalent to an ordinary explanatory comment merely because both use comment syntax.

A license header may be semantically irrelevant to program execution while still being mandatory for legal/materialization policy.

The style system must preserve these distinctions.

docs.title: 12. Lossy Projection Is Different from Semantic Deletion
docs.text:
A projection is lossy when canonical knowledge intentionally exists but is not represented in that projection.

For example:

canonical module
  Comment C
  Statement S

style hides ordinary comments

rendered projection
  Statement S

The absence of C from the rendered representation is not evidence that C was deleted from canonical knowledge.

This becomes critical when the projection is editable.

If the user edits the visible statement, reconciliation must not interpret all style-hidden entities as deletions.

Therefore:

An editable lossy projection requires a loss-aware reconciliation contract. If the adapter cannot provide one, the lossy projection must be read-only.

This is a capability/fidelity decision for the exact resolved style, not merely for the projection kind in the abstract.

docs.title: 13. Editable Reconciliation Is Bound to the Exact Baseline Projection
docs.text:
For editable projections, Scriberig must retain enough information to know exactly what the user was shown when editing began or when the external file was last synchronized.

Conceptually a reconciliation baseline includes:

semantic base snapshot
semantic scope
projection specification
exact resolved style
renderer version
exact rendered output identity/content reference
adapter version
projection-to-semantic mapping metadata when required
visibility/loss metadata when required

The purpose is to distinguish at least:

not present because the style omitted it

from:

was represented in the baseline and the user removed it

and from:

was concurrently changed in canonical state

A mere current parser result is insufficient for this distinction.

The existing base/current/external three-way model remains controlling; this document makes the exact baseline representation and its style part of the evidence supplied to reconciliation.

docs.title: 14. Fidelity and Editability Are Properties of the Resolved Projection
docs.text:
Do not assume that all styles for one projection kind have equal round-trip behavior.

For example:

TypeScript + full source style
  -> potentially lossless editable projection

TypeScript + hide ordinary comments
  -> lossy but potentially loss-aware editable projection

TypeScript + summary-only style
  -> likely read-only projection

A projection adapter should be able to describe a resolved projection as something equivalent to:

LosslessEditable
LossAwareEditable
ReadOnlyLossy

Exact names belong to Level 2.

Product surfaces should use this capability information rather than guessing from the selected style controls.

docs.title: 15. Materialization May Be Stricter Than Personal Viewing
docs.text:
A style can be acceptable for a private interactive projection while unacceptable for a shared source file.

Examples include:

  • hiding ordinary comments from a personal view while preserving them in checked-out source;
  • suppressing documentation in a compact personal view while materialization keeps documentation;
  • displaying semantic source using a preferred indentation width while repository files follow project policy.

Materialization policy may impose mandatory properties or categories that a personal view can override only locally.

This separation prevents personal presentation preferences from becoming repository churn or from violating repository/tool/legal requirements.

docs.title: 16. Style Resolution and Caching Must Be Reproducible
docs.text:
Rendering caches must include the exact resolved style and every other output-affecting input.

Changing user style should invalidate only projections whose output depends on that style. It must not invalidate semantic program identity or unrelated derived knowledge.

Where a style is composed from several sources, the renderer must receive an exact immutable resolved result rather than consult those mutable sources independently during rendering.

Provenance should remain inspectable so a user can understand why a style property has its current value.

Conceptually:

indent_width = 2
  from user profile "compact-typescript" revision R7

line_width = 100
  from repository policy revision R3

The exact provenance representation belongs to Level 2.

docs.title: 17. Source Projection Style Is Not Terminal Theme
docs.text:
The active terminal redesign delegates commodity terminal presentation to upstream rpi/rpi-tui according to Level-2 plan 032.

Keep these concepts distinct:

rpi-tui terminal theme/style
  -> colors, emphasis, layout primitives, terminal chrome

Scriberig projection style
  -> how canonical semantic code/document knowledge is represented

Upstream terminal theme machinery may render a source projection attractively. It must not become the authority for source indentation, comment visibility, repository materialization policy, or source projection reconciliation.

Conversely, Scriberig must not recreate a parallel terminal theme/widget system merely to expose projection-style selection.

A custom Scriberig source/projection component running on rpi-tui consumes projection results and shared style-selection/application contracts.

docs.title: 18. TUI, Web, CLI, Server, and Agents Share One Style Semantics
docs.text:
Product surfaces may offer different controls, layouts, and affordances, but they consume the same style-resolution and projection capabilities.

Do not implement separate rules such as:

TUI says user preference overrides repository
web says repository always wins
CLI reads formatter config directly
server ignores style provenance

Instead:

surface intent
  -> shared application style-selection/resolution operation
  -> exact resolved style
  -> projection adapter render/reconcile

Local/remote use must produce equivalent resolved style semantics from equivalent inputs.

Only state that genuinely belongs to one presentation instance, such as a temporary view override, remains presentation-local.

docs.title: 19. User Preference State Must Not Affect Execution Semantics Accidentally
docs.text:
Changing a personal projection style is presentation configuration unless the user explicitly requests a materialization/export policy change.

It must not by itself:

  • change canonical source entities;
  • create a code migration;
  • move a session navigation/reply/coordinator cursor;
  • change plan dependencies;
  • alter a model/provider assignment;
  • invalidate provider continuation;
  • rerun an agent/model operation;
  • rewrite shared files.

If an agent is explicitly supplied a styled projection as context, that exact projection becomes part of that invocation's declared context. Later UI style changes still do not retroactively alter the invocation.

docs.title: 20. Security, Policy, and Required Content
docs.text:
A projection style is not permission to bypass required content or trust policy.

Domains and materialization policies may mark some source elements as mandatory for a purpose.

Examples may include:

license notices
security annotations
generated-file warnings
compiler/lint directives required for the represented program
integrity markers required by an external format

A style resolver must surface an incompatibility when a requested style would violate such requirements instead of silently dropping them.

docs.title: 21. Conformance Requirements
docs.text:
The architecture should eventually prove at least the following cross-layer behaviors:

  1. The same semantic snapshot can be rendered under two different styles into different bytes while retaining the same semantic program identity.
  2. Changing style changes the render/cache identity but does not create a semantic content revision.
  3. Two users can concurrently view one semantic source scope using different styles.
  4. A user's private view style does not rewrite shared materialized files.
  5. Repository/materialization style remains deterministic and reproducible independently of the currently logged-in viewer.
  6. Style schemas and current resolved values are discoverable through shared application semantics.
  7. Domain adapters reject style settings they cannot safely support.
  8. Hiding safely omittable comments from a projection does not delete those comments from canonical state.
  9. A lossy editable projection reconciles against its exact baseline representation and exact style.
  10. A lossy style without loss-aware reconciliation is exposed as read-only.
  11. Local TUI and remote/web clients resolve equivalent style semantics through shared contracts.
  12. Terminal theme changes and source projection style changes remain independent.

docs.title: 22. Non-Goals
docs.text:
This document does not choose:

  • one universal formatter library;
  • a single style schema shared by all languages;
  • one UI layout for editing style properties;
  • whether TypeScript ultimately renders through Oxc, Biome, dprint, Prettier, or another implementation;
  • a database schema for user settings;
  • a filesystem watcher strategy;
  • exact Rust type names.

Those decisions belong in Level 2/3 or domain-specific implementation work.

docs.title: 23. Summary of Durable Invariants
docs.text:
The durable rules are:

canonical semantic content != rendered source bytes

style is an exact declared projection input

domain adapters own style meaning

personal view style != shared materialization style

renderer reads resolved style, not undeclared mutable globals

style may omit only content the domain/policy says is safe to omit

lossy editable projection -> loss-aware reconciliation
otherwise -> read-only

reconciliation is bound to exact baseline snapshot + style + renderer + output

source projection style != terminal theme

TUI/web/CLI/server share style semantics through application/projection contracts

These rules preserve the central Scriberig architecture: one canonical semantic knowledge world can support many simultaneous, purpose-specific representations without confusing representation preferences with semantic change.

docs.title: Compound Artifacts, Scalable Collections, and Rich Domain Editing
1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig is intended to edit structured project knowledge beyond source code and Markdown. Real projects may contain spreadsheets, rich documents, CAD drawings, geospatial datasets, QGIS projects, database-backed containers, and other artifacts whose logical structure is not equivalent to one text file.

This document extends the durable architecture in:

  • 001. vision and principles.md;
  • 002. universal knowledge model.md;
  • 003. identity revisions and snapshots.md;
  • 005. changes migrations branches and merge.md;
  • 006. projections and bidirectional editing.md;
  • 007. domain modeling and adapters.md;
  • 010. universal query and operation model.md;
  • 011. runtime libraries protocol and product surfaces.md;
  • 013. trust validation capabilities and provenance.md;
  • 014. extensibility ecosystem and licensing.md;
  • 019. semantic agent operations and projection-first editing.md;
  • 024. projection styles personalized representations and materialization policy.md.

It does not replace those documents. It defines the additional invariants needed when project knowledge is packaged, binary, spatial, very large, externally referenced, or only partially understood by Scriberig.

The central rule is:

Rich project artifacts are semantic domains over the same universal knowledge system. Their physical files, package members, database pages, external references, rendered canvases, and editor views are evidence or projections, not alternative canonical stores.

A second rule is:

Scriberig must be able to preserve exact external evidence and opaque author-significant content even when it understands only part of an artifact.

A third rule is:

Semantic addressability does not require eager one-record-per-object physical storage. Large tables, grids, feature sets, and drawings may use scalable indexed representations while remaining accessible through stable semantic handles and the universal query/change model.

docs.title: 2. Why Ordinary File Semantics Are Insufficient
docs.text:
The current file-oriented onboarding boundary is useful for discovery and source evidence, but richer formats expose several cases that cannot be modeled correctly as one path -> one independent editable blob.

Examples include:

.xlsx / .docx
  one ZIP package
  many related package parts
  relationships between parts
  semantic objects spanning several parts

.qgz
  one ZIP package
  project XML plus auxiliary members
  references to datasets outside the package

Shapefile dataset
  .shp + .dbf + .shx + .prj + optional sidecars
  several physical files represent one logical dataset

GeoPackage
  one SQLite file
  many logical vector/raster/attribute layers

DWG / DXF
  one drawing artifact
  many persistent drawing objects and cross references

The architecture therefore distinguishes physical source evidence from logical artifacts and their semantic contents.

docs.title: 3. External Artifact Is a Logical Boundary
docs.text:
Introduce the durable concept of an external artifact or equivalent semantic boundary.

Conceptually:

ExternalArtifact
  stable semantic identity
  artifact kind
  source evidence
  physical members
  logical parts
  external references
  adapter/schema identity
  synchronization/materialization policy
  provenance

The exact Rust type and storage layout belong in lower-level design.

An external artifact may correspond to:

  • one ordinary file;
  • one archive containing many package members;
  • several coordinated filesystem files;
  • one database/container file exposing many logical resources;
  • one project description that references independently owned datasets;
  • an externally hosted resource that is imported or synchronized under an explicit trust policy.

The artifact is not a second persistence system. It is semantic knowledge represented using the universal entity/revision/snapshot model.
