The reconciler must emit different semantic intent for content and collection changes.

Example:

before:
Section S -> [P1, P2]

candidate:
Section S -> [P1 changed, P3 inserted, P2]

Preferred result:

P1: new revision of same entity
P3: new entity
P2: reused unchanged entity
S: new structural revision because child collection changed

A changed paragraph must not force unrelated siblings to receive new identities.

docs.title: Formatting-only edits
docs.text:
If parsed candidate semantics are equivalent to the synchronization base/current semantic state, return NoSemanticChange.

The filesystem layer may rerender according to configured style and update synchronization state, but no semantic migration is created.

docs.title: Ambiguity
docs.text:
If continuity is uncertain, return structured ambiguity/conflict details containing candidate node, possible canonical matches, evidence, and affected parent/collection.

Do not silently select one identical paragraph over another when evidence is insufficient.

A conservative new entity is preferable to unsupported lineage, subject to collection reconciliation rules.

docs.title: Unrepresented knowledge
docs.text:
Markdown does not represent all relationships attached to document entities.

Editing a paragraph through Markdown must preserve unrelated canonical relations such as:

  • provenance;
  • decisions referring to it;
  • summaries;
  • citations represented elsewhere;
  • agent/session references.

The adapter therefore proposes changes only to semantic dimensions owned by the Markdown projection.

It must never rebuild the entire database state from the parsed file.

docs.title: Three-way reconciliation
docs.text:
When D != B, first derive semantic changes from B -> D and B -> C, then combine them through sr-change/domain-aware merge rules.

Disjoint block/entity changes should merge automatically.

Competing changes to the same paragraph/structure must produce structured conflict data rather than textual conflict markers as the canonical conflict representation.

A textual conflict view may be rendered later.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Before promotion, validate at least:

  • candidate document schema/structure;
  • renderer can render the proposed resulting document;
  • render-parse semantic equivalence of the resulting synchronized projection for supported constructs.

Invalid transient Markdown edits must not destroy the last valid canonical snapshot.

docs.title: Prescribed files
docs.text:
Implementation must create at least:

crates/sr-markdown/Cargo.toml
crates/sr-markdown/src/lib.rs
crates/sr-markdown/src/model.rs
crates/sr-markdown/src/candidate.rs
crates/sr-markdown/src/style.rs
crates/sr-markdown/src/parser.rs
crates/sr-markdown/src/render.rs
crates/sr-markdown/src/equivalence.rs
crates/sr-markdown/src/match_nodes.rs
crates/sr-markdown/src/reconcile.rs
crates/sr-markdown/src/diagnostic.rs
crates/sr-markdown/tests/round_trip.rs
crates/sr-markdown/tests/reconcile.rs
crates/sr-markdown/tests/file_sync.rs

Choose a mature CommonMark-compatible parser in implementation unless the repository has already standardized on another parser. The parser library choice is not part of semantic identity and must remain behind this crate.

docs.title: Edit a paragraph
docs.text:
Input semantic state contains P1 = "Objects are immutable.".

External Markdown changes only that paragraph to "Objects are immutable and content addressed.".

Expected: same paragraph entity, new revision, no unrelated structural churn.

docs.title: Insert a paragraph
docs.text:
External Markdown inserts a new paragraph between two unchanged paragraphs.

Expected: new entity for inserted paragraph; both unchanged neighbors retain identity; parent child collection gets a structural revision.

docs.title: Reformat only
docs.text:
Change list markers/spacing in a way defined as presentation-equivalent.

Expected: no semantic migration.

docs.title: Ambiguous duplicate paragraphs
docs.text:
Two equal paragraphs exist and an edit cannot be mapped confidently.

Expected: structured ambiguity instead of fabricated lineage.

docs.title: Concurrent edit
docs.text:
Database changes paragraph P1 while external file independently inserts P3 elsewhere.

Expected: automatic three-way merge when changes are disjoint.

docs.title: Invalid transient file
docs.text:
Parser cannot produce a valid supported candidate.

Expected: old canonical snapshot and synchronization base remain intact; diagnostics/retry state are retained.

docs.title: Completion criteria
docs.text: This design is satisfied when an ordinary Markdown file can be rendered from canonical document knowledge, edited with an external editor, parsed back into a candidate graph, reconciled without hidden IDs, converted into a semantic migration when meaning changed, treated as a no-op when only formatting changed, and rerendered as the new synchronization baseline.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document translates design/level-1/010. universal query and operation model.md into concrete Rust library boundaries and implementation contracts.

The Level 1 design defines one universal interaction grammar:

inspect
list
follow
find
query
diff
history
render
branch
apply
commit

This Level 2 design specifies where that grammar lives in the Rust workspace, the files required to implement it, the dependency boundaries between read-side queries and application operations, and the data structures that allow all later surfaces to share the same semantics.

This design intentionally does not define HTTP routes, CLI syntax, TypeScript packages, React hooks, TUI bindings, concrete agent tool schemas, authorization policy, or one database backend's indexes. Those are separate surface and persistence concerns.

The central implementation rule is:

scriberig-query owns reusable semantic read/query vocabulary; scriberig-app composes that vocabulary with history, projection, migration, validation, and branch services into the universal application-operation boundary.

docs.title: 2. Prerequisites and Existing Ownership
docs.text:
Before implementing this design, use the existing canonical workspace and crates described by:

  • design/level-1/002. universal knowledge model.md;
  • design/level-1/003. identity revisions and snapshots.md;
  • design/level-1/005. changes migrations branches and merge.md;
  • design/level-1/006. projections and bidirectional editing.md;
  • design/level-1/010. universal query and operation model.md;
  • design/level-2/001. workspace and package layout.md;
  • the Level 2 universal knowledge-model library design;
  • the Level 2 change/history design;
  • the Level 2 projection design.

The implementation must reuse the established equivalents of:

EntityId
RevisionId
SnapshotId
TypeId / EntityTypeId
RelationTypeId
CollectionTypeId
MigrationId
ProjectionId
StyleId

Do not redefine those identifiers inside the query or application crates.

The implementation must also reuse the established graph, change/history, and projection abstractions rather than introducing alternate persistence, branch, migration, diff, history, or render systems.

If a prerequisite crate has not been implemented yet, create only the files owned by this design that can compile against the agreed public contracts. Do not invent a duplicate substitute crate merely to make this lineage self-contained.

docs.title: 3. Files Prescribed by This Design
docs.text:
Within crates/scriberig-query/, create or extend:

Cargo.toml
src/lib.rs
src/handle.rs
src/scope.rs
src/pagination.rs
src/detail.rs
src/inspect.rs
src/traverse.rs
src/find.rs
src/query.rs
src/result.rs
src/error.rs

tests/universal_read_model.rs

Within crates/scriberig-app/, create or extend:

Cargo.toml
src/lib.rs
src/service.rs
src/request.rs
src/result.rs
src/capability.rs
src/operation.rs
src/error.rs

tests/universal_operation_model.rs

If one of these files already exists because workspace bootstrapping or another design created the crate skeleton, extend the existing file instead of creating a parallel module.

Do not create protocol, CLI, server, TUI, agent-runtime, or web files as part of this Level 2 design.

docs.title: 4. Dependency Direction
docs.text:
The intended dependency direction is:

scriberig-core
     |
     +--> scriberig-schema
     |
     +--> scriberig-store
              |
              v
        scriberig-graph
              |
              v
        scriberig-query
              |
              +-------------------+
                                  v
scriberig-migration ----------> scriberig-app
scriberig-projection ---------> scriberig-app
other domain/application -----> scriberig-app

s criberig-query must remain useful without:

  • an agent runtime;
  • an HTTP server;
  • CLI/TUI code;
  • React or TypeScript;
  • a concrete SQLite connection;
  • a specific domain adapter.

scriberig-app is allowed to depend on reusable domain-independent subsystems and later selected domain adapters, but no foundation crate may depend on scriberig-app.

docs.title: 5. Handle Types
docs.text:
src/handle.rs defines semantic references used by read operations.

The implementation should provide lightweight wrappers or enums for the Level 1 concepts:

EntityRef
RevisionRef
SnapshotRef
RelationRef
CollectionRef
ProjectionRef
OperationRef

Where an existing crate already owns the underlying identifier, the handle should wrap or reuse that type rather than duplicate identity semantics.

A useful exact object target is conceptually:

EntityAtRevision {
    entity: EntityId,
    revision: RevisionId,
}

A snapshot-resolved entity target is conceptually:

EntityInSnapshot {
    entity: EntityId,
    snapshot: SnapshotId,
}

The public API may choose a smaller unified enum if that produces clearer call sites.

The important invariant is that the caller can distinguish:

  • conceptual entity identity;
  • exact immutable revision identity;
  • snapshot-relative entity resolution.

docs.title: 6. Selection and Projection Anchors
docs.text:
The query crate should define a transport-neutral semantic selection model.

Conceptually:

Selection {
    snapshot: SnapshotId,
    entity: EntityId,
    revision: Option<RevisionId>,
    relation_path: Vec<RelationStep>,
    projection_anchor: Option<ProjectionAnchor>,
}

ProjectionAnchor must be extensible enough to represent opaque domain/projection-specific anchors without making line numbers, byte ranges, DOM nodes, or page rectangles canonical identity.

This type exists so later UI, editor, TUI, and agent layers can refer to one semantic selection.

Do not add UI toolkit types to the query crate.

docs.title: 7. Query Scope
docs.text:
src/scope.rs defines explicit search/query scope.

The model must support at least:

Snapshot
EntitySubtree / Entity
ExplicitEntitySet

Domain adapters may later expose named semantic scopes such as project, module, document, section, session, or branch as typed wrappers or expansions.

Every find and query request must carry a resolved SnapshotId, either supplied by the caller or resolved by scriberig-app before execution.

The query layer must never silently switch snapshots during one operation.

docs.title: 8. Pagination
docs.text:
src/pagination.rs defines bounded traversal without exposing storage-specific cursors.

Provide concepts equivalent to:

PageRequest {
    limit,
    continuation
}

Page<T> {
    items,
    next
}

The continuation token should be opaque at this layer.

The public contract must not expose SQL offsets, row IDs, B-tree keys, or backend-specific cursor structure.

The implementation may initially use a simple internal representation, but callers must treat it as opaque.

All potentially large list, follow, find, and query results should be representable as pages.

docs.title: 9. Progressive Detail
docs.text:
src/detail.rs defines a small transport-neutral vocabulary for progressive disclosure.

At minimum support concepts equivalent to:

Identity
Compact
Structure
Full

Do not hard-code domain-specific levels such as FunctionGroups or PdfLayout into the universal enum.

Domain-specific views are advertised separately.

The query result may also expose an optional InformationCost estimate, for example bytes, approximate tokens, item counts, or another coarse measure. Cost is advisory, not a correctness requirement.

docs.title: 10. Inspection Model
docs.text:
src/inspect.rs defines the universal orientation result.

An inspection result should be capable of carrying:

subject handle
resolved snapshot
resolved revision
entity type
short description
selected important properties
counts
available relations
available collections
available views
available operations
provenance summary
information-cost hints

The result must not require every field to be present for every domain.

Unknown or partially adapted resources must still be inspectable with whatever metadata is available.

Inspection is intended to be compact by default.

Do not make inspect return an unrestricted full graph dump.

docs.title: 11. Traversal Model
docs.text:
src/traverse.rs defines universal list and follow requests/results.

list is for a declared collection owned by or associated with an entity.

follow is for a typed relation.

Both must:

  • operate against one exact snapshot;
  • return semantic handles;
  • preserve relation/collection type information;
  • support bounded pagination;
  • return compact navigation entries by default;
  • distinguish canonical relations from derived relations when that information is available.

A navigation entry should support at least:

handle
type
short label/description
optional count/summary metadata

Do not force domain adapters to serialize full entity bodies merely to list children.

docs.title: 12. Discovery Model
docs.text:
src/find.rs defines find as a discovery operation.

The request must include:

scope
snapshot
search text or search expression
strategy
limit/page

Supported strategies should be extensible rather than a closed promise that every backend implements every strategy.

Initial universal strategy identifiers may include equivalents of:

ExactText
Token
StructuredName
Semantic
DomainSpecific(String)

A result hit must resolve to a semantic handle whenever possible and may additionally contain:

score/rank
preview
projection anchor
provenance / derivation metadata

The query layer should permit backends/domain indexes to declare unsupported strategies cleanly.

docs.title: 13. Structured Query AST
docs.text:
src/query.rs defines a declarative serializable query AST.

The AST must represent the Level 1 concepts without exposing SQL:

scope
type constraints
property predicates
relation traversal
collection membership
revision/snapshot constraints
ordering
limits

A reasonable initial shape is a small expression tree containing operations equivalent to:

All
TypeIs
PropertyEq
PropertyExists
Related
ContainedIn / MemberOf
And
Or
Not

plus explicit ordering and page/limit metadata outside the boolean expression.

Do not attempt to design a complete general-purpose query language in the first version.

The query AST should be:

  • clonable/debuggable;
  • serializable later without semantic redesign;
  • independent of one storage backend;
  • extensible by versioned domain predicates or query expansion rather than arbitrary SQL fragments.

The initial executor may support only a useful subset as long as unsupported nodes fail structurally and explicitly.

docs.title: 14. Result Types
docs.text:
src/result.rs defines common read-side result metadata.

Every result should be capable of reporting:

resolved snapshot
subject/scope
returned semantic handles
provenance where relevant
continuation where relevant
warnings/diagnostics where relevant

Results must be directly composable: handles returned by one operation should be valid inputs to later universal operations without reparsing display labels.

The result vocabulary should remain semantic rather than terminal/UI-specific.

docs.title: 15. Read-Side Errors
docs.text:
src/error.rs defines structured query/read failures.

The initial taxonomy should distinguish at least:

NotFound
WrongType / InvalidTarget
UnsupportedCapability
InvalidScope
InvalidQuery
InvalidContinuation
Ambiguous
SnapshotUnavailable
DerivedDataUnavailable
Internal

Every error should preserve operation context and relevant semantic handles where available.

Do not use unstructured strings as the only public failure representation.

Storage/driver errors may be retained as sources internally while being mapped to this semantic boundary.

docs.title: 16. Query Service Boundary
docs.text:
scriberig-query should expose a service trait or small set of traits that application code can implement over the established graph/store/index layers.

The read-side contract should cover equivalents of:

inspect
list
follow
find
query

diff, history, and render should not be reimplemented in scriberig-query if their canonical engines already belong to change/history and projection crates.

The query service should therefore be narrow enough that scriberig-app can compose it with those other systems.

docs.title: 17. Application Request Model
docs.text:
crates/scriberig-app/src/request.rs defines the transport-independent application request vocabulary.

Provide one enum or equivalent typed command model covering the universal grammar:

Inspect
List
Follow
Find
Query
Diff
History
Render
Branch
Apply
Commit

Each request must contain or resolve enough context to identify:

  • target/scope;
  • exact snapshot or branch base where required;
  • operation-specific options;
  • detail/profile request;
  • page request where relevant.

Do not add HTTP headers, command-line flags, terminal formatting, React state, or model-provider concepts.

docs.title: 18. Application Result Model
docs.text:
src/result.rs defines one corresponding application result vocabulary.

It should wrap the canonical result types produced by each subsystem rather than flattening them into strings.

Conceptually:

Inspect(...)
List(...)
Follow(...)
Find(...)
Query(...)
Diff(...)
History(...)
Render(...)
Branch(...)
Apply(...)
Commit(...)
OperationStarted(OperationRef)

All variants that describe canonical state must report the exact snapshot/revision/branch context used.

Later transports can serialize this model or map it to an equivalent wire model.

docs.title: 19. Capability Discovery
docs.text:
src/capability.rs defines descriptors advertised by inspect and other orientation results.

Provide transport-neutral descriptors equivalent to:

RelationCapability
CollectionCapability
ViewCapability
OperationCapability

Each descriptor should carry:

  • stable capability identifier/name;
  • short human-readable label/description;
  • applicability/target type information where practical;
  • whether the capability is canonical or derived where relevant;
  • optional cost/availability metadata;
  • enough metadata for later clients to formulate the next request without hard-coding every domain.

Domain adapters may register additional views and high-level operations.

High-level operations must still execute through the application/change boundary rather than bypassing branch/migration history.

docs.title: 20. Application Service
docs.text:
src/service.rs defines the shared application-operation boundary used later by CLI, server, TUI, web integration, agents, and third-party embedded callers.

The service composes existing engines:

inspect/list/follow/find/query -> scriberig-query

diff/history                 -> change/history subsystem

render                       -> scriberig-projection

branch/apply/commit          -> migration/change subsystem

The application service must not duplicate the algorithms owned by those subsystems.

It is responsible for cross-cutting behavior such as:

  • resolving an omitted current snapshot to one exact snapshot before execution;
  • preserving exact operation context;
  • normalizing structured application errors;
  • advertising applicable capabilities;
  • returning typed application results;
  • producing operation handles for work that is delegated as long-running.

docs.title: 21. Branch, Apply, and Commit Integration
docs.text:
The application crate does not own a second branch implementation.

Its Branch, Apply, and Commit request variants must adapt to the canonical change/migration subsystem defined elsewhere.

The application layer must preserve:

base snapshot
candidate snapshot/root
migration proposal
validation/conflict result
commit provenance

Apply does not advance the canonical named root.

Commit is the explicit promotion boundary.

If the change subsystem uses a workspace identifier rather than the word Branch, the application layer may adapt terminology without duplicating semantics.

docs.title: 22. Diff, History, and Render Integration
docs.text:
Diff and History must delegate to canonical history/change APIs.

Render must delegate to projection APIs.

The application result should preserve the domain-specific semantic result when available rather than converting everything to text.

For example, a semantic diff object should remain inspectable/renderable as structured data.

A raw textual diff is an optional rendering, not the core diff contract.

docs.title: 23. Structured Application Errors
docs.text:
crates/scriberig-app/src/error.rs maps lower subsystem failures into a transport-neutral application error taxonomy.

It must preserve at least these categories:

NotFound
InvalidRequest
UnsupportedCapability
Conflict
ValidationFailed
Ambiguous
PermissionDenied        # category only; policy is owned elsewhere
SnapshotUnavailable
OperationFailed
Internal

A structured error should carry relevant context such as:

operation kind
snapshot/branch
subject handles
candidate/conflicting handles
diagnostics
possible next capabilities where useful

Do not implement authorization policy here merely because the taxonomy includes PermissionDenied.

docs.title: 24. Long-Running Operation Handles
docs.text:
src/operation.rs defines the application-level representation of work that may outlive one immediate call.

The minimal lifecycle is:

Queued
Running
Completed
Failed
Cancelled

An operation record/handle should support:

OperationRef
kind
base snapshot/branch context
state
progress summary
produced result handles
diagnostics

This design defines the semantics, not an async scheduler or background worker implementation.

The application layer may return an immediate result for fast work or an OperationRef for delegated work without changing the meaning of the underlying operation.

docs.title: 25. Domain Extension Registration
docs.text:
The application/query boundary must allow domains to contribute:

  • relation descriptors;
  • collection descriptors;
  • specialized views;
  • find strategies;
  • query expansions/predicates;
  • high-level operations.

Do not implement domain behavior through a central match statement that must be edited for every future domain.

Use a registry/provider trait or another extensible mechanism.

Domain extensions may add convenience APIs but must ultimately consume universal handles and produce universal application/change results.

docs.title: 26. Conformance Tests
docs.text:
tests/universal_read_model.rs should verify at least:

  1. an entity-only reference is resolved against one exact snapshot;
  2. exact revision references remain stable across newer snapshots;
  3. inspect returns orientation metadata without requiring full content;
  4. list is bounded and returns a continuation when appropriate;
  5. follow preserves relation identity;
  6. find returns semantic handles;
  7. query can combine type and relation/property predicates;
  8. results from one operation can feed another directly;
  9. invalid continuation/scope/query errors are structured;
  10. unsupported capabilities fail explicitly rather than silently degrading.

tests/universal_operation_model.rs should verify at least:

  1. all eleven universal operations have application request/result representations;
  2. omitted current snapshot is resolved before execution and reported in the result;
  3. diff/history/render delegate to their owning subsystem interfaces;
  4. branch/apply/commit preserve explicit change semantics;
  5. apply does not promote a canonical root;
  6. commit is the only universal operation in this flow that may promote according to policy;
  7. inspection advertises available relations/views/operations;
  8. structured conflicts survive the application boundary;
  9. a long-running operation can be represented by OperationRef;
  10. no application result requires terminal/UI formatting to be useful.

Use memory/test doubles for graph, history, projection, and change services where possible. Do not make these conformance tests depend on SQLite.

docs.title: 27. Files Explicitly Not Created by This Design
docs.text:
Do not create or modify files under these areas solely for this design:

crates/scriberig-protocol/
crates/scriberig-server/
crates/scriberig-client/
crates/scriberig-cli/
crates/scriberig-tui/
crates/scriberig-agent-core/
crates/scriberig-agent-runtime/
web/

Those surfaces must later adapt the public scriberig-app semantics rather than defining competing operation models.

docs.title: 28. Completion Criteria
docs.text:
This Level 2 design is implemented when:

  • the universal handle, selection, scope, pagination, detail, and read-result vocabulary exists in scriberig-query;
  • inspect, list, follow, find, and structured query have reusable Rust contracts;
  • the query AST is semantic and storage-independent;
  • all canonical reads are bound to a resolved exact snapshot;
  • navigation results return reusable semantic handles;
  • progressive disclosure and capability discovery are represented in the public model;
  • scriberig-app exposes all eleven universal operations through one transport-independent application boundary;
  • diff/history/render and branch/apply/commit delegate to their canonical subsystems rather than being reimplemented;
  • conflicts and errors remain structured and referential;
  • long-running work has a universal operation-handle representation;
  • conformance tests prove composability and exact-state semantics;
  • no agent, CLI, server, TUI, or web-specific dependency is required to use these libraries.

docs.title: Application Operations, Protocol, and Runtime Boundaries
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document turns design/level-1/011. runtime libraries protocol and product surfaces.md into concrete Rust package boundaries and source-file responsibilities.

It complements design/level-2/001. workspace and package layout.md. That document establishes the overall monorepo shape; this document defines the runtime/application side that Level 1 intentionally left for Level 2.

The main implementation rule is:

Product surfaces are adapters over shared application operations. No product surface owns semantic business logic or bypasses the migration, validation, snapshot, and session models.

This document prescribes crate and source-file structure, but it does not define domain-specific behavior, database tables, web UI components, or a concrete HTTP framework.

docs.title: 2. Crates Added Above the Foundation
docs.text:
The Rust workspace must contain these runtime-facing packages in addition to the foundational crates already defined elsewhere:

crates/
├── scriberig-app/
├── scriberig-protocol/
├── scriberig-client/
├── scriberig-agent-core/
├── scriberig-agent-runtime/
├── scriberig-server/
├── scriberig-tui/
└── scriberig-cli/

apps/
└── scriberig/

These packages have distinct independent-use boundaries.

docs.title: scriberig-app
docs.text:
Owns user-visible application operations and orchestration over the knowledge platform.

It may depend on reusable semantic libraries and domain adapters, but not on server, CLI, TUI, remote client, or agent-runtime packages.

docs.title: scriberig-protocol
docs.text:
Owns the stable transport-facing contract.

It contains serializable references, requests, results, errors, operations, events, capability discovery, and protocol compatibility metadata.

It must not depend on server implementation details or expose persistence-backend structures.

docs.title: scriberig-client
docs.text:
Owns the reusable Rust remote client.

It depends on scriberig-protocol and transport support only. It must not depend on scriberig-server internals.

docs.title: scriberig-server
docs.text:
Adapts remote requests onto scriberig-app operations and converts results/events into scriberig-protocol forms.

The server is a transport host, not a semantic implementation.

docs.title: scriberig-agent-core
docs.text:
Owns reusable agent-facing adapters such as tool contracts, progressive-disclosure views, capability exposure, and context-input interfaces.

It composes application/session operations and must not access storage internals directly.

docs.title: scriberig-agent-runtime
docs.text:
Owns integrated model execution and orchestration.

It depends on scriberig-agent-core and the shared application/session layers. Lower layers must never depend on it.

docs.title: scriberig-tui
docs.text:
Owns terminal interaction and presentation over application operations or a public client boundary.

It must not own semantic mutations.

docs.title: scriberig-cli
docs.text:
Owns command parsing, command dispatch, human-readable terminal output, and selection of executable modes.

It must remain thin.

docs.title: apps/scriberig
docs.text:
Owns the final executable entry point and composition root.

It wires concrete implementations together but should contain almost no business logic.

docs.title: 3. Required Dependency Direction
docs.text:
The runtime crates must preserve this dependency direction:

foundation/domain crates
        |
        v
  scriberig-app
     /      \
    v        v
protocol   agent-core
   |          |
   v          v
client   agent-runtime
   |
   +------------------+
                      |
app + protocol ------> server
app/client ----------> tui
app/server/tui/
agent-runtime -------> cli
cli -----------------> apps/scriberig

More precisely:

  • scriberig-app may depend on scriberig-core, graph/query/migration/projection/session crates, and selected domain adapters.
  • scriberig-protocol may depend on scriberig-core for stable identifier/value types, but not on scriberig-app internals.
  • scriberig-client depends on scriberig-protocol.
  • scriberig-server depends on scriberig-app and scriberig-protocol.
  • scriberig-agent-core depends on scriberig-app, scriberig-session, and small shared types as required.
  • scriberig-agent-runtime depends on scriberig-agent-core and the application/session layers.
  • scriberig-tui may use either direct scriberig-app access for local mode or scriberig-client for remote mode; its presentation code must not be imported by lower layers.
  • scriberig-cli may compose app, server, TUI, client, and agent-runtime crates.
  • apps/scriberig depends on scriberig-cli and composition-only dependencies.

Cycles are forbidden.

docs.title: 4. scriberig-app Source Layout
docs.text:
Create the application crate with a small stable public surface and internal operation modules.

Target structure:

crates/scriberig-app/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs
    ├── error.rs
    ├── context.rs
    ├── query.rs
    ├── command.rs
    ├── operation.rs
    ├── event.rs
    └── capability.rs

Responsibilities:

  • context.rs: explicit snapshot, actor, capability, and request context passed to operations.
  • query.rs: application-level read operations such as inspect, list, follow, find, diff, and history.
  • command.rs: application-level state-changing operations such as branch, apply, reconcile, validate, merge, and commit.
  • operation.rs: stable identity and lifecycle for long-running work.
  • event.rs: application events that notify consumers without becoming authoritative state.
  • capability.rs: capability discovery and operation availability.
  • error.rs: semantic error categories shared by embedded callers and adapters.

The exact function names may evolve, but the query/command distinction and snapshot-aware context are required.

docs.title: 5. Queries and Commands
docs.text:
Application operations must distinguish reads from canonical-state-changing commands.

Queries include concepts equivalent to:

inspect
list
follow
find
query
diff
history

Commands include concepts equivalent to:

create branch
apply migration
reconcile projection
validate candidate
commit branch
merge branches
update projection configuration
start agent command

Expensive queries may populate derived caches but must not advance canonical snapshots merely because they ran.

Commands that can conflict must carry an explicit base snapshot or branch context.

docs.title: 6. Application Errors
docs.text:
Application errors must be machine-readable enums or equivalent structured values, not free-form text categories.

The application layer must be able to represent at least these semantic classes:

not found
schema violation
stale base snapshot
semantic conflict
validation failure
permission denied
unsupported operation
projection out of sync
operation cancelled
internal failure

Adapters may attach human-readable messages and transport metadata, but they must preserve the semantic category.

docs.title: 7. Operation Lifecycle
docs.text:
Long-running work is represented through stable OperationId values.

The application layer must provide a common lifecycle equivalent to:

queued
running
completed
failed
cancelled

An operation record/result must carry enough information to associate it with:

  • operation kind;
  • requester/provenance;
  • input snapshot or branch;
  • status;
  • progress where meaningful;
  • final result reference;
  • diagnostics or structured failure.

Streaming is an observation mechanism over this lifecycle, not a separate result model.

docs.title: 8. Events
docs.text:
The application event model should include semantic notification categories equivalent to:

snapshot changed
entity changed
projection changed
branch changed
migration created
operation started
operation progressed
operation completed
validation completed
agent output produced

Events should normally contain stable handles and concise metadata.

Consumers that need full state resolve it through normal query operations.

Event payloads must not become a second canonical representation of entities or snapshots.

docs.title: 9. scriberig-protocol Source Layout
docs.text:
Target structure:

crates/scriberig-protocol/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs
    ├── version.rs
    ├── refs.rs
    ├── request.rs
    ├── response.rs
    ├── error.rs
    ├── operation.rs
    ├── event.rs
    └── capability.rs

The protocol crate owns the public wire contract, not server routing.

The protocol should contain transport-neutral serializable values for:

  • entity/revision/snapshot references;
  • request and correlation IDs;
  • query and command requests;
  • typed summaries and results;
  • structured errors;
  • operation states and results;
  • runtime events;
  • capability discovery;
  • protocol version/compatibility metadata.

It must not expose SQLite row IDs, database page numbers, table names, or private application structs.

docs.title: 10. One Authoritative Wire Contract
docs.text:
The Rust protocol crate is the authoritative contract for the first implementation.

It must be possible to derive a machine-readable schema from the public protocol types and use that schema to generate or validate non-Rust client types.

Do not manually maintain an independently invented TypeScript wire model.

The exact generator/tool is an implementation decision, but these outputs must be reproducible from the authoritative contract.

Generated artifacts should be treated as build outputs, while hand-written TypeScript convenience clients belong in the web/client design.

docs.title: 11. Protocol Versioning
docs.text:
scriberig-protocol must define a protocol version independent of the crate/package version.

The first protocol version may be 1.

The contract must support:

  • client/server protocol-version exchange;
  • explicit rejection of unsupported major versions;
  • additive capability discovery;
  • unknown capability tolerance where safe;
  • structured unsupported-operation errors.

Do not use application package version strings as the sole compatibility mechanism.

docs.title: 12. scriberig-client
docs.text:
Target structure:

crates/scriberig-client/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs
    ├── client.rs
    ├── transport.rs
    ├── operation.rs
    └── subscription.rs

The public client API should expose semantic methods rather than raw endpoint assembly.

Examples include concepts equivalent to:

inspect
query
diff
apply
operation status
cancel operation
subscribe
capabilities

Transport-specific implementation belongs behind an internal/public transport abstraction so tests can use an in-memory fake transport.

docs.title: 13. scriberig-server
docs.text:
Target structure:

crates/scriberig-server/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs
    ├── server.rs
    ├── transport.rs
    ├── dispatch.rs
    ├── operation.rs
    └── subscription.rs

The server has four responsibilities:

  1. authenticate/authorize when configured;
  2. decode protocol requests;
  3. invoke scriberig-app operations;
  4. encode results and deliver events/operation progress.

dispatch.rs must not contain semantic implementations that cannot be called without the server.

The concrete HTTP/streaming framework is intentionally deferred to a focused implementation task.

docs.title: 14. Agent Runtime Boundary
docs.text:
The agent layer uses the same application semantics.

Target package responsibilities:

scriberig-agent-core
  tool definitions
  progressive-disclosure adapters
  capability filtering
  structured context inputs

scriberig-agent-runtime
  model-provider execution
  tool loop
  session branch orchestration
  operation tracking
  cancellation

Agent tools may combine several application operations into one simpler tool, but all canonical mutations must still pass through application migrations/validation.

docs.title: 15. CLI, TUI, and Executable Boundary
docs.text:
scriberig-cli parses commands and selects modes.

scriberig-tui renders interactive terminal state and invokes public operations.

apps/scriberig is a composition root.

The executable should eventually be able to host concepts equivalent to:

serve
tui
run one-shot command
run agent command
maintenance command

The exact command spelling belongs in the implementation-level task.

No command handler may directly manipulate database tables.

docs.title: 16. Snapshot Awareness Across Boundaries
docs.text:
Important query results must identify the snapshot/revision under which they were resolved.

Commands must identify the base state when conflict detection matters.

Client caches must key semantic data by immutable revision/snapshot identity rather than only by EntityId.

The protocol must preserve enough context to distinguish:

resolve this entity as of snapshot S

from:

resolve the current revision of this entity

docs.title: 17. Capability Discovery
docs.text:
Both embedded and remote consumers need a way to discover available operations.

Capability discovery should be able to report:

  • runtime-supported operation families;
  • protocol capabilities;
  • domain-contributed operations;
  • renderer/validator availability;
  • permission-filtered actions for a request context.

A generic consumer must be able to inspect an unknown domain using universal operations even when specialized commands are absent.

docs.title: 18. Testing Boundary
docs.text:
Each layer needs its own tests, but user-visible capabilities also require cross-surface conformance tests.

At minimum:

  • scriberig-app tests operation semantics without a network;
  • scriberig-protocol tests round-trip serialization and version compatibility;
  • scriberig-client tests against a fake transport;
  • scriberig-server tests dispatch without duplicating semantic assertions;
  • vertical tests compare embedded and remote results for semantic equivalence.

A separate Level 2 design defines the capability matrix and conformance harness.

docs.title: 19. Implementation Order
docs.text:
Implement in this order:

  1. scaffold runtime-facing crates and dependency edges;
  2. implement protocol references, errors, operation lifecycle, events, and version metadata;
  3. implement the application operation context and one read-only capability (inspect) end to end;
  4. add server/client transport around that capability;
  5. expose the same capability through CLI and agent adapters;
  6. add operation/event streaming and cancellation;
  7. add further capabilities vertically rather than building one surface far ahead of the others.

Do not implement broad domain behavior in this sequence merely to populate APIs.

docs.title: 20. Completion Criteria
docs.text:
This Level 2 design is satisfied when:

  • the prescribed runtime crates exist;
  • dependency direction is acyclic and enforced by manifests;
  • application operations are distinct from transport and presentation;
  • the protocol has one authoritative Rust contract and machine-readable generation path;
  • errors, operations, events, capabilities, and protocol versioning are structured;
  • server and client are adapters over the same semantics;
  • the agent runtime cannot bypass application operations for canonical mutations;
  • CLI/TUI/executable packages remain thin product hosts;
  • at least one capability can be exercised equivalently in embedded and remote form;
  • conformance work can test semantic equivalence without depending on presentation text.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
design/level-1/011. runtime libraries protocol and product surfaces.md requires user-level capabilities to evolve vertically across product surfaces and requires explicit conformance testing.

This document defines the concrete planning and test artifacts used to enforce that rule.

The central principle is:

A capability is implemented once semantically, then exposed and verified across each relevant surface. Missing surfaces are visible and intentional.

This design prescribes a machine-readable capability matrix and a dedicated conformance-test crate.

docs.title: 2. Files and Package to Create
docs.text:
Create these repository artifacts:

capabilities.toml

crates/scriberig-conformance/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   └── lib.rs
└── tests/
    ├── inspect.rs
    ├── protocol.rs
    ├── operations.rs
    └── events.rs

scriberig-conformance is a test/support package, not a foundational runtime dependency.

It must be marked publish = false.

Production crates must not depend on it.

docs.title: 3. Capability Matrix Format
docs.text:
capabilities.toml is the project-visible source of truth for cross-surface capability coverage.

It is not a runtime authorization file and not part of canonical project knowledge.

Each capability entry must include:

id
description
semantic_owner
surfaces

Recommended form:

[[capability]]
id = "inspect_entity"
description = "Inspect an entity under an explicit snapshot or current-state request."
semantic_owner = "scriberig-app"

[capability.surfaces]
library = "implemented"
protocol = "implemented"
server = "implemented"
client = "implemented"
cli = "implemented"
tui = "planned"
web = "planned"
agent = "implemented"

Allowed status vocabulary for the first version:

not_applicable
planned
implemented
verified

Do not add arbitrary status strings.

A surface may be not_applicable only when the reason is clear from the capability description or a nearby comment.

docs.title: 4. Initial Surface Names
docs.text:
The matrix should use these keys consistently:

library
app
protocol
server
client
cli
tui
web
agent

library means the reusable semantic/domain implementation when one exists.

app means the shared application-operation layer.

The remaining names refer to product or transport exposure.

The matrix may gain surfaces later, but existing keys should not be renamed casually because tooling may consume them.

docs.title: 5. Initial Capability Entries
docs.text:
Do not attempt to enumerate the final product.

Start with capabilities required to validate the runtime architecture:

inspect_entity
runtime_capabilities
operation_status
operation_cancel
event_subscription

Only mark a surface implemented when code exists.

Only mark it verified when a conformance or dedicated surface test proves the expected semantics.

Planned work remains planned.

docs.title: 6. Conformance Crate Responsibility
docs.text:
scriberig-conformance verifies that different surfaces expose equivalent semantics.

It does not own implementations.

Its tests may depend on public APIs from:

  • scriberig-app;
  • scriberig-protocol;
  • scriberig-client;
  • scriberig-server;
  • scriberig-agent-core when agent exposure is under test;
  • test fixtures from foundational/domain crates.

Avoid depending on private module paths.

The conformance crate should exercise the same fixed test world through different adapters.

docs.title: 7. Fixed Test World
docs.text:
Create reusable test setup inside src/lib.rs or a later src/fixture.rs when complexity justifies it.

The fixture should provide:

  • a deterministic in-memory or temporary store;
  • one known snapshot;
  • a small set of known entities/revisions;
  • an application instance wired to that state;
  • a server adapter or in-process transport where needed.

The fixture must not require external network access.

Do not make tests depend on user configuration, model providers, or external services.

docs.title: 8. inspect.rs
docs.text:
This is the first vertical acceptance test.

Given one known entity and snapshot, compare:

embedded application inspect
server/client inspect
CLI-facing result model where callable without scraping terminal text
agent inspect adapter result where available

The test compares semantic fields, references, snapshot context, and error category.

It must not require byte-identical presentation strings.

If TUI or web exposure is not yet implemented, the matrix records planned; this test does not invent fake UI implementations.

docs.title: 9. protocol.rs
docs.text:
Protocol conformance tests verify:

  • public request/response round trips;
  • operation state serialization;
  • structured error serialization;
  • event serialization;
  • protocol version metadata;
  • unknown/additive field tolerance according to the chosen serializer contract;
  • generated schema reproducibility when schema generation exists.

The test should catch accidental changes to public wire meaning.

Do not snapshot private Rust debug output as the protocol contract.

docs.title: 10. operations.rs
docs.text:
Operation tests verify that one long-running operation has the same stable identity and terminal result regardless of how it is observed.

At minimum verify:

  • operation ID remains stable;
  • lifecycle does not regress from terminal to non-terminal;
  • cancellation uses a structured result/error;
  • final result remains queryable after streaming observers disconnect;
  • input snapshot/base context is retained.

Use a deterministic fake operation rather than an external model or compiler.

docs.title: 11. events.rs
docs.text:
Event conformance tests verify:

  • an application event can be exposed through the server/client path;
  • event identity/subject handles survive transport;
  • consumers can resolve authoritative state after receiving an event;
  • events do not contain an independently mutable copy of canonical entity state;
  • reconnect/resubscribe behavior can recover current state even if a live event was missed.

The exact streaming transport can change without invalidating the semantic test.

docs.title: 12. Matrix Validation
docs.text:
The conformance crate or a small test helper should parse capabilities.toml and validate:

  • capability IDs are unique;
  • only known surface names are used;
  • only known status values are used;
  • every capability has a semantic owner;
  • entries marked verified have a corresponding declared conformance test mapping once such automation is introduced.

The first implementation may keep the last rule manual if building a full mapping system would distract from the initial vertical slice.

docs.title: 13. Development Rule
docs.text:
When adding a user-visible capability:

  1. add or update the semantic/application implementation;
  2. add protocol representation when remote use is relevant;
  3. expose it through server/client;
  4. expose it through relevant product surfaces;
  5. add conformance coverage;
  6. update capabilities.toml in the same change.

A capability may intentionally remain unavailable on some surfaces, but the matrix must make that explicit.

docs.title: 14. Do Not Turn the Matrix Into Build Configuration
docs.text:
capabilities.toml describes product coverage.

It must not silently decide which crates compile or which server permissions are granted.

Runtime capability discovery is a separate protocol/application concern.

Authorization is a separate trust concern.

Build features are a package-management concern.

Keeping these concepts separate prevents a planning artifact from becoming hidden runtime state.

docs.title: 15. Completion Criteria
docs.text:
This design is satisfied when:

  • capabilities.toml exists and follows the fixed vocabulary;
  • scriberig-conformance exists as a non-published test/support crate;
  • the initial capability entries are present with truthful statuses;
  • one deterministic fixture can be exercised without external services;
  • inspect_entity has an end-to-end semantic-equivalence test once its surfaces exist;
  • protocol, operation, and event conformance tests use public interfaces;
  • production crates do not depend on scriberig-conformance;
  • every future user-visible capability has an obvious place in the matrix and conformance model.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document translates the Level 1 identity model into a concrete first Rust implementation.

It implements the identity substrate only:

  • stable entity identity;
  • immutable content-addressed revision identity;
  • immutable snapshot identity;
  • snapshot-scoped entity resolution;
  • persistent structural sharing between snapshots;
  • named mutable roots with compare-and-swap updates;
  • exact snapshot diffing.

It does not implement domain schemas, migrations, projections, agents, sessions, SQLite persistence, or network APIs. Those systems must build on the contracts defined here.

The implementation must preserve the Level 1 rule:

Stable semantic identity is local. Exact immutable state is revisioned. Global certainty is provided by snapshots.

docs.title: 2. First Implementation Boundary
docs.text:
The repository currently has no Rust workspace. This design creates the minimum reusable Rust foundation needed to exercise the identity model without committing the project to a database backend.

Create these files:

Cargo.toml

crates/
├── sr-core/
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   └── src/
│       ├── lib.rs
│       ├── ids.rs
│       └── canonical.rs
│
└── sr-store/
    ├── Cargo.toml
    ├── src/
    │   ├── lib.rs
    │   ├── revision.rs
    │   ├── revision_store.rs
    │   ├── snapshot.rs
    │   ├── snapshot_trie.rs
    │   └── roots.rs
    └── tests/
        ├── revisions.rs
        ├── snapshots.rs
        └── roots.rs

Do not create a SQLite backend in this stage. The public traits must make a later durable backend possible without changing callers.

docs.title: 3.1 sr-core
docs.text:
sr-core contains backend-independent identity and canonical-encoding primitives.

It must not depend on sr-store, domain crates, agents, filesystems, servers, or UI code.

It owns:

  • EntityId;
  • RevisionId;
  • SnapshotId;
  • TypeId;
  • EncodingVersion;
  • canonical byte encoding helpers;
  • hashing helpers used to construct immutable IDs.

docs.title: 3.2 sr-store
docs.text:
sr-store contains immutable revision storage and snapshot state.

It owns:

  • canonical revision values;
  • a revision-store trait;
  • an in-memory revision-store implementation for conformance and tests;
  • the persistent snapshot map;
  • snapshot resolution and diffing;
  • mutable named roots;
  • compare-and-swap root updates.

sr-store depends on sr-core.

No higher product layer may be required to use either crate.

docs.title: 4.1 EntityId
docs.text:
EntityId represents conceptual continuity and must not be content-derived.

Use a 128-bit opaque value.

The initial implementation may generate it with UUID v4 semantics. The public type must not expose UUID-specific behavior as part of the architectural contract.

Required behavior:

EntityId::new()
EntityId::from_bytes([u8; 16])
EntityId::as_bytes()
Display
FromStr
Eq
Ord
Hash
Clone
Copy
Serialize/Deserialize if serde is enabled by the crate

Text representation must be deterministic and round-trippable.

Changing an entity's content must never require generating another EntityId unless reconciliation concludes that the new object is a different conceptual entity.

docs.title: 4.2 RevisionId
docs.text:
RevisionId identifies one exact canonical revision value.

Use a 256-bit BLAKE3 digest represented as an opaque newtype.

A revision ID must be computed from:

revision-domain tag
encoding version
type ID
canonical payload bytes

Do not include EntityId in the revision hash.

This allows identical canonical values of the same type and encoding version to deduplicate even when referenced by different entities.

docs.title: 4.3 SnapshotId
docs.text:
SnapshotId identifies one exact snapshot mapping.

Use a 256-bit BLAKE3 digest represented as a different opaque newtype from RevisionId.

A snapshot ID must be the hash of the persistent snapshot structure's root node representation, prefixed by a snapshot-domain tag and encoding version.

RevisionId and SnapshotId must not be interchangeable Rust types even though both contain 32 bytes.

docs.title: 4.4 TypeId
docs.text:
TypeId identifies the schema/domain type of a canonical revision.

Use a stable UTF-8 identifier wrapper in the initial implementation, for example:

markdown.paragraph
rust.function
session.branch

The value must participate in revision hashing.

The storage layer must not hard-code a registry of every possible type.

docs.title: 5. Canonical Encoding
docs.text:
Content addressing is only correct if byte encoding is deterministic.

sr-core::canonical must provide a small explicit canonical writer rather than relying on general-purpose JSON serialization.

The canonical writer must support at least:

  • fixed domain tags;
  • unsigned integers in a defined byte order;
  • byte strings prefixed by length;
  • UTF-8 strings prefixed by byte length;
  • booleans;
  • optional values with explicit discriminants;
  • ordered sequences with explicit element count;
  • maps only when callers supply entries in canonical sorted-key order.

Do not encode Rust memory layout, pointer values, platform endianness, Debug output, or unordered HashMap iteration.

Expose a trait similar to:

pub trait CanonicalEncode {
    fn encode_canonical(&self, out: &mut CanonicalWriter);
}

The concrete method names may differ, but the contract must remain explicit and deterministic.

docs.title: 5.1 Encoding version
docs.text:
Every content-addressed root must include an EncodingVersion.

Version 1 is the initial encoding.

Changing canonical encoding rules later requires a new encoding version; old IDs must continue to mean the old bytes.

docs.title: 6. Canonical Revision Value
docs.text:
sr-store::revision defines the stored immutable revision value.

It must contain:

encoding_version
TypeId
canonical_payload: bytes

The corresponding RevisionId is derived from exactly those canonical fields plus the fixed revision-domain tag.

The revision value does not contain:

  • parent identity;
  • position in a parent;
  • mutable aliases;
  • cache entries;
  • derived summaries;
  • current snapshot;
  • timestamps that are not part of domain semantics;
  • the EntityId that happens to reference it.

The revision type must provide a constructor that computes and exposes its RevisionId.

docs.title: 7. Revision Store Contract
docs.text:
Define a small trait for immutable revision persistence.

Required conceptual operations:

put(revision) -> RevisionId
get(RevisionId) -> Option<Revision>
contains(RevisionId) -> bool

put is idempotent.

Putting the same revision twice must return the same ID and must not create two logical copies.

The initial implementation is an in-memory store using a map keyed by RevisionId.

The trait must not expose implementation-specific locking or database handles.

A later SQLite implementation must be able to implement the same behavioral contract.

docs.title: 8. Snapshot Mapping
docs.text:
A snapshot is conceptually:

EntityId -> RevisionId

Do not represent the snapshot by recursively hashing semantic parents and descendants.

The snapshot structure is an independent persistent Merkle map.

docs.title: 8.1 Data structure
docs.text:
Implement the first version as an immutable 16-way radix trie over the 128 bits of EntityId.

Each level consumes one 4-bit nibble.

Maximum depth is therefore 32 branch levels.

Node kinds:

Empty
Branch(children[16])
Leaf(EntityId, RevisionId)

An implementation may compress empty children internally, but the canonical hash of a logical node must not depend on memory layout.

Each node caches its immutable node digest.

Updating one entity creates new trie nodes only along the path from the root to that entity. Unchanged branches are shared with Arc or an equivalent immutable shared pointer.

This gives bounded path copying and prevents semantic containment depth from controlling snapshot update cost.

docs.title: 8.2 Trie node hashes
docs.text:
Use separate canonical domain tags for empty, branch, and leaf nodes.

A leaf hash includes:

leaf tag
encoding version
EntityId
RevisionId

A branch hash includes:

branch tag
encoding version
16 child hashes in nibble order

The empty node has one defined hash for an encoding version.

The SnapshotId is derived from the root node hash using a separate snapshot-root domain tag so it cannot be confused with an internal node digest.

docs.title: 8.3 Snapshot operations
docs.text:
The snapshot type must support:

empty()
id() -> SnapshotId
resolve(EntityId) -> Option<RevisionId>
with_revision(EntityId, RevisionId) -> Snapshot
without_entity(EntityId) -> Snapshot
len() -> usize
iter() -> deterministic iteration
diff(&Snapshot) -> SnapshotDiff

All mutating-looking operations return a new snapshot and leave the old snapshot usable.

If with_revision sets an entity to the revision it already has, it should return a snapshot with the same SnapshotId.

If without_entity removes an absent entity, the ID should remain unchanged.

docs.title: 9. Snapshot Diff
docs.text:
Snapshot IDs answer whether global state differs. Snapshot diff explains which entity resolutions differ.

Represent differences using explicit cases:

Added {
    entity,
    revision
}

Removed {
    entity,
    revision
}

Changed {
    entity,
    from,
    to
}

Diff output must be deterministic, ordered by EntityId.

The first implementation may compare deterministic iterators if needed. A later optimization may recursively skip identical Merkle subtrees using their node hashes.

The public behavior must not depend on which diff algorithm is used.

docs.title: 10. Snapshot Storage Boundary
docs.text:
The first implementation keeps Snapshot values in memory and tests structural sharing directly.

Do not yet design a durable snapshot-node database schema in code.

However, keep internal trie nodes canonically encodable and hash-addressed so a later persistence backend can store them independently by digest.

No public API should require that a snapshot exist only as one large serialized map.

docs.title: 11. Named Roots and Aliases
docs.text:
Named roots are mutable pointers to immutable snapshot IDs.

Examples:

main -> SnapshotId
active-workspace -> SnapshotId

Define a root-store abstraction with these conceptual operations:

get(name) -> Option<SnapshotId>
set(name, SnapshotId)
compare_and_swap(name, expected, new) -> result

compare_and_swap is required for safe concurrent promotion.

It succeeds only when the current value equals expected.

The initial implementation may use an in-memory RwLock-protected map.

Named roots are never included in the immutable snapshot hash.

Changing a root pointer does not mutate either the old or new snapshot.

docs.title: 12. Snapshot-Scoped Resolution
docs.text:
The lowest exact read operation is:

resolve(snapshot, entity) -> RevisionId

The store layer must not provide an ambiguous operation that means "resolve this entity against whatever current state exists now" without naming the root or snapshot involved.

A higher application layer may define convenience operations using a named root, but it must resolve the name to a SnapshotId first.

This keeps reproducible reads possible under concurrent changes.

docs.title: 13. Error Model
docs.text:
Use explicit typed errors where failure is meaningful.

Examples:

  • malformed textual ID;
  • unsupported encoding version;
  • requested revision not found;
  • compare-and-swap root conflict.

Normal absence should use Option where appropriate rather than being an error.

Hash collisions are not handled as ordinary control flow. If storage observes the same digest with different canonical bytes, it must treat that as an integrity failure.

docs.title: 14. Serialization and Display
docs.text:
Public IDs need deterministic text forms for CLI, protocols, logs, and future APIs.

Use distinct prefixes so humans and parsers can distinguish them, for example:

ent_<...>
rev_<...>
snp_<...>

The exact alphabet may be hexadecimal for the first implementation.

Requirements:

  • parsing must reject the wrong prefix;
  • round-trip must be exact;
  • RevisionId text must never parse as SnapshotId;
  • display formatting must not depend on locale.

Binary protocol encodings may later use raw bytes.

docs.title: 15. Concurrency
docs.text:
Immutable revisions and snapshots need no in-place mutation locks.

Synchronization is required only around mutable implementation indexes and named-root updates.

The in-memory stores may use standard Rust synchronization primitives.

Do not leak those primitives through public traits.

The externally meaningful concurrent update operation is named-root compare-and-swap.

docs.title: 16. Tests Required Before Higher Layers Depend on This
16.1 Identity tests
docs.text:
Verify:

  • two new entities have different EntityId values;
  • text round-trip preserves each identity type;
  • prefixes prevent cross-type parsing;
  • identical canonical revision values have identical RevisionIds;
  • changing type, payload, or encoding version changes RevisionId.

docs.title: 16.2 Revision-store tests
docs.text:
Verify:

  • putting a revision and reading it returns identical canonical fields;
  • putting the same revision twice is idempotent;
  • missing revisions return None;
  • an integrity mismatch cannot silently overwrite an existing digest.

docs.title: 16.3 Snapshot tests
docs.text:
Verify:

  • empty snapshots have deterministic identity;
  • same logical mappings built in different insertion orders have identical SnapshotIds;
  • changing one entity changes SnapshotId;
  • unchanged mappings resolve to the same revisions;
  • old snapshots still resolve old revisions after a successor is created;
  • removing an entity changes the snapshot only when it existed;
  • reapplying the same entity revision preserves the snapshot ID;
  • iteration order is deterministic;
  • diff reports added, removed, and changed entities correctly.

docs.title: 16.4 Structural-sharing tests
docs.text:
Add test-only introspection if required.

Verify that changing one key reuses trie branches that are not on the changed radix path.

Do not require callers to observe storage internals in production APIs.

docs.title: 16.5 Root tests
docs.text:
Verify:

  • a root can point to a snapshot;
  • updating the root does not mutate either snapshot;
  • compare-and-swap succeeds with the expected old snapshot;
  • compare-and-swap fails without changing the root when the expected snapshot is stale.

docs.title: 17. Dependency Rules
docs.text:
Keep dependencies minimal.

Expected external dependencies are limited to purposes such as:

  • BLAKE3 hashing;
  • UUID/random entity generation;
  • optional serde support;
  • error derivation if desired.

Do not introduce async runtime, web framework, database driver, parser framework, or agent SDK dependencies into these crates.

docs.title: 18. Public API Stability Rules
docs.text:
The exact internal trie representation is private.

The following concepts are public contracts:

EntityId
RevisionId
SnapshotId
TypeId
CanonicalEncode
Revision
RevisionStore
Snapshot
SnapshotDiff
RootStore

Higher layers must not depend on:

  • trie node shape;
  • Arc usage;
  • in-memory map implementation;
  • BLAKE3 helper internals;
  • UUID library types;
  • lock types.

This allows persistence and performance implementations to evolve without changing semantic consumers.

docs.title: 19. Work Sequence
docs.text:
Implement in this order:

  1. workspace and sr-core identity types;
  2. canonical encoding and revision hashing;
  3. revision value and in-memory revision store;
  4. persistent snapshot trie and snapshot IDs;
  5. snapshot resolution, iteration, and diff;
  6. named roots with compare-and-swap;
  7. conformance and structural-sharing tests.

Each step must compile and test before the next step begins.

docs.title: 20. Completion Criteria
docs.text:
This Level 2 design is implemented when all of the following are true:

  • a caller can create a stable EntityId;
  • a canonical revision can be hashed, deduplicated, stored, and retrieved;
  • a snapshot can resolve entities to exact revision IDs;
  • editing one entity produces a new snapshot without modifying the old one;
  • unrelated trie branches are structurally shared;
  • equivalent logical snapshots have identical SnapshotIds regardless of insertion order;
  • snapshot diffs identify only changed entity resolutions;
  • a named root can be atomically advanced using compare-and-swap;
  • all identity, revision, snapshot, structural-sharing, and root tests pass;
  • neither crate depends on any agent or product layer.

After these criteria are satisfied, persistence backends, migrations, domains, projections, sessions, and agents can depend on the identity substrate without redefining its semantics.

docs.title: Licensing Artifacts, Package Metadata, and Notices
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document turns the licensing requirements in design/level-1/014. extensibility ecosystem and licensing.md into concrete repository artifacts and package-level rules.

It is intentionally limited to files and metadata required to make the platform/product licensing boundary visible and enforceable in the repository.

It does not redesign the architecture, introduce a plugin registry, define commercial licensing terms, or choose package names beyond packages that already exist when the implementation task runs.

The controlling rule is:

Reusable infrastructure is Apache-2.0. The integrated Scriberig product and runtime are AGPL-3.0. The repository must make that boundary obvious from documentation and package metadata.

docs.title: 2. Required Repository Artifacts
docs.text:
The repository must contain complete license texts for every license used by Scriberig components.

Create:

LICENSES/Apache-2.0.txt
LICENSES/AGPL-3.0.txt

The files must contain the complete authoritative license texts, not summaries or modified versions.

The repository must also contain a human-readable explanation of the licensing split.

Create:

LICENSING.md

LICENSING.md is the repository-level guide required by the Level 1 design. It explains how to determine the license of a component and links the architectural platform/product split to package metadata.

The repository should also expose contribution expectations in a normal contributor-facing location.

Create or update:

CONTRIBUTING.md

The contribution text must preserve the Level 1 rule that contributions are accepted under terms compatible with the component being modified. It must not silently introduce copyright assignment, a CLA, a DCO, or permission for future commercial relicensing unless a separate design explicitly adopts such a policy.

docs.title: 3. Repository-Level Licensing Guide
docs.text: LICENSING.md must explain the following points in plain language.

docs.title: 3.1 Reusable platform
docs.text:
Reusable infrastructure is licensed under Apache-2.0 by default.

This category includes reusable capabilities such as:

  • identity and core types;
  • storage abstractions and implementations;
  • graph and schema libraries;
  • query and migration libraries;
  • projection libraries;
  • domain adapters;
  • protocol definitions;
  • Rust and TypeScript clients;
  • client-side models;
  • framework bindings;
  • headless editor libraries;
  • neutral reusable UI components;
  • reusable opinionated component libraries such as MUI integrations;
  • reusable agent-facing interfaces that do not implement the integrated Scriberig runtime.

docs.title: 3.2 Integrated product
docs.text:
The integrated Scriberig product is licensed under AGPL-3.0 by default.

This category includes:

  • the reference Scriberig server application;
  • the integrated agent execution and orchestration runtime;
  • the complete Scriberig editor application;
  • product-specific workflows whose purpose is to operate the integrated Scriberig product.

docs.title: 3.3 Boundary rule
docs.text:
Licensing follows architectural responsibility, not file extension, programming language, or whether an artifact is a binary.

A CLI or executable that is only a reusable client may remain Apache-2.0. A component that embeds substantial integrated AGPL runtime behavior belongs on the AGPL side.

Reusable functionality must not be moved into AGPL packages merely to make the licensing boundary more restrictive.

docs.title: 3.4 Third-party applications
docs.text: LICENSING.md must make clear that a third-party application using Apache-licensed Scriberig platform components does not become part of the AGPL Scriberig product merely because it uses those components or interoperates with Scriberig.

docs.title: 3.5 Package metadata is authoritative at package scope
docs.text:
The guide must state that every distributable crate or package declares its own license in its package metadata.

Repository documentation explains the rule; package metadata identifies the license of a particular distributable component.

docs.title: 3.6 Third-party dependencies
docs.text: The guide must state that Scriberig licenses do not replace dependency licenses and that required notices and attribution must be preserved.

docs.title: 3.7 Future dual licensing
docs.text:
The guide must not promise commercial dual licensing.

It may state that commercial dual licensing of AGPL-covered components is a possible future decision, and that contributor terms would have to be designed deliberately before relying on that model.

docs.title: 4. Rust Package Metadata
docs.text:
Every distributable Rust crate must declare a license in Cargo.toml.

The implementation agent must classify the crate by architectural responsibility rather than by name alone.

Default classification:

Reusable platform crate -> Apache-2.0
Integrated product/runtime crate -> AGPL-3.0

Examples of reusable platform responsibilities:

core identities
storage
schemas
graph
queries
migrations
projections
domain adapters
protocol types
client SDKs
reusable agent interfaces

Examples of integrated product responsibilities:

reference server application
integrated agent runtime/orchestration
product-specific integrated workflows

A Rust CLI remains Apache-2.0 when it is primarily a reusable client over public APIs. If it embeds the integrated AGPL runtime, its classification must follow that responsibility.

Workspace-level inherited license metadata may be used only when all inheriting packages have the same correct license. Mixed-license workspaces must not hide the distinction behind one incorrect workspace-wide value.

docs.title: 5. TypeScript and Web Package Metadata
docs.text:
Every distributable TypeScript/JavaScript package must declare its license in package.json.

Default classification:

Reusable package -> Apache-2.0
Complete integrated Scriberig application -> AGPL-3.0

Reusable packages include protocol types, clients, semantic models, framework bindings, headless editor logic, neutral components, and MUI-based reusable component libraries.

The complete reference editor application belongs to the AGPL product layer.

Private packages should still declare their license when doing so clarifies the architectural boundary.

The implementation must not make MUI usage itself an AGPL boundary. Reusable MUI components remain part of the Apache platform unless they contain integrated product/runtime behavior.

docs.title: 6. SPDX Source Identifiers
docs.text:
The Level 1 design permits SPDX identifiers in source files where appropriate, but does not require a repository-wide source-header migration.

Therefore this design does not require adding headers to every source file.

Package metadata and complete license texts are mandatory. Source SPDX headers may be added later under a separate focused task if the repository adopts that convention.

docs.title: 7. Third-Party Notices and Attribution
docs.text:
The project must preserve notices and attribution required by third-party dependencies, assets, generated code, fonts, parsers, UI frameworks, and other distributed material.

The implementation must not invent attribution obligations where dependencies do not require them.

Use the following repository artifact when there is material that must or should be surfaced centrally:

THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md

If the initial repository has no distributable third-party material requiring a notice, the file may contain a short statement that dependency-specific notices will be added as distributable dependencies are introduced, or creation may be deferred until such material exists. The implementation agent must not fabricate a list of dependencies that are not present.

Dependency license review is required when adding a new externally distributed component.

docs.title: 8. Contribution Policy
docs.text:
CONTRIBUTING.md must include a licensing section with these rules:

  • contributions to Apache-licensed components are contributed under terms compatible with Apache-2.0;
  • contributions to AGPL-covered product components are contributed under terms compatible with AGPL-3.0;
  • contributors must not add third-party material without preserving its applicable license and notices;
  • the repository does not implicitly obtain rights to commercially relicense third-party contributions beyond the licenses and contributor terms actually in force;
  • no CLA, DCO, copyright assignment, or commercial relicensing grant is implied by this document.

If the project later adopts a formal CLA, DCO, or commercial relicensing policy, that must be introduced deliberately and the contributor documentation must be updated explicitly.

docs.title: 9. Protocol Specifications, Schemas, and Fixtures
docs.text:
The Level 1 design requires public protocol specifications, schemas, and conformance fixtures to live with the reusable platform rather than only inside the AGPL reference server.

This document does not create those protocol artifacts because their content is defined by protocol designs, not by licensing policy.

When those files are created, they must live in an Apache-licensed reusable package or platform directory and must not require the AGPL product runtime merely to be consumed.

No Level 3 implementation task in this licensing stream should invent protocol semantics merely to satisfy this placement rule.

docs.title: 10. Dependency Direction
docs.text:
The expected licensing dependency direction matches the architecture:

Apache reusable platform
        ^
        |
AGPL integrated product

AGPL product components may depend on Apache platform components.

Reusable Apache platform components must not depend on integrated AGPL product components.

This is an architectural rule first and a licensing clarity rule second.

An implementation agent that discovers such a reverse dependency must report it rather than hiding it with metadata changes.

docs.title: 11. Implementation Order
docs.text:
Apply this design in four focused steps.

  1. Create the repository license texts and LICENSING.md.
  2. Apply license declarations to Rust crates once their manifests exist.
  3. Apply license declarations to web/TypeScript packages once their manifests exist.
  4. Create or update contributor licensing guidance and preserve third-party notices required by dependencies that actually exist.

These steps are intentionally separable so a simple implementation agent does not have to classify the whole repository while also retrieving legal text.

docs.title: 12. Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
This design is implemented when all applicable statements below are true.

  • LICENSES/Apache-2.0.txt contains the complete Apache License 2.0 text.
  • LICENSES/AGPL-3.0.txt contains the complete GNU Affero General Public License version 3 text selected by the project.
  • LICENSING.md explains the platform/product split and points developers to package metadata for component-level licensing.
  • Every existing distributable Rust crate declares the license appropriate to its architectural responsibility.
  • Every existing distributable web package declares the license appropriate to its architectural responsibility.
  • The integrated server/runtime/editor are not accidentally labeled as permissive platform components.
  • Reusable libraries are not accidentally labeled AGPL merely because the reference product consumes them.
  • Contributor documentation preserves the two-license model without inventing relicensing rights.
  • Required third-party attribution is preserved for dependencies and assets actually present in distributed components.
  • No reusable Apache component depends on an integrated AGPL product component.

docs.title: 13. Non-Goals
docs.text:
Do not use this design to:

  • introduce a plugin registry;
  • define package publication policy;
  • define protocol semantics;
  • add a CLA or DCO;
  • promise commercial licensing;
  • choose a legal entity or copyright holder;
  • rewrite dependency licenses;
  • add speculative third-party notices;
  • make every source file carry a license header;
  • move reusable functionality into AGPL packages for licensing leverage.

Those decisions require separate designs when they become necessary.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document turns the persistence guarantees in design/level-1/004. persistence and storage model.md into Rust crate boundaries.

This level chooses implementation structure. It does not change the Level 1 model.

docs.title: Required crates
docs.text:
The initial persistence slice must create these workspace crates:

crates/
├── sr-core/
├── sr-store/
