  • periodic ticks when needed;
  • semantic operation results;
  • operation progress;
  • application/client events;
  • worker failures;
  • shutdown signals.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Actions express interaction intent or the arrival of a typed result. Examples include:

MoveSelection
ActivateSelection
GoBack
GoForward
ChangeFocus
OpenPalette
CloseOverlay
RunContextAction
InspectLoaded
HistoryLoaded
OperationUpdated
RequestQuit

Actions must not contain terminal-library handles or database connections.

docs.title: Reducer
docs.text: The reducer updates TUI state and returns zero or more semantic/presentation effects. It should be deterministic for a given state/action pair.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
Effects describe work outside pure state reduction, for example:

Inspect(reference)
List(reference, page)
Follow(reference, relation, page)
Find(query, scope)
History(reference)
Diff(left, right)
RenderProjection(reference, style)
DiscoverActions(context)
StartOperation(command)
CancelOperation(operation_id)
Refresh(reference)

No Ratatui widget may execute an effect directly.

docs.title: 7. Service Port
docs.text:
scriberig-tui needs a narrow presentation-facing service boundary so its state machine does not care whether operations are embedded or transported remotely.

Define a TUI service port whose methods correspond to public application operations, not storage primitives. The port may initially be implemented only by an embedded adapter over scriberig-app.

The port must preserve:

  • explicit application context;
  • snapshot or branch context;
  • structured application errors;
  • capability discovery;
  • stable operation identifiers;
  • pagination/cursors where the application API provides them;
  • cancellation and event observation when supported.

Do not create a TUI-specific semantic request language when an application request/result already exists. The service port should be an adapter that makes existing contracts convenient to consume from the runtime.

A future remote adapter should implement the same TUI service port through scriberig-client and protocol types.

docs.title: 8. Semantic Selection
docs.text:
The TUI keeps one primary semantic selection with optional comparison or parent context.

Represent selection using stable public references. Conceptually it must be able to point at at least:

entity
exact revision
snapshot
relation/list result item
projection
session object
operation
change or conflict object

Do not encode selection as a table row index. A view may maintain a cursor index, but activating that row resolves to the stable semantic reference stored in the row model.

Selection carries enough context to explain what is being observed, such as the active snapshot or branch. Exact-revision selections remain exact even when the current branch advances.

docs.title: 9. Navigation Model
docs.text: Navigation history and focus are independent concepts.

docs.title: Navigation history
docs.text:
Activating semantic references pushes locations onto a back/forward stack similar to a browser. A location includes:

semantic selection
active primary view
snapshot/branch context needed by the view
optional comparison target

Going back must not invoke a semantic mutation.

docs.title: Focus
docs.text: Focus identifies which visible interactive region receives navigation input. Focus moves among panes/overlays without changing semantic history unless the user activates a different semantic object.

docs.title: Cursor state
docs.text: Each list-like view may retain presentation cursor/scroll state keyed to its navigation location. This state is disposable and must never become semantic identity.

docs.title: 10. Rendering Contract
docs.text:
Rendering is a pure read of TuiState and the current terminal rectangle.

Rendering must not:

  • call application services;
  • read the filesystem;
  • sleep or wait on channels;
  • mutate canonical state;
  • update navigation history as a side effect;
  • change state merely because a region was too small.

The render layer may derive temporary layout rectangles and shortened display strings from state.

Where possible, views should render from small view models rather than domain-internal structures. This makes TestBackend assertions stable and keeps product presentation independent from storage representation.

docs.title: 11. Terminal Lifecycle
docs.text:
The terminal wrapper owns setup and restoration as one RAII-style responsibility.

Startup should perform the supported equivalents of:

verify interactive terminal when required
enable raw mode
enter alternate screen
hide cursor when appropriate
enable bracketed paste when input uses it
optionally enable mouse capture
clear/draw initial frame

Normal teardown performs the inverse.

The implementation must attempt restoration on:

  • normal quit;
  • an error returned by the event loop;
  • Ctrl-C/shutdown handling;
  • panic, by using a panic hook or another robust restoration strategy that composes with the process's existing hook.

Teardown must be idempotent enough that an error during shutdown does not intentionally skip the remaining restoration steps.

Do not put application/business cleanup into the terminal guard.

docs.title: 12. Event Loop and Responsiveness
docs.text:
The event loop should redraw when state changed, the terminal resized, or a bounded periodic refresh is required. It should not busy-spin at terminal frame rate when nothing changed.

Semantic work must happen outside the render function. The first local implementation may use a small worker/executor abstraction rather than committing the whole product to a specific async runtime.

The runtime must be able to accept result/progress events while the user continues navigating local UI state.

For request/result pairs where stale responses are possible, include a generation/request token in TUI state. A response for an obsolete view must not overwrite a newer selection's view model.

Cancellation should use the application's operation/cancellation mechanism when one exists. Dropping a TUI view alone must not falsely report an application operation as cancelled.

docs.title: 13. Loading and Error State
docs.text:
Every effect-backed view uses an explicit load state equivalent to:

NotRequested
Loading { request }
Ready { data, freshness }
Failed { structured_category, message }

Long-running operations use shared operation lifecycle states rather than inventing another terminal-only lifecycle.

A failed refresh may retain the last successful data as visibly stale if doing so is useful. Stale data must be labeled; it must not silently masquerade as current.

Structured error categories should drive presentation such as permission denied, stale base, conflict, validation failure, unsupported operation, cancellation, and internal failure.

docs.title: 14. Capability Discovery
docs.text:
The TUI maintains capability/action availability for the current context.

Global UI actions such as help, focus movement, and quit are local presentation commands. Semantic actions such as inspect, follow, diff, branch, validate, apply, reconcile, start agent work, or cancel an operation come from the shared operation/capability model.

A contextual action should carry:

stable action identifier
human label
whether it is currently available
reason when unavailable, when safe to disclose
input requirements
whether it is read-only or state-changing

If the application layer does not yet expose sufficient contextual action metadata, add that capability there rather than hard-coding privileged semantic decisions into the TUI.

docs.title: 15. Local Composition
docs.text:
The first supported product path is:

srig tui
   |
   v
scriberig-cli parses TUI arguments
   |
   v
apps/scriberig builds local store/application composition
   |
   v
embedded TUI service adapter
   |
   v
scriberig-tui::run(...)

s‍criberig-tui must not open the SQLite database itself. The composition root does so because concrete persistence selection is product composition.

The local principal should be explicit, for example a principal equivalent to local-tui, and its capabilities should be constructed by the same application capability model used elsewhere.

Do not grant unrestricted mutation capability merely because the caller is local.

docs.title: 16. Remote Composition
docs.text:
A later remote path may be:

srig tui --connect <endpoint>
   |
   v
scriberig-client
   |
   v
public server protocol
   |
   v
same TUI service port/state/views

Remote mode may add connection/authentication UI, latency states, reconnect behavior, and event-stream resubscription. It must not change the meaning of semantic actions.

Local-only actions, if any, are reported through capabilities and remain visibly local-only.

docs.title: 17. Public Crate Entry Point
docs.text:
The public API should be small. It should converge on concepts equivalent to:

TuiConfig
TuiService or adapter trait
run(service, context, config) -> Result<RunOutcome, TuiError>

RunOutcome should distinguish a normal user exit from any intentional product-level handoff if such handoffs are added later.

Do not expose Ratatui widget types as the main public integration contract. Ratatui is an implementation choice inside the product adapter.

docs.title: 18. Testing Boundary
docs.text:
The architecture must support four classes of tests:

  1. Reducer tests: actions produce expected state/effects without a terminal.
  2. Rendering tests: TestBackend frames for representative dimensions and states.
  3. Service-adapter tests: fixed semantic fixtures return the same references/errors as direct application operations.
  4. Runtime/lifecycle tests: terminal setup/teardown and event routing through abstractions that do not require corrupting the developer's real terminal.

Cross-surface semantic conformance remains owned by scriberig-conformance; TUI tests may provide a callable adapter/model so conformance does not scrape ANSI terminal text.

docs.title: 19. Initial Milestone Boundary
docs.text:
The first useful milestone includes:

terminal lifecycle
responsive shell
navigation/focus
semantic explorer + inspector
contextual command palette
structured errors
local embedded composition
help
rendering/reducer tests

History, diff, projection, change review, sessions, agents, remote mode, and richer operation observation may land in later Level 3 slices without redesigning the runtime.

The first milestone must not fake unsupported semantic operations merely to fill panels.

docs.title: 20. Implementation References
docs.text: Current Ratatui guidance should be consulted when implementing terminal lifecycle, event handling, backend selection, and TestBackend tests. The design intentionally follows Ratatui's separation between application state/event handling and frame rendering while preserving Scriberig's stricter semantic-operation boundary.

docs.title: Terminal UI Views, Interaction, and Conformance
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines the concrete product-facing view model and interaction contract for the Scriberig TUI.

It builds on:

  1. design/level-1/015. terminal user interface principles.md;
  2. design/level-2/021. terminal ui runtime and state architecture.md;
  3. design/level-2/010. universal query and operation implementation.md;
  4. design/level-2/012. capability matrix and cross surface conformance.md;
  5. design/level-2/020. repository scaffold conventions and native command surface.md.

This document is intentionally concrete about panes, views, default key behavior, responsive layout, contextual operations, and acceptance behavior. It does not move semantic ownership into the TUI.

docs.title: 2. Workspace Shell
docs.text:
The default shell has five logical regions:

+---------------------------------------------------------------+
| context bar: project / branch-or-snapshot / selection / state |
+------------------+-------------------------+------------------+
|                  |                         |                  |
| explorer         | primary view            | inspector        |
|                  |                         |                  |
|                  |                         |                  |
+------------------+-------------------------+------------------+
| status / operation / diagnostics                              |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
| contextual key hints                                          |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+

The three body regions are logical panes, not permanent rectangles. Responsive layout may collapse or replace them.

docs.title: Context bar
docs.text:
Shows enough context to answer:

Where am I?
What semantic object is selected?
Am I observing a branch, current snapshot, or exact historical revision?
Is the view stale, loading, conflicted, or validating?

Do not display full identifiers by default when a useful short form exists, but provide a way to reveal/copy the exact identifier.

docs.title: Status region
docs.text: Shows transient application status, structured errors, long-running operation progress, and connection state in remote mode.

docs.title: Key-hint region
docs.text: Shows a small set of actions relevant to the focused view. It is not the complete help system.

docs.title: 3. Responsive Layout
docs.text:
Use these initial width classes unless implementation testing demonstrates that a nearby threshold is materially better:

>= 120 columns: three-pane layout
80..119 columns: explorer + primary, inspector available as a view/overlay
< 80 columns: one primary pane, other regions become navigable views/overlays

At low height, remove decorative spacing and reduce status/key-hint rows before making semantic content unusable.

When the terminal is too small for safe interaction, render a clear minimum-size message that still permits help and quit. Do not panic because a layout region reached zero width or height.

Resize changes presentation only. It must not reset semantic selection or navigation history.

docs.title: 4. Focus and Overlay Rules
docs.text:
At most one pane or overlay owns keyboard focus at a time.

Focus order for the wide shell is:

Explorer -> Primary -> Inspector -> Explorer

An overlay temporarily owns focus until it closes. The underlying semantic selection remains visible where practical and is restored without a new semantic request unless refresh is required.

Overlay precedence from most modal to least modal is:

confirmation / review
text input
command palette
help
non-modal notification

Do not allow multiple modal overlays to compete for input. Opening a stronger modal replaces or suspends the weaker one according to explicit state transitions.

docs.title: 5. Default Global Keys
docs.text:
The initial global key contract is:

Ctrl-C        request quit, or cancel the active cancellable input/operation context
Esc           close overlay / cancel local interaction / move toward browse mode
Tab           focus next region
Shift-Tab     focus previous region
Enter         activate the focused semantic row or default contextual action
Up/Down       move within the focused list or scrollable region
Left/Right    collapse/expand where the focused view has hierarchy semantics
Backspace     navigate back when not editing text
:             open contextual command palette
/             open find/search input
?             open help
r             refresh current semantic view when no text input owns the key
q             request quit from ordinary browse state

h, j, k, and l may be provided as aliases for directional navigation in ordinary browse state, but arrow keys remain supported and documented.

Keys that would conflict with text input are interpreted as text while an input field owns focus.

The keymap implementation must be data-driven enough for help and key hints to derive labels from the same bindings rather than duplicating strings across widgets.

User-configurable keymaps are not required for the first implementation, but action identifiers must be separated from key chords so configuration can be added later.

docs.title: 6. Command Palette
docs.text:
The command palette is the universal discoverability surface.

It combines two action classes:

docs.title: Local presentation actions
docs.text:
Examples:

open help
switch primary view
focus inspector
go back
refresh
copy exact identifier
quit

docs.title: Semantic actions
docs.text:
These come from shared capability/operation availability for the current selection/context, for example:

inspect
list children
follow relation
show history
compare
render projection
validate candidate
review migration
apply
reconcile
start session
submit agent command
cancel operation

Semantic palette rows must not be enabled based solely on a hard-coded TUI list. The TUI may know how to render inputs for an action identifier, but availability comes from the application/client layer.

The palette supports fuzzy or substring filtering over labels and aliases. Filtering the palette is presentation logic; determining whether an action is authorized is not.

docs.title: 7. Semantic Explorer
docs.text:
The Explorer provides progressive navigation over semantic structure.

It must support rows with at least:

stable semantic reference
kind/type summary
human label or short description
expandability/navigation affordance
loading/error child state when expanded
optional trust/status marker

The explorer does not assume every object has filesystem-like children. Expansion may represent:

  • collection members;
  • typed relations;
  • session branches;
  • change/conflict groups;
  • snapshot roots;
  • projection/source links;
  • domain-advertised semantic children.

The application query model determines what can be listed or followed.

Expansion state is local presentation state keyed by stable references.

docs.title: 8. Inspector
docs.text:
The Inspector shows a progressive semantic summary for the primary selection.

The compact inspector should include, when available:

kind/schema
stable entity/reference identity
exact revision identity when relevant
short description
important properties
relation summaries
collection membership summary
snapshot/branch context
provenance/trust summary
available next operations

Deep provenance, large properties, long descriptions, and exhaustive relations are loaded or opened deliberately rather than overflowing the default inspector.

The inspector must clearly distinguish conceptual entity identity from exact revision identity.

docs.title: 9. Primary Views
docs.text: The Primary region switches among views while preserving the current semantic location when compatible.

docs.title: 9.1 Overview
docs.text: Shows a richer version of the selected object's summary, descriptions, properties, relations, and useful next actions.

docs.title: 9.2 Query and find results
docs.text: Shows bounded/paginated results. Every row stores a stable result handle. The view displays scope, query summary, result count information when available, and continuation state.

docs.title: 9.3 History
docs.text: Shows lineage/history returned by shared operations. Activating a historical revision creates an exact-revision semantic selection. The UI must not silently replace it with the current entity revision.

docs.title: 9.4 Diff
docs.text:
Shows semantic differences between two explicit references/snapshots/revisions. The left/base and right/target identities remain visible in the view header.

The TUI may render text-oriented diff blocks where returned by a projection/domain, but it must not infer semantic equality from terminal text.

docs.title: 9.5 Projection
docs.text:
Shows rendered projection content plus projection identity, style where relevant, source semantic reference, and synchronization state.

The initial view may be read-only. External editing or reconciliation actions are invoked through shared operations, not by writing files from the widget.

docs.title: 9.6 Changes, conflicts, and validation
docs.text:
Shows proposed migrations/changes, base snapshot, affected objects, conflicts, validation evidence, and approval/application actions.

This is the required review surface before canonical state-changing actions where a reviewable proposal exists.

docs.title: 9.7 Session
docs.text:
Shows session tree/branch structure, turns, summaries, tool invocations/results, durable promoted knowledge, and current agent-operation state where available.

Transient branches must be visibly distinct from canonical project state.

docs.title: 9.8 Operations
docs.text: Shows queued/running/completed/failed/cancelled operations using shared operation identifiers and lifecycle states. Users can inspect result references and request cancellation where the capability exists.

docs.title: 10. Text and Structured Content Rendering
docs.text:
Terminal rendering should preserve semantic structure without becoming a full text editor.

For structured text:

  • wrap at the current view width;
  • preserve paragraph and heading boundaries;
  • render code blocks with indentation and optional syntax styling when available;
  • allow vertical scrolling independent of semantic selection;
  • expose exact source/projection identity in metadata rather than embedding invisible terminal-only markers.

Do not rely on ANSI sequences embedded in application strings. Styling is applied by the TUI from structured or plain safe content.

Untrusted or externally sourced control characters must not be emitted to the terminal as executable control sequences. Normalize or visibly escape terminal control content before rendering.

docs.title: 11. Mutation and Review Workflow
docs.text:
Semantic actions are classified as read-only or state-changing.

Read-only actions may start immediately after required input is collected.

A state-changing action follows the logical flow:

select action
    |
    v
collect explicit inputs
    |
    v
obtain/construct reviewable proposal when supported
    |
    v
show base + affected objects + conflicts + validation/trust
    |
    v
user confirms intent
    |
    v
invoke shared application command
    |
    v
observe operation/result
    |
    v
refresh affected semantic locations

The confirmation overlay must include the action label and affected context. Destructive or canonical actions may require a stronger explicit confirmation than reversible presentation actions.

If the base becomes stale between review and application, show the shared stale-base/conflict result. Never silently recompute and apply against a different base without renewed user intent.

docs.title: 12. Trust, Permission, and Validation Presentation
docs.text:
Trust and permission state must remain visible enough for users to understand why an action is unavailable or risky.

Use textual/symbolic labels in addition to color for states such as:

trusted / authoritative
external
model-generated
derived
unvalidated
validated
validation failed
conflicted
permission denied
stale

The TUI may summarize evidence but must preserve links/handles needed to inspect full provenance and validation records through shared operations.

Do not expose sensitive denial reasons that the application layer intentionally redacts.

docs.title: 13. Sessions and Agent Input
docs.text:
Agent input uses an explicit text-input overlay or session composer. It must support multiline or pasted input without treating pasted control text as TUI commands.

Submitting agent input starts or extends a session through the shared session/agent application boundary. The TUI observes the resulting operation and session objects.

Streaming model text, if available, is presentation of an in-progress operation. It is not canonical project knowledge until the session/domain layer records it according to its own rules.

Users must be able to leave an agent view and inspect other knowledge while work continues, unless the application operation explicitly requires exclusive interaction.

docs.title: 14. Notifications and Errors
docs.text:
Notifications have bounded lifetime and severity but must not be the only place important failures are visible.

Recommended categories:

info
success
warning
error

Structured semantic failures that need action, such as conflicts or validation failures, should open or link to a durable result view rather than disappearing as a toast-like notification.

Internal failures may show a short safe message plus a correlation/operation identifier where available. Avoid dumping Rust debug output, secrets, raw SQL, or untrusted terminal control sequences into the UI.

docs.title: 15. Clipboard and External Terminal Integration
docs.text:
Core functionality must not require clipboard integration.

If copy support is implemented, prefer copying stable identifiers, references, or explicitly selected plain text. Do not emit terminal escape sequences for clipboard access unless the behavior is opt-in or the security implications are clearly understood for the supported terminal environment.

Opening an external editor/browser is outside the first milestone. Later integrations must suspend/restore terminal mode correctly and return through explicit product actions.

docs.title: 16. Local TUI Command Surface
docs.text:
design/level-2/020. repository scaffold conventions and native command surface.md already establishes:

srig tui

The first concrete implementation may add arguments without changing that top-level command. Recommended local option:

srig tui --db <PATH>

with the same development database default used by other local native modes where practical.

A later remote mode may add a mutually exclusive form equivalent to:

srig tui --connect <ENDPOINT>

The CLI crate owns parsing. The composition root owns constructing local or remote services. scriberig-tui owns neither database path parsing nor HTTP endpoint parsing.

docs.title: 17. Accessibility and Terminal Compatibility
docs.text:
Acceptance requirements include:

  • all core workflows usable without mouse input;
  • focus indicated by more than color alone;
  • important state represented by text or symbols plus styling;
  • usable behavior with reduced/no color;
  • resize at runtime without state loss or panic;
  • bounded behavior for narrow/small terminals;
  • control characters sanitized before terminal rendering;
  • paste handled as input data rather than key-command replay;
  • Unicode decoration not required for semantic comprehension.

A future theme system may customize appearance, but theme choices must not change semantic behavior.

docs.title: 18. Rendering and Interaction Tests
docs.text:
Use Ratatui's test backend or an equivalent in-memory backend to verify representative frames.

Do not snapshot the entire application for every change. Prefer focused assertions on semantic regions and a small number of high-value full-frame fixtures.

Required size classes include at least:

140x40 wide
100x30 medium
72x24 narrow
very small terminal guard case

Reducer/keymap tests should verify that the same action identifiers drive visible key hints/help.

Tests for pasted/untrusted text must verify that control sequences are rendered harmlessly.

docs.title: 19. Cross-Surface Conformance
docs.text:
The capability matrix must represent TUI coverage honestly.

A capability progresses through:

planned -> implemented -> verified

only when the corresponding TUI path exists and is tested.

For semantic conformance, expose a testable adapter/model boundary so scriberig-conformance can compare TUI-invoked semantics against application/server/client semantics without scraping terminal cells or ANSI output.

At minimum, the first verified TUI semantic slice should cover:

inspect_entity
runtime_capabilities

Later slices should add operation lifecycle, cancellation, event observation, history/diff, and mutation review as their underlying application capabilities become available.

docs.title: 20. Performance Acceptance
docs.text:
The TUI must remain responsive to local navigation and quit/help input while semantic work is pending.

Rendering work should be proportional to visible/bounded view models, not the total database size.

Lists use application pagination or bounded requests. The TUI must not fetch an unbounded universe merely to implement scrolling.

Redraw should be event-driven or bounded by a modest frame/tick rate. A static screen must not consume a CPU core through a busy loop.

Performance tests should prefer deterministic large synthetic view models over timing external services.

docs.title: 21. First-Version Non-Goals
docs.text:
The first TUI does not need:

  • user-authored theme files;
  • user-configurable keymaps;
  • plugin-defined terminal widgets;
  • arbitrary source-file editing;
  • a terminal emulator inside the TUI;
  • image rendering protocols;
  • mouse-only interactions;
  • a separate TUI persistence database;
  • direct SQL browsing.

These may be added later only if they preserve the Level 1 TUI invariants and shared operation model.

docs.title: Agent Runtime, Model Provider, and Branch Orchestration
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document turns design/level-1/016. model driven agent execution and branch isolation.md into concrete Rust subsystem boundaries.

It also depends on:

  1. design/level-1/009. agent interaction and sessions.md;
  2. design/level-2/011. application operations protocol and runtime boundaries.md;
  3. design/level-3/082. implement session domain structure and views.md.

The controlling rule is:

scriberig-agent-runtime owns provider communication and agent execution, but all semantic reads and mutations still flow through public application/session capabilities.

The implementation must support nested session branches, OpenAI-compatible model endpoints, progressive tool disclosure, model-request fingerprinting, cancellation, and deterministic testing without a real model service.

docs.title: 2. Package Ownership
docs.text:
Keep the existing package split:

crates/scriberig-agent-core/
crates/scriberig-agent-runtime/
crates/scriberig-session/
crates/scriberig-app/

Do not introduce provider dependencies into foundation/domain crates.

docs.title: scriberig-agent-core
docs.text:
Owns provider-neutral contracts that are useful independently of one concrete model transport:

agent profile descriptors
tool descriptors and JSON-schema-like argument contracts
tool result projections
context input blocks
branch execution policy descriptors
provider-neutral model input/output forms where reuse is useful

It must not perform HTTP.

docs.title: scriberig-agent-runtime
docs.text:
Owns:

OpenAI-compatible provider adapter
provider configuration and capability negotiation
model request execution and streaming
context compilation orchestration
request fingerprinting and cache lookup/write
model/tool loop
nested child-branch execution
operation cancellation
runtime events
execution budgets

docs.title: scriberig-session
docs.text:
Owns durable provider-neutral session entities and views:

Branch
Turn
ModelInvocation
ModelOutput
ToolInvocation
ToolResult
BranchResult
Summary

Raw provider request/response JSON, if retained, is optional external/audit artifact data and is not the canonical session shape.

docs.title: scriberig-app
docs.text: Owns public start/continue/cancel/query operations and capability enforcement. The runtime is invoked through an application-facing service boundary rather than directly from product UIs.

docs.title: 3. Target scriberig-agent-runtime Layout
docs.text:
Converge on a structure equivalent to:

crates/scriberig-agent-runtime/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs
    ├── config.rs
    ├── error.rs
    ├── runtime.rs
    ├── budget.rs
    ├── cancel.rs
    ├── event.rs
    ├── provider/
    │   ├── mod.rs
    │   ├── types.rs
    │   ├── openai_compatible.rs
    │   ├── stream.rs
    │   └── error.rs
    ├── context/
    │   ├── mod.rs
    │   ├── compiler.rs
    │   ├── policy.rs
    │   ├── dependencies.rs
    │   └── fingerprint.rs
    ├── tools/
    │   ├── mod.rs
    │   ├── catalog.rs
    │   ├── dispatch.rs
    │   └── projection.rs
    ├── branch/
    │   ├── mod.rs
    │   ├── orchestrator.rs
    │   ├── state.rs
    │   ├── result.rs
    │   └── policy.rs
    └── cache/
        ├── mod.rs
        ├── key.rs
        ├── record.rs
        └── repository.rs

Files may be split differently to remain below repository source-size limits, but the responsibilities must stay distinct.

docs.title: 4. Provider-Neutral Model Contract
docs.text:
Define an internal/public-as-needed provider trait conceptually equivalent to:

ModelProvider
  capabilities() -> ProviderCapabilities
  invoke(ModelRequest, Cancellation) -> ModelResponse/stream

The provider-neutral request must be able to represent:

model identifier
ordered context/messages/blocks
tool definitions
tool choice policy
structured-output schema when requested
output-affecting generation parameters
request metadata safe for logging

The provider-neutral response must be able to represent:

assistant text blocks
structured output
tool calls
finish/termination reason
usage metadata
provider request identifier
provider model/fingerprint metadata when available

Do not expose authorization headers or raw secret configuration through these structures.

docs.title: 5. OpenAI-Compatible Adapter
docs.text:
Implement the first provider adapter as an OpenAI-compatible HTTP client.

Compatibility is capability-based rather than assuming every endpoint implements every feature identically.

The adapter configuration includes at least:

base_url
model
credential source
request timeout
connect timeout
stream enabled/disabled
compatibility mode/profile
optional default generation parameters

Credentials are supplied through a secret source/environment/config mechanism owned by product composition. Never persist them in session records or cache keys.

The adapter must support a compatibility subset sufficient for:

  • text assistant output;
  • tool/function definitions;
  • tool calls with structured arguments;
  • streaming when enabled;
  • usage metadata when returned;
  • structured provider errors.

The exact HTTP path and wire envelope are adapter details. Support for multiple OpenAI-family endpoint styles may be added behind the same provider-neutral contract.

Do not make upstream session code depend on OpenAI wire type names.

docs.title: 6. HTTP and Async Boundary
docs.text:
Provider network I/O is asynchronous work owned by the agent runtime.

The first implementation should use a production HTTP client with:

TLS support
request timeout
stream/body limits
cancellation support
proxy behavior inherited/configured explicitly
structured status/body errors

reqwest is the preferred first implementation unless repository constraints established by the implementation task justify another client.

The async runtime must remain above foundation/application semantics. Product composition may host the runtime on Tokio; lower semantic crates must not gain a Tokio dependency merely because model transport is asynchronous.

Tests must be able to replace the HTTP provider with an in-memory fake provider.

docs.title: 7. Provider Capability Model
docs.text:
Represent provider support explicitly instead of scattering compatibility checks.

At minimum track concepts equivalent to:

streaming
function/tool calls
parallel tool calls
structured output
usage reporting
provider request IDs
reasoning controls, if exposed
maximum request context, when known

The context compiler/orchestrator asks the provider capability model before using optional features.

A provider lacking parallel tool-call support may serialize calls. A provider lacking structured-output support may use ordinary text/tool contracts where safe.

Unsupported required capability produces a structured runtime failure before sending a malformed request.

docs.title: 8. Agent Profile
docs.text:
An agent profile identifies reusable execution policy independent of one session.

Conceptually it includes:

profile id/revision
system instructions
preferred provider profile
preferred model
context policy id/revision
initial tool exposure policy
branching policy
runtime budgets
default model parameters
cache policy

Profiles must be versioned or otherwise fingerprintable so model request identity changes when behaviorally relevant profile content changes.

A profile is configuration, not session identity. A session branch records which profile revision executed it.

docs.title: 9. Context Compiler
docs.text:
The context compiler receives a BranchExecutionContext and returns a provider-neutral CompiledContext plus an exact dependency manifest.

Inputs may include:

branch identity and purpose
current user instruction
parent branch descriptor/result chain
recent current-branch turns
accepted decisions/open tasks
semantic selection
explicitly pinned knowledge handles
relevant derived summaries/descriptions
available tools after capability filtering
context/token budget
provider capabilities

The compiler must not simply concatenate the complete session transcript.

It applies a context policy in a deterministic order so tests can prove the same input state produces the same compiled context before provider-specific serialization.

docs.title: 10. Parent-to-Child Context Inheritance
docs.text:
Creating a child branch requires an explicit inheritance plan.

The plan may include:

parent branch descriptor
selected parent result handles
selected accepted decisions
selected semantic scope
explicit user/delegation instruction
capability subset
base snapshot/workspace

The child does not receive all parent turns by default.

A branch policy may allow a bounded recent parent excerpt, but that choice is explicit and participates in context identity.

When the child completes, the parent receives the child's BranchResult, not implicit access to the child transcript.

docs.title: 11. Tool Catalog
docs.text:
scriberig-agent-core exposes tool descriptors. scriberig-agent-runtime builds the tool catalog for each model step.

A descriptor includes at least:

stable tool id
human/model description
argument schema
result-shape description
read-only vs state-changing classification
atomic vs child-branch execution mode
capability requirement
optional semantic/domain applicability

The runtime must never execute an arbitrary provider-returned name without resolving it against the trusted catalog.

Tool schemas must be canonical/fingerprintable because they participate in model request identity.

docs.title: 12. Progressive Tool Disclosure
docs.text:
The initial catalog should be intentionally small.

A practical bootstrap set may expose concepts equivalent to:

inspect
list/follow
find/query
open referenced result
start focused branch

Domain-specific operations become available when:

  • the current selection/domain advertises them;
  • an inspected result advertises a next operation;
  • the current agent profile explicitly enables them;
  • the branch capability scope permits them.

The runtime recompiles tool definitions before the next model step when capability context changes.

docs.title: 13. Tool Dispatch
docs.text:
For every tool call:

  1. resolve tool id from the trusted catalog;
  2. parse and validate arguments;
  3. verify branch/application capability scope;
  4. determine execution mode;
  5. execute an atomic application operation or create a child branch;
  6. persist ToolInvocation and ToolResult session objects;
  7. construct a bounded tool-result projection for the next model step.

A state-changing atomic operation still uses the shared application mutation/validation path.

Provider tool-call identifiers may be recorded for correlation but are not semantic identity.

docs.title: 14. Child-Branch Tool Mode
docs.text:
A child-branch tool descriptor contains or resolves an execution specification equivalent to:

purpose template
expected result kind
context inheritance policy
capability subset
base selection/snapshot/workspace
budget override or inherited limits

The orchestrator creates the child branch before any child model request is made.

The child branch runs the same model/tool loop recursively.

When terminal, its compact result is returned to the parent as the tool result projection and durable BranchResult handle.

Recursion depth and total branch counts are budgeted to prevent unbounded delegation.

docs.title: 15. Branch Orchestrator State Machine
docs.text:
Use an explicit state machine conceptually equivalent to:

Created
-> CompilingContext
-> AwaitingModel
-> InterpretingModel
-> ExecutingTools / AwaitingChildren
-> CompilingContext ...
-> Completing
-> Completed

terminal alternatives:
Failed
Cancelled
BudgetExceeded

State transitions produce runtime/application events.

Durable session branch lifecycle may remain simpler (active/completed/abandoned) while runtime execution state is more granular. Do not overload canonical branch status with every transient scheduler state.

docs.title: 16. Model Loop
docs.text:
The core loop is:

compile context
-> fingerprint request
-> optionally reuse cache
-> invoke provider
-> persist complete model output metadata
-> if final answer: complete branch
-> if tool calls: dispatch calls
-> append structured results
-> repeat

The loop must enforce budgets before each expensive step.

The runtime must reject malformed tool-call arguments with a structured tool error. Whether that error is returned to the model for self-correction or terminates execution is controlled by policy and error class.

docs.title: 17. Parallel Tool Calls
docs.text:
Parallel provider tool calls are permitted only when runtime semantics allow them.

Safe parallel candidates are normally independent read-only atomic operations.

State-changing operations, branch-producing operations sharing a mutable workspace, or calls with ordering dependencies must be serialized or explicitly isolated into independent child workspaces/branches.

Provider support for parallel tool calls does not override Scriberig consistency rules.

docs.title: 18. Context Dependency Manifest
docs.text:
Every compiled context carries a manifest of exact dependencies used to construct it.

Dependency records include concepts such as:

session object + exact revision
project entity + exact revision
branch result + exact revision
agent profile revision
context policy revision
tool definition schema hash
derived summary record/revision

This manifest serves three purposes:

  1. provenance/explanation;
  2. model request fingerprinting;
  3. precise invalidation/recomputation.

The manifest must not include unrelated global snapshot state merely because a global snapshot exists.

docs.title: 19. Model Request Fingerprint
docs.text:
Construct a canonical hash over all output-relevant non-secret inputs.

Conceptual fields:

fingerprint format/version
provider compatibility profile
provider/model identifier
provider capability subset affecting serialization
agent profile revision
context policy revision
compiled provider-neutral context
exact dependency manifest
tool schemas and ordering
structured-output schema
model parameters

Do not include:

API keys
Authorization headers
random local request IDs
timestamps that do not affect model input
UI state
unrelated global snapshot changes

Canonical encoding must be deterministic.

docs.title: 20. Cache Repository
docs.text:
The runtime needs a cache repository independent of one storage backend.

A cache record includes:

request fingerprint
provider profile/model identity
provider fingerprint/version metadata when returned
successful complete response
usage metadata
original invocation provenance
creation time/retention metadata

Initial cache policies:

Disabled
RecordOnly
ReuseExact

ReuseExact returns the previous complete response without calling the provider and records a reuse relationship for the new model invocation.

Do not cache incomplete/cancelled streams as successful model responses.

Provider errors may have a separate short-lived retry cache only if a later design explicitly requires it.

docs.title: 21. Provider Payload Retention
docs.text:
Provider-neutral model inputs/outputs needed for execution provenance are stored through session/runtime records.

Raw HTTP request/response payload retention is optional.

If enabled:

  • redact credentials and sensitive headers;
  • do not persist transport TLS/proxy secrets;
  • mark raw payloads as external/audit artifacts;
  • keep them out of the canonical branch context unless deliberately inspected;
  • apply retention limits independently from durable branch results.

Correct replay/navigation must not require raw provider JSON.

docs.title: 22. Streaming
docs.text:
The provider adapter may emit a normalized stream:

ResponseStarted
TextDelta
ToolCallDelta
UsageUpdate
ResponseCompleted
ResponseFailed

The adapter assembles fragments into one complete provider-neutral response before durable model-output commit.

Runtime events may forward safe text/progress deltas to product surfaces.

Disconnecting a product client must not cancel the provider call unless the shared operation itself is cancelled.

docs.title: 23. Cancellation
docs.text:
Use one cancellation tree rooted in the shared agent operation.

Cancellation propagates to:

current provider request
pending atomic tools when cancellable
active child branches
runtime waits

A child may also fail/cancel independently without automatically cancelling its parent when branch policy permits the parent to recover.

The root operation reaches cancelled only after runtime cancellation handling reaches a stable terminal state.

docs.title: 24. Budgets and Limits
docs.text:
Execution budgets protect against runaway loops.

Support policy fields conceptually equivalent to:

maximum model steps per branch
maximum branch depth
maximum child branches
maximum tool calls
maximum context size/token estimate
maximum output size
maximum provider request duration
maximum total operation duration/cost when measurable

Limit exhaustion becomes a structured runtime failure/branch result rather than a panic.

Budgets participate in execution policy but do not need to be part of the model request fingerprint unless they change the serialized request itself.

docs.title: 25. Errors
docs.text:
Define structured runtime categories at least for:

provider configuration
provider authentication
provider transport
provider rate limit
provider unsupported capability
provider malformed response
context compilation
tool not found
tool argument validation
capability denied
application operation failure
child branch failure
budget exceeded
cancelled
cache corruption
internal runtime failure

Preserve safe provider diagnostics without leaking credentials or full sensitive prompts into ordinary error messages.

docs.title: 26. Testing Strategy
docs.text:
All orchestration tests use a deterministic fake provider and fake/embedded application tools.

The fake provider must be scriptable with a sequence such as:

return tool call inspect(X)
return tool call start_child(Y)
return final text

Tests must prove:

  • context compilation is deterministic;
  • provider serialization can be tested independently;
  • tool calls cannot escape the trusted catalog;
  • capability denial occurs before semantic execution;
  • child branches receive only selected inherited context;
  • child completion returns a compact result to the parent;
  • parent context does not automatically include child history;
  • nested recursion obeys budgets;
  • cache reuse avoids provider invocation and preserves provenance;
  • cancellation stops the execution tree;
  • no external network is required for runtime conformance tests.

Provider-adapter integration tests may use a local mock HTTP server.

docs.title: 27. Dependency Direction
docs.text:
The intended direction remains:

foundation/session/app
        |
        v
scriberig-agent-core
        |
        v
scriberig-agent-runtime
        |
        v
product composition

scriberig-agent-runtime may depend on scriberig-session, scriberig-app, scriberig-agent-core, HTTP/async libraries, and cache support.

No foundation/domain crate may depend on it.

scriberig-tui, web packages, and CLI must interact through shared app/protocol operation boundaries rather than importing provider internals.

docs.title: 28. Implementation Order
docs.text:
Implement in this order:

  1. extend provider-neutral session execution records;
  2. define provider-neutral model contract and fake provider;
  3. implement OpenAI-compatible adapter;
  4. implement deterministic context compiler and dependency manifest;
  5. implement request fingerprint and cache repository;
  6. implement trusted tool catalog/dispatch;
  7. implement branch orchestrator and nested child execution;
  8. expose execution through shared application operations;
  9. add product surfaces and cross-surface conformance.

docs.title: 29. Completion Criteria
docs.text:
This Level 2 design is satisfied when:

  • provider communication exists only in the agent runtime/product composition layers;
  • a fake provider can drive the complete agent loop without network access;
  • OpenAI-compatible text/tool calling is supported behind the provider-neutral boundary;
  • context compilation records exact dependencies and does not flatten the complete session by default;
  • tool exposure is capability filtered and progressive;
  • nested child branches execute recursively and return compact BranchResult values;
  • model requests have deterministic non-secret fingerprints;
  • cache policy can record and exactly reuse completed responses;
  • streaming is observable without making fragments canonical project state;
  • cancellation propagates through provider/tool/branch work;
  • runtime budgets prevent unbounded loops;
  • tests prove branch isolation and trusted tool dispatch.

docs.title: Agent Operations, Protocol, and Cross-Surface Product Contract
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines the public application/protocol contract through which one-shot CLI, TUI, web, remote clients, and other product surfaces start and observe model-driven agent work.

It refines:

  1. design/level-1/016. model driven agent execution and branch isolation.md;
  2. design/level-2/011. application operations protocol and runtime boundaries.md;
  3. design/level-2/017. web workspace packages and integrated editor.md;
  4. design/level-2/021. terminal ui runtime and state architecture.md;
  5. design/level-2/022. terminal ui views interaction and conformance.md;
  6. design/level-2/023. agent runtime model provider and branch orchestration.md.

The controlling rule is:

Product surfaces differ only in presentation and waiting behavior. They start and observe the same agent operation, session tree, branch results, and canonical mutation flow.

docs.title: 2. Semantic Owner
docs.text:
The semantic owner of agent execution requests is the application/session boundary, not CLI, TUI, web, server transport, or model provider code.

The public operation family should be represented in scriberig-app and serialized by scriberig-protocol.

The agent runtime is injected/composed as the executor behind those application operations.

A product surface must never call OpenAiCompatibleProvider or equivalent directly.

docs.title: 3. Public Operation Family
docs.text:
The first complete public agent/session operation family should contain concepts equivalent to:

agent_start
agent_continue
agent_cancel
agent_operation_status
session_inspect
session_list_branches
branch_inspect
branch_list_children
branch_list_activity
branch_result_inspect

Where an existing universal operation already covers inspection/listing/following, prefer reusing it over duplicating session-specific request types. Specialized agent operations are justified for starting/continuing execution and observing runtime-specific lifecycle.

docs.title: 4. Start Request
docs.text:
Define a transport-safe request conceptually equivalent to:

AgentStartRequest {
    prompt
    session: CreateNew | Existing(SessionRef)
    parent_branch: None | BranchRef
    selection: optional SemanticSelection
    base_snapshot: optional SnapshotRef
    agent_profile: optional AgentProfileRef
    context_policy: optional ContextPolicyRef
    retention: RetentionPolicy
    limits: optional AgentLimits
}

The caller does not supply provider credentials or raw provider request JSON.

docs.title: New session
docs.text: If session requests creation, the application creates a session and a root branch before model execution begins.

docs.title: Existing session
docs.text: If an existing session is supplied, the application verifies visibility/capabilities and either creates a child/root continuation branch according to request semantics.

docs.title: Existing parent branch
docs.text: Continuing from an existing branch creates new durable activity in that branch only when the branch lifecycle permits it. When completed branches are immutable by policy, continuation creates a child/sibling continuation branch instead of silently reopening history.

docs.title: 5. Start Response
docs.text:
Starting agent work returns stable handles immediately:

AgentStartResponse {
    operation: OperationRef
    session: SessionRef
    root_branch: BranchRef
    accepted_snapshot: optional SnapshotRef
}

The response does not wait for the model to finish.

A presentation surface that wants synchronous behavior waits by observing the returned operation.

docs.title: 6. Continue Request
docs.text:
A continue operation supports follow-up user input without requiring clients to understand provider message formats.

Conceptually:

AgentContinueRequest {
    session
    branch
    prompt
    selection: optional SemanticSelection
    limits: optional AgentLimits
}

Continuation records a new human input/turn and starts a new operation tied to the selected branch or a new continuation child according to branch lifecycle policy.

The application returns the same handle shape as agent_start.

docs.title: 7. Cancellation
docs.text:
Agent cancellation uses the shared operation cancellation model.

A specialized agent_cancel request may exist as a convenience wrapper, but it must resolve to the same OperationId cancellation semantics used by other long-running application work.

Cancellation request fields:

operation
optional reason

Cancellation response reports acceptance/rejection, not a false immediate terminal state.

The operation becomes terminal only when the runtime reports a stable cancelled/completed/failed state.

docs.title: 8. Operation Status
docs.text:
Agent work uses the shared operation lifecycle:

queued
running
completed
failed
cancelled

Status metadata may additionally expose:

session ref
root branch ref
current active branch refs
model/tool/validation phase summary
bounded progress counters
final result ref
structured failure

Do not expose raw provider prompts or secrets in ordinary operation status.

docs.title: 9. Agent Event Model
docs.text:
Extend the shared event system with stable, transport-safe agent/session event kinds.

At minimum support concepts equivalent to:

AgentOperationStarted
BranchCreated
BranchStateChanged
ModelInvocationStarted
ModelTextDelta
ToolInvocationStarted
ToolInvocationCompleted
ChildBranchStarted
ChildBranchCompleted
BranchResultProduced
AgentOutputCommitted
AgentOperationCompleted
AgentOperationFailed
AgentOperationCancelled

Not every event must be durable session state.

docs.title: Durable event references
docs.text: Events that correspond to durable knowledge carry stable references to the committed session object.

docs.title: Transient stream events
docs.text: Text deltas and low-level progress may be transient. They carry operation/branch correlation and sequence information but do not pretend to be canonical session objects.

docs.title: 10. Event Ordering and Reconnection
docs.text:
Within one agent operation, emitted events need a monotonically increasing sequence number or equivalent cursor.

Conceptually:

operation_id
sequence
kind
branch_ref
payload

This allows clients to:

  • order concurrently delivered events;
  • detect gaps;
  • resume when the transport supports replay;
  • fall back to authoritative operation/session refresh when replay is unavailable.

Correctness must never depend on receiving every transient event.

After reconnect, a client can always recover by querying:

operation status
session/branch tree
branch activity/result

docs.title: 11. Protocol Types
docs.text:
Add transport-neutral types under scriberig-protocol for:

SessionReference
BranchReference
BranchResultReference
AgentStartRequest/Response
AgentContinueRequest/Response
AgentLimits
RetentionPolicy
AgentEvent
AgentEventKind
AgentFailure

Reuse existing OperationReference, snapshot selectors, structured errors, and capability models where possible.

Do not serialize internal runtime scheduler structures or provider wire DTOs.

docs.title: 12. Application Service Boundary
docs.text:
scriberig-app exposes an injected agent execution service conceptually equivalent to:

AgentService
  start(context, request)
  continue(context, request)
  cancel(context, operation)

The default product composition wires this service to scriberig-agent-runtime.

Tests may wire it to a deterministic fake service.

This prevents the application/protocol crates from depending on concrete HTTP provider implementations while keeping product semantics stable.

docs.title: 13. Server Boundary
docs.text:
scriberig-server maps public agent requests onto scriberig-app.

The server owns:

authentication/authorization at transport entry
decoding/encoding
request correlation
event delivery/stream transport
operation lookup

It does not own:

prompt construction
provider credentials exposed to clients
branch orchestration
tool semantics
canonical mutations

For remote mode, the provider is configured on the server host, not in the browser or remote TUI.

docs.title: 14. Client Boundary
docs.text:
scriberig-client exposes semantic methods conceptually equivalent to:

start_agent(...)
continue_agent(...)
operation_status(...)
cancel_operation(...)
subscribe_agent_events(...)
inspect_session(...)
inspect_branch(...)

The Rust client hides envelope/correlation details.

The TypeScript client exposes equivalent concepts through @scriberig/client.

Neither client knows how to contact the model provider.

docs.title: 15. Capability Discovery
docs.text:
Add capability entries for at least:

agent_start
agent_continue
agent_events
agent_streaming_text
branch_tree
branch_activity
operation_cancel
model_cache_reuse   # informational/runtime feature, not caller privilege

Capability discovery should distinguish:

  • runtime feature availability;
  • caller authorization;
  • provider-dependent optional features such as streaming.

A UI must not show an enabled cancellation action when the operation/runtime says cancellation is unsupported or the caller lacks permission.

docs.title: 16. One-Shot CLI Contract
docs.text:
The canonical one-shot user flow is built on AgentStartResponse and operation observation.

Target behavior for srig run <PROMPT>:

parse command
-> compose local app/session/agent runtime/provider
-> AgentStartRequest(CreateNew session/root branch)
-> receive OperationId + SessionRef + BranchRef
-> observe until terminal
-> print final agent output/result
-> select exit status from structured terminal state

One-shot mode may choose a concise progress policy:

  • when stdout is a terminal, optionally show bounded progress on stderr;
  • when machine-readable output is requested, emit stable structured output without decorative progress;
  • final answer goes to stdout;
  • diagnostics/progress go to stderr.

The command does not implement its own model loop.

docs.title: srig agent
docs.text: The existing srig agent <PROMPT> spelling may remain as a compatibility/advanced alias or later accept explicit agent-profile controls. It must call the same shared start operation. The design does not permit run and agent to drift into separate orchestration engines.

docs.title: 17. One-Shot Exit Semantics
docs.text:
Define stable categories for process exit behavior.

Conceptually:

0   completed successfully
nonzero provider/runtime/application failure
130 user interrupt/cancellation where platform conventions permit
77  permission denied where existing CLI convention applies

The exact exit-code table should be finalized in the Level 3 CLI task and documented in CLI_REFERENCE.md.

A successful model answer with a failed candidate mutation is not automatically process success; the operation's semantic terminal result decides.

docs.title: 18. TUI Contract
docs.text:
The TUI uses its existing service/effect architecture.

Required service/effect concepts:

StartAgent(request)
ContinueAgent(request)
LoadSession(session)
LoadBranch(branch)
LoadBranchActivity(branch, page)
ObserveOperation(operation)
CancelOperation(operation)

The TUI reducer owns only presentation state.

docs.title: Session tree
docs.text:
Rows are loaded from authoritative session/branch queries and show:

branch title/purpose
status
compact outcome
child count
activity counts
result handles
active/running marker

Opening a child branch loads its activity on demand.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: ModelTextDelta may update an in-progress presentation buffer keyed by operation/branch. Once AgentOutputCommitted arrives, the durable object replaces the transient buffer as the authoritative view.

docs.title: Concurrent navigation
docs.text: The user can navigate away while an agent operation runs. Returning to the session view refreshes from durable state and operation status.

docs.title: 19. Web Client/Model Contract
docs.text:
Add the agent/session protocol to the generated/authoritative web protocol boundary.

@scriberig/client adds semantic methods for start/continue/status/cancel/events/session queries.

@scriberig/model adds reusable state for:

loaded session trees
loaded branch descriptors
branch activity pages
active agent operations
transient stream buffers
operation event cursors
reconnect/stale state

Canonical session objects and transient stream buffers must remain distinct.

docs.title: 20. @scriberig/agent-ui Responsibility
docs.text:
The existing @scriberig/agent-ui package becomes the reusable branch-aware interaction layer.

It should expose headless/view-model or React components/hooks for concepts equivalent to:

AgentComposer
SessionBranchTree
BranchSummaryCard
BranchActivity
ToolInvocationView
OperationProgress
AgentOutputView

It may depend on public protocol/client/model/react/editor-core packages as allowed by web workspace guidance.

It must not import server code or provider SDKs.

The reference web app composes these reusable pieces into SessionAgentView.

docs.title: 21. Web Interaction Contract
docs.text:
The web agent surface must support:

start work from current universal selection
continue selected branch
observe active operation
collapse/expand branch tree
open child branch history
open result semantic handles in other editor views
cancel when permitted
review/promote candidate changes through normal migration UI

The browser does not assume the live stream is the session transcript. Durable branch data comes from session queries.

On reload/reconnect, the app can reconstruct the session tree and operation terminal state without replaying the original stream.

docs.title: 22. Semantic Selection Binding
docs.text:
Starting agent work from TUI or web may include the current universal selection.

The runtime receives stable semantic references such as:

entity
optional exact revision
snapshot/branch context
projection location when meaningful

Do not convert the selection into only a filename/line-range string before passing it into the agent request.

Context compilation may later render projection text for the model while retaining the semantic handle/dependency identity.

docs.title: 23. Retention Policy
docs.text:
The public request may select among a small set of safe retention policies, for example:

ProjectDefault
RetainSession
EphemeralAfterResult

EphemeralAfterResult still uses real session/branch objects during execution; it only changes post-completion reachability/retention policy.

A product surface must not invent a separate non-session execution path merely to avoid long-term storage.

Audit/security policy may override a caller's request to discard records.

docs.title: 24. Structured Final Result
docs.text:
The terminal operation result should reference a structured agent result conceptually equivalent to:

AgentResult {
    session
    root_branch
    final_output: optional AgentOutputRef
    branch_result: BranchResultRef
    produced_changes: [SemanticRef]
    validation_results: [SemanticRef]
    unresolved_questions: [SemanticRef]
}

Product surfaces may render only final text by default, but machine-readable callers can inspect all result handles.

docs.title: 25. Security and Secrets
docs.text:
Provider secrets never cross the public Scriberig protocol.

The protocol may expose a safe provider/model display descriptor where authorized, such as:

profile name
model id
feature flags

It must not expose:

API keys
Authorization headers
secret environment variable values
provider private headers

Agent events and errors must sanitize provider diagnostics before transport.

docs.title: 26. Cross-Surface Conformance
docs.text:
Add conformance scenarios that invoke the same fake-backed agent operation through:

embedded application
Rust client/server dispatch
one-shot CLI adapter
TUI service adapter
web client/model adapter

Assertions compare semantic results, not presentation strings.

At minimum prove:

  • the same prompt/scope creates the same session/branch topology under a deterministic fake provider;
  • child branch results are visible on all surfaces;
  • cancellation resolves to the same terminal operation category;
  • provider secrets are absent from public DTOs/events;
  • stream loss does not prevent recovery from durable state;
  • result semantic handles navigate through existing query operations.

docs.title: 27. Capability Matrix
docs.text:
Extend capabilities.toml with agent/session coverage.

A capability must not become verified for a surface until an implementation and conformance test exist.

Suggested rows:

agent_start
agent_continue
session_branch_tree
session_branch_activity
agent_event_subscription
agent_streaming_output
agent_operation_cancel
agent_final_result

The semantic owner should normally be scriberig-app or scriberig-session, not the UI surface.

docs.title: 28. Implementation Order
docs.text:
Implement vertically:

  1. provider-neutral session execution records;
  2. agent runtime and fake provider;
  3. app-level agent_start with operation/session/branch handles;
  4. protocol/server/client mapping;
  5. event/status/cancellation path;
  6. one-shot CLI;
  7. TUI branch-aware session flow;
  8. web client/model/agent-ui flow;
  9. cross-surface conformance.

Do not complete the full web UI before the same operation can run through the application boundary.

docs.title: 29. Completion Criteria
docs.text:
This Level 2 design is satisfied when:

  • one public request starts model-driven branch execution;
  • start returns stable operation/session/root-branch handles before completion;
  • continue/cancel/status/event semantics are shared across surfaces;
  • the public protocol contains no provider credentials or provider-specific session schema;
  • one-shot CLI waits on the same operation instead of implementing a private model loop;
  • TUI renders authoritative branch/session state and treats streams as transient;
  • web uses public client/model/agent-ui packages and never contacts the model endpoint directly;
  • universal semantic selection can scope agent work;
  • reconnect can recover from durable operation/session state;
  • final results expose semantic handles beyond plain text;
  • deterministic conformance tests can compare all product adapters.

docs.title: First Useful Project Workflow Vertical Slice
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document implements the product-completion rule from design/level-1/013. vertical product completion and end to end usability.md for the first software-project workflow.

It is the concrete design for turning the existing onboarding, semantic store, code adapters, projection/change infrastructure, web editor, TUI, and agent runtime into one continuous useful workflow.

The target is deliberately narrow:

  • local Git-backed project;
  • Rust as the required editable language for the first slice;
  • browser editor and native TUI as required interactive surfaces;
  • CLI/application/protocol remain shared diagnostic and automation peers;
  • deterministic local test fixtures and deterministic agent provider;
  • no external network or model service is required for acceptance.

The goal is not to redesign the platform. The goal is to connect existing public layers so a user can inspect and safely change a real source project.

docs.title: 2. Existing Pieces and the Integration Gap
docs.text:
The repository already contains substantial pieces of the workflow:

  • project catalog, scan, import, ownership, and project-specific snapshots;
  • Rust syntax/domain import;
  • immutable snapshots and history;
  • application operations and protocol/client/server layers;
  • projection and reconciliation infrastructure;
  • migration/change/validation machinery;
  • filesystem projection ownership and atomic I/O support;
  • native TUI views;
  • reusable web packages and the reference web app;
  • session/agent operations and branch-aware product views;
  • browser and native terminal E2E harnesses.

The missing contract is composition.

An import response that says imported is not enough. The product must know which project/snapshot/root is active, navigate meaningful symbols, render the source representation, route edits through migrations, materialize accepted output, refresh to the successor snapshot, and preserve semantic scope for agents.

This document specifies those connections.

docs.title: 3. Non-Goals
docs.text:
Do not expand this slice into unrelated platform work.

Not required for first acceptance:

  • full IDE language-server functionality;
  • arbitrary multi-file refactoring UI;
  • every imported programming language becoming editable;
  • syntax highlighting parity with a dedicated code editor;
  • remote cloud project upload;
  • collaborative multi-user editing;
  • desktop shell integration;
  • persistent docking/layout systems;
  • external model-provider access in CI;
  • generalized build-system execution beyond the deterministic fixture requirement;
  • replacing the universal graph with a code-specific store.

If a missing foundational capability blocks the golden path, implement the smallest reusable public capability needed and keep it domain/surface boundaries-correct.

docs.title: 4. Golden Fixture
docs.text:
Create one repository-controlled fixture specifically for product E2E tests.

Recommended location:

tests/fixtures/golden-rust-project/
  Cargo.toml
  src/
    lib.rs

The fixture must have no external Cargo dependencies.

Its source must contain stable names and a stable editable expression. Use the following semantic content unless an equivalent existing fixture is already shared by both web and TUI tests:

pub mod math {
    pub struct Calculator;

    impl Calculator {
        pub fn add(&self, left: i32, right: i32) -> i32 {
            left + right
        }
    }
}

The exact formatting may follow repository Rust formatting rules, but these strings are acceptance anchors:

math
Calculator
add
left + right

The accepted edited form for the primary scenario is:

left.saturating_add(right)

The fixture must compile with a local cargo check without downloading dependencies.

Every E2E run copies the fixture to a fresh temporary directory and initializes Git there if the checked-in fixture itself is not a nested Git repository. Tests must never mutate the checked-in fixture or Scriberig's own working tree.

docs.title: 5.1 Server/application project record remains canonical catalog data
docs.text:
The existing project service remains the owner of:

  • ProjectId;
  • canonical project path;
  • display name;
  • import status;
  • current project snapshot;
  • project semantic root/ownership data.

Do not add a separate web-only or TUI-only project database.

docs.title: 5.2 Active project is client/product state
docs.text:
The active project is not one global mutable server setting.

Each interactive client maintains an ActiveProjectWorkspace equivalent containing at least:

project_id
project_name
canonical_path or path metadata appropriate to the client
snapshot_id
root_entity_id

The public server/client contract must provide enough information to construct this value from ProjectId.

If the existing project status/import response does not expose the exact project root reference required for semantic browsing, extend the shared application operation and public protocol response. Do not infer the root by scanning database tables or by assuming the server's global capability root belongs to the project.

docs.title: 5.3 Required activation operations
docs.text:
The product runtime must support these conceptual actions:

list projects
resolve/open workspace for project_id
activate resolved workspace locally
refresh active workspace after project snapshot changes

The exact method names may fit existing project-operation conventions.

Do not create a server-side set_current_project_for_everyone mutation.

docs.title: 5.4 Import-to-activation behavior
docs.text:
After successful import in web or TUI:

  1. resolve the imported project's current workspace/root;
  2. make it the active workspace in that client;
  3. reset/rebase navigation tree to that project root;
  4. clear a selection that points to a different project's snapshot;
  5. navigate to the semantic/raw project browser or otherwise provide an explicit Open project action that the E2E test exercises;
  6. show project identity and current snapshot visibly.

The user must never have to restart the server or manually copy an entity ID after import.

docs.title: 6. Workspace Events and Refresh
docs.text:
The client runtime must be able to refresh active workspace state after:

  • import creates a new project snapshot;
  • a migration is applied;
  • external reconciliation creates a successor snapshot;
  • an event reports that the active project's current snapshot changed.

Refresh means resolving the authoritative project status/root again, not modifying local snapshot IDs optimistically without server confirmation.

When semantic identity survives the change, preserve selection by entity identity and resolve it against the new snapshot.

When it does not survive, clear the invalid selection and show a meaningful state rather than silently selecting an unrelated object.

docs.title: 7.1 Public semantic data owns display names
docs.text:
The Rust/code adapter must expose display metadata through the shared semantic object model.

For named source concepts, at least the following must be represented when applicable:

display label / symbol name
semantic kind
source-relative path
source range or projection mapping
parent/containment relation

Frontends may decorate these fields but must not parse serialized syntax trees privately to recover names.

docs.title: 7.2 Required fixture navigation
docs.text:
From the active golden fixture workspace, the public semantic/navigation API must let a client reach the fixture method add through recognizable labels.

The exact intermediate hierarchy may depend on current code-domain modeling, but product output must expose enough context that a human can identify:

src/lib.rs
math
Calculator
add

If the universal tree contains low-level syntax nodes as well, products may hide/collapse them by default in a semantic mode. Raw knowledge mode may still expose them.

docs.title: 7.3 Raw and semantic modes
docs.text:
The integrated products may retain both:

  • raw graph/knowledge navigation for debugging;
  • semantic/domain navigation for ordinary work.

The golden-path test uses semantic/domain navigation, not opaque raw node indices.

docs.title: 7.4 Stable labels
docs.text:
Labels must not depend on enumeration order such as #17 when a symbol name exists.

A label may include disambiguating context, e.g. add · method · src/lib.rs, but add must be available as semantic data.

docs.title: 8.1 What projection must return
docs.text:
For the selected add method, source projection must expose at least:

projection identifier
project identifier
snapshot/base identifier
source-relative path
rendered source text
semantic-to-source mapping covering the selected entity
editable/read-only capability
stale/conflict state

For the fixture selection, the rendered text must include left + right before the edit.

docs.title: 8.2 Projection granularity
docs.text:
The implementation may render:

  • the entire source file with selection range; or
  • a bounded semantic source region with enough context.

The web E2E test must be able to edit the selected source deterministically.

The TUI must be able to inspect the same source and create the same candidate through a terminal-appropriate interaction.

docs.title: 8.3 No inspector fallback for required source capability
docs.text:
If a Rust source projection is supported, showing only object metadata/description does not satisfy this contract.

Generic inspector fallback remains valid for unsupported domains.

docs.title: 9.1 Web edit
docs.text:
The web editor must allow the E2E test to replace:

left + right

with:

left.saturating_add(right)

through a public projection/change API.

The edit must not immediately write the filesystem or advance current canonical state.

It produces a candidate/migration based on the exact active snapshot.

docs.title: 9.2 TUI edit
docs.text:
The TUI does not need a full-screen IDE editor for this milestone.

It must nevertheless expose a deterministic terminal interaction that creates the same kind of candidate through the public change path. Acceptable first forms include:

  • an edit command that opens/edits a projection buffer within the TUI;
  • a command palette action that supplies replacement text for the selected mapped range;
  • an external $EDITOR handoff only if the test harness can deterministically drive it and the edited result returns through reconciliation rather than direct canonical mutation.

Do not implement a TUI-only direct filesystem patch command.

docs.title: 9.3 Candidate invariants
docs.text:
A candidate must include or resolve:

migration/proposal identity
exact base snapshot
candidate/result snapshot when materialized
changed semantic entities
changed source projection(s)
validation state
stale/conflict state
provenance identifying human/agent source

docs.title: 10. Diff and Review Contract
docs.text:
Before application, both web and TUI must let the user review the candidate.

For the fixture, review must show enough information to establish that:

old: left + right
new: left.saturating_add(right)

Review should prefer semantic diff plus a source/text diff when source is editable.

At minimum the candidate review must expose:

  • base snapshot ID;
  • changed file src/lib.rs;
  • affected semantic object add or its stable entity identity plus human label;
